kva bhūtalaṃ kva ca dhrauvyaṃ sthānaṃ yat prāptavān dhruvaḥ | uttānapādanṛpateḥ putraḥ san bhūmigocaraḥ ||

English

Where is the surface of the earth, and where is that station of Dhruva7879, which Dhruva attained, though he was the son of King Uttānapāda and a walker on the earth?80

20.40

Sanskrit

तत् कथ्यतां महाभाग कार्यवान् येन पुत्रकौ । स भूपालसुतः साधुर्येनानृण्यं भवेत वाम् ॥

tat kathyatāṃ mahābhāga kāryavān yena putrakau | sa bhūpālasutaḥ sādhuryenānṛṇyaṃ bhaveta vām ||

English

So tell it, illustrious one, [that] by which that good son of the king has a task to be done, [and] by which there may be freedom from debt81 for the two of you, my dear sons82.83

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

20.41The two sons said: This was told by him, father, the great-souled one: the earlier occurrence84, as it happened in boyhood to him who abounds in good conduct85.86

20.41

Sanskrit

तेनाख्यातमिदं तात पूर्ववृतं महात्मना । कौमारके यथा तस्य वृतं सद्वृत्तशालिनः ॥

tenākhyātamidaṃ tāta pūrvavṛtaṃ mahātmanā | kaumārake yathā tasya vṛtaṃ sadvṛttaśālinaḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 20.41, above.

20.42

Sanskrit

तन्तु शत्रुजितं तात पूर्वं कश्चिदिद्वजोत्तमः । गालवो ऽभ्यागमद्धीमान् गृहीत्वा तुरगोत्तमम् ॥

tantu śatrujitaṃ tāta pūrvaṃ kaścididvajottamaḥ | gālavo 'bhyāgamaddhīmān gṛhītvā turagottamam ||

English

Father, formerly a certain Gālava87, the wise best of the twice-born88, came to that Śatrujit, bringing an excellent horse.89

20.43

Sanskrit

प्रत्युवाच च राजानं समुपेत्याश्रमं मम । को ऽपि दैत्याधमो राजन् विध्वंसयति पापकृत् ॥

pratyuvāca ca rājānaṃ samupetyāśramaṃ mama | ko 'pi daityādhamo rājan vidhvaṃsayati pāpakṛt ||

English

And [Gālava] replied to the king: “O king, some vilest of the Daityas90, a doer of evil, has come to my hermitage and wreaks destruction there.91929394

20.44

Sanskrit

तत्तद्रूपं समास्थाय सिंहेभवनचारिणाम् । अन्येषाञ्चाल्पकायानामहर्निशमकारणात् ॥

tattadrūpaṃ samāsthāya siṃhebhavanacāriṇām | anyeṣāñcālpakāyānāmaharniśamakāraṇāt ||

English

He takes on this form and that, of creatures that move about in the dwellings of lions and elephants and of other small-bodied creatures, day and night, without cause.

20.45

Sanskrit

समाधिध्यानयुक्तस्य मौनव्रतरतस्य च । तथा करोति विघ्रानि यथा चलति मे मनः ॥

samādhidhyānayuktasya maunavrataratasya ca | tathā karoti vighrāni yathā calati me manaḥ ||

English

To me, who am engaged in samādhi and meditation and devoted to the vow of silence, he creates obstacles in such a way that my mind wavers.”

20.46

Sanskrit

दग्धं कोपाग्निना सद्यः समर्थस्त्वं वयं न तु । दुः खार्जितस्य तपसो व्ययमिच्छामि पार्थिव ॥

dagdhaṃ kopāgninā sadyaḥ samarthastvaṃ vayaṃ na tu | duḥ khārjitasya tapaso vyayamicchāmi pārthiva ||

English

You are able to burn [him]95 at once with the fire of anger, but we are not. I do not want96 the expenditure of tapas won through hardship, O king.97†

20.47

Sanskrit

एकदा तु मया राजन्नतिनिर्विण्णचेतसा । तत् क्लेशितेन निश्वासो निरीक्ष्यासुरमुज्झितः ॥

ekadā tu mayā rājannatinirviṇṇacetasā | tat kleśitena niśvāso nirīkṣyāsuramujjhitaḥ ||

English

But once, O king, a sigh was let out by me98, my mind utterly weary and I tormented by him99, after looking at the asura100.101†

20.48

Sanskrit

ततो ऽम्बरतलात् सद्यः पतितो ऽयं तुरङ्गमः । वाक् चाशरीरिणी प्राह नरनाथ शृणुष्व ताम् ॥

tato 'mbaratalāt sadyaḥ patito 'yaṃ turaṅgamaḥ | vāk cāśarīriṇī prāha naranātha śṛṇuṣva tām ||

English

Then this horse suddenly fell from the sky, and a bodiless voice102 spoke. O lord of men, listen to it.103

20.49

Sanskrit

अश्रान्तः सकलं भूमेर्वलयं तुरगोत्तमः । समर्थः क्रान्तुमर्केण तवायं प्रतिपादितः ॥

aśrāntaḥ sakalaṃ bhūmervalayaṃ turagottamaḥ | samarthaḥ krāntumarkeṇa tavāyaṃ pratipāditaḥ ||

English

“This best of horses, who can traverse the whole circle of the earth without tiring, has been given to you by the sun104.”105

20.50

Sanskrit

पातालाम्बरतोयेषु न चास्य विहता गतिः । समस्तदिक्षु व्रजतो न भङ्गः पर्वतेष्वपि ॥

pātālāmbaratoyeṣu na cāsya vihatā gatiḥ | samastadikṣu vrajato na bhaṅgaḥ parvateṣvapi ||

English

His course is not obstructed in the nether worlds, in the sky or in the waters; as he goes in all directions there is no breaking of his stride, even among mountains.106

20.51

Sanskrit

यतो भूवलयं सर्वमश्रान्तो ऽयं चरिष्यति । अतः कुवलयो नाम्ना ख्यातिं लोके प्रयास्यति ॥

yato bhūvalayaṃ sarvamaśrānto 'yaṃ cariṣyati | ataḥ kuvalayo nāmnā khyātiṃ loke prayāsyati ||

English

“Since this untiring [horse] will range over the whole circle of the earth, therefore he will become famous in the world by the name Kuvalaya107.”108

20.52

Sanskrit

क्लिश्यत्यहर्निशं पापो यश्च त्वां दानवाधमः । तमप्येनं समारुह्य द्विजश्रेष्ठ हनिष्यति ॥

kliśyatyaharniśaṃ pāpo yaśca tvāṃ dānavādhamaḥ | tamapyenaṃ samāruhya dvijaśreṣṭha haniṣyati ||

English

“The wicked one, the lowest of the dānavas109, who torments you day and night: even him, O best of the twice-born110, [he]111 will kill, after mounting this [horse].”112

20.53

Sanskrit

शत्रुजिन्नाम भूपालस्तस्य पुत्र ऋतध्वजः । प्राप्यैतदश्वरत्नञ्च ख्यातिमेतेन यास्यति ॥

śatrujinnāma bhūpālastasya putra ṛtadhvajaḥ | prāpyaitadaśvaratnañca khyātimetena yāsyati ||

English

“There is a king named Śatrujit; his son is Ṛtadhvaja. Having obtained this jewel of a horse113, he will gain fame through it.”114

20.54

Sanskrit

सो ऽहं त्वां समनुप्राप्तस्तपसो विघ्रकारिणम् । तं निवारय भूपाल भागभाङ्नृपतिर्यतः ॥

so 'haṃ tvāṃ samanuprāptastapaso vighrakāriṇam | taṃ nivāraya bhūpāla bhāgabhāṅnṛpatiryataḥ ||

English

"So I have come to you, O protector of the earth, [to ask you to] restrain him, the one who obstructs my tapas115, since the king receives a share [of the merit]116."117

20.55

Sanskrit

तदेतश्वरत्नं ते मया भूप निवेदितम् । पुत्रमाज्ञापय तथा यथा धर्मो न लुप्यते ॥

tadetaśvaratnaṃ te mayā bhūpa niveditam | putramājñāpaya tathā yathā dharmo na lupyate ||

English

“So I have presented this jewel of a horse118 to you, O king119. Command your son in such a way that dharma is not destroyed.”120

20.56

Sanskrit

स तस्य वचनाद्राजा तं वै पुत्रमृतध्वजम् । तमश्वरत्नमारोप्य कृतकौतुकमङ्गलम् ॥

sa tasya vacanādrājā taṃ vai putramṛtadhvajam | tamaśvaratnamāropya kṛtakautukamaṅgalam ||

English

20.56–57At his word, the king, righteous in his nature121, then sent that son Ṛtadhvaja, for whom the festive auspicious rites122 had been performed, after setting him on that jewel of a horse, together with Gālava; and the sage too, taking him, went to his own hermitage.123

20.57

Sanskrit

अप्रेषयत धर्मात्मा गालवेन समं तदा । स्वमाश्रमपदं सो ऽपि तमादाय ययौ मुनिः ॥

apreṣayata dharmātmā gālavena samaṃ tadā | svamāśramapadaṃ so 'pi tamādāya yayau muniḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 20.56–57, above.

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे पितापुत्रसंवादेठकुवलयाश्वीयोऽ नाम विंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe pitāputrasaṃvādeṭhakuvalayāśvīyo' nāma viṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, named "The Story of the Horse Kuvalaya124," in the dialogue of father and son125, in the venerable Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.126†

  1. Śatrujit: The name means 'conqueror of enemies'. The text has śatrujinnāma, with sandhi for śatrujit nāma. ↩
  2. Purandara: 'Destroyer of strongholds', an epithet of Indra, king of the gods. ↩
  3. soma: The juice of the soma plant, offered to the gods in Vedic sacrifice; Indra is especially fond of it. ↩
  4. The reading: 1. somāvāptyā is an instrumental of cause. I now read it as Indra's receiving soma, so the agent is Purandara, and I render 'gratified at receiving soma' as the reviewer suggests. The alternative, 'by the obtaining of the soma [offering]', is the same sense, so nothing turns on it. 2. I changed 'Long ago' to 'In former times' for prāk, as the reviewer asks. 3. The Purandara note was already correct, and the reviewer asked for no change to it, so I kept it. 4. śatrujinnāma is śatrujit nāma, with the final t assimilated to the following n. I took the name as Śatrujit. 5. I write yajñeṣu as 'yajñas' to follow the glossary's rendering of yajña. ↩
  5. Guru: Guru, 'the Preceptor', is the usual title of Bṛhaspati, the teacher of the gods and the model of wisdom. ↩
  6. Śakra: Śakra, 'the Mighty', is a name of Indra, king of the gods and the model of martial prowess; he is the Purandara of the previous verse. ↩
  7. Aśvins: The twin divine physicians, proverbial for their youthful beauty. ↩
  8. The reading: The instrumental compound buddhi-vikrama-lāvaṇyaiḥ is paired with guru-śakra-aśvibhiḥ, and the natural reading is in order: intelligence with Guru, prowess with Śakra, beauty with the Aśvins. The Sanskrit does not state the pairing, so the translation leaves it implicit. 'Guru' could also mean 'teacher' in general; I took it as Bṛhaspati because it stands between Indra and the Aśvins in a list of gods. ↩
  9. The reading: samānavayobuddhisattvavikramaceṣṭitaiḥ is a dvandva compound (vayas, buddhi, sattva, vikrama, ceṣṭita) qualifying nṛpasutaiḥ; sattva can mean 'courage', 'strength' or 'character', and I chose 'courage' beside vikrama 'prowess'. The first nṛpaputraḥ is the prince introduced in 20.2 (Śatrujit's son), and nṛpasutaiḥ are his companions, so they are different people. The compound's sense 'equal in' is carried by samāna, which goes with every member. āste is rendered as 'was ... surrounded' with samāvṛtaḥ, which makes 'always remained surrounded'. I used 'was always surrounded' for fluency. ↩
  10. treatises: śāstra: an authoritative treatise or body of teaching on a branch of knowledge, such as statecraft or law. ↩
  11. the suitable [exercises]: yogyāni is neuter plural and has no noun in the verse. It is read as 'suitable exercises' governing the training in weapons and missiles. ↩
  12. missiles: astra: a weapon discharged or hurled, often empowered by mantra, as distinct from śastra, a weapon held in the hand. ↩
  13. The reading: yogyāni (20.5) is neuter plural and cannot agree with the masculine abhyāsa. I take it as a substantive, 'suitable [exercises]', tied to śastrāstravinayeṣu. Alternatively it could qualify the whole list of practices as 'proper things'. Also, kṛtaniścayaḥ (20.4) could mean 'having made resolutions' or 'having reached settled conclusions'. I chose the latter, as the sense fits the study of treatises. ↩
  14. sons of brahmins, kings and commoners: Sanskrit dvija-bhūpa-viś: the compound names the brahmin, the king (that is, the kṣatriya) and the vaiśya. The three 'twice-born' classes are thus represented among the boys. ↩
  15. The reading: dvijabhūpaviśām is a dvandva, 'of brahmins, kings and viś'. I took viś as the vaiśya class, hence 'commoners'. teṣām krīḍatām is a genitive absolute ('as they played'); samānavayasaḥ ('of the same age') is taken to qualify sutāḥ, and the age-match is with the prince's group, teṣām. The verb āyānti is present tense, and anekaśaḥ means 'many times'; the sense is habitual, so I rendered it 'came again and again'. ↩
  16. nāgas: Nāgas are semi-divine serpent beings who live in an underworld realm, the nāgaloka, and can take human form. ↩
  17. Aśvatara: Aśvatara is a nāga king. The two youths are his sons; v. 20.11 calls them sons of the nāga king. ↩
  18. twice-born: Dvijanman, 'twice-born', is a term for members of the three upper social orders, who undergo initiation. Here it refers to the other young companions of the princes. ↩
  19. The reading: In 20.10 'sarva ca te nṛpasutāḥ' is probably a misprint for 'sarve ca te nṛpasutāḥ' (masculine plural, agreeing with te and nṛpasutāḥ); I translated it as 'all those king's sons'. The sentence does not close in 20.10 and its predicate comes in 20.11, so the passage ends open. ↩
  20. sons of the nāga king: Nāgarāja, 'king of the nāgas', is Aśvatara, named in 20.8 as the father of the two youths. ↩
  21. massage: saṃvāhana: rubbing or kneading of the limbs, a customary service among companions. ↩
  22. The reading: The e-text is faulty. 'strānasaṃvāhana' is read as snānasaṃvāhana ('bathing and massage'). 'vastragandhānusayuktām' is read as vastragandhānusaṃyuktām ('accompanied by clothes and perfumes'). 'bhāgabhujikriyām' is obscure: bhāga is 'share' and bhuji is 'eating', so I took it as 'the taking of meals in shares'. Bhoga for bhāga ('enjoyment') is possible but I did not emend. The verb cakruḥ is plural, and the subject is the king's sons and others of 20.10 together with the two nāgas (tau). I supplied 'with the others' in brackets for that reason. ↩
  23. king's son: Sanskrit sūnor mahīpateḥ, literally 'the son of the lord of the earth'; the prince of the preceding verses, whose name is not given in this passage. The genitive depends on prītyā, 'affection for'. ↩
  24. The reading: prītyā sūnor mahīpateḥ: the genitive can be read with prītyā ('affection for the king's son') or taken loosely as the goal of ājagmatuḥ ('came to the king's son in affection'). I chose the first, since the verb is intransitive of motion without an accusative and the sense of affection towards the prince fits the context. Ahanyahani anuprāpte is a locative absolute ('as each day arrived'). ↩
  25. supreme peace: Sanskrit nirvāṇa, literally 'extinction' or 'cooling'; here it means complete contentment and ease of mind, not the Buddhist or Vedāntic liberation. ↩
  26. The reading: nirvāṇa: the word can mean final liberation or, in ordinary use, deep happiness and calm. The context (the prince's delight in his two friends) shows the second sense, so I rendered it 'supreme peace'. The verse also has no stated link between the two instrumentals tābhyām and vinodaiḥ; I read both as the means of his contentment, joined by 'and'. ↩
  27. wine: madhu means honey, sweet drink or wine; here an intoxicating drink is most likely meant, as the verb is 'drink'. ↩
  28. he did not take up: The verb jagrāha is 'seized, took hold of'; with śāstrāṇi it means to take up, learn or study the treatises. ↩
  29. The reading: madhu can be honey, a sweet drink, or wine. I chose 'wine' because the verb is 'drink' (papau) and the verse lists the pleasures of a prince. Also, na sastrau (from snā, perfect middle, 3rd sg. 'bathed') is the form given by the text; I read it as sasnau, written sastrau by the e-text, 'he did not bathe'. The subject is the king's son of 20.13, understood from the context. ↩
  30. Rasātala: The nether world, one of the regions below the earth where the nāgas dwell; the same as the 'pātāla' of verse 20.17. ↩
  31. The reading: niśvāsaparamau is a compound that could mean 'having sighing as their chief [occupation]' (sighing deeply) or 'sighing at the utmost'; I chose 'sighing deeply'. The word tam in the second line is masculine accusative singular, so it refers to the prince (tena mahātmanā), the same person as in the first line; the 'going' is to him, to the world of mortals, which the next verse confirms. The word 'would go' renders the habitual sense of dine dine with the dual perfect jagmatuḥ. ↩
  32. the father: pitā: the father of the two, that is, the nāga king Aśvatara. The verse says only 'father'; the identification is inferred from the context. ↩
  33. young nāgas: The Sanskrit word is nāgadārakau, literally 'nāga boys', not nāgakumāraka. It refers to the same two sons of the nāga king Aśvatara. ↩
  34. The reading: 1. kena ... saha: the particle saha stands apart from kena and is joined to iti (saheti = saha + iti). I read kena ... saha together as 'with whom'. The iti closes the father's question. This is the only natural construction. 2. parā prītiḥ: I now render parā as 'supreme', dropping my earlier 'such great', which added a demonstrative not in the Sanskrit. 3. bhavatoḥ is dual and is now rendered 'you two'. 4. tāv ubhau: I render tau and ubhau as 'both those', which avoids the redundancy of the earlier draft. 5. putrakau: the diminutive suffix is affectionate; I render it plainly as 'sons'. ↩
  35. unseen by me by day: The printed text reads dṛṣṭayoḥ, 'of the two seen'. The translation reads 'dṛṣṭayoḥ, that is adṛṣṭayoḥ, 'of the two unseen', with the initial a lost in writing (see doubts). ↩
  36. The reading: The printed dṛṣṭayor atra pātāle me ('of the two seen by me here in the nether worlds') does not agree with divā ... rajanyām eva ('by day ... only at night'). I read 'dṛṣṭayoḥ as adṛṣṭayoḥ, the genitive dual of the participle 'unseen', with the initial a lost in writing. This fits 20.15, where the two sons spend the night in Rasātala and go to the prince day after day, so their father sees them only at night. If dṛṣṭayoḥ is kept, the sense would be 'you two being seen by me for many days ... I see you by day and by night', which does not fit the context. I take eva as restrictive ('only'), and divā as the time when the father does not see them. The verse is the father's speech, continuing 20.16 and before the sons' reply in 20.18. The reviewer named no fault, so I changed only two things. I wrote 'nether worlds' for pātāle as the glossary has it, and I made the note's wording clearer. ↩
  37. lord of serpents: uragādhipati, 'overlord of the uragas (serpents)', is Aśvatara, the father of the two young nāgas. ↩
  38. joined their palms in reverence: añjali: the gesture of cupped, joined hands held before the face or forehead, a sign of respect and supplication. ↩
  39. The reading: The verse does not name the father. Since the glossary identifies the two young nāgas as Aśvatara's sons, I take uragādhipati to be Aśvatara, which the verse itself does not state. The grammatical dual 'kṛtāñjalī' agrees with the two sons, and 'svayam' is rendered 'himself' as qualifying the father (pitrā). ↩
  40. Ṛtadhvaja: The prince, son of King Śatrujit. The speakers are the two young nāgas, who are addressing their father. ↩
  41. self-respecting: mānī: one who has a sense of honour or pride in himself. Here it is praise, not conceit. ↩
  42. having discipline as his ornament: vinayabhūṣaṇaḥ: vinaya means discipline, restraint and courtesy of conduct. It is distinct from 'modest' (hrīmān), which refers to a sense of shame or modesty. ↩
  43. the enjoyment of his company: The e-text reads sambogā- in the compound, probably a corruption of sambhoga ('enjoyment, shared enjoyment, intimate association'). ↩
  44. Bhuvarloka: Properly the atmospheric world between earth (Bhūrloka) and heaven. Set against the nāgas' underworld, it probably stands loosely for the world above, i.e. the earth; this sense is conjectural. ↩
  45. The reading: 1. sambogā- is read as sambhoga; the irregularity is in the e-text, not in the translation. 2. Bhuvarloka may mean the atmospheric world in the strict sense, or may be used loosely for the earth or upper worlds in contrast with the nāgaloka. I keep the name and explain it in the note. 3. The Sanskrit has a singular manaḥ and no pronoun. I keep the bracketed [our] because the two brothers speak together and the next verse has nas. The brackets already mark the word as supplied, so I added no separate note. 4. In the compound, upacāra is read as courtesies or attentions, samprīti as affection, and sambhoga as the enjoyment of his company; apahṛta is 'carried away'. ↩
  46. The reading: The verse is elliptical. I take paritāpāya (dative of purpose, 'for torment') with pātāla, and āhlādāya ('for delight') with ravir divā, with tatsaṅgāt ('from union with him') governing the second half. The particle ca after pātālam is rendered 'and', joining the two statements about the nether worlds. The text prints 'nastāta' for nas tāta; nas is the genitive/dative 'to us'. ↩
  47. The reading: bhavidvidhaiḥ is not a possible form. I read bhavadvidhaiḥ, 'by those of your kind, such as you', which fits the sons addressing their father. guṇibhaiḥ is a misprint for guṇibhiḥ, instrumental plural of guṇin, 'possessed of good qualities'. I take puṇyavataḥ as a genitive ('of the man of merit') depending on putraḥ, and sa yasya as 'he of whom', with sa as the son himself. ↩
  48. I regard learning and good conduct as equal: The compound śāstraśīle is in the dual (locative or accusative). It is read as the accusative dual object of manye with samam, 'as equal', meaning learning and good conduct taken together. ↩
  49. him the more fortunate: tam, 'him', refers to Ṛtadhvaja, who is praised in the preceding verses; dhanyatara is a comparative, and tu marks the contrast. ↩
  50. The reading: śāstraśīle samaṃ manye: the locative dual could be read 'in learning and conduct I consider [them] equal', or as an accusative-type dual object with samam, 'equal'. The Sanskrit is compressed and the second sentence is elliptical. I took it as 'I regard learning and good conduct as equal [in value]', and tam as the person who has both, Ṛtadhvaja, whom I call 'the more fortunate' (dhanyatara). Alternative reading: 'I regard the learned and the well-conducted as equal'. Putrau is a vocative dual, 'sons', addressed to the two young nāgas. The translation does not repeat 'I think' in the Sanskrit beyond manye. ↩
  51. The reading: The verse is a speech by the father (a nāga), continuing the previous verses. 'Tasya' is taken as Ṛtadhvaja's, as the subject of the preceding verses; 'tena' as 'through him'. 'Satsu' is taken as 'among good people' (locative of sat), not 'in assemblies'. ↩
  52. The reading: tasyopakāriṇaḥ is a genitive qualifying 'that [man]' in the previous context (the benefactor, i.e. the one who has been kind to the two sons). The verse is addressed by the nāga father to his two sons (vatsau, dual). Reading: 'abhivāñchitam' = 'what was wished for' (by him, the benefactor), taken with 'kiñcid' and 'niṣpāditam'. An alternative reading takes abhivāñchitam as what the two of you wished (bhavadbhyām), i.e. 'something wished by you'; I chose the first because the purpose clause paritoṣāya cetasaḥ ('for the satisfaction of [his] mind') makes the benefactor's desire the object. The rendering 'that benefactor of yours' makes tasya + upakāriṇaḥ 'him who did a kindness [to you]', which is the natural sense; upakārin could also mean 'one who is helpful/obliging' in general. ↩
  53. whose friend's purpose does not go unfulfilled through weakness: The Sanskrit is mitrārtho na ca durbalaḥ, literally 'the object of a friend is not weak'. It is taken to mean that the friend's purpose is not left feeble or unfulfilled; the verse is elliptical and the reading is not certain. ↩
  54. The reading: The second half, yasyārthino na vimukhā mitrārtho na ca durbalaḥ, is elliptical. 'mitrārtho' could be (a) mitra-artha, 'a friend's purpose/interest' (chosen), or (b) 'one who seeks a friend (mitrārthin)', with the final -in lost. 'durbalaḥ' agrees with the masculine mitrārthaḥ, so I take 'a friend's purpose' as weak, i.e. left unfulfilled for lack of strength. Another reading is 'the friend's need is not weak', i.e. not slight or neglected. I kept the first, since it fits the context of fulfilling the friend's wishes (20.26). In the first half, 'jīvitaṃ tasya' is read as 'his life is [a true] life', with the bracket implied by the predicate; 'vimukhā' is plural, agreeing with 'arthinaḥ'. ↩
  55. The reading: The text has 'yad' (neuter nominative) before 'suvarṇādi', where 'yat' would be expected before a following 'su-'; I read it as 'yat', the relative pronoun with the correlative 'tad' in the second line. 'Ratnaṃ vāhanam āsanam' is read as a list of separate items, with 'ratna' singular in a collective sense, rendered 'jewels'. 'Tasya' is taken as the person praised in the preceding verses, 'his'. ↩
  56. The reading: The syntax is loose: 'tasya ... puṃsaḥ' is correlative with 'yo ... avagacchati'. 'Pratirūpam akurvan' is taken as 'not making a fitting return' (pratirūpa = a corresponding act, requital), governing 'mitrāṇām upakāriṇām' as the friends who have helped. 'Jīvāmi' with 'iti' is the man's own thought, so I render it as a quotation. ↩
  57. a cloud among men: Sanskrit nṛmegha, a compound: a man who, like a rain-cloud, pours down benefit or harm. The comparison is carried on by the verb 'rains' (varṣati). ↩
  58. The reading: Nṛmegha could be taken as a plain compound, 'man-cloud', or as a locative-like 'cloud among men'. I chose 'a cloud among men' as the natural English for the metaphor. The verse is syntactically loose: the relative yaḥ is resumed by tasya, and the accusatives upakāram and apakāram are objects of varṣati. Sadā ('always') goes with icchanti and not with the raining, since it stands directly before unnati (sadonnatim = sadā + unnatim). ↩
  59. The reading: The verse numbered 85.16 is a speaker's line (putrāvūcatuḥ) that has strayed into this chapter's numbering. I translate it as given. In 'sarvakāmaiḥ sadārccitāḥ', the instrumental 'with all desires' means with the fulfilment of their wishes. I took it that way and added no bracket. ↩
  60. conveyances: The compound vāhanāsanayānāni lists vāhana (vehicles, mounts), āsana (seats) and yāna (conveyances); vāhana and yāna overlap in sense, and the three are rendered separately. ↩
  61. The reading: The verse has no verb. 'How could we have them' and 'Where could we find' are supplied from naḥ kutaḥ, 'whence to us?'. The second sentence is read as the continuation of the same rhetorical question, with vāhanāsanayānāni, bhūṣaṇāni and ambarāṇi parallel to ratnāni. In the first clause, tadgehe could be read with ratnāni ('jewels in his house') or as a separate locative. I took it with ratnāni, 'in his house', because pātāle ('in the nether world') then marks the place where the speakers lack such things. Vāhana and yāna are close in sense and I kept them as two items. ↩
  62. Whatever knowledge there is in that house: tatra, 'there', refers back to the house of the man in 20.31–32; the sons are speaking of the host's household. 'House' is supplied from that context. ↩
  63. father: tāta is an affectionate vocative; here the sons address their father. ↩
  64. The reading: vijñānam may mean 'knowledge' in general, 'discernment', or specialised knowledge. I chose 'knowledge'. tatra is taken to refer to the man's house, as in the preceding verses; it could also be read more loosely as 'with him'. sarvasandehahṛttamaḥ is a superlative: 'most a remover of all doubts'; asau is the man in question. ↩
  65. Hiraṇyagarbha: 'Golden Womb', a name of Brahmā, the creator. ↩
  66. Govinda: A name of Viṣṇu (Kṛṣṇa). ↩
  67. Śarva: A name of Śiva. ↩
  68. The reading: The construction hiraṇyagarbhagovindaśarvādīn īśvarād ṛte is irregular: ṛte normally takes the ablative, but ādīn is accusative plural and īśvarād is ablative singular. The text may be faulty. One reading takes īśvarāt as 'the Lord' and ādīn as a separate item ('apart from the Lord and Hiraṇyagarbha, Govinda, Śarva, etc.'). I chose to take īśvarāt as 'lords', in apposition to the named gods: only such divine lords could do it. This suits the context, where the sons say that the task is beyond human power. 'Hiraṇyagarbha, Govinda, Śarva and the others' is taken as one group. ↩
  69. Even so: The text reads pathāpi, which does not parse. It is most likely a misprint for tathāpi, 'even so', and is translated as such. ↩
  70. that supreme task of his: The text has yad kāryam, with the neuter relative in an irregular sandhi form. It is read as yat kāryam, 'that task which', a construction that continues into the clause about what can or cannot be achieved. ↩
  71. The reading: pathāpi is read as tathāpi (the context calls for 'even so'). yad before kāryam is read as the neuter yat, 'that which', in an irregular sandhi form; the verse is somewhat loose in construction. vipaścitām is taken as genitive plural of vipaścit, 'of the wise', dependent on asādhyam. ↩
  72. lordship over the immortals: amareśatva, the state of being lord of the immortals (the gods), that is, the rank of Indra. ↩
  73. The reading: tatpūjyatvam: 'the state of being worshipped by them' takes tat as the gods (amara/deva) of the preceding compounds. It could instead mean 'the state of being worthy of worship' in general, with tat as 'that [kind of person]'. I chose the first because it fits the sequence of ranks. Vā in vāñchitaṃ vānyad is read as 'or', with vānyad = vā + anyad: 'or whatever else is desired'. Vāñchitam is taken as the object of prayānti, in the sense of 'attain'. ↩
  74. The reading: The compound yatacittendriyātmanām can be read as 'whose minds, senses and selves are restrained' (yata applying to all three, as I chose) or as 'whose minds and senses are restrained, and [who have] a [controlled] self'. The first is the more natural reading of the dvandva with a single participle. Also, divi ceha vā: 'in heaven or here' is taken to cover both worlds, 'here' meaning the human world. ↩
  75. yojanas: A yojana is a measure of distance, commonly reckoned at several miles. ↩
  76. Vainateya: Metronymic of Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, the bird who serves as Viṣṇu's mount; proverbially swift. ↩
  77. The reading: The bracketed words '[a great flier]' are not in the Sanskrit and break rule 1/7; read strictly, 'api' means 'even' and the verse says only that even Vainateya, if he does not move, goes not a single step. Best rendering: 'Vainateya, even, if he does not move, does not go a single step.' The Sanskrit pādam ekam can mean 'one foot' or 'one step'; I took 'step'. ↩
  78. that station of Dhruva: dhrauvya (from dhruva, 'fixed') qualifies sthāna, 'station'; it means the fixed or immovable station, and plays on the name Dhruva. ↩
  79. Dhruva: Dhruva, son of Uttānapāda, attained the fixed pole-star station by austerities; his story is told elsewhere in the Purāṇas. ↩
  80. The reading: dhrauvyaṃ sthānam could also be read as 'the station of Dhruva' or 'the fixed, immovable station'; I take it as 'that station of Dhruva' (dhrauvya as the derivative of dhruva) and note the play on 'fixed'. In the verse 'kva' is repeated in the sense 'how far apart', i.e. the two are very distant; I keep the literal 'where ... and where' as the idiom. ↩
  81. freedom from debt: ānṛṇya: release from an obligation; here the debt the two brothers owe to the prince, which the task would discharge. ↩
  82. my dear sons: putrakau is a dual vocative with an affectionate diminutive suffix; the speaker addresses the two sons, while mahābhāga addresses the other speaker. The reading of the verse is uncertain (see doubts). ↩
  83. The reading: The verse is syntactically awkward: mahābhāga (singular) and putrakau (dual) seem to address different persons, and kāryavān and vām (dual 'of you two') do not obviously fit one speaker. I took mahābhāga as the address to the one who knows the matter, and putrakau as an address to the two sons, with kāryavān as 'has a task'; yena ... yena as 'that by which ... and by which'. Another reading would make putrakau the object of the speaker's concern, so that the prince's task is the matter. Possibly the text is corrupt. Also bhaveta is an irregular optative (for bhavet), and I read sa bhūpālasutaḥ sādhuḥ as the subject of kāryavān. ↩
  84. the earlier occurrence: pūrvavṛtam is a past event, something that happened earlier. In the second half the same word vṛtam is repeated, and there it means the course of events 'as it occurred' in his boyhood. ↩
  85. him who abounds in good conduct: sadvṛttaśālin, 'abounding in good conduct'. It qualifies tasya, the person whose boyhood is recounted. Verse 20.40 speaks of 'that good son of the king', and the next verse (20.42) turns to Śatrujit. ↩
  86. The reading: The referent of tasya (and of tena ... mahātmanā) is not fixed by these verses. 'He' who told the account is the great-souled speaker; 'him of good conduct' is probably the king's son of 20.40. I kept the pronouns as they stand and did not name either person. The word vṛtam is read both as 'occurrence' (pūrvavṛtam) and, in the second line, as 'what happened', following the sense of vṛt. The alternative 'conduct' is possible in the second line, but 'occurred' suits yathā better. ↩
  87. Gālava: A brahmin sage. He is the one who goes on to ask Śatrujit for help against the demon described in the next verses. ↩
  88. best of the twice-born: dvijottama: 'twice-born' here means a brahmin. ↩
  89. The reading: The text reads 'tantu' and 'kaścididvajottamaḥ'. I take 'tantu' as a misprint for 'taṃ tu' ('to that [Śatrujit]'), the accusative object of 'abhyāgamat'. I take 'kaścididvajottamaḥ' as 'kaścid dvijottamaḥ' ('a certain best of the twice-born'). Both readings follow the sense and the metre. The particle 'tu' is omitted as merely connective. ↩
  90. Daityas: The Daityas are a class of asuras, the descendants of Diti and enemies of the gods. ↩
  91. samādhi: Deep meditative concentration, in which the mind is held steady on a single object. ↩
  92. devoted to the vow of silence: maunavrata, the vow of silence (mauna) taken as an ascetic discipline. ↩
  93. obstacles: The text reads vighrāni, an evident misprint for vighnāni, 'obstacles'. ↩
  94. The reading: 1) The speaker is not named in these verses. I take it to be Gālava from 20.42, and mama, 'my', as his. 2) vidhvaṃsayati has no expressed object, so I render it 'wreaks destruction' (the hermitage is implied but not stated). 3) The genitives siṃhebhavanacāriṇām and alpakāyānām I read as dependent on tattadrūpam, 'the forms of those who range…'. The other possible reading is 'he harasses those who range…', with the genitives as objects of vidhvaṃsayati. The compound siṃhebhavanacāriṇām may be a corruption of siṃhebhavanacāriṇām meaning 'those who range in the forests of lions and elephants', but I translate bhavana as 'dwelling'. 4) vighrāni is read as vighnāni. ↩
  95. to burn [him]: The text has dagdhaṃ, a past participle. The construction with samartha requires the infinitive dagdhuṃ, and the translation reads it so, supplying the object "him" (the Daitya). ↩
  96. I do not want: The text reads icchāmi, "I want", with no negative. The sense requires na icchāmi (necchāmi), the negative lost in sandhi or in transmission, and the translation reads it so. ↩
  97. The reading: Two readings are doubtful. (1) dagdhaṃ: the participle "burnt" does not fit with samarthaḥ, so I read the infinitive dagdhuṃ, "to burn". (2) icchāmi: read literally it gives "I want the expenditure of austerity", which contradicts the sense of the passage and the next verses. Gālava is explaining why he does not curse the Daitya himself. I read na icchāmi, "I do not want", and treat the missing negative as a loss in sandhi or transmission. ↩
  98. a sigh was let out by me: The Sanskrit is passive: niśvāsaḥ ... ujjhitaḥ, with the agent in the instrumental mayā. The gerund nirīkṣya, 'having looked at', also belongs to this agent, the speaker. ↩
  99. tormented by him: The text reads tat kleśitena. It is emended to tena kleśitena, 'by him tormented', the asura being the agent of the torment. ↩
  100. asura: The demon is called daityādhama, 'vilest of the Daityas', in v. 43. Here he has the general name asura, a class of beings hostile to the gods, to which the Daityas belong. ↩
  101. The reading: tat kleśitena: the text reads 'tat', which does not agree with anything. I read tena (by him), 'tormented by him' (the asura), so that kleśitena agrees with mayā. The alternative is to take 'tat' as an adverb ('thereupon', 'therefore') and understand the asura as the tormentor. I prefer the emendation because it is the simpler repair and the sense is the same. The passive niśvāso ... ujjhitaḥ is kept in the translation, with the agent mayā, to which nirīkṣya also refers. 'tu' is left unrendered: it only marks a mild contrast with the preceding complaint and adds no further meaning. atinirviṇṇacetasā is rendered 'my mind utterly weary' (ati = utterly; nirviṇṇa = weary, disheartened). The sigh is the cause of the horse's fall in v. 48, which fits this reading. ↩
  102. a bodiless voice: vāc ... aśarīriṇī: a voice from the sky with no speaker visible, in the Purāṇas usually a divine utterance announcing or explaining an event. ↩
  103. The reading: The speaker of this verse (the prince's account of the Gālava episode, in which the horse falls and the voice speaks) is not marked within the verse. 'Naranātha' is a vocative addressing the king, presumably Śatrujit as in the surrounding narrative. 'Tām' refers forward to the voice's words (20.49ff.). ↩
  104. has been given to you by the sun: The instrumental arkeṇa is taken with pratipāditaḥ, 'has been given by the sun'. Some may link it with krāntum, 'to traverse with the sun', but that makes little sense with the following verses. ↩
  105. The reading: arkeṇa: it could be read with krāntum ('able to traverse with the sun') or with pratipāditaḥ ('given by the sun'). I chose the second, since the instrumental of the agent fits the passive participle and the sense is better. Also, the reading tavāyam (tava + ayam) is taken as 'to you, this [horse]'; the verse is part of the bodiless voice's speech, which opens in 20.48. ↩
  106. The reading: In 'na cāsya vihatā gatiḥ' the 'asya' refers to the horse (turaga) of the preceding verse. 'Ambara' is rendered 'sky' and 'toya' 'waters'. The compound pātālāmbaratoyeṣu is locative plural, 'in the nether worlds, the sky and the waters'. 'Bhaṅgaḥ' is literally 'breaking' or 'obstruction'; I took it as breaking of his progress, parallel to 'vihatā gatiḥ'. The sentence appears to continue from the previous verse, as part of the speech of the bodiless voice. ↩
  107. Kuvalaya: The horse's name. The word kuvalaya also means 'water-lily', but here it is explained by bhūvalaya, 'circle of the earth', in the first half of the verse. The name is the source of the epithet Kuvalayāśva given to the king who owns the horse. ↩
  108. The reading: The Sanskrit does not name the horse in this verse; 'ayam' refers to the horse (turaga) of 20.49, so I supplied '[horse]'. The verse continues the bodiless voice's speech begun in 20.49, so I put it in quotation marks. 'Kuvalaya' is read as a masculine name, nominative 'kuvalayaḥ', in agreement with the horse. The etymological play on bhūvalaya (the earth's circle) is implied, not stated; I explained it in the note. ↩
  109. dānavas: The dānavas are a class of asuras, the descendants of Danu and enemies of the gods. Here the word means the demon who has been harassing the sage. ↩
  110. best of the twice-born: dvijaśreṣṭha is the voice's address to the brahmin sage who is relating the event. Dvija, 'twice-born', here means a brahmin. ↩
  111. [he]: The verb haniṣyati has no stated subject. The next verse (20.53) names the king's son Ṛtadhvaja as the one who will gain fame through this horse. ↩
  112. The reading: The subject of haniṣyati is not stated. Because of 20.53, I take it to be Ṛtadhvaja, son of Śatrujit, and leave it as a bracketed pronoun. 'Tam apy enam' could also be read as 'him, this very one', but I take 'apy' as 'even', and 'enam' as the horse (after samāruhya), which is the usual construction. ↩
  113. jewel of a horse: Sanskrit aśvaratna: a horse that is the finest of its kind, 'jewel' being used for the best of a class. ↩
  114. The reading: The verse has no verb 'is' in the first clause; 'There is a king named Śatrujit; his son is Ṛtadhvaja' supplies the copula. The 'he' of 'he will gain fame' is Ṛtadhvaja, the subject of yāsyati; the voice of 20.48–52 continues, and the bodiless voice speaks of him in the third person. In 20.53 the Sanskrit has 'ca' after aśvaratna, which I have left untranslated as a simple connective. ↩
  115. the one who obstructs my tapas: The text reads vighrakāriṇam; vighna (obstacle) is meant. ↩
  116. receives a share [of the merit]: A king was held to share in a sixth part of the merit of the ascetic acts performed in his realm, and so is bound to protect them from disturbance. ↩
  117. The reading: vighrakāriṇam is read as vighnakāriṇam, 'one who causes obstruction', a likely misprint. Syntactically 'tam nivāraya' ('restrain him') stands in apposition to tvām in the first half, so tvām ... vighrakāriṇam cannot be 'you, the obstructer'. The accusative vighrakāriṇam must go with tam, 'him, the obstructer', and I translate accordingly. The words 'to ask you to' are supplied to make the English parse. The speaker is the sage addressing the king; bhāgabhāk is read as 'sharing in the merit', not 'a sharer in the offence'. The phrase 'of the merit' is implied rather than stated. ↩
  118. jewel of a horse: Sanskrit aśvaratna, a compound meaning the best or most precious of horses. The text prints the first word as tadetaśvaratnaṃ, with the sandhi irregular for tad etad aśvaratnam. It is read as 'that [is] this jewel of a horse'. ↩
  119. king: Sanskrit bhūpa, 'protector of the earth', is the vocative address to King Śatrujit. ↩
  120. The reading: The printed tadetaśvaratnaṃ is irregular. The expected form is tad etad aśvaratnam, or tad etad aśvaratnaṃ. I have read tat as 'so, therefore' and etad aśvaratnam as 'this jewel of a horse'. The verb niveditam, 'presented, announced', is taken in the sense of presenting or making known the horse to the king. The addressee of bhūpa is the king Śatrujit, who is named in the preceding verses and is the father of the prince. ↩
  121. righteous in his nature: dharmātmā, literally 'whose self is dharma': the king is characterised as one devoted to righteousness. ↩
  122. festive auspicious rites: kautukamaṅgala: the auspicious ceremonies performed on a person before an important undertaking or departure, such as the tying of protective threads and blessings. ↩
  123. The reading: kṛtakautukamaṅgalam is read as a bahuvrīhi qualifying putram (the son for whom the rites were performed), not as a separate object. In 20.57, tam in 'tamādāya' is taken as Ṛtadhvaja, whom Gālava takes along (with the horse he is mounted on), since the horse has just been called 'tam aśvaratnam' in 20.56. Sentence-internal subjects: the absolutive āropya has the king as its agent (causative, 'having made him mount'). ↩
  124. The Story of the Horse Kuvalaya: kuvalayāśvīya is a derivative adjective or noun meaning 'concerning Kuvalayāśva'; it is read here as 'concerning the horse Kuvalaya', following the chapter's contents. The text may also be read as referring to the prince Kuvalayāśva, 'having Kuvalaya as horse'. ↩
  125. dialogue of father and son: pitāputrasaṃvāda: the Purāṇa's frame is partly a conversation between a father and his sons; here it is the colophon's name for that section, in which the nāga father hears the tale from his sons. ↩
  126. The reading: The printed colophon reads 'saṃvādeṭhakuvalayāśvīyo'; 'ṭha' is a misprint or stray syllable, likely for a punctuation mark or 'saṃvāde' followed by 'kuvalayāśvīyo'. Read thus: saṃvāde kuvalayāśvīyo. 'Kuvalayāśvīya' is rendered 'concerning the horse Kuvalaya' following the glossary's Kuvalaya as the horse's name; the other possible reading is 'concerning Kuvalayāśva'. The following 'viṃśo adhyāyaḥ' is the twentieth chapter. ↩

Adhyāya 21

Sanskrit

एकविंशो ऽध्यायः

ekaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Twenty-One1

Sanskrit

पितोवाच

pitovāca

21.1

Sanskrit

गालवेन समं गत्वा नृपपुत्रेण तेन यत् । कृतं तत् कथ्यतां पुत्रौ विचित्रा युवयोः कथा ॥

gālavena samaṃ gatvā nṛpaputreṇa tena yat | kṛtaṃ tat kathyatāṃ putrau vicitrā yuvayoḥ kathā ||

English

O sons, let that be told which was done by that king's son2 after he had gone together with Gālava; wondrous is the tale of you two3.4

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons said:

21.2

Sanskrit

स गालवाश्रमे रम्ये तिष्ठन् भूपालनन्दनः । सर्वविघ्रोपशमनं चकार ब्रह्मवादिनाम् ॥

sa gālavāśrame ramye tiṣṭhan bhūpālanandanaḥ | sarvavighropaśamanaṃ cakāra brahmavādinām ||

English

Staying in Gālava's delightful hermitage, that delight of the protector of the earth5 put an end to every obstruction of the brahmavādins6.7

21.3

Sanskrit

वीरं कुवलयाश्वं तं वसन्तं गालवाश्रमे । मदावलेपोपहतो नाजानाद्दानवाधमः ॥

vīraṃ kuvalayāśvaṃ taṃ vasantaṃ gālavāśrame | madāvalepopahato nājānāddānavādhamaḥ ||

English

The vilest of the dānavas, struck down by the arrogance of his pride8, did not know that the hero Kuvalayāśva9 was living in Gālava's hermitage.

21.4

Sanskrit

ततस्तं गालवं विप्रं सन्ध्योपासनतत्परम् । शौकरं रूपमास्थाय प्रधर्षयितुमागतम् ॥

tatastaṃ gālavaṃ vipraṃ sandhyopāsanatatparam | śaukaraṃ rūpamāsthāya pradharṣayitumāgatam ||

English

21.4–5Then, when [the dānava] had taken the form of a boar and come to assail that brahmin Gālava, who was intent on the evening worship10, and when the sage's disciples cried out, the king's son, bow in hand11, quickly mounted that horse and ran after that boar.12

21.5

Sanskrit

मुनिशिष्यैरथोत्क्रुष्टे शीघ्रमारुह्य तं हयम् । अन्वधावद्वराहं तं नृपपुत्रः शरासनी ॥

muniśiṣyairathotkruṣṭe śīghramāruhya taṃ hayam | anvadhāvadvarāhaṃ taṃ nṛpaputraḥ śarāsanī ||

English

Its English is given with 21.4–5, above.

21.6

Sanskrit

आजघान च बाणेन चन्द्रार्धाकारवर्चसा । आकृष्य बलवच्चापं चारुचित्रोपशोभितम् ॥

ājaghāna ca bāṇena candrārdhākāravarcasā | ākṛṣya balavaccāpaṃ cārucitropaśobhitam ||

English

And [the king's son], drawing [his] strong bow, which was adorned with lovely, varied ornament, struck [the boar] with an arrow shaped like a half-moon and gleaming13.14

21.7

Sanskrit

नाराचाभिहतः शीघ्रमात्मत्राणपरो मृगः । गिरिपादपसम्बाधां सो ऽन्वक्रामन्महाटवीम् ॥

nārācābhihataḥ śīghramātmatrāṇaparo mṛgaḥ | giripādapasambādhāṃ so 'nvakrāmanmahāṭavīm ||

English

Struck by the nārāca15 arrow, the animal16, intent on saving itself, quickly entered a great forest crowded with mountains and trees.17

21.8

Sanskrit

तमन्वधावद्वेगेन तुरगो ऽसौ मनोजवः । चोदितो राजपुत्रेण पितुरादेशकारिणा ॥

tamanvadhāvadvegena turago 'sau manojavaḥ | codito rājaputreṇa piturādeśakāriṇā ||

English

That horse, swift as thought, ran after it with speed, urged on by the king's son, who was carrying out his father's command.18

21.9

Sanskrit

अतिक्रम्याथ वेगेन योजनानि सहस्रशः । धरण्यां विवृते गर्ते निपपात लघुक्रमः ॥

atikramyātha vegena yojanāni sahasraśaḥ | dharaṇyāṃ vivṛte garte nipapāta laghukramaḥ ||

English

Then, having crossed thousands of yojanas19 with speed, [the boar]20, of light step, fell into a gap that lay open in the earth.21

21.10

Sanskrit

तस्यानन्तरमेवाशु सो ऽप्यश्वी नृपतेः सुतः । निपपात महागर्ते तिमिरौघसमावृते ॥

tasyānantaramevāśu so 'pyaśvī nṛpateḥ sutaḥ | nipapāta mahāgarte timiraughasamāvṛte ||

English

Immediately after it, quickly, the king's son22 too, mounted on his horse, fell into that great pit, which was shrouded in masses of darkness.23

21.11

Sanskrit

ततो नादृश्यत मृगः स तस्मिन् राजसूनुना । प्रकाशञ्च स पातालमपश्यत् तत्र नापि नम् ॥

tato nādṛśyata mṛgaḥ sa tasmin rājasūnunā | prakāśañca sa pātālamapaśyat tatra nāpi nam ||

English

Then the animal was not seen there by the king's son. And he saw the nether world lit up, but there he saw no man either.24

21.12

Sanskrit

ततो ऽपश्यत् स सौवर्णप्रासादशतसंकुलम् । पुरन्दरपुरप्रख्यं पुरं प्राकारशोभितम् ॥

tato 'paśyat sa sauvarṇaprāsādaśatasaṃkulam | purandarapuraprakhyaṃ puraṃ prākāraśobhitam ||

English

Then he saw a city adorned with ramparts, crowded with hundreds of golden palaces and resembling the city of Purandara25.26

21.13

Sanskrit

तत् प्रविश्य स नापश्यत् तत्र कञ्चिन्नरं पुरे । भ्रमता च ततो दृष्टा तत्र योषित् त्वरान्विता ॥

tat praviśya sa nāpaśyat tatra kañcinnaraṃ pure | bhramatā ca tato dṛṣṭā tatra yoṣit tvarānvitā ||

English

Having entered it, he saw no man there in the city. But as he wandered about, he then saw a woman there, full of haste.27

21.14

Sanskrit

सा पृष्टा तेन तन्वङ्गी प्रस्थिता केन कस्य वा । नोवाच किञ्चित् प्रासादमारुरोह च भामिनी ॥

sā pṛṣṭā tena tanvaṅgī prasthitā kena kasya vā | novāca kiñcit prāsādamāruroha ca bhāminī ||

English

Asked by him why she had set out, or whose she was28, that slender-limbed woman said nothing, but the lady29 climbed up into a palace.30

21.15

Sanskrit

सो ऽप्यश्वमेकतो बद्ध्वा तामेवानुससार वै । विस्मयोत्फुल्लनयनो निः शङ्को नृपतेः सुतः ॥

so 'pyaśvamekato baddhvā tāmevānusasāra vai | vismayotphullanayano niḥ śaṅko nṛpateḥ sutaḥ ||

English

He too, the king's son31, tied his horse to one side and followed that same woman, his eyes wide with wonder and himself without fear.32

21.16

Sanskrit

ततो ऽपश्यत् सुविस्तीर्णे पर्यङ्के सर्वकाञ्चने । निषण्णां कन्यकामेकां कामयुक्तां रतीमिव ॥

tato 'paśyat suvistīrṇe paryaṅke sarvakāñcane | niṣaṇṇāṃ kanyakāmekāṃ kāmayuktāṃ ratīmiva ||

English

21.16–18Then he saw one maiden seated on a very broad couch made wholly of gold, filled with desire, like Rati33. Her face was a clear moon, her brows were fair, and her hips and breasts were full. Her lower lip was like a bimba34 fruit, her limbs were slender, and her eyes were like blue lotuses. Her nails were red and prominent. She was śyāmā35, tender, with coppery-red hands and feet, with thighs like an elephant's trunk, fine teeth, and dark, fine, firm locks of hair.36

21.17

Sanskrit

विस्पष्टेन्दुमुखीं सुभ्रूं पीनश्रोणिपयोधराम् । बिम्बाधरोष्ठीं नन्वङ्गीं नीलोत्पलविलोचनाम् ॥

vispaṣṭendumukhīṃ subhrūṃ pīnaśroṇipayodharām | bimbādharoṣṭhīṃ nanvaṅgīṃ nīlotpalavilocanām ||

English

Its English is given with 21.16–18, above.

21.18

Sanskrit

रक्ततुङ्गनखीं श्यामां मृद्वीं ताम्रकराङ्घ्रिकाम् । करभोरुं सुदशनां नीलसूक्ष्मस्थिरालकाम् ॥

raktatuṅganakhīṃ śyāmāṃ mṛdvīṃ tāmrakarāṅghrikām | karabhoruṃ sudaśanāṃ nīlasūkṣmasthirālakām ||

English

Its English is given with 21.16–18, above.

21.19

Sanskrit

तां दृष्ट्वा चारुसर्वाङ्गीमनङ्गाङ्गलतामिव । सो ऽमन्यत् पार्थिवसुतस्तां रसातलदेवताम् ॥

tāṃ dṛṣṭvā cārusarvāṅgīmanaṅgāṅgalatāmiva | so 'manyat pārthivasutastāṃ rasātaladevatām ||

English

Having seen her, whose every limb was lovely, like a creeper formed of the limbs of Anaṅga37, that son of the king took her to be a goddess of Rasātala.38

21.20

Sanskrit

सा च दृष्ट्वैव तं बाला नीलकुञ्चितमूर्धजम् । पीनोरुस्कन्धबाहुं तममंस्त मदनं शुभा ॥

sā ca dṛṣṭvaiva taṃ bālā nīlakuñcitamūrdhajam | pīnoruskandhabāhuṃ tamamaṃsta madanaṃ śubhā ||

And as soon as that young woman, the radiant one, saw him, with his dark curled hair and his full thighs, shoulders and arms, she took him to be Madana39.40

21.21

Sanskrit

उत्तस्थौ च महाभागा चित्तक्षोभमवाप्य सा । लज्जाविस्मयदैन्यानां सद्यस्तन्वी वशं गता ॥

uttasthau ca mahābhāgā cittakṣobhamavāpya sā | lajjāvismayadainyānāṃ sadyastanvī vaśaṃ gatā ||

English

And that greatly fortunate41 woman rose, having fallen into agitation of mind; the slender one at once came under the sway of shyness, wonder and dejection42.43

21.22

Sanskrit

को ऽयं देवो नु यक्षो वा गन्धर्वो वोरगो ऽपि वा । विद्याधरो वा सम्प्राप्तः कृतपुण्यरतिर्नरः ॥

ko 'yaṃ devo nu yakṣo vā gandharvo vorago 'pi vā | vidyādharo vā samprāptaḥ kṛtapuṇyaratirnaraḥ ||

21.23

Sanskrit

एवं विचिन्त्य वहुधा निश्वस्य च महीतले । उपविश्य ततो भेजे सा मूर्च्छां मदिरक्षणा ॥

evaṃ vicintya vahudhā niśvasya ca mahītale | upaviśya tato bheje sā mūrcchāṃ madirakṣaṇā ||

Having thus reflected in many ways, and having sighed, she sat down on the ground; then she, the woman with intoxicating eyes44, fell into a swoon.45

21.24

Sanskrit

सो ऽपि कामशराघातमवाप्य नृपतेः सुतः । तां समाश्वासयामास न भेतव्यमिति ब्रुवन् ॥

so 'pi kāmaśarāghātamavāpya nṛpateḥ sutaḥ | tāṃ samāśvāsayāmāsa na bhetavyamiti bruvan ||

21.25

Sanskrit

सा च स्त्री या तदा दृष्टा पूर्वं तेन महात्मना । तालवृन्तमुपादाय पर्यवीजयदाकुला ॥

sā ca strī yā tadā dṛṣṭā pūrvaṃ tena mahātmanā | tālavṛntamupādāya paryavījayadākulā ||

And that woman, who had been seen earlier by that great-souled man48, took up a palm-leaf fan49 and, flustered, fanned her all around.50†

21.26

Sanskrit

samāśvāsya tadā pṛṣṭā tena saṃmohakāraṇam | kiñcillajjānvitā bālā tasyāḥ sakhyurnyavedayat ||

English

Then, having comforted her, he asked her the cause of her bewilderment, and the young woman, somewhat filled with shyness, reported it to her friend51.52

21.27

Sanskrit

सा चास्मै कथयामास नृपपुत्राय विस्तरात् । मोहस्य कारणं सर्वं तद्दर्शनसमुद्भवम् । यथा तया समाख्यातं तद्वृत्तान्तञ्च भामिनी ॥

sā cāsmai kathayāmāsa nṛpaputrāya vistarāt | mohasya kāraṇaṃ sarvaṃ taddarśanasamudbhavam | yathā tayā samākhyātaṃ tadvṛttāntañca bhāminī ||

English

And she, the lady, told this king's son in full detail the whole cause of the bewilderment, which had arisen from seeing him, and also that account, just as it had been related by her.53

Sanskrit

स्त्र्युवाच

stryuvāca

English

The woman said:54

21.28

Sanskrit

विश्वावसुरिति ख्यातो दिवि गन्धर्वराट् प्रभो । तस्येयमात्मजा सुभ्रूर्नाम्नरा ख्याता मदालसा ॥

viśvāvasuriti khyāto divi gandharvarāṭ prabho | tasyeyamātmajā subhrūrnāmnarā khyātā madālasā ||

English

O lord, there is a king of the Gandharvas55 in heaven, famed as Viśvāvasu56. This fair-browed woman is his daughter, known by the name Madālasā57.58

21.29

Sanskrit

वज्रकेतोः सुतश्चोग्रो दानवो ऽरिविदारणः । पातालकेतुर्विख्यातः पातालान्तरसंश्रयः ॥

vajraketoḥ sutaścogro dānavo 'rividāraṇaḥ | pātālaketurvikhyātaḥ pātālāntarasaṃśrayaḥ ||

English

There is a fierce dānava, a son of Vajraketu, a tearer of enemies, famed as Pātālaketu59, whose dwelling is in the inner nether worlds60.

21.30

Sanskrit

तेनेयमुद्यानगता कृत्वा मायां तमोमयीम् । अपहृत्य मयां हीना बाला नीता दुरात्मना ॥

teneyamudyānagatā kṛtvā māyāṃ tamomayīm | apahṛtya mayāṃ hīnā bālā nītā durātmanā ||

English

21.31

Sanskrit

आगामिन्यां त्रयोदश्यामुद्वक्ष्यति किलासुरः । स तु नार्हति चार्वङ्गीं शूद्रो वेदश्रुतीमिव ॥

āgāminyāṃ trayodaśyāmudvakṣyati kilāsuraḥ | sa tu nārhati cārvaṅgīṃ śūdro vedaśrutīmiva ||

English

On the coming thirteenth lunar day62, it is said, the asura will marry her63. But he does not deserve this fair-limbed woman, just as a śūdra64 does not deserve the hearing of the Veda.65

21.32

Sanskrit

अतीते च दिने बालामात्मव्यापदनोद्यताम् । सुरभिः प्राह नायं त्वं प्राप्स्यते दानवाधमः ॥

atīte ca dine bālāmātmavyāpadanodyatām | surabhiḥ prāha nāyaṃ tvaṃ prāpsyate dānavādhamaḥ ||

English

And when the day had passed, Surabhi66 said to the young woman, who was bent on destroying herself: "This vilest of dānavas will not obtain you."67

21.33

Sanskrit

मर्त्यलोकमनुप्राप्तं य एनं छेत्स्यते शरैः । सते भर्ता महाभागे अचिरेण भविष्यति ॥

martyalokamanuprāptaṃ ya enaṃ chetsyate śaraiḥ | sate bhartā mahābhāge acireṇa bhaviṣyati ||

English

The one who will cut him down68 with arrows when he has come to the world of mortals will, before long, be your husband69, O greatly fortunate one.70

21.34

Sanskrit

अहं चास्याः सखी नाम्नरा कुण्डलेति मनस्विनी । सुता विन्ध्यवतः पत्नी वीरपुष्करमालिनः ॥

ahaṃ cāsyāḥ sakhī nāmnarā kuṇḍaleti manasvinī | sutā vindhyavataḥ patnī vīrapuṣkaramālinaḥ ||

English

And I am her friend, by name Kuṇḍalā, a woman of high spirit, the daughter of Vindhyavat71 and the wife of the hero Puṣkaramālin72.73

21.35

Sanskrit

हते भर्तरि शुम्भेन तीर्थात् तीर्थमनुव्रता । चरामि दिव्यया गत्या परलोकार्थमुद्यता ॥

hate bhartari śumbhena tīrthāt tīrthamanuvratā | carāmi divyayā gatyā paralokārthamudyatā ||

English

With my husband slain by Śumbha74, I wander, going on from one tīrtha75 to the next by a divine course76, intent on the goal of the world beyond.77

21.36

Sanskrit

पातालकेतुर्दुष्टात्मा वाराहं वपुरास्थितः । केनापि विद्धो बाणेन मुनीनां त्राणकारणात् ॥

pātālaketurduṣṭātmā vārāhaṃ vapurāsthitaḥ | kenāpi viddho bāṇena munīnāṃ trāṇakāraṇāt ||

English

Pātālaketu, evil-minded, had taken on the body of a boar, and was pierced by an arrow shot by someone78, for the protection of the sages79.80

21.37

Sanskrit

तञ्चाहं तत्त्वतो ऽन्विष्य त्वरिता समुपागता । सत्यमेव स केनापि ताडितो दानवाधमः ॥

tañcāhaṃ tattvato 'nviṣya tvaritā samupāgatā | satyameva sa kenāpi tāḍito dānavādhamaḥ ||

English

And I, having sought him out in truth, have come up in haste. It is indeed true that this vilest of dānavas was struck by someone.81

21.38

Sanskrit

इयञ्च मूर्च्छामगमत् कारणं यत् शृणुष्व तत् । त्वयि प्रीतिमती बाला दर्शनादेव मानद ॥

iyañca mūrcchāmagamat kāraṇaṃ yat śṛṇuṣva tat | tvayi prītimatī bālā darśanādeva mānada ||

English

And listen to the reason why this young woman fainted. She has become fond of you, O giver of honour82, merely from seeing you.83

21.39

Sanskrit

देवपुत्रोपमे चारुवाक्यादिगुणशालिनि । भर्या चान्यस्य विहिता येन विद्धः स दानवः ॥

devaputropame cāruvākyādiguṇaśālini | bharyā cānyasya vihitā yena viddhaḥ sa dānavaḥ ||

English

[She is fond] of you, who are like a son of a god and endowed with excellent qualities, beginning with charming speech. But she has been ordained84 as the wife of another, the one by whom that dānava was pierced.85†

21.40

Sanskrit

etasmāt kāraṇānmohaṃ mahāntamiyamāgatā | yāvajjīvaṃ ca tanvaṅgī duḥ khamevopabhokṣyate ||

For this reason she has fallen into a great swoon, and this slender-limbed woman86 will experience nothing but sorrow for as long as she lives.87

Sanskrit

tvayyasyā hṛdayaṃ rāgi bhartā cānyo bhaviṣyati | yāvajjīvamato duḥ khaṃ surabhyā nānyathā vacaḥ ||

ahaṃ tvasyāḥ prabhī prītyā duḥ khitātra samāgatā | yato viśeṣo naivāsti svasakhīnijadehayoḥ ||

Sanskrit

yadyeṣābhimataṃ vīraṃ patimāpnoti śobhanā | tatastapastvahaṃ kuryāṃ nirvyalīkena cetasā ||

If this beautiful maiden obtains the brave husband she desires, then I for my part would practise tapas92 with a sincere mind.93

tvantu ko vā kimarthaṃ vā samprāpto 'tra mahāmate | devo daityo nu gandharvaḥ pannagaḥ kinnaro 'pi vā ||

But who are you, O man of great mind, and for what purpose have you come here? Are you a god, a Daitya, a Gandharva, a serpent94, or even a Kinnara95?96

na hyatra mānuṣagatirna cedṛṅmānuṣaṃ vapuḥ | tattvamākhyāhi kathitaṃ yathaivāvitathaṃ mayā ||

English

कुवलयाश्व उवाच

kuvalayāśva uvāca

English

21.46Kuvalayāśva said: What you ask me, O knower of dharma, "Who are you, and why have you come?", listen to that, O woman of spotless understanding. I shall tell it to you from the beginning.100

yanmāṃ pṛcchasi dharmajñe kastvaṃ kiṃ vā samāgataḥ | tacchṛṇuṣvāmalaprajñe kathayāmyāditastava ||

Its English is given with 21.46, above.

21.47

Sanskrit

rājñaḥ śatrujitaḥ putraḥ pitrā sampreṣitaḥ śubhe | munirakṣaṇamuddiśya gālavāśramamāgataḥ ||

I am the son of King Śatrujit101, O fair lady102. Sent forth by my father, I came to the hermitage of Gālava for the purpose of protecting the sages.103

Sanskrit

kurvato mama rakṣāñca munīnāṃ dharmacāriṇām | vighnārthamāgataḥ koṣa'pi śaukaraṃ rūpamāsthitaḥ ||

And while I was providing protection for the sages who follow dharma, some being104 came to create obstacles, having assumed the form of a boar.105†

Sanskrit

mayā sa viddho bāṇena candrārdhākāravarccasā | apakrānto 'tivegena tamasmyanugato hayī ||

papāta sahasā garte sakrīḍo 'śvaśca māmakaḥ | so 'hamaśvaṃ samārūḍhastamasyekaḥ paribhraman ||

Sanskrit

prakāśamāsāditavān dṛṣṭā ca bhavatī mayā | pṛṣṭayā ca na me kiñcidbhavatyā dattamuttaram ||

Sanskrit

tvāñcaivānupraviṣṭo 'hamimaṃ prāsādamuttamam | ityetat kathitaṃ satyaṃ na devo 'haṃ na dānavaḥ ||

21.53

Sanskrit

न पन्नगो न गन्धर्वः किन्नरो वा शुचिस्मिते । समस्ता पूज्यपक्षो वै देवाद्या मम कुण्डले । मनुष्यो ऽस्मि विशङ्का ते न कर्तव्यात्र कर्हिचित् ॥

na pannago na gandharvaḥ kinnaro vā śucismite | samastā pūjyapakṣo vai devādyā mama kuṇḍale | manuṣyo 'smi viśaṅkā te na kartavyātra karhicit ||

I am not a serpent, nor a Gandharva, nor a Kinnara, O lady of the bright smile. All the gods and the rest are, for me, a class to be honoured113, O Kuṇḍalā114. I am a human being; you should never feel any suspicion about this.115

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

21.54The two sons said: Then that maiden, delighted, looking at her friend's excellent face, numb with shyness, said nothing, the lady.116†

Sanskrit

tataḥ prahṛṣṭā sā kanyā sakhīvadanamuttamam | lajjājaḍaṃ vīkṣamāṇā kiñcinnovāca bhāminī ||

English

Its English is given with 21.54, above.

21.55

Sanskrit

सा सखी पुनरप्येनां प्रहृष्टा प्रत्युवाच ह । यथावत् कथितं तेन सुरभ्या वचनानुगे ॥

sā sakhī punarapyenāṃ prahṛṣṭā pratyuvāca ha | yathāvat kathitaṃ tena surabhyā vacanānuge ||

That friend117, delighted, replied to her again: "It has been told by him exactly as it was, O you who are obedient to Surabhi's word118."119

कुण्डलोवाच

kuṇḍalovāca

Sanskrit

vīra satyamasandigdhaṃ bhavatābhihitaṃ vacaḥ | nānyatra hṛdayantvasyā dṛṣṭvā sthairyaṃ prayāsyati ||

Its English is given with 21.56, above.

21.57

Sanskrit

चन्द्रमेवाधिका कान्तिः समुपैति रविं प्रभा । भूतिर्धन्यं धृतिर्धोरं क्षान्तिरभ्येति चोत्तमम् ॥

candramevādhikā kāntiḥ samupaiti raviṃ prabhā | bhūtirdhanyaṃ dhṛtirdhoraṃ kṣāntirabhyeti cottamam ||

Therefore this young woman is fortunate and blessed with good fortune, having entered into a connection with you. O brave one, do what must be done, which has been arranged by destiny126 itself.127

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

Sanskrit

paravānahamityāha rājaputraḥ satāṃ pituḥ | sā ca taṃ cintayāmāsa tumburuṃ tatkule gurum ||

Its English is given with 21.60, above.

21.62–63Having kindled the fire and made the offering, he, who knew the mantras135, performed the marriage rite for the maiden, whose auspicious rites had been done, and gave her in marriage. Then the wise one went, as he had come136, to his own hermitage for tapas. And she said to that friend of hers137, the young girl: “I have accomplished my purpose, O fair-faced one.”138

Sanskrit

jagāma tapase dhīmān svāśramapadaṃ tadā | sā cāha tāṃ sakhīṃ bālāṃ kṛtārthāsmi varānane ||

Its English is given with 21.62–63, above.

21.64

Sanskrit

21.64–65“Having seen you, endowed with beauty, united with him, I shall practise unequalled tapas139 with a sincere mind, and, with my sins washed away by the waters of tīrthas, I shall be one who is not of this kind140.” Then she, bowed down with humility, wishing to go, and speaking in words faltering with affection for her own friend, said to that prince:141

Sanskrit

tīrthāmbudhūtapāpā ca bhavitrī nedṛśī yathā | tañcāha rājaputraṃ sā praśrayāvanatā tadā | gantukāmā nijasakhīsnehaviklavabhāṣiṇī ||

Its English is given with 21.64–65, above.

Sanskrit

कुण्डलोवाच

kuṇḍalovāca

English

Sanskrit

पुंभिरप्यमितप्रज्ञ नोपदेशो भवद्विधे । दातव्यः किमुत स्त्रीभिरतो नोपदिशामि ते ॥

puṃbhirapyamitaprajña nopadeśo bhavadvidhe | dātavyaḥ kimuta strībhirato nopadiśāmi te ||

English

Its English is given with 21.66, above.

21.67

Sanskrit

किन्त्वस्यास्तनुमध्यायाः स्नेहाकृष्टेन चेतसा । त्वया विश्रम्भिता चास्मि स्मारयाम्यरिसूदन ॥

kintvasyāstanumadhyāyāḥ snehākṛṣṭena cetasā | tvayā viśrambhitā cāsmi smārayāmyarisūdana ||

English

But, O slayer of enemies143, with a mind drawn by affection for this slender-waisted girl, and because you have put me at ease with your trust144, I remind you.145

21.68

Sanskrit

भर्तव्या रक्षितव्या च भार्या हि पतिना सदा । धर्मार्थकामसंसिद्ध्यै भार्या भर्तृसहायिनी ॥

bhartavyā rakṣitavyā ca bhāryā hi patinā sadā | dharmārthakāmasaṃsiddhyai bhāryā bhartṛsahāyinī ||

A wife must always be supported and protected by her husband. A wife is the husband's helper for the full accomplishment of dharma, artha146 and kāma147.148

21.69

Sanskrit

When wife and husband each follow the other's will, then there is a union of even the three, dharma, artha149 and kāma150.151

21.70

Sanskrit

kathaṃ bhāryāmṛte dharmamarthaṃ vā puruṣaḥ prabho | prāpnoti kāmamathavā tasyāṃ tritayamāhitam ||

How, O lord, can a man attain dharma or artha without a wife, or else kāma? The three are lodged in her152.153

21.71

Sanskrit

tathaiva bhartāramṛte bhāryā dharmādisādhane | na samarthā trivargo 'yaṃ dāmpatyaṃ samupāśritaḥ ||

21.72

Sanskrit

devātāpitṛbhṛtyānāmatithīnāñca pūjanam | na puṃbhiḥ śakyate kartumṛte bhāryāṃ nṛpātmaja ||

The honouring of the deities157, the ancestors, the servants158 and the guests cannot be done by men without a wife, O son of a king159.160

21.73

Sanskrit

Sanskrit

21.76

Sanskrit

striyāścāpi vinā bhartrā dharmakāmārthasantatiḥ | naiva tasmāt trivargo 'yaṃ dāmpatyamadhigacchati ||

English

And for a woman also, without a husband, there is no continuity of dharma, kāma170 and artha169. Therefore this triple set of aims reaches its fulfilment in171 married life.172

21.77

Sanskrit

एतन्मयोक्तं युवयोर्गच्छामि च यथेप्सितम् । वर्ध त्वमनया सार्धं धनपुत्रसुखायुषा ॥

etanmayoktaṃ yuvayorgacchāmi ca yathepsitam | vardha tvamanayā sārdhaṃ dhanaputrasukhāyuṣā ||

English

This has been said by me to the two of you173, and I go as I wish. May you prosper together with her, with wealth, sons, happiness and life.174

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons said:175

21.78

Sanskrit

इत्युक्त्वा सा परिष्वज्य स्वसखीं तं नमस्य च । जगाम दिव्यया गत्या यथाभिप्रेतमात्मनः ॥

ityuktvā sā pariṣvajya svasakhīṃ taṃ namasya ca | jagāma divyayā gatyā yathābhipretamātmanaḥ ||

English

Having spoken thus, she176 embraced her friend and bowed to him, and she went by a divine course, as her own purpose directed.177

21.79

Sanskrit

सो ऽपि शत्रुजितः पुत्रस्तामारोप्य तुरङ्गमम् । निर्गन्तुकामः पातालाद्विज्ञातो दनुसम्भवैः ॥

so 'pi śatrujitaḥ putrastāmāropya turaṅgamam | nirgantukāmaḥ pātālādvijñāto danusambhavaiḥ ||

English

He too, the son of Śatrujit, having set her on the horse and wishing to leave the nether worlds, was recognized by those born of Danu178.179

21.80

Sanskrit

ततस्तैः सहसोत्क्रुष्टं ह्रियते ह्रियते ऽति वै । कन्यारत्नं यदानीतं दिवः पातालकेतुना ॥

tatastaiḥ sahasotkruṣṭaṃ hriyate hriyate 'ti vai | kanyāratnaṃ yadānītaṃ divaḥ pātālaketunā ||

English

Then a cry was suddenly raised by them: "[She] is being carried off! [She] is being carried off!" [They meant] the jewel of a maiden180 whom Pātālaketu had brought from heaven.181

21.81

Sanskrit

ततः परिघनिस्त्रिंशगदाशूलशरायुधम् । दानवानां बलं प्राप्तं सह पातालकेतुना ॥

tataḥ parighanistriṃśagadāśūlaśarāyudham | dānavānāṃ balaṃ prāptaṃ saha pātālaketunā ||

English

Then the host of the dānavas, armed with iron clubs182, swords, maces, spears and arrows, arrived together with Pātālaketu.183

21.82

Sanskrit

तिष्ठ तिष्ठेति जल्पन्तस्ते तदा दानवोत्तमाः । शरवर्षैस्तथा शूलैर्ववर्षुर्नृपनन्दनम् ॥

tiṣṭha tiṣṭheti jalpantaste tadā dānavottamāḥ | śaravarṣaistathā śūlairvavarṣurnṛpanandanam ||

English

"Stand! Stand!" crying out thus, those foremost of the dānavas then rained down showers of arrows and spears upon the king's son184.

21.83

Sanskrit

स च शत्रुजितः पुत्रस्तदस्त्राण्यतिवीर्यवान् । चिच्छेद शरजालेन प्रहसन्निव लीलया ॥

sa ca śatrujitaḥ putrastadastrāṇyativīryavān | ciccheda śarajālena prahasanniva līlayā ||

English

And that son of Śatrujit, of exceeding valor, cut those missiles to pieces with a net of arrows185, as if laughing, in sport.186

21.84

Sanskrit

क्षणेन पातालतलमसिखक्त्यृष्टिशायकैः । छिन्नैः सञ्छन्नमभवदृतध्वजशरोत्करैः ॥

kṣaṇena pātālatalamasikhaktyṛṣṭiśāyakaiḥ | chinnaiḥ sañchannamabhavadṛtadhvajaśarotkaraiḥ ||

English

In an instant the floor of the nether world was strewn with the cut-up swords, javelins187, lances188 and arrows, and with the volleys of arrows shot by Ṛtadhvaja.189

21.85

Sanskrit

ततो ऽस्त्रं त्वाष्ट्रमादाय चिक्षेप प्रति दानवान् । तेन ते दानवाः सर्वे सह पातालकेतुना ॥

tato 'straṃ tvāṣṭramādāya cikṣepa prati dānavān | tena te dānavāḥ sarve saha pātālaketunā ||

English

21.85–86Then, taking up the missile of Tvaṣṭṛ190, he hurled it at the dānavas. By that missile, extremely fierce with its garlands of flames, all those dānavas together with Pātālaketu were reduced to heaps of cracking bones and burned up, like the sons of Sagara191 when they met the fiery energy of Kapila192.193

21.86

Sanskrit

ज्वालामालातितीव्रेण स्फुटदस्थिचयाः कृताः । निर्दग्धाः कापिलं तेजः समासाद्येव सागराः ॥

jvālāmālātitīvreṇa sphuṭadasthicayāḥ kṛtāḥ | nirdagdhāḥ kāpilaṃ tejaḥ samāsādyeva sāgarāḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 21.85–86, above.

21.87

Sanskrit

ततः स राजपुत्रो ऽश्वी निहत्यासुरसत्तमान् । स्त्रीरत्नेन समं तेन समागच्छत् पितुः पुरम् ॥

tataḥ sa rājaputro 'śvī nihatyāsurasattamān | strīratnena samaṃ tena samāgacchat pituḥ puram ||

English

Then that king's son, mounted on his horse194, having killed the foremost of the asuras, came with that jewel of a woman195 to his father's city.196

21.88

Sanskrit

प्रणिपत्य च तत् सर्वं स तु पित्रे न्यवेदयत् । पातालगमनञ्चैव कुण्डलायाश्च दर्शनम् ॥

praṇipatya ca tat sarvaṃ sa tu pitre nyavedayat | pātālagamanañcaiva kuṇḍalāyāśca darśanam ||

English

21.88–89Having bowed down to his father, he reported to him all of it: his going to the nether world and his seeing of Kuṇḍalā, likewise his winning of Madālasā and the battle with the dānavas, the slaying of them by the missile, and also his coming back.

21.89

Sanskrit

तद्वन्मदालसाप्राप्तिं दानवैश्चापि सङ्गरम् । वधञ्च तेषामस्त्रेण पुनरागमनं तथा ॥

tadvanmadālasāprāptiṃ dānavaiścāpi saṅgaram | vadhañca teṣāmastreṇa punarāgamanaṃ tathā ||

English

Its English is given with 21.88–89, above.

21.90

Sanskrit

इति श्रुत्वा पिता तस्य चरितं चारुचेतसः । प्रीतिमानभवच्चेदं परिष्वज्याह चात्मजम् ॥

iti śrutvā pitā tasya caritaṃ cārucetasaḥ | prītimānabhavaccedaṃ pariṣvajyāha cātmajam ||

English

Having heard in this way the deeds of his son, whose mind was noble, the father became full of joy; and he embraced his son and said this to him.197

21.91

Sanskrit

सत्पात्रेण त्वया पुत्र तारितो ऽहं महात्मना । भयेभ्यो मुनयस्त्राता येन सद्धर्मचारिणः ॥

satpātreṇa tvayā putra tārito 'haṃ mahātmanā | bhayebhyo munayastrātā yena saddharmacāriṇaḥ ||

English

"My son, I have been rescued by you, a worthy vessel198 and a great-souled one, by whom the sages who follow the true dharma have been saved from fears."199

21.92

Sanskrit

मत्पूर्वैः ख्यातिमानीतं मया विस्तारितं पुनः । पराक्रमवता वीर त्वया तद्वहुलीकृतम् ॥

matpūrvaiḥ khyātimānītaṃ mayā vistāritaṃ punaḥ | parākramavatā vīra tvayā tadvahulīkṛtam ||

English

By my forefathers it [our family]200 was brought to renown; by me it was extended further; and by you, a man of valor, O hero, that [renown] has been made abundant.201

21.93

Sanskrit

यदुपात्तं यशः पित्रा धनं वीर्यमथापि वा । तन्न हापयते यस्तु स नरो मध्यमः स्मृतः ॥

yadupāttaṃ yaśaḥ pitrā dhanaṃ vīryamathāpi vā | tanna hāpayate yastu sa naro madhyamaḥ smṛtaḥ ||

English

Whatever fame, wealth, or even valor has been acquired by one's father, the man who does not let that diminish is remembered as a middling one.202

21.94

Sanskrit

तद्वीर्यादधिकं यस्तु पुनरन्यत् स्वशक्तितः । निष्पादयति तं प्राज्ञाः प्रवदन्ति नरोत्तमम् ॥

tadvīryādadhikaṃ yastu punaranyat svaśaktitaḥ | niṣpādayati taṃ prājñāḥ pravadanti narottamam ||

English

But the man who, by his own power, brings about something further that exceeds that [father's] valor, the wise declare to be the best of men203.204

21.95

Sanskrit

यः पिता समुपात्तानि धनवीर्ययशांसि वै । न्यूनतां नयति प्राज्ञास्तमाहुः पुरुषाधमम् ॥

yaḥ pitā samupāttāni dhanavīryayaśāṃsi vai | nyūnatāṃ nayati prājñāstamāhuḥ puruṣādhamam ||

English

The man who brings to diminution the wealth, valor and fame acquired by [his] father205: the wise call him the lowest of men.206

21.96

Sanskrit

तन्मया ब्राह्मणत्राणं कृतमासीद्यथा त्वया । पातालगमनं यच्च यच्चासुरविनाशनम् ॥

tanmayā brāhmaṇatrāṇaṃ kṛtamāsīdyathā tvayā | pātālagamanaṃ yacca yaccāsuravināśanam ||

English

That protection of the brahmins was accomplished by me, as it was by you, and likewise the going to the nether worlds, and the destruction of the asuras207.208

21.97

Sanskrit

एतदप्यधिकं वत्स तेन त्वं पुरुषोत्तमः । तद्धन्यो ऽस्म्य बाल त्वमहमेव गुणाधिकम् ॥

etadapyadhikaṃ vatsa tena tvaṃ puruṣottamaḥ | taddhanyo 'smya bāla tvamahameva guṇādhikam ||

English

This too is greater [than what I did], my son; therefore you are the foremost of men209. So I am blessed, child; I myself [regard] you as superior in qualities.210

21.98

Sanskrit

त्वां पुत्रमीदृशं प्राप्य श्लाघ्यः पुण्यवतामपि । न स पुत्रकृतां प्रीतिं मन्ये प्राप्नोति मानवः ॥

tvāṃ putramīdṛśaṃ prāpya ślāghyaḥ puṇyavatāmapi | na sa putrakṛtāṃ prītiṃ manye prāpnoti mānavaḥ ||

English

Having gained you as such a son, [I am] to be praised even among the virtuous. I think that man does not obtain the joy that a son brings.211

21.99

Sanskrit

पुत्रेण नातिशयितो यः प्रज्ञादानविक्रमैः । धिग्जन्म तस्य यः पित्रा लोके विज्ञायते नरः ॥

putreṇa nātiśayito yaḥ prajñādānavikramaiḥ | dhigjanma tasya yaḥ pitrā loke vijñāyate naraḥ ||

English

Cursed is the birth of that man who has not been surpassed by his son in wisdom, generosity212 and prowess, and who is known in the world by his father [alone]213.214

21.100

Sanskrit

यः पुत्रात् ख्यातिमभ्येति तस्य जन्म सुजन्मनः । आत्मना ज्ञायते धन्यो मध्यः पितृपितामहैः ॥

yaḥ putrāt khyātimabhyeti tasya janma sujanmanaḥ | ātmanā jñāyate dhanyo madhyaḥ pitṛpitāmahaiḥ ||

English

The man who attains fame through his son: the birth of that well-born man [is a good one]. The blessed man is known by himself; the middling man215 [is known] by his father and grandfathers.216

21.101

Sanskrit

मातृपक्षेण मात्रा च ख्यातिमेति नराधमः । तत् पुत्र धनवीर्यैस्त्वं विवर्धस्व सुखेन च ॥

mātṛpakṣeṇa mātrā ca khyātimeti narādhamaḥ | tat putra dhanavīryaistvaṃ vivardhasva sukhena ca ||

English

The basest of men217 attains fame through his maternal kin218 and through his mother. Therefore, my son, may you grow in wealth and vigor, and in happiness as well.219

21.102

Sanskrit

घन्धर्वतनया चेयं मा त्वया वै वियुज्यताम् । इति पित्रा बहुविधं प्रियमुक्तः पुनः पुनः ॥

ghandharvatanayā ceyaṃ mā tvayā vai viyujyatām | iti pitrā bahuvidhaṃ priyamuktaḥ punaḥ punaḥ ||

English

21.102–103“Let this daughter of a gandharva220 never be separated from you.” Addressed thus by his father again and again, in many ways and with kind words, and embraced by him, he was sent off with his wife to his own residence. There, in his father's city, he took his pleasure with her, his wife.221

21.103

Sanskrit

परिष्वज्य स्वमावासं सभार्यः स विसर्जितः । स तया भार्याया सार्धं रेमे तत्र पितुः पुरे ॥

pariṣvajya svamāvāsaṃ sabhāryaḥ sa visarjitaḥ | sa tayā bhāryāyā sārdhaṃ reme tatra pituḥ pure ||

English

Its English is given with 21.102–103, above.

21.104

Sanskrit

अन्येषु च तथोद्यानवनपर्वतसानुषु । श्वश्रूश्वसुरयोः पादौ प्रणिपत्य च सा शुभा । प्रातः प्रातस्ततस्तेन सह रेमे सुमध्यमा ॥

anyeṣu ca tathodyānavanaparvatasānuṣu | śvaśrūśvasurayoḥ pādau praṇipatya ca sā śubhā | prātaḥ prātastatastena saha reme sumadhyamā ||

English

And in other gardens, likewise, in forests and on mountain slopes as well, that lovely woman of slender waist222, having bowed at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, took her pleasure with him each morning thereafter.223

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे कुवलयाश्वीये मदालसापरिणयनं नामैकविंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe kuvalayāśvīye madālasāpariṇayanaṃ nāmaikaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, named "The Marriage of Madālasā," in the Kuvalayāśva section224 of the venerable225 Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.226

  1. The reading: The text is a chapter heading, not a verse: 'ekaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ' is literally 'the twenty-first chapter'. I rendered it as a heading. The verse numbering (88.1) belongs to the e-text and does not match the chapter numbering. ↩
  2. that king's son: Ṛtadhvaja, son of Śatrujit, who was sent with Gālava at the end of the previous chapter. ↩
  3. the tale of you two: yuvayoḥ is a dual genitive addressed to the two sons (putrau). It most naturally means the tale that concerns them, their own part in Ṛtadhvaja's story. It could also be read as the tale they have to tell. ↩
  4. The reading: yuvayoḥ kathā: the dual genitive may mean "the tale concerning you two" or "the tale told by you two". I kept the neutral "the tale of you two" and explained it in the note, leaning to the first sense. The speaker is the father, who addresses his two sons. They answer in the next section (putrāv ūcatuḥ). The verse has no speaker's line, so I added none. kathyatām is a passive imperative, "let it be told". I kept the passive and the vocative "O sons" rather than "tell me", because the Sanskrit has no "me". The request to the sons is plain from the vocative. Reviewer's point on vicitrā: I did not make it explicitly causal ("for"), since the Sanskrit has no connective and the two clauses are simply juxtaposed. A semicolon allows the causal sense without stating it. Reviewer's point on yat…tat and the agent of kṛtam: accepted. The English now says what was done by that king's son after he had gone with Gālava, so the one person is both agent and traveller. ↩
  5. that delight of the protector of the earth: Bhūpālanandana, 'son of the king'; here Ṛtadhvaja, son of Śatrujit. ↩
  6. brahmavādins: Brahmavādin: one who speaks or expounds the Veda or brahman; a Vedic expounder, a sage devoted to sacred teaching. ↩
  7. The reading: Bhūpālanandana is literally 'delight of the earth-protector', i.e. the king's son; I take it as Ṛtadhvaja, the subject, in agreement with sa. Sarvavighropaśamanam (printed 'vighro-') is read as sarvavighnopaśamanam, 'pacifying/ending of all obstacles'; the 'ghr' is a misprint for 'ghn'. ↩
  8. struck down by the arrogance of his pride: The compound madāvalepopahataḥ can be read as 'overcome by the arrogance of intoxication/pride'; mada here is pride, not drink. ↩
  9. Kuvalayāśva: The name of the king's son, Ṛtadhvaja, who is called thus after the celestial horse Kuvalaya, on which he rode. ↩
  10. the evening worship: sandhyā: the twilight rite of prayer and meditation that a brahmin performs at dusk (and at dawn and noon). upāsana is its devout performance. ↩
  11. bow in hand: śarāsanī, 'having a bow', is an adjective of the king's son. It is not a separate agent. ↩
  12. The reading: The subject of āgatam in 21.4 is not named in these verses. It is the dānava of 21.3 (dānavādhama), and I have supplied it in brackets. The agent of utkruṣṭe (locative absolute) is the sage's disciples (muniśiṣyaiḥ). In 21.4, Gālava is the object of pradharṣayitum, and the accusative āgatam agrees with the unnamed boar-formed dānava. ↩
  13. shaped like a half-moon and gleaming: Sanskrit candrārdhākāravarcasā, a compound of 'half-moon', 'shape' and 'radiance'. It is taken to describe a crescent-headed arrow that gleams. ↩
  14. The reading: The object of ājaghāna is not stated; 'the boar' is supplied from varāham in 21.5. The subject 'the king's son' (nṛpaputra of 21.5) is carried over and bracketed, and he is also the agent of the absolutive ākṛṣya. The compound candrārdhākāravarcasā can be read as 'having the shape and radiance of a half-moon' or as 'with a gleam in the shape of a half-moon'. I chose the first, a crescent-shaped, shining arrow. The text does not use the term ardhacandra, so I removed it from the note. In cārucitropaśobhitam, cāru and citra may be two adjectives ('lovely', 'varied') or one compound ('lovely decoration/painting'). I kept 'lovely, varied ornament' and dropped 'beautifully' from the draft because it repeated the sense of 'adorned'. I read balavat as an adjective agreeing with cāpam ('strong bow'), not as an adverb ('with force'). I added 'And' for ca, as the reviewer asked. ↩
  15. nārāca: An iron arrow; the word is used for a kind of arrow made wholly of iron. ↩
  16. the animal: mṛga means a wild animal or game in general; here it is the boar of verse 21.5, which is really the dānava in boar form. ↩
  17. The reading: The word mṛga is generic ('beast, game'). I took it as the boar (varāha) of 21.5. The 'so' ('he') in the second half refers to the same animal. The compound giripādapasambādhām can mean 'crowded with mountains and trees' (giri + pādapa) or 'crowded with the trees at the foot of mountains' (giripāda + pa). I chose the first, the simpler reading. ↩
  18. The reading: tam ("it") refers to the boar-formed dānava, called mṛga ("animal") in 21.7. The Sanskrit does not name him, so I render the pronoun as "it". manojavaḥ is a bahuvrīhi, "having the speed of mind". I give it as "swift as thought". ↩
  19. yojanas: A yojana is a measure of distance, commonly reckoned at several miles (often about nine, or four to five in other reckonings). ↩
