  20. [the boar]: The subject of nipapāta is not named in this verse. Since laghukramaḥ ('of light step') is nominative singular masculine, it could refer to the boar or the horse. Verse 21.10 says that the king's son also fell 'after him' (tasyānantaram), which indicates that the boar fell first. ↩
  21. The reading: The subject of nipapāta and laghukramaḥ is not named. The boar is the likely subject, because 21.10 says 'after him' the king's son also fell, and 21.11 says the boar was no longer seen. The horse (21.8) is a grammatically possible alternative. I chose the boar, supplied in brackets, because it fits the sequence of verses 21.10–11. ↩
  22. the king's son: Sanskrit nṛpateḥ sutaḥ, 'son of the king'; he is Ṛtadhvaja (Kuvalayāśva), the same person as the 'king's son' of the previous verses, son of Śatrujit. ↩
  23. The reading: aśvī is read as 'possessing a horse', i.e. mounted on his horse (aśvin), with so 'pi nṛpateḥ sutaḥ as subject. 'So 'pi' is 'he too', referring back to the boar of v. 9 that fell into the gap. The singular 'great pit' (mahāgarte) is taken as the same gap (vivṛte garte) of verse 9, now described as dark. ↩
  24. The reading: The last word, 'nam', is doubtful. It is probably a misprint or a metrical contraction. (a) 'naram' or 'nṛ', 'a man', which I chose. It suits the next verses, where he enters the city and sees no one, and 'api' ('either') then fits as well. (b) A pronoun, 'him', that is, the boar, for 'enam'. Reading (b) would repeat the first half of the verse. 'Prakāśam' could be an adverb or a noun ('light, brightness'), or an adjective agreeing with 'pātālam'. I took it as an adjective, 'lit up', since the nether world is seen after the fall into darkness. ↩
  25. Purandara: 'Destroyer of cities', a name of Indra; 'the city of Purandara' is Amarāvatī, Indra's capital in heaven. ↩
  26. The reading: The compound sauvarṇaprāsādaśatasaṃkulam could be taken as 'crowded with a hundred golden palaces' or 'with hundreds'; I chose 'hundreds', since śata in such compounds usually means a great number. The subject 'he' (sa) is the king's son, as in the preceding verses. ↩
  27. The reading: In the second half, 'bhramatā ... dṛṣṭā' is a construction with the agent in the instrumental: 'by him wandering'. The masculine singular instrumental participle bhramatā refers to the king's son, the subject of 'sa'. The word 'tatra' occurs twice, in the first half as 'in the city (pure)' and in the second as 'there'; I rendered both as 'there'. In the first half, 'tat' is read as the neuter accusative 'that [city]', object of 'praviśya', referring to the 'puram' of 21.12; I wrote 'it'. ↩
  28. why she had set out, or whose she was: The question is elliptical. kena is taken as 'for what reason'. kasya is a genitive of possession: whose woman she was, that is, to whom she belonged. ↩
  29. the lady: bhāminī is a term for a beautiful, spirited or passionate woman. It is used here as a descriptive epithet, not as a name. ↩
  30. The reading: kena prasthitā: 'for what reason has she set out' (chosen, because it pairs naturally with the question 'whose is she') or 'by whom [sent]'. I dropped my earlier 'with whom', which the Sanskrit does not support, and replaced the unidiomatic 'by what [cause]' with 'why'. kasya vā is taken as a genitive of possession, 'or whose she was'. bhāminī: 'lady' kept. The reviewer allows it, and the context (haste and silence) does not clearly point to 'haughty' or 'passionate', so I have not forced a stronger sense. The reviewer's point on ca is accepted: it is rendered 'but', since the sentence sets her silence against her action. ↩
  31. the king's son: Ṛtadhvaja (Kuvalayāśva); the Sanskrit has nṛpateḥ sutaḥ, 'son of the king'. ↩
  32. The reading: ekatas ('to one side', 'in one place') could also be read as 'by himself' or 'together'. I took it as the place where he tied the horse. The e-text reads niḥ śaṅko as two words; I read it as the single word niḥśaṅka, 'without fear'. The reading nanv aṅgīm in 21.17 is not part of this verse. ↩
  33. Rati: Rati is the goddess of desire and the wife of Kāma, the god of love; she is the type of loveliness and passion. ↩
  34. bimba: The bimba is a bright red gourd-like fruit, the usual comparison for red, full lips. ↩
  35. śyāmā: śyāmā means dark-complexioned, or a young woman in the bloom of youth. The poets also use it for a woman who is warm in winter and cool in summer. The sense here is uncertain. ↩
  36. The reading: (1) nanvaṅgīm (21.17) is probably corrupt or misprinted for tanvaṅgīm 'slender-limbed' (cf. tanvaṅgī in 21.14); I translated 'slender' on that assumption. As it stands, nanu + aṅgī gives no clear sense. (2) śyāmā may mean 'dark-complexioned' or 'a young woman in her prime'; I kept the word in IAST. (3) karabha can mean an elephant's trunk, a young camel or the forearm; I chose 'elephant's trunk' as the usual image for rounded, tapering thighs. (4) vispaṣṭendumukhī: I read vispaṣṭa as 'clear', giving 'her face a clear moon', in the sense of a spotless full moon. ↩
  37. Anaṅga: 'The Bodiless One', a name of Kāma, the god of desire, who was burned to ashes by Śiva and so lost his body. The simile likens her to a creeper made of his limbs. ↩
  38. The reading: The compound anaṅgāṅgalatām could also be read as 'the creeper-like body of Anaṅga'. I take it as 'a creeper formed of the limbs of Anaṅga', which suits the comparison with her lovely limbs. Pārthivasuta is rendered 'son of the king', the same prince as 'the king's son' (nṛpateḥ sutaḥ) in 21.15. ↩
  39. Madana: 'The Intoxicator', a name of Kāma, the god of love, who is called Anaṅga in verse 21.19. ↩
  40. The reading: Śubhā may be read as an adjective ('the auspicious, radiant one') or as a proper name. I took it as an adjective in apposition to bālā, since the verse gives no other sign of a name. Pīnoruskandhabāhum is a compound: I read it as 'whose thighs, shoulders and arms were full', with pīna qualifying all three members. Dṛṣṭvaiva: eva gives the sense 'as soon as'. Mūrdhaja ('hair') is rendered in the singular collective. ↩
  41. greatly fortunate: Translates mahābhāgā, the feminine of mahābhāga; here it describes the maiden, not any other person. ↩
  42. came under the sway of shyness, wonder and dejection: Literally 'went into the power of' the three feelings (genitive plural with vaśaṃ gatā); the three are named together as the cause of her state. ↩
  43. The reading: The sense of cittakṣobham is 'agitation of mind'; it may also be rendered 'disturbance of heart'. I chose the former as the closer literal rendering. The genitive lajjāvismayadainyānām with vaśaṃ gatā is taken as dependent on vaśa ('into the power of'), not partitive. ↩
  44. the woman with intoxicating eyes: madirakṣaṇā, 'she whose eyes are intoxicating' (or 'wine-like'); an epithet of the maiden, here standing as an apposition to the subject. ↩
  45. The reading: vahudhā is printed for bahudhā ('in many ways'); I read it as bahudhā. madirakṣaṇā may mean 'with intoxicating eyes' or 'with eyes like wine / intoxicated eyes'; I chose 'intoxicating eyes' as the usual sense of the compound. ↩
  46. Kāma's arrows: Kāma, the god of love, is imagined as shooting flower-tipped arrows that cause desire in those they strike. ↩
  47. The reading: The compound kāmaśarāghātam may be read as 'the blow of the arrows of Kāma' (chosen, taking kāma as the god) or as 'the blow of the arrows of desire'. Since the glossary identifies Madana and Anaṅga with the god of love, the god is the more natural reading. The 'son of the king' is the same prince mentioned in 21.19, not a new person. ↩
  48. that woman, who had been seen earlier by that great-souled man: She is the maiden's companion, whom the prince had seen earlier, before the maiden herself came into view. The verses that follow call her the maiden's sakhī (friend). ↩
  49. palm-leaf fan: tālavṛnta: a fan made from a palm leaf. ↩
  50. The reading: The verse does not name the object of paryavījayat. I read it as the swooning maiden of verse 23, and the English supplies 'her' without brackets because the verb's sense implies it. The subject sā strī is the maiden's friend, as verse 26 (tasyāḥ sakhyuḥ) shows, and not the maiden herself. The pronoun tena mahātmanā refers to the prince. ↩
  51. to her friend: The Sanskrit has the genitive tasyāḥ sakhyuḥ, 'of her friend', used in the sense of the dative. The friend is the woman with the palm-leaf fan in 21.25, and in 21.27 she tells the prince the whole story. ↩
  52. The reading: tasyāḥ sakhyuḥ: the genitive can be read as the object 'to her friend' (genitive for dative, or an error for sakhyai), or as dependent on a missing noun. I chose 'to her friend' because 21.27 shows the friend passing the account on to the prince. Also, samāśvāsya has no expressed subject. I took its agent to be tena, 'he', the subject of the asking, not the young woman. ↩
  53. The reading: The pronouns are ambiguous. I take 'sā' and 'bhāminī' to be the friend, who fanned the maiden in 21.25 and received her confession in 21.26. I take 'tayā' to be the maiden, whose own account the friend repeats. I take 'tad-' in 'taddarśana' to be the prince, so the cause is 'seeing him'. In 'tadvṛttānta', 'tad-' could refer to the maiden (her story) or to the whole episode. I chose the maiden, but kept the English neutral ('that account'). 'yathā tayā samākhyātam' may also be read as the friend telling it exactly as the maiden had told it, which is what I have rendered. ↩
  54. The reading: The reference '89.11' does not match the chapter 21 context. The verse is only the speaker's line 'stryuvāca', and I took it to introduce the speech at 21.28. The speaker is the woman (strī) who has just been called bhāminī in 21.27; she is the maiden's friend, not the maiden herself. The glossary notes that bhāminī is 'the woman of the city', which also suggests a different woman from the maiden. ↩
  55. Gandharvas: Gandharvas are celestial beings, famed as musicians, who dwell in the heavenly world. ↩
  56. Viśvāvasu: Viśvāvasu is a well-known chief of the Gandharvas. ↩
  57. Madālasā: The name means 'languid with intoxication or passion'. It echoes the earlier epithet madirakṣaṇā, 'the woman with intoxicating eyes'. ↩
  58. The reading: The reading nāmnarā in the e-text is corrupt or misprinted. It is probably nāmnā tu, nāmnā ca or nāmnā rā, and the sense 'by name' is certain. I translated 'known by the name Madālasā'. subhrūḥ ('fair-browed') is taken as an epithet of the daughter and is rendered rather than kept in IAST. ↩
  59. Pātālaketu: "Whose banner is Pātāla"; the asura who carried Madālasā off, as the next verses tell. ↩
  60. inner nether worlds: The compound pātālāntarasaṃśrayaḥ may also be read "taking refuge in the interior of Pātāla"; both readings give the same sense. ↩
  61. The reading: The text reads 'mayāṃ hīnā', which does not parse as it stands: 'mayā' is a cognate of māyā and the accusative 'mayām' would not go with 'hīnā'. I take it as a misprint for 'mayā hīnā', 'bereft of me', with the instrumental that 'hīna' takes. The speaker is the young woman's friend, who was with her in the garden. The alternative would be to read 'mayāṃ' as a variant of 'māyām' and make it the object of 'apahṛtya', but that leaves 'hīnā' without a complement and repeats 'māyām' from the first half of the verse, so I rejected it. ↩
  62. thirteenth lunar day: trayodaśī, the thirteenth tithi of a lunar fortnight, fixed here as the day of the wedding. ↩
  63. will marry her: udvakṣyati is from ud-√vah, 'to lead up', the usual verb for taking a bride in marriage. The object is understood from the next half-verse, cārvaṅgīm. ↩
  64. śūdra: A member of the fourth social order, traditionally barred from hearing or studying the Veda. ↩
  65. The reading: The particle kila ('it is said', 'indeed') may mark hearsay or be merely assertive. I chose 'it is said', since the speaker is reporting the demon's plan. The object of udvakṣyati is not stated; 'her' is supplied from cārvaṅgīm in the second half-verse. I did not bracket it, because the second half names her. Vedaśrutīm can mean 'the Veda as heard' or 'the hearing of the Veda'. I chose 'the hearing of the Veda' as the likelier sense, since it fits the śūdra's exclusion from hearing. ↩
  66. Surabhi: Taken as a proper name, probably the divine cow Surabhi, who speaks to the girl in her despair. The word can also mean 'fragrant'; see doubts. ↩
  67. The reading: 1) surabhiḥ: a proper name (the divine cow Surabhi) or the adjective 'fragrant'. As the subject of prāha it is best read as a name, and I chose this. 2) tvaṃ prāpsyate: the nominative tvam with the middle prāpsyate does not parse as it stands. I read tvāṃ for tvaṃ (object 'you') and prāpsyate as an irregular middle for prāpsyati, giving 'will not obtain you' with ayam dānavādhamaḥ as subject. 3) dine: 'on the day' or 'when the day had passed'. I took atīte dine as a locative absolute. The sense of 'the day' is not fixed by this verse alone; the context suggests the day before the wedding. ↩
  68. will cut him down: 'chetsyate' is a middle-voice future of the root chid, used here where classical Sanskrit would normally have 'chetsyati'. ↩
  69. will, before long, be your husband: The printed 'sate' is read as 'sa te' ('he [will be] to you'), the usual sense of the construction 'te bhartā bhaviṣyati'. ↩
  70. The reading: 'sate' is not a possible form in this context. I read it as 'sa te' ('he, to you'), which gives the sense 'he will be your husband', with 'ya' in the first half as the correlative of 'sa'. 'Enam' is taken to refer to the dānava Pātālaketu, who is the subject of the preceding verses. ↩
  71. Vindhyavat: Vindhyavat (nominative Vindhyavān) is the father of Kuṇḍalā. The text does not say who he is. The name suggests a link with the Vindhya range. ↩
  72. the hero Puṣkaramālin: The compound vīra-puṣkaramālin is read as the name Puṣkaramālin with the epithet vīra, 'hero'. Puṣkaramālin means 'wearing a garland of lotuses'. The next verse says he was killed by Śumbha. ↩
  73. The reading: The text reads nāmnarā, which does not parse. The same form appears in 21.28, so it is probably an e-text corruption, most likely of nāmnā 'by name' with a particle. I read it as nāmnā, 'by name'. Kuṇḍaleti is kuṇḍalā + iti, giving the name Kuṇḍalā. Manasvinī can mean 'high-spirited', 'resolute' or 'wise'. I chose 'of high spirit'. ↩
  74. Śumbha: Name of the slayer of Puṣkaramālin. The identification is unclear; perhaps the asura Śumbha. ↩
  75. tīrtha: A sacred ford or holy place of pilgrimage, usually on a river or the sea, where bathing gives merit. ↩
  76. divine course: divyayā gatyā: a divine or celestial manner of going, perhaps a supernatural way of travelling. ↩
  77. The reading: Anuvratā: the root anu-√vrat gives 'following, going after', and with tīrthāt tīrtham it is taken as 'going on from one tīrtha to the next'. The alternative, 'devoted to', is rejected because it hides the sequence. Paralokārtham udyatā: artha can mean 'purpose', 'goal' or 'sake', so the phrase is 'intent on the goal of the other world'. The earlier reading 'for her husband's welfare there' is dropped because the verse does not say it. Śumbhena is the instrumental agent of hate, 'slain by Śumbha'. Whether he is the well-known asura is not stated. Hate bhartari is a locative absolute, and carāmi is present, so the English uses a single present tense. ↩
  78. someone: kenāpi, "by someone or other": the archer is not named here. Verse 21.37 repeats that the dānava was struck by "someone". ↩
  79. for the protection of the sages: The phrase (munīnāṃ trāṇakāraṇāt) may state the archer's purpose in shooting, as taken here, or the reason for the whole episode. The Sanskrit does not settle this. ↩
  80. The reading: The phrase munīnāṃ trāṇakāraṇāt could be read as the archer's motive, which is how I took it with viddhaḥ, or as a general reason. The agent of vidhyate is kenāpi, "someone", and is not identified. ↩
  81. The reading: tam: the object of anviṣya is taken as the boar-shaped Pātālaketu of v. 36, the one just mentioned. The other possibility is the unknown archer, but the sentence goes on to say that the dānava was struck by someone, so tam is most naturally the dānava. tattvataḥ is taken as an adverb ('truly', 'in reality') qualifying anviṣya, not as its object, so the earlier draft's 'searched out the truth about him' is dropped. ca is the plain conjunction 'and'. The earlier note, which called it an enclitic taking up the object and said she 'verified the report', is withdrawn, so no note remains. satyam eva is rendered 'it is indeed true', since the emphasis affirms the fact. I use a full stop, not a colon, between the two clauses, because the Sanskrit does not make the second explain the first. 'Here' is dropped from samupāgatā. ↩
  82. O giver of honour: Vocative of mānada, 'one who gives honour'; here addressed to the man whom Madālasā has just seen. ↩
  83. The reading: iyañca mūrcchām agamat kāraṇaṃ yat śṛṇuṣva tat: the sentence is loosely built. I take 'kāraṇaṃ yat ... tat' as 'the reason (for) which ... that, listen to', and 'iyam ... mūrcchām agamat' as 'she fainted'. The 'ca' is rendered as 'And'. The next verse's 'devaputropame' suggests that tvayi and mānada refer to the same hero, who is the one addressed. ↩
  84. ordained: vihitā means arranged or decreed, here by destiny. It is the same decree stated in 21.33, which names the slayer of the dānava as her future husband. ↩
  85. The reading: The locatives devaputropame and cāruvākyādiguṇaśālini have no verb of their own. I take them as continuing tvayi prītimatī of 21.38, and supply 'She is fond' in brackets. cāruvākyādiguṇa is read as 'qualities beginning with charming speech'. anyasya is 'of another', that is, of someone other than the addressee, who is the one who pierced the dānava. ↩
  86. slender-limbed woman: Sanskrit tanvaṅgī, 'one whose limbs are slender', a common term for a young woman, here the maiden Madālasā; compare tanvī in the glossary. ↩
  87. The reading: The e-text reads duḥ khameva with a stray space; I take it as duḥkham eva, 'only sorrow'. The text has upabhokṣyate, a middle form of upa-√bhuj, 'will experience'; I render it in the future with the sense of experiencing or undergoing. ↩
  88. The word spoken by Surabhi: Surabhyā is an instrumental, 'by Surabhi'. It is taken as the agent of the word (vacaḥ). The speaker seems to name herself in the third person. ↩
  89. The reading: Surabhyā vacaḥ could also be read as 'a word [given] by Surabhi' or as an instrumental of agency with an understood participle. I took it as 'the word spoken by Surabhi', which fits the glossary, where Surabhi is the speaker. Rāgi is read as 'attached, full of love' (literally 'coloured, passionate'), not as a technical term. ↩
  90. O lord: The printed text reads prabhī. This is probably a corruption or misprint of the vocative prabho. ↩
  91. The reading: prabhī is not a regular vocative. Possible readings: (1) a misprint for prabho, 'O lord', addressed to the man the speaker is talking to, which I chose because it fits the address and the metre; (2) a feminine noun 'mistress', which would have to qualify asyāḥ and does not fit the syntax. Also, 'grieving for her' supplies the object of duḥkhitā from asyāḥ, which the sense requires. I take tu as a mild contrast with the preceding verses and render it 'But'. ↩
  92. tapas: Austerity or ascetic discipline; here the speaker offers to undertake it for her friend's sake. ↩
  93. The reading: The speaker (Madālasā's friend, Kuvalayāśva being addressed) is not named in the verse. 'I' is the friend speaking. 'Sincere' renders nirvyalīka (without deceit or pain); 'without guile' is also possible. The optative kuryām is rendered 'would practise', as a conditional resolve. ↩
  94. serpent: Translates pannaga, a snake-being of the nāga kind, living beneath the earth. ↩
  95. Kinnara: A class of semi-divine beings, associated with music and usually counted among the attendants of Kubera. ↩
  96. The reading: The particle nu in 'devo daityo nu' marks the question, 'is it a god, a Daitya...?'; I render it by the interrogative form of the sentence. The speaker is presumably the woman addressing Kuvalayāśva, but the verse itself does not say so. ↩
  97. no human access exists here: mānuṣagati may be read as 'human course of movement, access' (the place is beyond men's reach) or 'human state or condition'. The translation takes the first sense, which suits the context of his arrival in a place men cannot reach. ↩
  98. just as I have told you [the truth] without falsehood: The clause kathitaṃ yathaivāvitathaṃ mayā is compressed. It is taken as: 'as I have spoken truly (about myself and my fears)'. The words 'the truth' are supplied to complete the sense. ↩
  99. The reading: mānuṣagati: 'human access/movement' vs 'human condition'; I chose access/movement because the place is unreachable by men. The last pāda is elliptical; kathitaṃ yathaiva avitathaṃ mayā is read as 'as I have spoken without falsehood', with 'the truth' supplied, though it could also mean 'as it was truly told by me' (i.e. in the preceding speech). The compression leaves the exact reference slightly uncertain. ↩
  100. The reading: The reference '90.10' for the speaker line is evidently an error in the e-text numbering (it should belong to the sequence of chapter 21); I treated it as the speaker line introducing 21.46. In 'kastvaṃ kiṃ vā samāgataḥ' the verb is not repeated and 'tvam' is used in the quoted question; I took it as a loose quotation of Madālasā's question in 21.44, 'Who are you, and why have you come?', and rendered it accordingly. ↩
  101. Śatrujit: The speaker, Kuvalayāśva (Ṛtadhvaja), names his father; the Sanskrit says "the son of King Śatrujit" without stating the pronoun. ↩
  102. O fair lady: Vocative śubhe, addressed to Madālasā, the woman he is speaking to; it may also be read as a general address, 'O auspicious one'. ↩
  103. The reading: munirakṣaṇam is rendered 'protecting the sages' (muni as object of rakṣaṇa); 'protection of the sage' (Gālava alone) is possible, but the plural fits the next verse, which mentions the sages (munīnām). Putraḥ pitrā sampreṣitaḥ is read as one sentence: 'I am the son... sent by my father'; the verse has no first-person verb, so 'I am' is supplied from the context of the answer to 'who are you'. ↩
  104. some being: The printed text reads koṣa'pi, which is not a word. It is emended to ko 'pi (kaḥ + api), 'someone' or 'some being'. The sense and the metre both require this. ↩
  105. The reading: 1. koṣa'pi is read as ko 'pi (kaḥ + api), 'some being'. The printed form is a misprint, and I have marked the emendation in a note. 2. The 'ca' in rakṣāṃ ca is not filler, as my earlier draft guessed. It can be read as 'and', joining this sentence to the previous verse (the hermitage and the protection of the sages), or as 'also' ('protection too'). It could also be a metrical expletive, though this is less certain. I render it as an opening 'And', which keeps the connective sense without adding anything. 3. dharmacāriṇām means 'those who conduct themselves according to dharma'. I take 'who follow dharma' as the closest rendering, and 'righteous sages' would be an acceptable alternative. 4. I did not add 'to obstruct them', as one finding suggested. vighnārtham says only 'for the purpose of obstruction' and names no object. Naming one would add to the Sanskrit. 5. The genitive absolute kurvato mama is rendered 'while I was providing', so 'mama' is carried by the 'I' of the clause. ↩
  106. an arrow that had the shape and lustre of a half-moon: The compound candrārdhākāravarccasā most likely describes a crescent-headed arrow (ardhacandra). Its literal sense is 'having the shape and radiance of a half-moon'. ↩
  107. he fled away: The subject, sa, is the being that had taken the form of a boar (śaukaraṁ rūpam) in the previous verse. ↩
  108. The reading: candrārdhākāravarccasā: it can be read as 'with the shape and lustre of a half-moon', as I have it, or as 'with a lustre of crescent shape'. The first reading is chosen as the more natural. The spelling varccasā is a variant of varcasā. hayī (literally 'possessing a horse') is rendered 'on horseback'. ↩
  109. the boar: The e-text reads sakrīḍo. I take it as sa kroḍo (or sa krīḍo, with krīḍa as a variant of kroḍa), 'that boar', the creature in boar form of 21.48–49. The reading is a conjecture. ↩
  110. The reading: The e-text's sakrīḍo is obscure. (a) sakrīḍa, 'sportive' or 'with play', agreeing with aśva: this is the draft's reading, and I withdraw it, because a horse that is 'sporting' as it falls into a pit makes no sense in the narrative. (b) sa kroḍo, or sa krīḍo with krīḍa for kroḍa, 'that boar': chosen. It gives the subject of papāta that the previous verses lead us to expect, the creature in boar form that Kuvalayāśva had pierced and was chasing, and ca then adds the horse. Both readings fit the metre. The singular verb papāta serves both subjects, so I bracket the repeated 'fell' for the horse. samārūḍhaḥ is a past participle used actively, 'having mounted'. The sentence continues into 21.51 (prakāśam āsāditavān, 'reached light'), so the translation stops mid-sentence. ↩
  111. The reading: The verse is the continuation of a sentence begun in 21.50, where the speaker, riding his horse, wanders alone in the darkness (tamasi). 'prakāśam āsāditavān' is read as 'I reached a place of light', with the subject understood from 21.50. In the second half, 'pṛṣṭayā ca' (instrumental feminine) agrees with 'bhavatyā', so the sense is 'by you, although asked'. The clause is made to run in the English as 'when you were asked by me', taking the agent as the speaker, as the construction is a loose one: the instrumental 'pṛṣṭayā' with 'bhavatyā' and 'me' (by me) is syntactically awkward, and the sense 'I asked you and you gave no answer' is clear from context. ↩
  112. The reading: The first half is joined to the preceding verse by the particle ca. The text reads 'tvāñcaivānupraviṣṭo', with 'tvām' as the object of the participle. Strictly 'anupraviṣṭaḥ' takes the accusative, so 'followed you into' is the natural rendering, with 'imaṃ prāsādam' as the second object. The sense is that he entered after her. The text is slightly irregular because the verse has two accusatives, but it is not corrupt. 'Ityetat kathitaṃ satyam' could also be read as 'thus this has been told [to you] truly', and I took 'satyam' as predicative ('it is the truth') rather than adverbial. The difference in meaning is slight. ↩
  113. a class to be honoured: pūjyapakṣa: literally 'the side or party of those worthy of worship'. The speaker means that he ranks the gods and other celestial beings among those he reveres, not among his own kind. ↩
  114. O Kuṇḍalā: Kuṇḍale is read as the vocative of Kuṇḍalā, the friend of Madālasā, and not as a dual or locative of kuṇḍala, 'earring'. The prince addresses the friend, and perhaps the lady too, as the story requires. ↩
  115. The reading: samastā pūjyapakṣo vai devādyā mama: the grammar is irregular. samastā (feminine singular or neuter plural) does not agree with pūjyapakṣaḥ (masculine singular) or with devādyāḥ, so the text may be corrupt, with samastāḥ intended. I take samastā devādyāḥ as 'all the gods and the rest' and pūjyapakṣaḥ as the predicate, 'a class to be honoured'. The alternative reading of kuṇḍale as 'earrings' makes no sense here, so I take it as a vocative of Kuṇḍalā. ↩
  116. The reading: 1. lajjājaḍam can be read as an adverb of vīkṣamāṇā (the maiden is numb with shyness as she looks), or as an adjective of sakhīvadanam (her friend's face is numb with shyness). I chose the adverbial reading because the shyness suits the maiden, who has just heard the stranger's declaration, and not the friend. 2. The header putrāvūcatuḥ is numbered 90.19, which does not fit the sequence of chapter 21. It is probably a displaced or misplaced speaker's line from the e-text. I translated it as given. Who the 'two sons' are cannot be told from these verses. ↩
  117. That friend: Sakhī is Kuṇḍalā, the friend of Madālasā. Enām, 'her', is Madālasā, the kanyā (maiden) of 21.54, who had stayed silent. ↩
  118. O you who are obedient to Surabhi's word: Surabhyā vacanānuge is a crux. It is read here as surabhyā(ḥ) vacanānuge, a feminine vocative addressed to Madālasā. A possible emendation is surabhyā vacanānugam or -ānugā, 'in accord with Surabhi's word'. ↩
  119. The reading: The second half-verse, yathāvat kathitaṃ tena surabhyā vacanānuge, looks corrupt. Surabhyā is an instrumental, but vacanānuge can only be a feminine vocative, and an instrumental does not govern -anuga naturally. I follow the reviewer on two points. I have dropped 'too' from the draft, since the Sanskrit has no 'also' and tena and surabhyā are not joint agents of kathitam; the only agent is tena, 'by him'. I have also made the relation of vacanānuge explicit: 'O you who are obedient to Surabhi's word', so that the vocative is clearly Madālasā and Surabhi is the one whose word she follows. This assumes the genitive surabhyāḥ. The alternative is the adverbial 'told by him in accord with Surabhi's word', after emending to vacanānugam. I did not adopt it because it changes the text more and leaves the sense unsure. Another problem is that the next verse (21.56) addresses the hero (vīra), while enām here is Madālasā. I have kept enām as the addressee of this verse and treated the sentence a ↩
  120. The reading: 21.56cd: nānyatra hṛdayaṃ tv asyā dṛṣṭvā sthairyaṃ prayāsyati. I had read it as 'it will not go elsewhere, but will attain steadiness'. The reviewer is right, and I now take na with anyatra and with the verb: 'will not attain steadiness elsewhere'. This is the natural reading of na ... anyatra ... prayāsyati. It also suits 21.57, where each thing (radiance, light, and so on) goes to its own proper place. The earlier draft invented a separate clause, 'will not go elsewhere', that the Sanskrit does not state. dṛṣṭvā has no expressed object; its agent is the heart (hṛdayam), and I supply [you] in brackets so the English parses. The particle tu (hṛdayaṃ tv asyā, printed hṛdayantvasyā by sandhi) is only mildly contrastive, and I leave it untranslated. asandigdham qualifies vacaḥ: 'free of doubt'. The label 91.2 for kuṇḍalovāca looks like a numbering slip in the e-text, and probably belongs with the end of 21.55 or the start of 21.56. The speaker tag is rendered as it stands. ↩
  121. the steadfast: The text reads dhoram. It is probably a form related to dhaureya or dhorita, 'one who bears a burden steadily'. The sense 'steadfast' suits dhṛti (firmness) in the parallel. ↩
  122. The reading: dhoram is obscure: it may be a corrupt or Prakritic form of dhaureya or dhorita ('steady, bearing a load'), or a misprint. I took it as 'steadfast', which pairs naturally with dhṛti. Also, eva after candram could be read as 'to the moon alone' or as a comparative 'just as to the moon'. I treated it as merely emphatic and left it out. ↩
  123. pierced by you alone: Refers to the earlier episode in which the dānava who had carried off Madālasā was struck down by her suitor's arrow; the speaker is the hero addressed in the preceding verses. ↩
  124. Surabhi: The divine cow, called here 'mother of cows'; her words to Madālasā are the authority on which Kuṇḍalā relies. ↩
  125. The reading: viddhaḥ: 'pierced' (struck by a weapon) is the plain sense; the text does not say with what. 'tvayaiva' is taken as 'by you alone' because the emphasis carries meaning (the deed is credited to him). The verse could also be read as addressed to the hero in the singular, which is what I have done. ↩
  126. destiny: vidhi: ordinance, fate, or prescribed rite. Here it most probably means the ordering of destiny; the sense 'by proper rite' is also possible. ↩
  127. The reading: vidhinā may mean 'by destiny/providence' or 'by the prescribed rule/rite'; I chose 'destiny' because the preceding verses stress that Surabhi's word has settled the matter. Also, samāhitam may mean 'arranged, settled' or 'composed, concentrated'; I took 'arranged'. The first half is also grammatically loose (taddhanyā iyaṃ, with tad as 'therefore'), and sametya has no explicit subject beyond iyam, so I took iyam as the subject of the absolutive. ↩
  128. The two sons said:: The speaker line putrāvūcatuḥ, with its verse number 91.7, has no speech after it. It looks like a stray or misplaced speaker tag, or an interpolation in the e-text. It is kept as given. ↩
  129. the father of the good: Sanskrit satāṃ pituḥ: both words are genitive (plural and singular) and are read together. The phrase is unclear and may be corrupt. It may mean the prince's own father as protector of the good, but that is not certain. ↩
  130. Tumburu: Tumburu is a celestial musician (gandharva). Here he is the family preceptor (guru) of Madālasā's line. ↩
  131. The reading: (1) putrāvūcatuḥ ('the two sons said') is followed by no speech, only by a narrative verse. It looks misplaced or interpolated. I kept it as its own segment and flagged it in a note. (2) satāṃ pituḥ is doubtful. The reviewer is right that satām (gen. pl.) and pituḥ (gen. sg.) probably belong together, so I withdrew 'as is the way among the good', which the Sanskrit does not support. I also withdrew the 'ablative' reading and the added 'my'. Paravān can take a genitive ('dependent on'), so pituḥ is taken as the person depended on, qualified by satām: 'the father of the good'. Alternatives: 'among the good, [dependent] on [my] father', or an emendation. The text may be corrupt, and I do not resolve it. (3) tatkule: tat may refer to the bride's family or to the prince's. Since the subject is sā (Madālasā), who calls on her own family preceptor, I took 'her family'. Tumburu is a gandharva, which suits her line. (4) taṃ is read as agreeing with tumburum, hence 'that Tumburu'. The note calls ↩
  132. Tumburu: Named in the previous verse as the family preceptor (guru) of Madālasā's line, whom she called to mind; 'he' (sa) refers to him. ↩
  133. kuśa: A sacred grass used as seating and in ritual; here it is brought for the marriage rite. ↩
  134. The reading: 'sa' is not named in this verse; I take it as Tumburu, the guru she thought of in 21.60 (tumburuṃ ... gurum). 'Kuṇḍalāgauraveṇa' is read as 'out of respect for Kuṇḍalā' (objective genitive compound); the alternative, 'out of respect shown by Kuṇḍalā', is less natural. 'Samprītyā' is read as 'affection' for Madālasā, which I take to be a motive for his coming. ↩
  135. mantras: Mantra: a sacred formula or verse, recited at rites. Here the marriage ritual is performed with them. ↩
  136. went, as he had come: yathāgatam is adverbial: he left in the manner of his arrival, that is, as suddenly as he had come in 21.61. ↩
  137. she said to that friend of hers: The speaker 'she' (sā) is Kuṇḍalā, and the friend addressed is Madālasā, as the following verses show. ↩
  138. The reading: (1) pratipādya with vaivāhikavidhiṃ kanyām: it can mean 'having accomplished (the rite)' or 'having given (the maiden)'. I rendered both, as the rite performed and the maiden given in marriage. (2) The speaker sā in 21.63 is taken as Kuṇḍalā, not Madālasā, because 21.64 has the speaker praising 'you' (Madālasā) united with him, and 21.65 introduces Madālasā as speaking to the prince. The phrase tāṃ sakhīṃ bālām is therefore Madālasā. ↩
  139. I shall practise unequalled tapas: The text reads tamas tapsye, which is not idiomatic. It is most likely a corruption of tapas tapsye, 'I shall practise austerity', and is translated so. ↩
  140. I shall be one who is not of this kind: bhavitrī nedṛśī yathā is obscure. It is taken as 'I shall become one such that I shall not be of this sort', that is, no longer like the speaker's present self. ↩
  141. The reading: (1) tamas tapsye: read as tapas tapsye, with tamas taken as a corruption; 'darkness' makes no sense with tap- 'to practise'. (2) bhavitrī nedṛśī yathā: the sense is uncertain. I take bhavitrī as 'I shall become', with the yathā clause giving the result ('so that I shall not be of this kind'). The alternatives are 'so that no one will be like this' or a reference to Kuṇḍalā's own state. The speaker is taken to be Kuṇḍalā (sā), speaking first to Madālasā and then turning to the prince, as the context of 21.63 suggests. ↩
  142. The reading: The reference "91.14" is evidently a misprint for a number in chapter 21 (the speaker's line falls between 21.65 and 21.66). The verse is translated as given. The locative bhavadvidhe is read as 'to one such as you', governed by upadeśaḥ dātavyaḥ. The speech continues in 21.67, so the closing quotation mark is left open. ↩
  143. slayer of enemies: Arisūdana, a vocative addressed to the prince (rājaputra) of the preceding verse. ↩
  144. put me at ease with your trust: viśrambhitā is a causative participle: 'made confident, put at ease' by the prince, which gives Kuṇḍalā the freedom to speak. ↩
  145. The reading: The verb smārayāmi ('I remind', causative of smṛ) has no object expressed; it is understood from the next verse, which gives the reminder. The reading viśrambhitā cāsmi is taken as 'I have been put at ease (made confident) by you'; a sense 'I have been trusted' is also possible, and the two overlap closely. ↩
  146. artha: Material welfare and the means of livelihood, wealth and worldly success; with dharma and kāma it forms the traditional triple set of aims of life (trivarga). ↩
  147. kāma: Desire, pleasure, especially sensual and erotic enjoyment; the third of the three aims of life. It is distinct from the god Kāma, who is named in the glossary. ↩
  148. The reading: The verse has two parts, each with bhāryā, and the second does not repeat the first: the first sentence is about the husband's duty (bhartavyā rakṣitavyā), the second about the wife's role. I read the second bhāryā as a new subject, not as part of the first, which keeps the sense. The particle hi is left untranslated as emphatic or explanatory. Reading dharmārthakāmasaṃsiddhyai as a dative of purpose, 'for the full accomplishment of dharma, artha and kāma'. ↩
  149. artha: Material welfare, wealth and worldly advantage. With dharma and kāma it forms the triple set of human aims (trivarga). ↩
  150. kāma: Desire, pleasure, especially sensual and conjugal love, as the third human aim. It is not the god Kāma here. ↩
  151. The reading: 1. saṅgatam is a neuter participle used as a noun, 'union, concord, coming together'. I take it as 'there is a union' and keep the three aims in the genitive after it, as the reviewer asks. 'Fulfilment, attainment' is possible, but 'union' fits the following verses, which treat the three aims as lodged together in marriage. 2. In trayāṇām api, api is rendered 'even', so the sense is that even all three, not merely one, are joined. 3. On parasparavaśānugau I accept the reviewer's point that 'obedient' was too strong. The compound is vaśa + anuga in the dual, 'each following the other's control or will', and I now render it 'each follow the other's will'. I keep 'follow' rather than 'submit', since anuga means 'follower' and does not imply submission. ↩
  152. The three are lodged in her: tritayam āhitam: the triad dharma, artha and kāma is said to be placed or deposited in the wife, as in a receptacle. ↩
  153. The reading: prabho is a vocative, taken as addressed to the prince, the same person as Arisūdana in 21.67. vā ... athavā is taken as a loose alternation: 'dharma or artha, or else kāma'. āhitam could also mean 'established, deposited'; I kept 'lodged'. ↩
  154. triple set of aims: trivarga: the three aims of life, dharma, artha and kāma, named in the preceding verses; dharmādi ("dharma and the rest") refers to the same three. ↩
  155. married life: dāmpatya: the state of being a couple (dampatī), that is, the joint life of husband and wife. ↩
  156. The reading: samupāśritaḥ is masculine singular, agreeing with trivargaḥ. I took it as 'depends on, rests on' (upa-ā-śri with the accusative dāmpatyam). Another possible reading is 'has recourse to', but that does not fit a thing as subject. I rendered tathaiva ('in the same way') as completing the parallel with the previous verse, where the husband needs the wife. The verse is not in the usual form of a single sentence, so I joined its two halves as two English sentences. ↩
  157. the deities: The text reads devātā-, which is not a regular compound form. It is taken as devatā-, 'deities', with a lengthened vowel that is either metrical or a misprint. The metre does not need the long vowel. ↩
  158. servants: bhṛtya means one who is maintained, that is, a servant or dependent of the household. The householder's duty to provide for such persons is meant. ↩
  159. O son of a king: Nṛpātmaja, 'son of a king', addresses the prince Puṣkaramālin. He is the same person as Arisūdana and prabhu in the preceding verses. ↩
  160. The reading: devātā-pitṛ-bhṛtyānām: devātā- is not a regular compound form. Options: (a) devatā-, 'deities', with a lengthened vowel or a misprint; (b) some other form of devatā or deva. I chose (a). It gives a regular list of four objects of honouring, matching the four-fold pūjanam. The reviewer's suggestion 'deity-protected' is not supported by the construction and is rejected. I kept the passive, as the reviewer suggests: 'cannot be done by men' for na puṃbhiḥ śakyate kartum. For bhṛtya I took 'servants' as the primary sense and explained 'dependents' in the note. Pūjanam is rendered 'honouring' for all four groups, since 'worship' does not suit servants and guests. ↩
  161. The reading: The reading 'apī' in the text is a metrical/typographical form of 'api'. The phrase 'kubhāryāsaṃśraye 'pi vā' could mean 'or even in reliance on a bad wife' (the choice here: when they depend on a bad wife) or 'in the keeping of a bad wife'. The subject 'arthaḥ' is singular and collective, so 'wealth ... comes' is rendered with 'men' (plural) supplied as 'they' in the last clause, following the agents manujaiḥ. ↩
  162. [this] is perceived by direct observation: pratyakṣeṇopalakṣyate stands oddly after naivāsti, and the text may be corrupt. Possible repairs are pratyakṣeṇa na lakṣyate ('it is not observed in practice') or pratyakṣaṃ copalakṣyate. The transmitted reading is kept. ↩
  163. joint dharma: sahadharma: religious duty performed together by husband and wife, especially shared rites. ↩
  164. the dharma of the three Vedas: trayīdharma: the rites and duties enjoined by the triple Veda (Ṛg, Yajur and Sāman). It is not the triple set of aims (trivarga) of 21.71. ↩
  165. The reading: (1) Reading of the first half. I keep the transmitted text and take pratyakṣeṇopalakṣyate as a second predicate: kāma does not exist for him, and this is seen by direct observation. This does not contradict naiva, because the observation confirms the absence. The bracketed [this] is needed for the English to parse. If the text is emended to pratyakṣeṇa na lakṣyate, the sense would be 'nor is it observed in practice'. The reviewer's finding that the earlier bracket '[only in the married]' was an addition is accepted and the bracket is removed. (2) 'tasya' is taken as the man without a wife (21.73), and 'tu' marks the contrast with the loss of wealth in that verse. (3) The subject of avāpnuyāt is unexpressed and is supplied as [a man]. (4) 'trayīdharma' is read as the Vedic dharma and not as the trivarga, since trayī normally means the three Vedas. ↩
  166. protects: avati (root av) means 'protects, favours, gratifies, sustains'. The single verb serves all four objects, and its sense is stretched to fit each: sons keep the ancestors' offerings going, food gratifies guests, worship gratifies the gods, and the husband protects his wife. ↩
  167. the immortals: amara, 'the undying', is a common word for the gods. ↩
  168. The reading: The verse is elliptical and the construction is loose. I take avati as the verb of all four clauses, with naraḥ as subject: the man protects (or gratifies) the ancestors by sons, the guests by food, the gods by worship, and likewise a faithful wife. The sense required by the context (vv. 72–74), that a man honours ancestors, guests and gods through a faithful wife, may be intended, but the text does not say so, so I have followed the words as they stand. Annasādhanaiḥ could also be read as 'with the means of preparing food'; I chose 'means of providing food' as the wider reading. ↩
  169. continuity of dharma, kāma and artha: The compound dharmakāmārthasantatiḥ can be read as 'the continuity (santati) of dharma, kāma and artha' or as 'the offspring (santati) born of them'. The translation takes the first sense, which fits the context of the verse. ↩
  170. kāma: Kāma: desire, pleasure, especially sexual and sensual enjoyment; the third of the three aims of life. ↩
  171. reaches its fulfilment in: adhigacchati literally means 'goes to', 'attains' or 'reaches'. Here the triple set of aims is the subject and married life is the object that it reaches or rests upon. ↩
  172. The reading: santati in dharmakāmārthasantatiḥ: 'continuity/succession' or 'offspring'. I chose 'continuity' since the verse concerns how the three aims are sustained through married life. Also, the sense of nominal clause: no verb is expressed in the first half, so 'there is no' is supplied from naiva. The tasmāt ('therefore') links the two halves. adhigacchati could also be 'obtains, resorts to'; I chose 'reaches its fulfilment in' as the gloss for the relation of trivarga to dāmpatya. ↩
  173. to the two of you: yuvayoḥ is a dual genitive used where English expects a dative: 'said for the two of you'. The pair are the man addressed and the woman who is called 'her' in the next phrase. ↩
  174. The reading: vardha is the imperative of vṛdh and is read as a wish, 'may you prosper'. Taken as a plain command it would be 'grow' or 'thrive'. The compound dhanaputrasukhāyuṣā is a single instrumental singular and is read as a series, 'wealth, sons, happiness and life'. The Sanskrit does not say whether the speaker means long life, so only 'life' is given. ↩
  175. The reading: The verse reference given (92.7) does not match the chapter and verse numbering of the surrounding text (21.72–21.79), and the line stands in a context where a speaker is unexpected (21.77 is spoken by a woman addressing a pair, and 21.78 opens with 'iti uktvā'). The Sanskrit putrāvūcatuḥ is putrau ūcatuḥ, a dual subject: 'the two sons said'. I translate it as it stands. The text may be a stray line or a misplaced verse marker from another chapter. ↩
  176. she: The speaker of 21.77 is a woman (a divine maiden), who here takes leave of her friend and of the prince; the verse gives only the pronoun sā. ↩
  177. The reading: svasakhīm is read as 'her own friend' (sva + sakhī). The verse does not name the friend, and taṃ is taken as the man to whom she bows, i.e. the hero addressed in 21.77. yathābhipretamātmanaḥ is taken as 'according to her own wish/purpose', modifying jagāma adverbially; it could also be read as 'to the destination intended by herself'. ↩
  178. those born of Danu: Danusambhava: 'born of Danu', that is, the Dānavas, the demons, descendants of Danu. ↩
  179. The reading: Two of the reviewer's findings are only partly accepted. (1) 'But' is dropped and the verse is now one sentence with the absolutive āropya ('having set') and nirgantukāmaḥ ('wishing to leave') both attached to the son of Śatrujit, the subject. I keep 'wishing to leave' rather than 'about to leave', since kāma expresses desire, not imminence. (2) pātāla is singular in the Sanskrit, but I keep the glossary rendering 'nether worlds', as the glossary requires, because the word names the whole subterranean region. The note label is changed from 'epithet' to 'name', and the note now names the Dānavas as descendants of Danu. ↩
  180. jewel of a maiden: kanyāratna: a maiden who is the best of her kind. Here it is Madālasā, whom Pātālaketu had carried off. ↩
  181. The reading: The Sanskrit gives no subject for hriyate. I supplied 'She', since the clause yad ānītam makes the maiden the one carried off, and 'They meant' to link the relative clause. Divaḥ is ablative, 'from heaven' or 'from the sky'. I chose 'from heaven' as the literal sense, although the story elsewhere has Pātālaketu take her from the earth. The text may be loose here. ↩
  182. iron clubs: Sanskrit parigha: a heavy iron bar or club, used as a weapon. ↩
  183. The reading: The compound parighanistriṃśagadāśūlaśarāyudham is a bahuvrīhi qualifying balam ('host whose weapons are...'). I read the first member as parigha, nistriṃśa, gadā, śūla and śara, five weapons. Prāptam is taken as 'arrived', agreeing with balam. ↩
  184. the king's son: nṛpanandana, 'delight of the king': the son of King Śatrujit, who is carrying off Madālasā. ↩
  185. net of arrows: śarajāla: a dense volley of arrows, likened to a net. ↩
  186. The reading: The verse does not say 'the king's son' by name. 'sa ca śatrujitaḥ putraḥ' is the same prince as in 21.79 and 21.82. In 'tadastrāṇi', tad (those) refers to the arrows and spears of the dānavas in 21.82, which the text here calls astras (missiles). 'prahasann iva' is rendered 'as if laughing'; the 'iva' is kept because it carries meaning. ↩
  187. javelins: śakti: a throwing spear or javelin with a pointed head, distinct from the śūla (spear) mentioned earlier. ↩
  188. lances: ṛṣṭi: a long, double-edged lance or spear. ↩
  189. The reading: The printed text reads 'asikhakti', which is evidently a misprint for 'asiśakti' (sword and javelin). I read it as asi-śakti. 'Chinnaiḥ' (cut to pieces) agrees with the weapons of the dānavas (swords, javelins, lances, arrows). The 'śarotkaraiḥ' (volleys of arrows) belong to Ṛtadhvaja, and I take them as a second instrument of 'sañchannam' (covered, strewn). 'Ṛtadhvaja' is therefore the possessor of the arrows, not the one cut. ↩
  190. the missile of Tvaṣṭṛ: The tvāṣṭra missile belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine craftsman. It is a mantra-empowered weapon that burns the enemy. ↩
  191. the sons of Sagara: The sixty thousand sons of King Sagara were burned to ashes when they disturbed the sage Kapila while searching for their father's sacrificial horse. ↩
  192. fiery energy of Kapila: Kāpila is the adjective from Kapila, the sage. Tejas, here 'fiery energy', is the burning power of an ascetic or a god. ↩
  193. The reading: sphuṭadasthicayāḥ: sphuṭat can mean 'bursting', 'splitting' or 'cracking'. I chose 'cracking', as the bones split in the heat. kṛtāḥ and nirdagdhāḥ are both predicated of the dānavas, 'made into heaps of bones' and 'burned up'. I have joined them in one clause. ↩
  194. mounted on his horse: The Sanskrit is aśvī, 'having a horse' or 'possessed of a horse'. It is read here as 'mounted on his horse', and refers to the prince's horse in this story. ↩
  195. jewel of a woman: strīratna, a woman who is the finest of her kind, counted as a 'jewel' among a man's possessions. Here it refers to Madālasā, whom the prince has just won back. ↩
  196. The reading: aśvī is ambiguous: 'possessed of a horse', i.e. mounted, or a reference to his special horse in the story. I chose 'mounted on his horse'. The verse does not name Madālasā; strīratnena tena is taken to be her, since 21.89 speaks of recovering her (Madālasāprāpti). ↩
  197. The reading: The father is Śatrujit, though the verse does not name him; it says only "the father" (pitā), the one to whom Ṛtadhvaja made his report in 21.88. "Whose mind was noble" renders cārucetasaḥ, a compound whose reading is clear. The verse closes with "said this" (idam āha), and the speech itself begins in 21.91. ↩
  198. a worthy vessel: satpātra: literally 'a good vessel', a person fit to receive and bear gifts, trust and responsibility; here a son worthy of his father's hopes. ↩
  199. The reading: The Sanskrit has tārito 'haṃ, 'I have been delivered'. 'Rescued' renders tārita, which can also mean 'brought across' (as over a danger or a sea). The verse is the father's direct speech and continues in 21.92-93; 'trātāḥ' is read in the text as trātā (munayastrātā), a probable sandhi/printing irregularity for trātāḥ, 'protected' (plural, agreeing with munayaḥ). I take it as plural. ↩
  200. [our family]: The verse has no stated subject for ākhyātimānītam beyond the implied family or lineage; the neuter participle agrees with the 'it' that is later called tat. The bracket gives the most natural referent, though the 'it' may refer simply to renown. ↩
  201. The reading: The Sanskrit khyātim ānītam ('brought to renown') has no stated object. I take 'it' to be the family or lineage, and tat in the second half to be the renown (khyāti). The alternative is that the entire thing is the renown itself, in which case 'brought to renown' is somewhat tautological. The verse also leaves the sense of 'extended' and 'made abundant' unmarked as to subject, but the neuter singular participles agree with the implied family or its fame. ↩
  202. The reading: The verse has no explicit object for yaḥ; I take 'tat' (that) as the object of 'na hāpayate', with the three items (fame, wealth, valor) as its content. 'Vā' after 'atha api' is read as a loose 'or even', not as marking a strict alternative. ↩
  203. the best of men: narottama, the counterpart of the 'middling' man (madhyama) in the previous verse; verse 21.95 then names the lowest of men, puruṣādhama. ↩
  204. The reading: tadvīryāt: 'that valor' refers back to the fame, wealth or valor acquired by the father in 21.93. 'Valor' (vīrya) is taken as standing for the whole set. Alternatively, tad could be read as only 'that [of the father]'. anyat ('something else', 'further') is taken as the object of niṣpādayati, qualified by adhikam. ↩
  205. father: The transmitted text reads yaḥ pitā, which cannot be construed with samupāttāni ('acquired'). The translation emends to pitrā, 'by the father', as in 21.93 (yad upāttaṃ yaśaḥ pitrā). pitā for pitrā is a simple omission of r. This is a departure from the transmitted text. ↩
  206. The reading: yaḥ pitā samupāttāni: the transmitted pitā is nominative singular. Read literally, it gives 'the father who brings to diminution the wealth, valor and fame acquired'. The passive participle samupāttāni then has no agent, and the verse would leave the son's relation to his father's gains, which 21.93–94 discuss, and speak of a father instead. I therefore emend to pitrā (instrumental, 'by the father'), taking pitā as a loss of r, and I have marked this in the note. yaḥ is then the man in general, parallel to 21.93 yas tu and 21.94 yas tu. If one keeps pitā, the alternative is 'The father who brings to diminution the wealth, valor and fame that have been acquired'. I rejected that as out of keeping with the sequence. nyūnatāṃ nayati: I now translate 'brings to diminution', in line with hāpayate ('lets diminish') in 21.93. I have not added 'indeed' for vai, since here it is a purely expletive particle with no meaning to carry; the reviewer's suggestion is therefore not adopted. puruṣādhama ↩
  207. asuras: The asuras are the demonic opponents of the gods and of the sacrificial order. Here they are the enemies who threatened the brahmins. ↩
  208. The reading: tat (tanmayā) is taken as a resumptive 'that', pointing back to the achievements the father lists. The two relatives yat ca ... yat ca are taken as standing in apposition to brāhmaṇatrāṇam and so as further objects of kṛtam āsīt. The alternative is a relative construction ('what was the going to Pātāla and what was the destruction of the asuras'), which would leave the main clause incomplete. The text is not corrupt. The pluperfect-like kṛtam āsīt is rendered as a simple past, 'was accomplished'. ↩
  209. the foremost of men: puruṣottama, a different word from narottama in verse 94 but the same idea: the son who surpasses his father's achievements. ↩
  210. The reading: The last pāda, tvam ahameva guṇādhikam, has no verb and looks corrupt or elliptical. Possible readings: (a) 'I myself [regard] you as superior in qualities', which I chose because it fits the father's praise in the surrounding verses; (b) 'you are superior to me in qualities'; or (c) an emendation such as tvayāham eva guṇādhikaḥ. The verb in my rendering is supplied in brackets. Also etad apy adhikam: 'this too is greater' is taken to mean greater than the father's own deeds named in verse 96; the comparison is implied, not stated. ↩
  211. The reading: Two points. (1) ślāghyaḥ has no stated subject. I supply the speaker, the father addressing his son, in brackets as "[I am]". (2) "sa ... mānavaḥ" ("that man") looks forward to the relative "yaḥ" in the next verse (21.99), "he who is not surpassed by his son". I therefore keep "that man" without further specification here. "manye" ("I think") could also be read as parenthetical, which I have followed in the English. ↩
  212. generosity: The compound prajñādānavikramaiḥ is taken as 'wisdom, giving and prowess'. The printed text reads 'prajñā-', although 'dāna' could in principle be read otherwise. ↩
  213. known in the world by his father [alone]: The verse is a compressed statement. 'Pitrā vijñāyate' means he is identified only through his father, with no distinction of his own; the word 'alone' is supplied from the sense. The following verse (21.100) contrasts the man who gains renown from his son. ↩
  214. The reading: Two points in the verse are uncertain. (1) 'vijñāyate pitrā' may mean 'is known by (through) his father', as I take it, or 'is recognised as [his father's son]'. Both give the same sense of a man with no identity of his own. (2) The compound 'prajñādānavikramaiḥ' is taken as three separate qualities (wisdom, generosity, prowess), not as a compound with 'dānava'. The glossary entry dānava (class of asuras) might tempt a reading 'prajñā-dānava-vikramaiḥ', but the sense and the verse's context rule it out. ↩
  215. the middling man: The verse ranks men by the source of their fame: through a son (the highest), through oneself (blessed), through father and grandfathers (middling). Verse 21.101 goes on to the lowest, who is known through the mother's side. ↩
  216. The reading: The first half has no finite verb. I take tasya ... sujanmanaḥ as one phrase, with sujanmanaḥ agreeing with tasya in the genitive, and supply 'is a good one' for janma, as the reviewer suggests; the draft's 'is the birth of one well born' was clumsy and is replaced. For dhanyaḥ I keep 'blessed' as the second rank, with 'known by himself' as the predicate, as the reviewer accepts. pitṛpitāmahaiḥ is a dvandva, 'father and grandfathers'. Here pitṛ means the living father, not the glossary's 'ancestor' in the sense of the departed forefathers, so I use 'father'. I have dropped the draft's note on the sense of pitṛ because it is unnecessary. Reading tasya janma as 'his birth' with the genitive absolute-like sense is the same in meaning, so I keep one reading. ↩
  217. The basest of men: narādhama is a synonym of puruṣādhama, which occurs in 21.95. It is rendered differently here so that the two words stay distinct. ↩
  218. his maternal kin: mātṛpakṣeṇa, literally 'by the mother's side', means the mother's relatives. The verse adds the mother herself with mātrā. ↩
  219. The reading: 'Tat' is read as the adverbial 'therefore', not as a pronoun. 'Vivardhasva' is the middle imperative of vṛdh, 'grow' or 'may you prosper'. I accept the reviewer's change of vīrya to 'vigor', which keeps it distinct from vikrama, 'prowess'. I also accept the change of narādhama to 'the basest of men', so that 'the lowest of men' stays reserved for puruṣādhama. I corrected the note that wrongly said narādhama occurs in 21.95, and removed the word 'only', which is not in the Sanskrit. ↩
  220. gandharva: A class of semi-divine beings, celestial musicians, often fathers of lovely maidens. The reference is to the bride, the daughter of a gandharva. ↩
  221. The reading: The text reads 'ghandharva-', a misspelling of gandharva; I read gandharva. In 21.103 'bhāryāyā' (genitive/dative in form) after 'tayā' looks like a misprint for the instrumental 'bhāryayā'; I take 'tayā bhāryayā sārdham' as 'together with her, his wife'. The embracing in 21.103 is by the father, since the absolutive 'pariṣvajya' shares the agent of the father's speaking; the grammatical subject 'sa' would otherwise be the son. ↩
  222. slender waist: sumadhyamā, 'she of the fine waist', a conventional epithet of a beautiful woman; here it qualifies the wife, the gandharva's daughter, who is not named in this verse. ↩
  223. The reading: The verse has no explicit subject-name; 'sā śubhā ... sumadhyamā' is the gandharva's daughter (the wife) of 21.102-103, and 'tena' is her husband. Also, 'prātaḥ prātaḥ' (each morning) can be taken with the bowing to the in-laws or with the pleasure-taking; I take it with the whole sequence, as the main clause. 'Tathā' links 'anyeṣu' with the preceding verse's 'tatra pituḥ pure' (his father's city), so I render 'in other gardens, likewise'. ↩
  224. Kuvalayāśva section: kuvalayāśvīya: the portion of the text concerned with Kuvalayāśva (Ṛtadhvaja), the story of the king and his horse Kuvalaya; here used as a sub-title within the Purāṇa. ↩
  225. venerable: śrī, an honorific prefixed to the title of the work. ↩
  226. The reading: The e-text number 93.15 is a GRETIL running count; the verse is the chapter colophon, not metrical text. 'Kuvalayāśvīye' is taken as a locative qualifying the Purāṇa (the Kuvalayāśva section), not as a separate title. 'madālasāpariṇayanaṃ nāma' is taken as the chapter's name. ↩

Adhyāya 22

Sanskrit

द्वाविंशो ऽध्यायः

dvāviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

The twenty-second chapter1.

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons2 said:3

22.1

Sanskrit

ततः काले वहुतिथे गते राजा पुनः सुतम् । प्राह गच्छाशु विप्राणां त्राणाय चर मेदिनीम् ॥

tataḥ kāle vahutithe gate rājā punaḥ sutam | prāha gacchāśu viprāṇāṃ trāṇāya cara medinīm ||

English

Then, when a good many days4 had passed, the king spoke to his son again: "Go quickly and roam the earth to protect the brahmins5."6

22.2

Sanskrit

अश्वमेनं समारुह्य प्रातः प्रातर्दिने दिने । अबाधा द्विजमुख्यानामन्वेष्टव्या सदैव हि ॥

aśvamenaṃ samāruhya prātaḥ prātardine dine | abādhā dvijamukhyānāmanveṣṭavyā sadaiva hi ||

English

"Mount this horse7 and, every morning, day after day, you must always look to see that the foremost of the brahmins8 are free from harm."9

22.3

Sanskrit

दुर्वृत्ताः सन्ति शतशो दानवाः पापयोनयः । तेभ्यो न स्याद्यथा बाधा मुनीनां त्वं तथा कुरु ॥

durvṛttāḥ santi śataśo dānavāḥ pāpayonayaḥ | tebhyo na syādyathā bādhā munīnāṃ tvaṃ tathā kuru ||

English

"There are dānavas10 by the hundreds, evil in conduct and of sinful birth11. Act in such a way that the sages suffer no harm from them."12

22.4

Sanskrit

स यथोक्तस्ततः पित्रा तथा चक्रे नृपात्मजः । परिक्रम्य महीं सर्वां ववन्दे चरणौ पितुः ॥

sa yathoktastataḥ pitrā tathā cakre nṛpātmajaḥ | parikramya mahīṃ sarvāṃ vavande caraṇau pituḥ ||

English

As his father had instructed him, he, the king's son, then did exactly so. Having gone round the whole earth, he bowed at his father's feet.13

22.5

Sanskrit

अहन्यहन्यनुप्राप्ते पूर्वाह्ने नृपनन्दनः । ततश्च शेषं दिवसं तया रेमे सुमध्यया ॥

ahanyahanyanuprāpte pūrvāhne nṛpanandanaḥ | tataśca śeṣaṃ divasaṃ tayā reme sumadhyayā ||

English

Each day, when the forenoon had come, the king's son [went out on his rounds]14; and then he spent the rest of the day in pleasure with that slender-waisted woman15.16†

22.6

Sanskrit

एकदा तु चारन् सो ऽथ ददर्श यमुनातटे । पातालकेतोरनुजं तालकेतुं कृताश्रमम् ॥

ekadā tu cāran so 'tha dadarśa yamunātaṭe | pātālaketoranujaṃ tālaketuṃ kṛtāśramam ||

English

Then, one day, as he was roaming, he saw on the bank of the Yamunā17 Tālaketu18, the younger brother of Pātālaketu, who had made a hermitage there.19

22.7

Sanskrit

मायावी दानवः सो ऽथ मुनिरूपं समास्थितः । स प्राह राजपुत्रं तं पूर्ववैरमनुस्मरन् ॥

māyāvī dānavaḥ so 'tha munirūpaṃ samāsthitaḥ | sa prāha rājaputraṃ taṃ pūrvavairamanusmaran ||

English

That dānava, a master of māyā20, had now taken on the form of a sage. Remembering the old enmity21, he spoke to the king's son.22

22.8

Sanskrit

राजपुत्र ब्रीवीमि त्वां तत् कुरुष्व यदीच्छसि । न च ते प्रार्थनाभङ्गः कार्यः सत्यप्रतिश्रव ॥

rājaputra brīvīmi tvāṃ tat kuruṣva yadīcchasi | na ca te prārthanābhaṅgaḥ kāryaḥ satyapratiśrava ||

English

"King's son, I am speaking to you; do that, if you are willing. And, you whose promise is true23, you must not refuse my request."24†

22.9

Sanskrit

यक्ष्ये यज्ञेन धर्माय कर्तव्याश्च तथेष्टयः । चितयस्तत्र कर्तव्या नास्ति मे दक्षैणा यतः ॥

yakṣye yajñena dharmāya kartavyāśca tatheṣṭayaḥ | citayastatra kartavyā nāsti me dakṣaiṇā yataḥ ||

English

I shall sacrifice with a yajña for the sake of dharma, and the offerings25 must also be made; the fire-altars26 must be built there as well. Since I have no sacrificial fee27, [I ask you for this].28†

22.10

Sanskrit

अतः प्रयच्छ मे वीर हिरण्यार्थं स्वभूषणम् । यदेतत् कण्ठलग्नं ते रक्ष चेमं माश्रमम् ॥

ataḥ prayaccha me vīra hiraṇyārthaṃ svabhūṣaṇam | yadetat kaṇṭhalagnaṃ te rakṣa cemaṃ māśramam ||

English

"Therefore, brave one, give me your own ornament for the sake of gold29: this one that clings to your neck. And protect this hermitage of mine as well30,31

22.11

Sanskrit

यावदन्तर्जले देवं वरुणं यादसां पतिम् । वैदिकैर्वारुणैर्मन्त्रैः प्रजानां पुष्टिहेतुकैः ॥

yāvadantarjale devaṃ varuṇaṃ yādasāṃ patim | vaidikairvāruṇairmantraiḥ prajānāṃ puṣṭihetukaiḥ ||

English

22.11–12until, in the water, I have praised the god Varuṇa, lord of the aquatic creatures32, with Vedic mantras of Varuṇa33, which are the cause of the prosperity of creatures, and return in haste." He bowed to him34 as he spoke thus, and then gave him the ornament for his neck.

22.12

Sanskrit

अभिष्टूय त्वरायुक्तः समभ्येमीति वादिनम् । तं प्रणम्य ततः प्रादात् स तस्मै कण्ठभूषणम् ॥

abhiṣṭūya tvarāyuktaḥ samabhyemīti vādinam | taṃ praṇamya tataḥ prādāt sa tasmai kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇam ||

English

Its English is given with 22.11–12, above.

22.13

Sanskrit

प्राह यैनं भवान् यातु निर्व्यलीकेन चेतसा । स्थास्यामि तावदत्रैव तवाश्रमसमीपतः ॥

prāha yainaṃ bhavān yātu nirvyalīkena cetasā | sthāsyāmi tāvadatraiva tavāśramasamīpataḥ ||

English

He said to him: "Let your honour35 go with an untroubled36 mind. In the meantime I shall stay right here, near your hermitage.37

22.14

Sanskrit

तवादेशान्महाभाग यावदागमनं तव । न ते ऽत्र कश्चिदाबाधां करिष्यति मयि स्थिते । विश्रब्धश्चात्वरन् ब्रह्मन् कुरुष्व त्वं मनोगतम् ॥

tavādeśānmahābhāga yāvadāgamanaṃ tava | na te 'tra kaścidābādhāṃ kariṣyati mayi sthite | viśrabdhaścātvaran brahman kuruṣva tvaṃ manogatam ||

English

At your command38, greatly fortunate one, until you return, no one here will cause you any harm while I am standing by. Trusting me and without haste, brahmin39, do what is in your mind."40

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons41 said:42

22.15

Sanskrit

एकमुक्तस्ततस्तेन स ममज्ज नदीजले । ररक्ष सो ऽपि तस्यैव मायाविहितमाश्रमम् ॥

ekamuktastatastena sa mamajja nadījale | rarakṣa so 'pi tasyaiva māyāvihitamāśramam ||

English

Thus addressed43 by him, he then dived into the water of the river. And the other, for his part, guarded that same man's hermitage, which had been fashioned by māyā44.45

22.16

Sanskrit

गत्वा जलाशयात् तस्मात् तालकेतुश्च तत्परम् । मदालसायाः प्रत्यक्षमन्येषाञ्चैतदुक्तवान् ॥

gatvā jalāśayāt tasmāt tālaketuśca tatparam | madālasāyāḥ pratyakṣamanyeṣāñcaitaduktavān ||

English

Having gone from that body of water, Tālaketu then said this in the presence of Madālasā and of others.46

Sanskrit

तालकेतुरुवाच

tālaketuruvāca

English

Tālaketu said:

22.17

Sanskrit

वीरः कुवलयाश्वो ऽसौ ममाश्रमसमीपतः । केनापि दुष्टदैत्येन कुर्वन् रक्षां तपस्विनाम् ॥

vīraḥ kuvalayāśvo 'sau mamāśramasamīpataḥ | kenāpi duṣṭadaityena kurvan rakṣāṃ tapasvinām ||

English

22.17–18That brave Kuvalayāśva, near my hermitage, was providing protection for the ascetics. He was fighting to the best of his power and striking down the haters of brahmins in battle. Then he was pierced in the chest47 with a spear48 by some wicked Daitya, that sinful one, who had resorted to māyā.49

22.18

Sanskrit

युध्यमानो यथाशक्ति निघ्नन् ब्रह्मद्विषो युधि । मायामाश्रित्य पापेन भिन्नः शूलेन वक्षसी ॥

yudhyamāno yathāśakti nighnan brahmadviṣo yudhi | māyāmāśritya pāpena bhinnaḥ śūlena vakṣasī ||

English

Its English is given with 22.17–18, above.

22.19

Sanskrit

म्रियमाणेन तेनेदं दत्तं मे कण्ठभूषणम् । प्रापितश्चाग्निसंयोगं स वने शूद्रतापसैः ॥

mriyamāṇena tenedaṃ dattaṃ me kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇam | prāpitaścāgnisaṃyogaṃ sa vane śūdratāpasaiḥ ||

English

As he was dying, he gave me this ornament for the neck. And in the forest he was brought into contact with fire50 by śūdra ascetics.51

22.20

Sanskrit

कृतार्तह्रेषाशब्दो वै त्रस्तः साश्रुविलोचनः । नीतः सो ऽश्वश्च तेनैव दानवेन दुरात्मना ॥

kṛtārtahreṣāśabdo vai trastaḥ sāśruvilocanaḥ | nītaḥ so 'śvaśca tenaiva dānavena durātmanā ||

English

And that horse too, which had uttered a cry of anguish in its neighing, terrified and with tears in its eyes, was led away by that same wicked-minded dānava.52

22.21

Sanskrit

एतन्मया नृशंसेन दृष्टं दुष्कृतकारिणा । यदत्रानन्तरं कृत्यं क्रियतां तदकालिकम् ॥

etanmayā nṛśaṃsena dṛṣṭaṃ duṣkṛtakāriṇā | yadatrānantaraṃ kṛtyaṃ kriyatāṃ tadakālikam ||

English

I, a cruel man and a doer of evil deeds, saw this. Let whatever should be done next in this matter be done at once, without delay53.54

22.22

Sanskrit

हृदयाश्वासनञ्चैतद् गृह्यतां कण्ठभूषणम् । नास्माकं हि सुवर्णेन कृत्यमस्ति तपस्विनाम् ॥

hṛdayāśvāsanañcaitad gṛhyatāṃ kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇam | nāsmākaṃ hi suvarṇena kṛtyamasti tapasvinām ||

English

And take this ornament for the neck, which will comfort your heart; for we ascetics have no use for gold.55

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons said:56

22.23

Sanskrit

इत्युक्त्वोत्सृज्य दत्भूमौ स जगाम यथागतम् । निपपात जनः सो ऽथ शोकार्तो मूर्च्छयाऽतुरः ॥

ityuktvotsṛjya datbhūmau sa jagāma yathāgatam | nipapāta janaḥ so 'tha śokārto mūrcchayā'turaḥ ||

English

Having said this, and having laid it down on the ground, he went away the way he had come. Then that company of people fell down, stricken with grief and overcome by fainting.57

22.24

Sanskrit

तत्क्षणात् चेतनां प्राप्य सर्वास्ता नृपयोषितः । राजपत्न्यश्च राजा च विलेपुरतिदुः खिताः ॥

tatkṣaṇāt cetanāṃ prāpya sarvāstā nṛpayoṣitaḥ | rājapatnyaśca rājā ca vilepuratiduḥ khitāḥ ||

English

At that very moment, having regained consciousness, all those women of the king's household, the royal wives, and the king himself lamented, exceedingly distressed.58

22.25

Sanskrit

मदालसा तु द् दृष्ट्वा तदीयं कण्ठभूषणम् । तत्याजाशु प्रियान् प्राणान् श्रुत्वा च निहन्त पतिम् ॥

madālasā tu d dṛṣṭvā tadīyaṃ kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇam | tatyājāśu priyān prāṇān śrutvā ca nihanta patim ||

English

But Madālasā, having seen that ornament for the neck, which was his59, and having heard that her husband had been killed, quickly gave up her dear life-breaths60.61

22.26

Sanskrit

ततस्तथा महाक्रन्दः पौराणां भवनेष्वभूत् । यथैव तस्य नृपतेः स्वगेहे समवर्तत ॥

tatastathā mahākrandaḥ paurāṇāṃ bhavaneṣvabhūt | yathaiva tasya nṛpateḥ svagehe samavartata ||

English

Then a great wailing arose in the houses of the townspeople, just as it had arisen in the king's own palace.62

22.27

Sanskrit

राजा च तां मृतां दृष्ट्वा विना भर्त्रा मदालसाम् । प्रत्युवाच जनं सर्वं विमृश्य सुस्थमानसः ॥

rājā ca tāṃ mṛtāṃ dṛṣṭvā vinā bhartrā madālasām | pratyuvāca janaṃ sarvaṃ vimṛśya susthamānasaḥ ||

English

And the king, having seen Madālasā dead, deprived of her husband, reflected, and with a composed mind replied to all the people.63

22.28

Sanskrit

न रोदितव्यं पश्यामि भवतामात्मनस्तथा । सर्वेषामेव संचिन्त्य सम्बन्धानामनित्यताम् ॥

na roditavyaṃ paśyāmi bhavatāmātmanastathā | sarveṣāmeva saṃcintya sambandhānāmanityatām ||

English

I see no reason for weeping, either for you or for myself, when I reflect on the impermanence of all relationships.64

22.29

Sanskrit

किन्नु शोचामि तनयं किन्नु शोचाम्यहं स्नुषाम् । विमृश्य कृतकृत्यत्वाम्नम्ये ऽशोच्यावुभावपि ॥

kinnu śocāmi tanayaṃ kinnu śocāmyahaṃ snuṣām | vimṛśya kṛtakṛtyatvāmnamye 'śocyāvubhāvapi ||

English

Why indeed should I grieve for my son? Why indeed should I grieve for my daughter-in-law? Having reflected, I consider both of them not to be grieved for, because they have accomplished what was to be done65.66†

22.30

Sanskrit

मच्छ्रु श्रुपुर्मद्वचनाद्द्विजरक्षणतत्परः । प्राप्तो मे यः सुतो मृत्युं कथं शोच्यः स धीमताम् ॥

macchru śrupurmadvacanāddvijarakṣaṇatatparaḥ | prāpto me yaḥ suto mṛtyuṃ kathaṃ śocyaḥ sa dhīmatām ||

English

How should that son of mine, who at my word67 was intent on the protection of the brahmins and met his death, be mourned by the wise?68

22.31

Sanskrit

अवश्यं याति यद्देहं तद्द्विजानां कृते यदि । मम पुत्रेण संत्यक्तं नन्वभ्युदयकारि तत् ॥

avaśyaṃ yāti yaddehaṃ taddvijānāṃ kṛte yadi | mama putreṇa saṃtyaktaṃ nanvabhyudayakāri tat ||

English

The body that inevitably departs: if that body, cast off by my son, is [given] for the sake of the brahmins, surely that brings prosperity69.70

22.32

Sanskrit

इयञ्च सत्कुलोत्पन्ना भर्तर्येवमनुव्रतां । कथन्नु शोच्या नारीणां भर्तुरन्यन्न दैवतम् ॥

iyañca satkulotpannā bhartaryevamanuvratāṃ | kathannu śocyā nārīṇāṃ bharturanyanna daivatam ||

English

And how should this woman, born in a good family and so devoted to her husband71, be mourned? For women there is no deity other than the husband.72

22.33

Sanskrit

अस्माकं बान्धवानाञ्च तथान्येषां दयावताम् । शोच्या ह्येषा भवेदेवं यदि भर्त्रा वियोगिनी ॥

asmākaṃ bāndhavānāñca tathānyeṣāṃ dayāvatām | śocyā hyeṣā bhavedevaṃ yadi bhartrā viyoginī ||

English

She would indeed be worthy of mourning by us, by [our] kinsmen, and likewise by others who are compassionate, only if she were thus separated from her husband.73

22.34

Sanskrit

या तु भर्तुर्वधं श्रुत्वा तत्क्षणादेव भामिनी । भर्तारमनुयातेयं न शोच्यातो विपश्चिताम् ॥

yā tu bharturvadhaṃ śrutvā tatkṣaṇādeva bhāminī | bhartāramanuyāteyaṃ na śocyāto vipaścitām ||

English

But this lady, who, on hearing of her husband's killing, followed her husband74 at that very moment, is therefore not to be mourned by the wise.75

22.35

Sanskrit

ताः शोच्या या वियोगिन्यो न शोच्या या मृताः सह । भर्त्रा वियोगस्त्वनया नानुभूतः कृतज्ञया ॥

tāḥ śocyā yā viyoginyo na śocyā yā mṛtāḥ saha | bhartrā viyogastvanayā nānubhūtaḥ kṛtajñayā ||

English

Those women are to be mourned who are separated from their husbands; those who have died together with them are not to be mourned. But this grateful woman has not experienced separation from her husband.76

22.36

Sanskrit

दातारं सर्वसौख्यानामिह चामुत्र चोभयोः । लोकयोः का हि भर्तारं नारी मन्येत मानुषम् ॥

dātāraṃ sarvasaukhyānāmiha cāmutra cobhayoḥ | lokayoḥ kā hi bhartāraṃ nārī manyeta mānuṣam ||

English

What woman would regard her husband as a mere human being, when he is the giver of every happiness in both worlds77, here and in the next?78

22.37

Sanskrit

नासौ शोच्यो न चैवेयं नाहं तज्जननी न च । त्यजता ब्राह्मणार्थाय प्राणान् सर्वे स्म तारिताः ॥

nāsau śocyo na caiveyaṃ nāhaṃ tajjananī na ca | tyajatā brāhmaṇārthāya prāṇān sarve sma tāritāḥ ||

English

He is not to be mourned, nor is she, nor am I, his mother, nor [is anyone else]79; for by giving up his prāṇas for the sake of a brahmin, he has carried all of us across80.81†

22.38

Sanskrit

विप्राणं मम धर्मस्य गतः स हि महामतिः । आनृण्यमर्धभुक्तस्य त्यागाद् देहस्य मे सुतः ॥

viprāṇaṃ mama dharmasya gataḥ sa hi mahāmatiḥ | ānṛṇyamardhabhuktasya tyāgād dehasya me sutaḥ ||

English

My son, that man of great mind, has attained freedom from debt towards the brahmins, towards me, and towards dharma, through the abandonment of his body, which he had enjoyed only by half82.83

22.39

Sanskrit

मातुः सतीत्वं मद्वंशवैमल्यं शौर्यमात्मनः । संग्रामे संत्यजन् प्राणान् नात्यजद् द्विजरक्षणम् ॥

mātuḥ satītvaṃ madvaṃśavaimalyaṃ śauryamātmanaḥ | saṃgrāme saṃtyajan prāṇān nātyajad dvijarakṣaṇam ||

English

In giving up his life in battle, he did not abandon his mother's chastity84, the purity of my lineage, his own valor, or the protection of the brahmins.85

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons said:86

22.40

Sanskrit

ततः कुवलयाश्वस्य माता भर्तुरनन्तरम् । श्रुत्वा पुत्रवधं तादृक् प्राह दृष्ट्वा तु तं पतिम् ॥

tataḥ kuvalayāśvasya mātā bharturanantaram | śrutvā putravadhaṃ tādṛk prāha dṛṣṭvā tu taṃ patim ||

English

Then, after her husband [had spoken], Kuvalayāśva's mother, having heard of her son's killing, of such a kind87, and having looked at that husband of hers, spoke.88

22.41

Sanskrit

मातोवाच न मे मात्रा न मे स्वस्त्रा प्राप्ता प्रीतिर्नृपेदृशी । श्रुत्वा मुनिपरित्राणे हतं पुत्रं यथा मया ॥

mātovāca na me mātrā na me svastrā prāptā prītirnṛpedṛśī | śrutvā muniparitrāṇe hataṃ putraṃ yathā mayā ||

English

The mother said: Such joy, O king, as has been obtained by me on hearing that my son was slain in the protection of the sages, was obtained neither by my mother nor by my sister.

22.42

Sanskrit

शोचतां बान्धवानां ये निः श्वसन्तो ऽतिदुः खिताः । म्रियन्ते व्याधिना क्लिष्टास्तेषां माता वृथाप्रजा ॥

śocatāṃ bāndhavānāṃ ye niḥ śvasanto 'tiduḥ khitāḥ | mriyante vyādhinā kliṣṭāsteṣāṃ mātā vṛthāprajā ||

English

22.42–43Of those who die afflicted by disease, sighing and in great suffering while their kinsmen89 grieve, the mother has borne children in vain; but those who fight in battle unafraid, in the protection of cows and brahmins, and perish crushed by weapons, they alone are men on earth.9091

22.43

Sanskrit

संग्रामे युध्यमाना ये ऽभीता गोद्विजरक्षणे । क्षुण्णाः शस्त्रैर्विपद्यन्ते त एव भुवि मानवाः ॥

saṃgrāme yudhyamānā ye 'bhītā godvijarakṣaṇe | kṣuṇṇāḥ śastrairvipadyante ta eva bhuvi mānavāḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 22.42–43, above.

22.44

Sanskrit

अर्थिनां मित्रवर्गस्य विद्विषाञ्च पराङ्मुखः । यो न याति पिता तेन पुत्री माता च वीरसूः ॥

arthināṃ mitravargasya vidviṣāñca parāṅmukhaḥ | yo na yāti pitā tena putrī mātā ca vīrasūḥ ||

English

22.44–45The man who does not go away with his back turned on92 petitioners, on his circle of friends, or on enemies, through him a father has a son and a mother is the mother of a brave son93. I think that a woman's pain of pregnancy attains its fruit then, when her son is either a conqueror of his enemies or slain in battle.94

22.45

Sanskrit

गर्भक्लेशः स्त्रियो मन्ये साफल्यं भजते तदा । यदारिविजयी वा स्यात् संग्रामे वा हतः सुतः ॥

garbhakleśaḥ striyo manye sāphalyaṃ bhajate tadā | yadārivijayī vā syāt saṃgrāme vā hataḥ sutaḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 22.44–45, above.

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons95 said:96

22.46

Sanskrit

ततः स राजा संस्कारं पुत्रपत्नीमलम्भयत् । निर्गम्य च बहिः स्नातो ददौ पुत्राय चोदकम् ॥

tataḥ sa rājā saṃskāraṃ putrapatnīmalambhayat | nirgamya ca bahiḥ snāto dadau putrāya codakam ||

English

Then that king had the rites performed97 for his son's wife. And he went out, bathed outside, and offered water to his son98.99

22.47

Sanskrit

तालकेतुश्च निर्गम्य तथैव यमुनाजलात् । राजपुत्रमुवाचेदं प्रणयान्मधुरं वचः ॥

tālaketuśca nirgamya tathaiva yamunājalāt | rājaputramuvācedaṃ praṇayānmadhuraṃ vacaḥ ||

English

22.47–48And Tālaketu, having come out of the water of the Yamunā in the same way100, spoke these sweet words to the king's son out of affection: "Go, you, son of the protector of the earth101. By you I have been made one whose purpose is accomplished. The long-desired task [is accomplished], with you standing unshaken here."102

22.48

Sanskrit
