गच्छ भूपालपुत्र ! त्वं कृतार्थो ऽहं कृतस्त्वया । कार्यं चिराभिलषितं त्वय्यत्राविचले स्थिते ॥

gaccha bhūpālaputra ! tvaṃ kṛtārtho 'haṃ kṛtastvayā | kāryaṃ cirābhilaṣitaṃ tvayyatrāvicale sthite ||

English

Its English is given with 22.47–48, above.

22.49

Sanskrit

वारुणं यज्ञकार्यञ्च जलेशस्य महात्मनः । तन्मया साधितं सर्वं यन्ममासीदभीप्सितम् ॥

vāruṇaṃ yajñakāryañca jaleśasya mahātmanaḥ | tanmayā sādhitaṃ sarvaṃ yanmamāsīdabhīpsitam ||

English

The rite of the yajña belonging to Varuṇa, the great-souled lord of the waters103, has been accomplished by me in full; all that I desired has been achieved.104

22.50

Sanskrit

प्रणिपत्य स तं प्रायाद्राजपुत्रः पुरं पितुः । समारुह्य तमेवाश्वं सुपर्णानिलविक्रमम् ॥

praṇipatya sa taṃ prāyādrājaputraḥ puraṃ pituḥ | samāruhya tamevāśvaṃ suparṇānilavikramam ||

English

Having bowed low to him, the prince departed for his father's city, mounting that same horse, whose prowess was like that of Suparṇa105 and the wind.106

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे कुवलयाश्वीये मदालसावियोगो नाम द्वाविंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe kuvalayāśvīye madālasāviyogo nāma dvāviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, named "The Separation from Madālasā," in the Kuvalayāśva section107 of the venerable Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

  1. chapter: This line is a chapter heading, not a verse of the narrative. The GRETIL numbering (94.1) runs on from the previous chapter's colophon (93.15). The next chapter's verses are numbered 22.1 onward. ↩
  2. The two sons: The dual putrau does not say which two sons speak. The line may be a stray or misplaced speaker's formula, since the verses that follow (22.1–2) are narrative and do not read as a speech by two sons. ↩
  3. The reading: putrāvūcatuḥ = putrau + ūcatuḥ, 'the two sons said'. The two speakers are not named and the next verses are narrative, so the line may be a displaced or intrusive formula. One possibility is the two sons of Droṇa, the speaking birds of the Purāṇa's frame story, but the text does not say so. I translate the words as they stand and add no names. ↩
  4. a good many days: The text reads vahutithe; this is taken as a misprint for bahutithe, 'of many days'. ↩
  5. brahmins: Rendering viprāṇām; the brahmins are the priestly class, here the sages and twice-born whom the son is to protect. ↩
  6. The reading: vahutithe is read as bahutithe (b/v confusion in the e-text), 'after many days'. The subject of prāha, rājā, is the king (Śatrujit in the story, not named here); sutam is his son Kuvalayāśva (Ṛtadhvaja). ↩
  7. this horse: The horse is Kuvalaya, the celestial horse by which the prince is known as Kuvalayāśva; the verse itself does not name it. ↩
  8. foremost of the brahmins: dvijamukhya, 'chief of the twice-born', here means the leading brahmins; the sense is the same as vipra in the preceding verse. ↩
  9. The reading: anveṣṭavyā is a gerundive of anu-√iṣ, 'to be sought out'. The sense is that the king's son must look into (see to) the brahmins' freedom from harm; I render it as 'you must look to see that ... are free from harm'. The sentence continues from 22.1, where the king is speaking, so I have kept it as his quoted speech. The absolutive samāruhya has the prince as its agent. ↩
  10. dānavas: Descendants of Danu, a class of asuras, hostile to gods and brahmins. Here the threat is from such beings in general, not from one named dānava. ↩
  11. of sinful birth: pāpayonayaḥ is literally 'having a sinful womb or origin'. The compound can also be read as 'sources of sin', but the sense of sinful birth suits the context. ↩
  12. The reading: pāpayonayaḥ: 'of sinful birth' (bahuvrīhi, yoni = womb or origin) or 'sources of sin'. I chose 'of sinful birth' as the usual sense of the compound when applied to persons. ↩
  13. The reading: (1) The first finding is accepted. The draft left out tathā and so lost the yathā…tathā correlative, and 'then' (tataḥ) was not placed against the verb. The translation now follows the Sanskrit: 'As his father had instructed him … he … then did exactly so.' The pronoun sa is rendered 'he', in apposition to nṛpātmajaḥ. (2) parikramya: 'having gone round' is kept, not 'circumambulated'. The sense is a circuit of the earth, as ordered in 22.1–2, and nothing in the context points to a ritual pradakṣiṇā. I withdraw the draft's earlier remark that sarvām might be hyperbole: it simply qualifies mahīm, 'the whole earth'. (3) nṛpātmajaḥ is nominative singular and the subject here. The glossary describes it as a vocative, but that applies to its other occurrences; this is not a vocative, so no change is needed. The verse does not name the prince, but he is the king's son of the preceding verses, so 'the king's son' is kept. ↩
  14. [went out on his rounds]: The verb is not stated for the first half; the locative absolute ahanyahani anuprāpte pūrvāhne sets the time, and the sense of the previous verses (his protective circuit) supplies the activity. ↩
  15. that slender-waisted woman: Sumadhyā, 'she of the fair waist', refers to the woman the prince brought back earlier in the story; she is not named in this verse. Here tayā ... sumadhyayā is read as 'that fair-waisted one'. ↩
  16. The reading: sumadhyayā may be an epithet ('the slender-waisted one') or a proper name; I take it as an epithet because tayā precedes it. The first half has no finite verb; the sense 'went out on his rounds' is supplied from the context, and the verse may also be read as 'when the forenoon had come, [he did his duty]'. ↩
  17. Yamunā: The river Yamunā, a tributary of the Gaṅgā. ↩
  18. Tālaketu: A dānava, younger brother of Pātālaketu; in the next verse he takes the form of a sage and addresses the prince. ↩
  19. The reading: The e-text reads 'cāran so 'tha', with 'cāran' for the expected 'caran'; I take it as the present participle 'roaming', and the subject 'saḥ' is the king's son (Nṛpātmaja) of the preceding verses. 'Kṛtāśramam' could grammatically qualify either Tālaketu or the bank, but it agrees in case and gender with Tālaketu, so I take it as 'who had made a hermitage'. ↩
  20. a master of māyā: māyāvī means one who possesses or practises māyā, here the power of deceptive disguise, which lets the dānava appear as an ascetic. ↩
  21. the old enmity: The hostility between the dānava brothers and the prince's family, arising from Pātālaketu's earlier abduction of Madālasā and his defeat, told earlier in the narrative. ↩
  22. The reading: The verse does not name Tālaketu; 'that dānava' (so 'tha dānavaḥ) is taken to be Tālaketu, the subject of the preceding verse. 'So 'tha' is read as 'sa atha', 'now'. Munirūpam samāsthitaḥ is rendered 'taken on the form of a sage'; 'having assumed' is equally possible. 'Pūrvavaira' might refer to enmity with the prince's father or with the prince himself; the translation keeps it neutral as 'the old enmity'. ↩
  23. you whose promise is true: Vocative, satyapratiśrava: one whose promises are kept. Tālaketu uses it to bind the prince before stating his request, which comes in 22.9–10. ↩
  24. The reading: brīvīmi is a corrupt or irregular form of bravīmi ('I say'); I translate it as bravīmi. yadīcchasi is read yad īcchasi ('if you wish'), with the lengthened vowel as a metrical or scribal variant of yadicchasi. The text also offers no speaker's line here, since 22.7 has already introduced Tālaketu's speech (sa prāha). ↩
  25. the offerings: iṣṭi: a class of Vedic sacrificial offering; the plural here refers to the offerings required in the rite. ↩
  26. fire-altars: citi: the layered brick fire-altar built for certain large Vedic rites; the sense here is that they must be constructed. ↩
  27. sacrificial fee: dakṣiṇā: the gift made to the priests at a sacrifice. The verse leads to the request in 22.10 for the prince's ornament. ↩
  28. The reading: The text reads dakṣaiṇā, evidently a misprint for dakṣiṇā, and I translate it so. The verse lacks a main verb for the final clause. Verse 22.10 supplies it with 'therefore give me', so I added '[I ask you for this]' in brackets to carry the sense. Also, ca tathā is rendered 'also… as well', and iṣṭayaḥ is rendered 'offerings', but the exact sense may be 'sacrificial rites'. ↩
  29. for the sake of gold: hiraṇyārtham: 'for the purpose of gold', that is, to obtain gold for the sacrifice; the dakṣiṇā (sacrificial fee) was lacking in the previous verse. ↩
  30. protect this hermitage of mine as well: The sentence continues into 22.11, where the dānava says he will return once he has praised Varuṇa in the water; the protection is for that interval. ↩
  31. The reading: māśramam: read as mā + āśramam, 'my hermitage' (mā for me/mama, as Vedic-style form), rather than the negative particle mā ('do not protect'), which makes no sense here. Also, 'cemaṃ' is ca + imaṃ. The verse does not end the sentence: yāvat in 22.11 continues it, so the translation is left open at its close, with ' //' added by convention. ↩
  32. lord of the aquatic creatures: Translates yādasāṃ pati, a standard epithet of Varuṇa as ruler of the waters and the creatures in them. ↩
  33. Vedic mantras of Varuṇa: vāruṇa means 'belonging to Varuṇa', that is, Vedic hymns and formulas addressed to him. ↩
  34. He bowed to him: The subject 'he' (sa) is the king's son, Puṣkaramālin. 'Him' (taṃ) is Tālaketu, the false sage who has just said 'I shall return'. ↩
  35. your honour: bhavān is the respectful form of address, used with a third-person verb (yātu, 'let him go'). ↩
  36. untroubled: nirvyalīka means 'free of vyalīka', which can be offence, displeasure, anxiety or falsehood. Here it means a mind without misgiving or ill will. ↩
  37. The reading: The first word-group prāha yainaṃ is metrically and syntactically faulty, since yā has nothing to agree with. I take it as a corruption of prāha cainam ('and said to him'), or prāhainam. The subject is the king's son, who is answering the false sage. The speech continues in 22.14. ↩
  38. At your command: tavādeśāt is an ablative: 'by your order', 'in accordance with your instruction'. It links to the prince's promise to remain and guard the hermitage. ↩
  39. brahmin: Vocative brahman: the speaker, the prince, addresses the sage as a brahmin. The word is not the neuter brahman of the absolute. ↩
  40. The reading: The verse is a single sentence. 'tavādeśāt' may be read either as 'at your command' (with the guarding) or as 'by your instruction' (with the staying). I took it with the opening clause as a general ground for the whole promise. The pair 'viśrabdhaḥ ... acvaran' is rendered as two qualifiers, 'trusting' and 'without haste'; 'viśrabdha' may also mean 'free from anxiety'. ↩
  41. The two sons: putrau is a dual form: two sons speak together. The Sanskrit does not name them; the speech that follows is not given in this verse. ↩
  42. The reading: The reference 94.17 does not match the context given (chapter 22, verses 9-16). The Sanskrit line putrāvūcatuḥ is only a speaker's line; its speech is not in the verses supplied. Who the two sons are, and what they say, cannot be told from the verses given, so the translation renders only the line itself. Its place in the sequence is also doubtful: the surrounding verses are numbered 22.9-22.16, while this line is numbered 94.17. ↩
  43. Thus addressed: The text reads ekam uktaḥ. This is probably a misprint for evam uktaḥ, 'thus addressed'. ↩
  44. fashioned by māyā: The hermitage is an illusion produced by the pretended sage, who is the demon Tālaketu in disguise. The following verse names him and shows that the whole scene is a deception. ↩
  45. The reading: ekamuktaḥ: read literally it would be 'told one thing' or 'told once'. That gives poor sense after the speeches in 22.13-14. I take it as a corruption of evam uktaḥ, 'thus addressed', the usual formula. The pronouns sa (the pretended sage) and so 'pi (the other, who has promised to guard the hermitage) are resolved from the context of 22.10-14. ↩
  46. The reading: tatparam: it can be read as an adverb, 'thereafter, after that', or as 'intent on that [purpose]'. I chose 'then' because it fits the sequence of events after the dive in 22.15. Also, jalāśayāt tasmāt ('from that body of water') presumably refers to the river in which he dived in 22.15. ↩
  47. pierced in the chest: vakṣasī is the dual accusative of respect, literally 'pierced as to the two sides of the chest'. It means pierced through the chest. ↩
  48. with a spear: śūla is a spear or pike, a piercing weapon. It is not the śakti (javelin) of the glossary. ↩
  49. The reading: yathāśakti is read as 'to the best of his power' (śakti as strength, ability), not as 'according to the javelin' (the glossary's śakti). The adverbial compound makes the sense of strength certain. kenāpi duṣṭadaityena and pāpena are taken as one agent, the Daitya who used māyā. The speaker, Tālaketu, is himself that deceiver, and his account is false. ↩
  50. brought into contact with fire: agnisaṃyoga is here a euphemism for cremation. The causative participle prāpitaḥ means he was made to reach it, and the śūdra ascetics are the agents. ↩
  51. The reading: śūdratāpasaiḥ is taken as a compound meaning 'ascetics who are śūdras'. It could also be read as 'ascetics of the śūdras', but the first reading is the natural one. kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇa is translated as 'ornament for the neck', that is, a necklace. ↩
  52. The reading: The text has 'so 'śvaś ca' (that horse too). The horse is the Kuvalaya, mentioned in the glossary, but the verse does not name it. 'Tenaiva dānavena' is taken to be the Daitya of 22.17, the same wicked one who struck Kuvalayāśva; here he is called a dānava. 'Vai' is left untranslated as a mere particle of emphasis. 'Kṛtārtahreṣāśabdaḥ' is taken as a bahuvrīhi qualifying the horse: 'one by whom a cry of neighing in distress was made'. ↩
  53. without delay: akālikam is read as 'not subject to delay, immediate'. Another sense, 'untimely', would not suit the context. ↩
  54. The reading: akālikam: 'immediate, without delay' (chosen, since the speaker urges prompt action) or 'untimely, out of season'. Also, nṛśaṃsena duṣkṛtakāriṇā is the speaker's self-description as a cruel man and evildoer (Tālaketu's deceit), taken as agent of dṛṣṭam with mayā. The text is accepted as given. ↩
  55. The reading: The Sanskrit text reads hṛdayāśvāsanañ caitad, 'and this [is] a comfort of the heart'. I take it as a predicate of kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇam ('as a comfort to the heart'), rendered as a relative clause. The verb gṛhyatām is a passive imperative, translated 'let it be taken', and rendered here in the natural English imperative 'take'. The particle hi is taken as giving the reason ('for'). ↩
  56. The reading: The verse reference is given as 95.7 but the surrounding verses are numbered 22.17–22.24, so the label looks like a misprint in the e-text. The line is a speaker's line only: putrāvūcatuḥ is putrau + ūcatuḥ, 'the two sons said' (dual). The two sons are not named here and are not identified in this verse, so I have not named them. The speech that follows is not part of this verse. ↩
  57. The reading: (1) 'datbhūmau' is not a valid form and is metrically faulty. It is probably a misprint for 'tad bhūmau' ("it [the ornament] on the ground") or 'dattvā bhūmau'. I read it as 'tad bhūmau' with utsṛjya, 'laid it down on the ground', the object being the kaṇṭhabhūṣaṇa of the preceding verses. (2) 'janaḥ so' is grammatically singular, 'that person', but verse 22.24 shows the whole court, the women, the queens and the king, falling and reviving. I therefore took 'janaḥ' as a collective, 'that company of people'. ↩
  58. The reading: The text reads 'tatkṣaṇāt cetanāṃ' and 'duḥ khitāḥ' with a stray space; I read tatkṣaṇāt cetanāṃ and atiduḥkhitāḥ. 'nṛpayoṣitaḥ' (women of the king, i.e. the household women) and 'rājapatnyaḥ' (royal wives) are given as two groups, and 'sarvāḥ tāḥ' qualifies the former; the king is a third subject. The verb vilepuḥ is plural and governs all three subjects. 'Tatkṣaṇāt' is rendered 'at that very moment', i.e. immediately after the swoon; it could also be 'after a moment', but the ablative of time here favours the former. ↩
  59. which was his: tadīya means "belonging to him", that is, to her husband. Madālasā recognizes the ornament as his, which is why it convinces her that he is dead. ↩
  60. life-breaths: prāṇa: the vital breaths or life-force. "To give up the prāṇas" is the idiom for dying. ↩
  61. The reading: The printed text is corrupt in two places. (1) "d dṛṣṭvā" is read as "tad dṛṣṭvā", "having seen that", with the initial ta lost. (2) "nihanta" is not a form that parses. I read "nihataṃ", the accusative singular agreeing with patim: "heard [that her] husband [was] killed". This gives the construction śrutvā ... nihataṃ patim and fits the context of the verses before and after, which describe the false report of his death. Another conjecture, "nihantā", would make the husband a "slayer", which does not suit the sense. ↩
  62. The reading: samavartata is the imperfect of sam-√vṛt, 'took place, occurred'. It is used here with mahākrandaḥ understood as the subject, which I have rendered 'had arisen' to parallel abhūt. The word svagehe, 'in his own house', I have rendered 'palace' because the house belongs to a king (nṛpateḥ). ↩
  63. The reading: The syntax is loose. 'vinā bhartrā' (without her husband) is taken with 'tāṃ mṛtāṃ madālasām' as 'deprived of her husband'. 'pratyuvāca' is taken as 'replied', since the king answers the lamenting people; the verb is preceded by the absolutives 'dṛṣṭvā' and 'vimṛśya', both with the king as agent. 'susthamānasaḥ' is rendered 'with a composed mind' (literally 'of well-settled mind'). The 'ca' is rendered 'and' to join this verse to the preceding narrative. ↩
  64. The reading: The text reads bhavatām ātmanaḥ tathā, 'of you [all] and likewise of oneself'. I took ātmanaḥ as 'myself', since the king is the speaker, rather than the impersonal 'oneself'. The verse has no verb of weeping beyond roditavyam (gerundive, 'is to be wept'), so 'no reason for weeping' renders na roditavyaṃ paśyāmi, literally 'I do not see [that it is] to be wept'. The genitives bhavatām and ātmanaḥ are read as genitives of the agent or of the person concerned, 'by you and by me'. I chose 'for you or for myself' to keep the sense, and the alternative 'by you and by me' is also possible. The sandhi form bhavatāmātmanas is for bhavatām ātmanaḥ. ↩
  65. they have accomplished what was to be done: Sanskrit kṛtakṛtyatva, the state of one who has done what was to be done, that is, has fulfilled his or her task. For the son this is the protection of the brahmins (see the following verses); for Madālasā it is faithfulness to her husband. ↩
  66. The reading: The printed text reads 'kṛtakṛtyatvāmnamye', which is corrupt. I emend it to 'kṛtakṛtyatvān manye', 'because of having accomplished what was to be done, I consider'. The ablative abstract noun gives the reason, and 'manye' governs 'aśocyau ubhau api' (both as not to be grieved for). This fits the sense and the metre. ↩
  67. at my word: The opening words, 'macchru śrupur', are corrupt in the e-text and give no sense. They are left untranslated. 'madvacanāt' is clear. ↩
  68. The reading: The first pāda begins 'macchru śrupur', which is unintelligible and looks like a misprint or a garbled repetition. It might stand for something like 'mat-' plus a form of √śru or 'pura', but I found no secure reading, so I translate only the intelligible words: madvacanāt ('at my word'), dvijarakṣaṇatatparaḥ ('intent on protecting the brahmins') and prāpto ... mṛtyum ('met death'). I read 'dhīmatām' as an agent genitive, 'by the wise', with śocyaḥ. I take 'me' with 'sutaḥ', 'my son'. ↩
  69. brings prosperity: abhyudayakāri, 'productive of abhyudaya': rise, welfare, prosperity; here the good fortune or merit that follows from such a death. ↩
  70. The reading: Construction: yad deham avaśyaṃ yāti, tad ... saṃtyaktam, nanu tad abhyudayakāri. Both correlatives are now shown. Both 'saṃtyaktam' and the final 'tat' agree with 'deham'. I accept the reviewer's points on 'in any case' (dropped; 'avaśyam' is 'inevitably'), on the agent (now 'cast off by my son', following the instrumental putreṇa) and on the correlative. I partly disagree on 'yadi': it governs the whole clause 'tad dvijānāṃ kṛte ... putreṇa saṃtyaktam', so the condition is the body's being given up for the brahmins, and the son's act is part of it. The draft's placement was not wrong, but the new rendering shows this scope more clearly. 'nanu' is rendered 'surely', as an emphatic assertion. The earlier remark that it marks a rhetorical question is withdrawn. 'kṛte' ('for the sake of') takes the genitive dvijānām. The words 'is [given]' are supplied for the English to parse. ↩
  71. so devoted to her husband: The text reads anuvratāṃ, an accusative form. It is taken as a misprint for the nominative anuvratā, agreeing with iyam, 'this woman'. ↩
  72. The reading: anuvratāṃ (accusative singular) does not agree with the nominative iyam and śocyā. I read it as anuvratā, 'devoted', a misprint of the e-text, or perhaps a metrical licence. The alternative is to join it to a missing governing verb, but nothing in the verse supports that. evam, 'thus', is taken to refer to her devotion as shown in her death after her husband. ↩
  73. The reading: bhavet ... yadi: the optative with yadi is a condition contrary to what has happened, since the next verse says she followed her husband in death. I took 'evam' as 'thus', pointing to separation from her husband, and rendered 'eva' in 'evam' as part of that word. 'Asmākam bāndhavānām ca tathānyeṣām dayāvatām' is taken as three parallel genitives (us, kinsmen, other compassionate people), each in the sense of 'by' with the gerundive śocyā. The text 'bhavedevaṃ' could also be read 'bhaved eva' (emphatic); I kept 'evam'. The adjective viyoginī is rendered as 'separated', not 'widowed', because it is not specifically a widow's term here. ↩
  74. followed her husband: anvā-√yā here means that she followed her husband in death, that is, died after him; it is not said how, and she is understood to have died on hearing the news. ↩
  75. The reading: anuyātā (from anu-√yā) literally means 'went after, followed'. I take it as 'followed in death', as the context of the preceding verses (22.33) and the following verse (22.35, 'who died along with their husbands') indicates. The word atas is rendered 'therefore'. The verse has a feminine form iyam, so the 'lady' is the daughter-in-law mentioned in 22.29 and 22.32. ↩
  76. The reading: The verse has no speaker's line. The 'yā mṛtāḥ saha' is read as 'who have died together with [their husbands]', with bhartrā in pāda c as the implied companion; 'saha' governs bhartrā by sense. 'viyoginyaḥ' is read as separated from the husband, as in the preceding verse. 'Kṛtajñayā' (instrumental, agreeing with anayā) is rendered 'grateful', meaning she acknowledges what her husband has done for her. ↩
  77. both worlds: loka: this world and the world beyond, as named by iha and amutra in the verse. ↩
  78. The reading: mānuṣam can be read as 'merely human, an ordinary man' (chosen, since the rhetorical question implies that a husband giving happiness in both worlds is more than human) or simply 'human'. The word hi is rendered by the form of the rhetorical question. The clause 'when he is the giver...' is the sense of the accusative dātāram in apposition with bhartāram. ↩
  79. nor [is anyone else]: The last na ca of the first half-verse has no stated object. It is read as 'nor [is any other member of the family]'; the bracketed words are supplied to make the English parse. ↩
  80. carried all of us across: tārita is from the verb tṛ, 'to cross over'. The son's sacrifice is said to bring the family safely across, that is, to rescue or save it. The 'all' (sarve) are the speaker, the wife and the son himself. ↩
  81. The reading: The first half-verse ends with 'na ca' and has no stated predicate. I read it as 'nor [is anyone else] to be mourned', as a closing negation after the three persons named. An alternative is to take 'na ca' as only completing the series 'nor I, his mother', with 'na ca' as a metrical filler. I chose the first reading because the following clause says 'all of us' (sarve). ↩
  82. enjoyed only by half: ardhabhuktasya dehasya: of the body only half enjoyed, that is, a life cut off midway. The verse does not say whether the son's death in battle (see 22.39) or his youth is meant; the sense is a life not lived to its full span. ↩
  83. The reading: viprāṇaṃ is metrically and grammatically irregular. The normal genitive plural is viprāṇām, and I read it so, in series with mama and dharmasya, all dependent on ānṛṇyam (freedom from debt towards brahmins, me, and dharma). A reading viprāṇāṃ ... dharmasya as 'the dharma of brahmins' is possible but leaves mama unattached, so I did not choose it. The sense of the three genitives as creditors is inferred from ānṛṇya. ↩
  84. his mother's chastity: satītva is the state of being a satī, a wife wholly faithful to her husband. A son who upholds his family's honor is said to keep his mother's satītva unstained. ↩
  85. The reading: The accusatives satītvam, vaimalyam and śauryam have no verb of their own. I take all three as objects of nātyajat, along with dvijarakṣaṇam: he did not abandon them. Another possibility is that a verb such as 'upheld' or 'proved' is understood for the first three. I chose the simpler reading, since it needs no word added. The subject is the son of v. 38, who is not named in this verse. ↩
  86. The reading: The reference '96.5' does not match the chapter 22 context given. The verse is only the speaker's line 'putrāvūcatuḥ' ('the two sons said'). The dual putrau with ūcatuḥ ('the two sons spoke') is grammatically sound. The surrounding verses (22.34–22.41) do not show who the two sons are, so I have not named them. Verse 22.41 has mātovāca, a separate speaker's line, so this line may be misplaced or a variant reading in the e-text. ↩
  87. of such a kind: tādṛk qualifies putravadham: the killing as it has just been described, that is, the son's death in defence of the brahmin sage. ↩
  88. The reading: dṛṣṭvā tu taṃ patim: the participle has no object other than taṃ patim, so I take it as 'having looked at that husband', that is, after he had spoken. It is not a separate sight of the husband's grief or of the dead son. ↩
  89. men: Sanskrit mānavāḥ, literally 'descendants of Manu', the usual word for human beings; here it implies men worthy of the name. ↩
  90. have borne children in vain: Sanskrit vṛthāprajā, a compound meaning 'one whose offspring is in vain'; rendered here as a predicate of the mother. ↩
  91. The reading: In 22.42, 'niḥśvasanto 'tiduḥkhitāḥ' could qualify the grieving kinsmen or the dying. I took it as describing the dying, since it agrees in case with 'ye ... mriyante'; the kinsmen are in the genitive. ↩
  92. with his back turned on: parāṅmukhaḥ ('with face turned away') takes the genitives arthināṃ, mitravargasya and vidviṣām. For petitioners and friends it means turning away from their need. For enemies it means turning away in flight. ↩
  93. the mother of a brave son: vīrasūḥ, 'one who bears a hero'. It is a traditional title of honour for a mother. ↩
  94. The reading: The genitive vidviṣām after parāṅmukhaḥ can mean either 'turning away from enemies' (that is, fleeing) or 'turning away from the enemies' request'. I chose the first, flight, because the context is the battle death of a son. In 22.44 'arthin' is read as 'petitioner' (one who asks for something); 'seeker of wealth' is also possible. ↩
  95. The two sons: putrau is a dual nominative, so two sons speak together. The reference 96.12 does not match the surrounding chapter 22 numbering, and the speakers are not identified in this verse. ↩
  96. The reading: The verse reference (96.12) differs from the chapter 22 context. The verse is only a speaker's line, so it has no further content. Dual putrau is rendered as 'the two sons' without naming them, since the text does not. ↩
  97. had the rites performed: saṃskāra here means the funeral rites (cremation) for the dead woman, who is the wife of the king's son. ↩
  98. offered water to his son: The offering of water (udaka) to the dead is the funerary libation, made after bathing. ↩
  99. The reading: putrapatnīm: 'the son's wife' (the king's son's wife) is taken as the object of alambhayat, i.e. the rites were performed for her. The causative alambhayat (from labh) literally means 'caused her to obtain' the rites. Whose son putrāya refers to is not stated; it is read as the king's own son, since the king performs the water-offering. The text before and after (Tālaketu, the son who died) supports this reading only loosely, and the identification of the dead persons is not certain from this verse alone. ↩
  100. in the same way: tathaiva: the text does not say what the comparison is with; it probably refers back to the participle nirgamya, 'having come out', used of persons in 22.46. ↩
  101. son of the protector of the earth: bhūpālaputra: a vocative addressing the prince, the same person as 'the king's son' in the previous verse. ↩
  102. The reading: (1) In 22.48 the clause 'kāryaṃ cirābhilaṣitaṃ tvayi ... sthite' has no finite verb. I took it as a nominative subject with a locative absolute ('tvayi ... sthite', 'with you standing unshaken here') and supplied '[is accomplished]' in brackets, as the sense requires and as 22.49 ('that was accomplished by me') confirms. The alternative, 'the long-desired task rests on you, who stand unshaken here', suits the context less well. I took cirābhilaṣitam as 'long desired' without specifying by whom, though it is plainly Tālaketu. (2) tathaiva: I give it as 'in the same way', leaving the point of comparison open, and I removed the earlier note's claim that the king came out of water in 22.46. There he came out and bathed outside (bahiḥ snātaḥ). (3) sthite could be 'standing' or 'remaining, being firm'. I kept 'standing', which goes with avicale 'unshaken'. ↩
  103. Varuṇa, the great-souled lord of the waters: jaleśa, 'lord of the waters', is Varuṇa, the god of the waters; the rite is the yajña Tālaketu was performing for him. ↩
  104. The reading: vāruṇaṃ yajñakārya may be read as 'the sacrificial task pertaining to Varuṇa' (chosen) or 'the sacrificial duty enjoined by Varuṇa'. The text does not name Varuṇa; he is identified from vāruṇa and jaleśa. The yajña is therefore Tālaketu's rite for Varuṇa, not a previous sacrifice. ↩
  105. Suparṇa: Suparṇa is another name of Garuḍa, the bird who carries Viṣṇu, proverbial for swiftness. ↩
  106. The reading: The compound suparṇānilavikramam may be read as 'whose prowess equals that of Suparṇa and the wind' (a comparison, as chosen) or, less likely, as 'whose prowess was that of Suparṇa and the wind' taken as a plain list. The sense is the same. The tam before aśvam is read as qualifying the horse by tameva, 'that very horse', the one on which he had come. The tam after praṇipatya refers to Tālaketu. ↩
  107. Kuvalayāśva section: The Kuvalayāśva episode within the Purāṇa, here called kuvalayāśvīya; the story of Ṛtadhvaja, called Kuvalayāśva after his horse, and of Madālasā. ↩

Adhyāya 23

Sanskrit

त्रयोविंशो ऽध्यायः

trayoviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Twenty-Three1

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons2 said:3

23.1

Sanskrit

स राजपुत्रः संप्राप्य वेगादात्मपुरं ततः । पित्रोर्ववन्दिषुः पादौ दिदृक्षुश्च मदालसाम् ॥

sa rājaputraḥ saṃprāpya vegādātmapuraṃ tataḥ | pitrorvavandiṣuḥ pādau didṛkṣuśca madālasām ||

English

That prince, having then quickly reached his own city, wished to bow at the feet of his parents4 and wished to see Madālasā.5

23.2

Sanskrit

ददर्श जनमुद्विग्नमप्रहृष्टमुखं पुरः । पुनश्च विस्मिताकारं प्रहृष्टवदनं ततः ॥

dadarśa janamudvignamaprahṛṣṭamukhaṃ puraḥ | punaśca vismitākāraṃ prahṛṣṭavadanaṃ tataḥ ||

English

23.2–3He saw before him people6, agitated, their faces joyless; and then again [he saw people] with an astonished look and glad faces; and [he saw] another group, eyes wide open, crying, "Thank heaven! Thank heaven!"7, embracing one another, full of great curiosity.8

23.3

Sanskrit

अन्यमुत्फुल्लनयनं दिष्ट्या दिष्ट्येतिवादिनम् । परिष्वजन्तमन्योन्यमतिकौतूहलान्वितम् ॥

anyamutphullanayanaṃ diṣṭyā diṣṭyetivādinam | pariṣvajantamanyonyamatikautūhalānvitam ||

English

Its English is given with 23.2–3, above.

23.4

Sanskrit

चिरं जीवोरुकल्याण ! हतास्ते परिपन्थिनः । पित्रोः प्रह्लादय मनस्तथास्माकमकण्टकम् ॥

ciraṃ jīvorukalyāṇa ! hatāste paripanthinaḥ | pitroḥ prahlādaya manastathāsmākamakaṇṭakam ||

English

"Live long, O you of great good fortune9! Your enemies have been slain. Gladden the minds of your parents, and likewise make our kingdom free of thorns10."11†

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons12 said:13

23.5

Sanskrit

इत्येवं वादिभिः पौरैः पुरः पृष्ठे च संवृतः । तत्क्षणप्रभवानन्दः प्रविवेश पितुर्गृहम् ॥

ityevaṃ vādibhiḥ pauraiḥ puraḥ pṛṣṭhe ca saṃvṛtaḥ | tatkṣaṇaprabhavānandaḥ praviveśa piturgṛham ||

English

Surrounded in front and behind by townsmen who spoke in this way, and with joy arising at that very moment, he entered his father's house.

23.6

Sanskrit

पिता च तं परिष्वज्य माता चान्ये च बान्धवाः । चिरं जीवेति कल्याणीर्ददुस्तस्मै तदाशिषः ॥

pitā ca taṃ pariṣvajya mātā cānye ca bāndhavāḥ | ciraṃ jīveti kalyāṇīrdadustasmai tadāśiṣaḥ ||

English

His father, his mother and his other kinsmen embraced him, and then they gave him those auspicious blessings14, saying, "Live long!"15

23.7

Sanskrit

प्रणिपत्य ततः सो ऽथ किमेतदिति विस्मितः । पप्रच्छ पितरं तात ! सो ऽस्मै सम्यक् तदुक्तवान् ॥

praṇipatya tataḥ so 'tha kimetaditi vismitaḥ | papraccha pitaraṃ tāta ! so 'smai samyak taduktavān ||

English

Then he bowed down, and astonished, he asked his father, "What is this, father?" And the father told him all of it fully.16

23.8

Sanskrit

स भार्यां तां मृतां श्रुत्वा हृदयेष्टां मदालसाम् । पितरौ च पुरो दृष्ट्वा लज्जाशोकाब्धिमध्यगः ॥

sa bhāryāṃ tāṃ mṛtāṃ śrutvā hṛdayeṣṭāṃ madālasām | pitarau ca puro dṛṣṭvā lajjāśokābdhimadhyagaḥ ||

English

23.8–9Hearing that his wife Madālasā, dear to his heart, was dead, and seeing his parents before him, he sank into the middle of an ocean of shame and grief17. He thought: "That young girl, a faithful wife, heard that I had met my death18, and gave up her life. Shame on me, whose heart is so hard!"19

23.9

Sanskrit

चिन्तयामास सा बाला मां श्रुत्वा निधनं गतम् । तत्याज जीवितं साध्वी धिङ्मां निष्ठुरमानसम् ॥

cintayāmāsa sā bālā māṃ śrutvā nidhanaṃ gatam | tatyāja jīvitaṃ sādhvī dhiṅmāṃ niṣṭhuramānasam ||

English

Its English is given with 23.8–9, above.

23.10

Sanskrit

नृशंसो ऽहमनार्यो ऽहं विना तां मृगलोचनाम् । मत्कृते निधनं प्राप्तां यज्जीवाम्यतिनिर्घृणः ॥

nṛśaṃso 'hamanāryo 'haṃ vinā tāṃ mṛgalocanām | matkṛte nidhanaṃ prāptāṃ yajjīvāmyatinirghṛṇaḥ ||

English

I am cruel, I am ignoble, since I live on, utterly pitiless, without her, the deer-eyed one20, who met her death because of me.

23.11

Sanskrit

पुनः स चिन्तयामास परिसंस्तभ्य मानसम् । मोहोद्गममपास्याशु निः श्वस्योच्छवस्य चातरः ॥

punaḥ sa cintayāmāsa parisaṃstabhya mānasam | mohodgamamapāsyāśu niḥ śvasyocchavasya cātaraḥ ||

English

23.11–12Again he reflected, distressed, having steadied his mind, quickly thrown off the onset of delusion, and sighed and drawn breath: “‘She is dead’ on my account. If I give up my life [for that], what favour have I done her? This, however, is praiseworthy in women.”21

23.12

Sanskrit

मृतेति सा मन्नमित्तं त्यजामि यदि जीवितम् । किं मयोपकृतं तस्याः श्लाघ्यमेतत्तु योषिताम् ॥

mṛteti sā mannamittaṃ tyajāmi yadi jīvitam | kiṃ mayopakṛtaṃ tasyāḥ ślāghyametattu yoṣitām ||

English

Its English is given with 23.11–12, above.

23.13

Sanskrit

यदि रोदिमि वा दीनो हा प्रियेति ! वदन्मुहुः । तथाप्यश्लाघ्यमेतन्नो वयं हि पुरुषाः किल ॥

yadi rodimi vā dīno hā priyeti ! vadanmuhuḥ | tathāpyaślāghyametanno vayaṃ hi puruṣāḥ kila ||

English

Or if I weep in my misery, crying out again and again, "Alas, my beloved!", even so this would not be praiseworthy for us, for we are men, after all.22

Sanskrit

अथ शोकजडो दीनो स्त्रजा हीनो मलान्वितः ।

atha śokajaḍo dīno strajā hīno malānvitaḥ |

English

Then [he was] numbed by grief, wretched, bereft of a garland, and covered with dirt.23

23.14

Sanskrit

विपक्षस्य भविष्यामि ततः परिभवास्पदम् ॥

vipakṣasya bhaviṣyāmi tataḥ paribhavāspadam ||

English

As a result I shall become an object of the enemy's contempt24.25

23.15

Sanskrit

मयारिशातनं कार्यं राज्ञः शुश्रुषणं पितुः । जीवितं तस्य चायत्तं सन्त्याज्यं तत्कथं मया ॥

mayāriśātanaṃ kāryaṃ rājñaḥ śuśruṣaṇaṃ pituḥ | jīvitaṃ tasya cāyattaṃ santyājyaṃ tatkathaṃ mayā ||

English

The destruction of enemies must be accomplished by me, and service to the king, [my] father; and his life is dependent [on me]26. How then can that [life of mine] be abandoned by me?27†

23.16

Sanskrit

किन्त्वत्र मन्ये कर्तव्यस्त्यागो भागस्य योषितः । स चापि नोपकाराय तन्वङ्ग्याः किन्तु सर्वथा ॥

kintvatra manye kartavyastyāgo bhāgasya yoṣitaḥ | sa cāpi nopakārāya tanvaṅgyāḥ kintu sarvathā ||

English

But in this matter I think that the abandonment of the woman's share28 is what must be done. And that too is not for the benefit of the slender-limbed one, but in every way.29†

23.17

Sanskrit

मया नृशंस्यं कर्तव्यं नोपकार्यपकारि च । या मदर्थे ऽत्यजत् प्राणांस्तदर्थे ऽल्पमिदं मम ॥

mayā nṛśaṃsyaṃ kartavyaṃ nopakāryapakāri ca | yā madarthe 'tyajat prāṇāṃstadarthe 'lpamidaṃ mama ||

English

Cruelty must be done by me30, which is not beneficial and does harm. She gave up her life-breaths for my sake; for her sake this is small for me.31†

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons said:32

23.18

Sanskrit

इति कृत्वा मतिं सो ऽथ निष्पाद्योदकदानिकम् । क्रियाश्चानन्तरं कृत्वा प्रत्युवाच ऋतध्वजः ॥

iti kṛtvā matiṃ so 'tha niṣpādyodakadānikam | kriyāścānantaraṃ kṛtvā pratyuvāca ṛtadhvajaḥ ||

English

Having thus made up his mind, Ṛtadhvaja then performed the water-offering33, and after that the other rites as well, and replied.34

Sanskrit

ऋतध्वज उवाच

ṛtadhvaja uvāca

English

Ṛtadhvaja said:

23.19

Sanskrit

यदि सा मम तन्वङ्गी न स्याद्भार्या मदालसा । अस्मिन् जन्मनि नान्या मे भवित्री सहचारिणी ॥

yadi sā mama tanvaṅgī na syādbhāryā madālasā | asmin janmani nānyā me bhavitrī sahacāriṇī ||

English

If that slender-limbed Madālasā is not to be my wife, then in this birth no other woman will be my companion.35

23.20

Sanskrit

तामृते मृगशावाक्षीं गन्धर्वतनयामहम् । न भोक्ष्ये योषितं काञ्चिदिति सत्यं मयोदितम् ॥

tāmṛte mṛgaśāvākṣīṃ gandharvatanayāmaham | na bhokṣye yoṣitaṃ kāñciditi satyaṃ mayoditam ||

English

Except for her, the fawn-eyed daughter of the Gandharva, I will not enjoy36 any woman. This is the truth I have spoken.

23.21

Sanskrit

सद्धर्मचारिणीं पत्नीं तां मुक्त्वा गजगामिनीम्, । काञ्चिन्नाङ्गीकरिष्यामीत्येतत् सत्यं मयोदितम् ॥

saddharmacāriṇīṃ patnīṃ tāṃ muktvā gajagāminīm, | kāñcinnāṅgīkariṣyāmītyetat satyaṃ mayoditam ||

English

Leaving aside her, my wife, the elephant-gaited37 maiden who walks in the true dharma38, I will not take any other woman as my own. This is the truth that I have spoken.39†

Sanskrit

पुत्रावूचतुः

putrāvūcatuḥ

English

The two sons40 said:41

23.22

Sanskrit

परित्यज्य च स्त्रीभोगान् तात ! सर्वंस्तया विना । क्रीडन्नास्ते समं तुल्यैर्वयस्यैः शीलसम्पदा ॥

parityajya ca strībhogān tāta ! sarvaṃstayā vinā | krīḍannāste samaṃ tulyairvayasyaiḥ śīlasampadā ||

English

Father, he has given up all enjoyments of women, since he is without her, and he stays on, playing together with friends of his own age who are his equals in the wealth of good conduct.42

23.23

Sanskrit

एतत्तस्य परं कार्यं तात ! तत् केन शक्यते । कर्तुमत्यर्थदुष्प्राप्यमीश्वरैः किमुतेतरैः ॥

etattasya paraṃ kāryaṃ tāta ! tat kena śakyate | kartumatyarthaduṣprāpyamīśvaraiḥ kimutetaraiḥ ||

English

This is his supreme task, father. Who is able to do that? It is exceedingly hard to achieve by lords, how much less by others?43

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

23.24

Sanskrit

इति वाक्यं तयोः श्रुत्वा विमर्शमगमत्पिता । विमृश्य चाह तौ पुत्रौ नागराट् प्रहसन्निव ॥

iti vākyaṃ tayoḥ śrutvā vimarśamagamatpitā | vimṛśya cāha tau putrau nāgarāṭ prahasanniva ||

English

Having heard this speech of the two, their father fell into deliberation; and after deliberating, the king of the nāgas44, as if laughing45, said to those two sons:46

Sanskrit

नागराडश्वतर उवाच

nāgarāḍaśvatara uvāca

English

23.25The nāga king Aśvatara said: If men, knowing "it cannot be done," will not make an effort in action, then from the loss of exertion there comes a further loss beyond that.47

23.25

Sanskrit

यद्यशक्यमिति ज्ञात्वा न करिष्यन्ति मानवाः । कर्मण्युद्यममुद्योगहान्या हानिस्ततः परम् ॥

yadyaśakyamiti jñātvā na kariṣyanti mānavāḥ | karmaṇyudyamamudyogahānyā hānistataḥ param ||

English

Its English is given with 23.25, above.

23.26

Sanskrit

आरभेत नरः कर्म स्वपौरुषमहापयन् । निष्पत्तिः कर्मणो दैवे पौरुषे च व्यवसथिता ॥

ārabheta naraḥ karma svapauruṣamahāpayan | niṣpattiḥ karmaṇo daive pauruṣe ca vyavasathitā ||

English

A man should undertake an action without letting his own manly effort48 go to waste. The accomplishment of an action rests on fate49 and on manly effort.50

23.27

Sanskrit

तस्मादहं तथा यत्नं करिष्ये पुत्रकावितः । तपश्चर्यां समास्थाय यथैतत् साध्यते ऽचिरात् ॥

tasmādahaṃ tathā yatnaṃ kariṣye putrakāvitaḥ | tapaścaryāṃ samāsthāya yathaitat sādhyate 'cirāt ||

English

Therefore, my two dear sons51, from now on I shall make such an effort, resorting to the practice of austerities52, that this may be accomplished before long.53

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

23.28

Sanskrit

एवमुक्त्वा स नागेन्द्रः प्लक्षावतरणं गिरेः । तीर्थं हिमवतो गत्वा तपस्तेपे सुदुश्चरम् ॥

evamuktvā sa nāgendraḥ plakṣāvataraṇaṃ gireḥ | tīrthaṃ himavato gatvā tapastepe suduścaram ||

English

Having spoken thus, that lord of the nāgas went to Plakṣāvataraṇa54, a tīrtha on the mountain Himavat55, and performed extremely hard austerities.56

23.29

Sanskrit

तुष्टाव गीर्भिश्च ततस्तत्र देवीं सरस्वतीम् । तन्मना नियताहारो भूत्वा त्रिषवणाप्लुतः ॥

tuṣṭāva gīrbhiśca tatastatra devīṃ sarasvatīm | tanmanā niyatāhāro bhūtvā triṣavaṇāplutaḥ ||

English

Then, in that place, having become intent on her in mind, restrained in food, and bathing at the three savanas57, he praised the goddess Sarasvatī58 with words of praise.59

Sanskrit

अश्वतर उवाच

aśvatara uvāca

English

Aśvatara said:

23.30

Sanskrit

जगद्धात्रीमहं देवीमारिराधयिषुः शुभाम् । स्तोष्ये प्रणम्य शिरसा ब्रह्मयोनिं सरस्वतीम् ॥

jagaddhātrīmahaṃ devīmārirādhayiṣuḥ śubhām | stoṣye praṇamya śirasā brahmayoniṃ sarasvatīm ||

English

I, wishing to propitiate the auspicious goddess, the sustainer of the world, shall bow with my head and praise Sarasvatī, whose source is Brahmā60.61

23.31

Sanskrit

सदसद्देवि ! सय् किञ्चिन्मोक्षवच्चार्थवत् पदम् । तत्सर्वं त्वय्यसंयोगं योगवद्देवि ! संस्थितम् ॥

sadasaddevi ! say kiñcinmokṣavaccārthavat padam | tatsarvaṃ tvayyasaṃyogaṃ yogavaddevi ! saṃsthitam ||

English

O goddess, whatever there is, being or non-being, and whatever word62 has liberation63 and meaning in it: all that stands in you, goddess, without conjunction, yet as though joined in yoga64.65

23.32

Sanskrit

त्वमक्षरं परं देवि ! यत्र सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितम् । अक्षरं परमं देवि ! संस्थितं परमाणुवत् ॥

tvamakṣaraṃ paraṃ devi ! yatra sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitam | akṣaraṃ paramaṃ devi ! saṃsthitaṃ paramāṇuvat ||

English

You are the imperishable66, the supreme, O goddess, in whom everything is established. O goddess, the supreme imperishable abides [in you] like an atom67.68†

23.33

Sanskrit

अक्षरं परमं ब्रह्म विश्वञ्चैतत् क्षरात्मकम् । दारुण्यवस्थितो वह्निर्भौमाश्च परमाणवः ॥

akṣaraṃ paramaṃ brahma viśvañcaitat kṣarātmakam | dāruṇyavasthito vahnirbhaumāśca paramāṇavaḥ ||

English

The imperishable is the supreme brahman69, and this universe is of the nature of the perishable. Fire abides in wood, and the atoms are of the earth.7071

23.34

Sanskrit

तथा त्वयि स्थितं ब्रह्म जगच्चेदमशेषतः । ओङ्काराक्षरसंस्थानं यत्तु देवि ! स्थिरास्थिरम् ॥

tathā tvayi sthitaṃ brahma jagaccedamaśeṣataḥ | oṅkārākṣarasaṃsthānaṃ yattu devi ! sthirāsthiram ||

English

So too brahman72 abides in you, and this whole world without remainder, O goddess—that which is steady and unsteady, whose form is established in the syllable oṅkāra73.74

23.35

Sanskrit

तत्र मात्रात्रयं सर्वमस्ति यद्देवि नास्ति च । त्रयो लोकास्त्रयो वेदास्त्रैविद्यं पावकत्रयम् ॥

tatra mātrātrayaṃ sarvamasti yaddevi nāsti ca | trayo lokāstrayo vedāstraividyaṃ pāvakatrayam ||

English

There, in that syllable75, is the triple mātrā76: everything that exists, O goddess, and what does not exist. There are the three worlds, the three Vedas, the threefold knowledge77, and the three fires78.79

23.36

Sanskrit

त्रीणि ज्योतींषि वर्णाश्च त्रयो धर्मागमास्तथा । त्रयो गुणास्त्रयः शब्दस्त्रयो वेदास्तथाश्रमाः ॥

trīṇi jyotīṃṣi varṇāśca trayo dharmāgamāstathā | trayo guṇāstrayaḥ śabdastrayo vedāstathāśramāḥ ||

English

The three lights, and the varṇas80; likewise the three sources of dharma81; the three guṇas82, the three sounds, the three Vedas83, and likewise the āśramas84.85

23.37

Sanskrit

त्रयः कालास्तथावस्थाः पितरो ऽहर्निशादयः । एतन्मात्रात्रयं देवि ! तव रूपं सरस्वति ॥

trayaḥ kālāstathāvasthāḥ pitaro 'harniśādayaḥ | etanmātrātrayaṃ devi ! tava rūpaṃ sarasvati ||

English

The three times, likewise the [three] states, the ancestors86, and day and night and the rest: this triad of mātrās87 is your form, O goddess Sarasvatī.88

Sanskrit

विभिन्नदर्शिनामाद्या ब्रह्मणो हि सनातनाः ।

vibhinnadarśināmādyā brahmaṇo hi sanātanāḥ |

English

[They are] the primeval and eternal [forms] of Brahman89 for those who see things as distinct90.91

23.38

Sanskrit

सोमसंस्था हविः संस्थाः पाकसंस्थाश्च सप्त याः ॥

somasaṃsthā haviḥ saṃsthāḥ pākasaṃsthāśca sapta yāḥ ||

English

23.38–39The seven soma sacrificial modes92, the seven oblation modes and the seven cooking modes: these, O goddess, are performed by the brahmavādins93 through uttering you. And likewise there is another, indescribable, supreme, joined with a half-mātrā94.95

23.39

Sanskrit

तास्त्वदुच्चारणाद्देवि ! क्रियन्ते ब्रह्मवादिभिः । अनिर्देश्यं तथा चान्यदर्धमात्रान्वितं परम् ॥

tāstvaduccāraṇāddevi ! kriyante brahmavādibhiḥ | anirdeśyaṃ tathā cānyadardhamātrānvitaṃ param ||

English

Its English is given with 23.38–39, above.

23.40

Sanskrit

अविकार्यक्षयं दिव्यं परिणामविवर्जितम् । तवैतत्परमं रूपं यन्न शक्यं मयोदितुम् ॥

avikāryakṣayaṃ divyaṃ pariṇāmavivarjitam | tavaitatparamaṃ rūpaṃ yanna śakyaṃ mayoditum ||

English

This highest form of yours96 is divine, unchangeable and imperishable, free from all transformation; it is something that I am not able to express.97

23.41

Sanskrit

न चास्ये न च तज्जिह्वा ताम्रोष्ठादिभिरुच्यते । इन्द्रो ऽपि वसवो ब्रह्मा चन्द्राकौ ज्योतिरेव च ॥

na cāsye na ca tajjihvā tāmroṣṭhādibhirucyate | indro 'pi vasavo brahmā candrākau jyotireva ca ||

English

It is spoken of neither in the mouth, nor [by] its tongue98, nor by the copper-red lips and the rest. Indra too, the Vasus99, Brahmā, the moon and the sun, and light itself100†

23.42

Sanskrit
