Having joined them, his own sons and the king's son244, that lord of the great serpents245, truthful in his speech, self-possessed and filled with joy, took the foods and the wines as each was fitting, he who was an enjoyer of pleasures.246

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे मदालसोपाख्याने कुवलयाश्वपातालगमनं नाम त्रयोविंसो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe madālasopākhyāne kuvalayāśvapātālagamanaṃ nāma trayoviṃso 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, named "The Descent of Kuvalayāśva247 to Pātāla248," in the Madālasā episode249 of the revered Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.250

  1. Chapter Twenty-Three: The e-text gives this chapter heading as verse 97.1, though it is only a chapter title (trayoviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ, 'the twenty-third chapter'). The numbering of the e-text is irregular here. ↩
  2. The two sons: putrau is a dual form, so two sons speak. The e-text's verse numbering is irregular here: this line stands where the next chapter's opening was expected, and the sons are not named. They are presumably the two sons of Ṛtadhvaja (Kuvalayāśva) and Madālasā, but the preceding lines do not say so. ↩
  3. The reading: putrāvūcatuḥ: the verse has no context. The two sons are not identified in the lines given, and the line does not fit the sequence of chapters 22 and 23 (the speech introduced here is not found in the following verses). It looks like a stray or misplaced speaker line in the e-text. I have translated it literally as a speaker's line, with no closing mark. ↩
  4. bow at the feet of his parents: Touching or bowing at the feet is the customary mark of reverence toward elders. ↩
  5. The reading: The sentence has no finite verb in this verse. The absolutive 'saṃprāpya' and the desideratives 'vavandiṣuḥ' and 'didṛkṣuḥ' stay open until 23.2, where 'dadarśa' (he saw) supplies the main verb. I render the verse as a self-contained clause, with the two desiderative adjectives treated as predicates ('wished to...'). The reading 'pitror vavandiṣuḥ' is taken as pitroḥ (genitive dual) + vavandiṣuḥ, with sandhi giving 'pitrorvavandiṣuḥ'. 'Pādau' (accusative dual) is the object of the desiderative 'vavandiṣuḥ', 'wishing to bow to', so 'pitroḥ pādau' means 'the feet of his parents'. ↩
  6. people: Sanskrit janam and anyam are singular collectives. Anyonyam ("one another") and pariṣvajantam ("embracing") imply several persons, so a group is meant. ↩
  7. "Thank heaven! Thank heaven!": Sanskrit diṣṭyā, literally "by good fortune", is an exclamation of joy at welcome news. It is repeated here. ↩
  8. The reading: 1. Janam and anyam are singular but collective, and the participles agree with them in the singular. English needs the plural ("their faces", "embracing one another"). I rendered anyam as "another group", as the reviewer asks, and took the participles with it. 2. In punaś ca ... tataḥ the Sanskrit gives no object and does not say whether the people are the same as in the first clause. I removed the draft's "them" and supplied only "[people]", which is neutral. Whether the mood changes in the same crowd or a different crowd is shown is left open. 3. I kept the final " //" although the reviewer asks to remove it as stray. The series rule requires every passage to end with it. The two verse segments are given separately and carry no " //". 4. Udvigna is rendered "agitated", which suits it better than "uneasy". ↩
  9. O you of great good fortune: The vocative urukalyāṇa is addressed by the people to the prince, who is the subject of the preceding verses. ↩
  10. free of thorns: akaṇṭaka, "thornless": a standard expression for a realm cleared of enemies and troublemakers. ↩
  11. The reading: asmākam akaṇṭakam: the Sanskrit has only "thornless for us" and does not say what is to be thornless. I supply "our kingdom" in the translation, not in brackets, which is an interpretive choice. Literally: "[make] thornless for us". Another reading takes akaṇṭakam as an adverb, "make our [minds/lives] free from thorns". Since manas stands in the preceding clause, "gladden our minds free of thorns" is also possible. I chose the kingdom reading as the usual sense of akaṇṭaka. The speakers are the townsfolk of 23.3, not the two sons who speak in 97.2. The vocative with the space before the exclamation mark is a printing feature. ↩
  12. The two sons: putrau ūcatuḥ is a dual: two sons speak. In this passage the pair are presumably Śatrujit's two sons, Ṛtadhvaja and his brother, who narrate the story to their father; the verse itself does not name them. ↩
  13. The reading: The verse is only a speaker's line, a dual 'putrau ūcatuḥ'. Its numbering (97.7) and the placement before chapter 23's verses are an artifact of the e-text, where the speaker line is stored out of order. The speakers' identity is not stated in the line itself, so I give the plain dual and leave the identification to the note as a conjecture. ↩
  14. those auspicious blessings: The verse has kalyāṇīḥ ('auspicious') and tadāśiṣaḥ ('those blessings'); tad refers to the blessing of long life quoted in the verse (ciraṃ jīva). ↩
  15. The reading: Reading of tadāśiṣaḥ: taken as tad + āśiṣaḥ ('those blessings'), with kalyāṇīḥ as its adjective. The quoted words 'ciraṃ jīva' are the content of the blessings. ↩
  16. The reading: The vocative 'tāta' is placed inside the son's question, 'What is this, father?', since it follows 'papraccha pitaraṃ' in the verse and is the son's address to his father. The second 'saḥ' (so 'smai) is the father, the subject of 'uktavān', and 'asmai' is the son. 'Tat' (taduktavān) is rendered 'all of it', meaning the matter just asked about, i.e. 'that' the son enquired of. ↩
  17. he sank into the middle of an ocean of shame and grief: lajjāśokābdhimadhyagaḥ is a compound: 'gone to the middle of the ocean of shame and grief'. The subject is the same prince as in 23.7, understood from the context and not named in these verses; the speaker of 23.7 is Puṣkaramālin. ↩
  18. had met my death: nidhanaṃ gatam is literally 'gone to death'. The participle agrees with māṃ, 'me'. ↩
  19. The reading: The subject of the verses is not named. It is the prince from the previous verse, Puṣkaramālin in the glossary, so 'he' is used. The sentence in 23.9 begins with sā bālā, which is read as the content of his thought; no 'saying' verb appears, only cintayāmāsa. The fifth word of 23.9 is dhiṅ, 'shame on', with the accusative māṃ. ↩
  20. deer-eyed one: Translates mṛgalocanā, a conventional epithet of a beautiful woman, here said of Madālasā. ↩
  21. The reading: 1) ātaraḥ (23.11) is probably a misprint for āturaḥ, "distressed, afflicted"; I translated it as "distressed", as the sense requires. 2) mannamittam (23.12) is evidently a misprint for mannimittam, "because of me, on my account". 3) mṛteti is read as mṛtā iti, "[she is] dead", the quoted ground of his grief. The clause mṛteti sā mannimittam can be taken either as an independent thought or as the ground for giving up life. I took it as the former, with the "if" clause following. ↩
  22. The reading: Reading of 'etanno': etad + naḥ ('this ... for us'), with 'naḥ' as a genitive of the speaker used for 'me'. I took it as 'for us' because the verse goes on with 'vayam ... puruṣāḥ' (we are men). The 'hā priyeti' is taken as quoted speech: hā priye iti, with priyā in the vocative, 'Alas, beloved!'. I rendered it 'my beloved' for natural English. The verse ends with the particles 'hi ... kila'. I rendered them together as 'after all', since they carry the sense of a reminder or a reason. ↩
  23. The reading: Both findings are accepted. (1) 'strajā' is not a word. I read 'srajā', instrumental of 'sraj' (garland), the regular complement of 'hīnaḥ' ('deprived of'); the 't' is an intrusive misprint. I removed the possessive 'his' from the draft because the Sanskrit has none. (2) 'dīno' is irregular before an initial 's', where 'dīnaḥ' would stand. I read it as 'dīnaḥ', nominative singular, 'wretched'. It may be a slip, or a trace of a lost 'dīno ’srajā' that was misread. (3) The verse has no finite verb and no named subject, so I supplied only '[he was]'. The adjectives describe a man, presumably the king's son who has been brooding over Madālasā's death in 23.8–13. (4) The reference '97.17' does not belong to chapter 23. The verse also interrupts the sequence: 23.13 ends with 'vayaṃ hi puruṣāḥ kila' and 23.14 begins 'vipakṣasya bhaviṣyāmi', which has its own subject 'I'. It may be an intrusive or misplaced line. I translated it as given and did not try to join it to the surrounding sentences. ↩
  24. an object of the enemy's contempt: paribhavāspadam is a compound of paribhava (contempt, humiliation) and āspada (seat, place, object), and is the predicate of bhaviṣyāmi. The genitive vipakṣasya depends on it. The verse completes the speaker's reasoning in 23.12–13, where he considers dying (tyajāmi yadi jīvitam) or weeping (yadi rodimi) and judges both unworthy of a man. ↩
  25. The reading: tataḥ can mean 'then', 'therefore' or 'from that'. I now take it in the ablative sense 'as a result', since the contempt follows from the conduct considered in 23.12–13 (dying or weeping). vipakṣasya is a genitive. I now keep it as 'of the enemy' and have dropped the 'my' and the dative 'to', neither of which is in the Sanskrit. It could also be read as 'of the opposing party', but 'enemy' is the usual sense of vipakṣa. The reviewer notes that dīno in 23.13 is not echoed here. That is right, but it is not in this verse and needs no rendering. I do not call the 'if'-clauses a strict protasis of this verse: 23.13 ends with a complete statement (tathāpy aślāghyam etat), so the note now describes only the reasoning. ↩
  26. his life is dependent [on me]: tasya is the father-king, so jīvitam here is his life, which rests on the speaker; mayi is understood. The speaker offers this as the reason he must not give up his own life. The tat of santyājyam then refers to the speaker's own life, which supports his father. ↩
  27. The reading: tasya cāyattaṃ jīvitam: (1) 'his (the father-king's) life is dependent [on me]'; (2) 'my life is dependent on him', with āyatta taking the genitive of the controller. I now choose (1), as the reviewer asks. tasya stands next to jīvitam and most naturally means 'his life'. The son's giving the father's dependence on him as the reason he cannot abandon his own life suits the argument of 23.12–17. I withdraw my earlier claim that the grammar of āyatta settles the matter, since it does not exclude (1). The antecedent of tat in santyājyam is the speaker's own life, which the Sanskrit does not state, so I bracket 'of mine'. tat could also be read as an adverbial 'therefore' (tat katham, 'how then'). I render it as 'how then' and also take it as the pronoun, which gives the same sense. Likewise 'my' with 'father' and 'on me' are implied, not stated, so they are bracketed. Verse 23.14 is printed with a stray verse from chapter 97 before it. This does not affect the present verse. ↩
  28. the woman's share: bhāgasya yoṣitaḥ is read as two genitives, "of the share, of the woman". What "share" (bhāga) means here is not stated; it probably refers to the woman's claim on the king, such as following her in death or in grief. ↩
  29. The reading: bhāgasya yoṣitaḥ is obscure. Other readings are "the share of life [to be given] for the woman" or "the portion that belongs to the woman". I kept the literal "the woman's share" and did not interpret it. The clause kintu sarvathā is left incomplete, and the sentence seems to continue in 23.17. I translated it as it stands and supplied nothing. ↩
  30. Cruelty must be done by me: The sense is that Ṛtadhvaja's staying alive would itself be the cruelty. The following clause then takes the sacrifice of his own life as the small return for her sacrifice. ↩
  31. The reading: nopakāryapakāri ca: the text is metrically and grammatically awkward. I read na upakāri apakāri ca, with both words as neuter nominatives agreeing with nṛśaṃsyam ('not beneficial, and harmful'). The alternative is to take upakārin as 'one who benefits' and read 'no benefactor [to her] but a wrongdoer', which gives much the same sense. The reading is uncertain and the line may be corrupt. 'This' (idam) is left unexplained because the Sanskrit does not say what it refers to; I take it to be the giving up of his own life. ↩
  32. The reading: The reference 98.2 and the neighbouring verses appear to be mismatched in the e-text, so the speaker's line cannot be placed in context. The line itself is clear: putrau is the dual nominative, 'the two sons', and ūcatuḥ is the dual perfect of vac, 'the two said'. The sons are not named in the line, so I give no names. ↩
  33. water-offering: udakadānika: the offering of water to the dead, made by relatives after a death; here Ṛtadhvaja performs it for Madālasā, whom he believes dead. ↩
  34. The reading: kriyāḥ ('rites') is left general; it presumably means the further funeral rites after the water-offering. matim kṛtvā is rendered 'made up his mind' (literally 'having made a resolve'), referring to the resolve stated in the preceding verses. pratyuvāca ('replied') has no stated object here; the reply follows in the next verses, and the speaker's line there is not translated. ↩
  35. The reading: The verse is a conditional sentence. 'yadi ... na syāt ... nānyā bhavitrī' reads as 'if she is not to be my wife, no other will be my companion.' I take 'bhāryā' as predicate of 'sā' and 'sahacāriṇī' as predicate of 'anyā'. 'bhavitrī' is a future agent noun, 'she who will be', so I render it 'will be'. ↩
  36. enjoy: The verb bhokṣye (from √bhuj) means 'enjoy' or 'take as one's own'; here it refers to taking a woman as wife or sexual partner. ↩
  37. elephant-gaited: gajagāminī: a conventional epithet of beauty, a woman whose gait is stately like an elephant's. ↩
  38. walks in the true dharma: saddharmacāriṇī: a wife who practises the good or true dharma, that is, one who shares her husband's duties. ↩
  39. The reading: The verse has no named subject; 'tām' refers to Madālasā, as the preceding verses make plain. 'Muktvā' (absolutive of muc) is rendered 'leaving aside', with the speaker Ṛtadhvaja as its agent, i.e. 'except for her'. The reading 'aṅgīkariṣyāmi' means 'I will accept/take'; 'kāñcit' with 'na' means 'no woman at all'. The word 'strī' is implied by the feminine kāñcit and supplied as 'woman'. I treat 'patnīm' as in apposition to 'tām', 'my wife', with 'my' implied. ↩
  40. The two sons: putrau ... ūcatuḥ: the dual shows that two speakers are meant. The verse does not name them; by the context they are the two young nāgas, sons of Aśvatara, who speak of Ṛtadhvaja. ↩
  41. The reading: The verse number 98.8 is out of sequence with the surrounding chapter 23 numbering, which suggests a misplaced or interpolated speaker line in the e-text. The identity of the two sons is not given in the verse. I took them to be the two nāga youths from the context, but this is inferred. ↩
  42. The reading: śīlasampadā (instrumental) can be read two ways. (a) It qualifies tulyaiḥ vayasyaiḥ: 'equal [to him] in the wealth of good conduct'. (b) It is adverbial and goes with krīḍan: 'sporting with [or in] excellent conduct'. I chose (a), because the instrumental of respect regularly goes with tulya. Also, tayā vinā ('without her') could go with parityajya (he has given up the pleasures of women, being without her) or with strībhogān. I took it as the reason for the renunciation, in the sense that without her he has no wish for any woman. ↩
  43. The reading: I accepted the reviewer's points on 'paraṃ kāryam', on the passive construction with 'kena' and 'īśvaraiḥ', and on the removal of 'but'. My earlier doubt about 'tat' was unnecessary, so I withdraw it. 'Tat' is the object of 'kartum' and refers to the 'kāryam' (the task). 'Atyarthaduṣprāpyam' agrees with that task: 'extremely hard to achieve'. It does not qualify Madālasā. 'Etat' points back to what the sons have just described, Ṛtadhvaja's resolve to win Madālasā and no other. I left it as 'this', since the verse does not name her. I translated 'kimuta' as 'how much less' because the sense is negative: if lords cannot achieve it, others still less. The spacing before the daṇḍa and after 'tāta' is only a typographical feature of the e-text, and no emendation is needed. ↩
  44. the king of the nāgas: Nāgarāj (nāgarāṭ) is the father of the two sons, identified in the following verse-heading as Aśvatara. ↩
  45. as if laughing: prahasann iva: literally 'smiling/laughing as it were'; a faint, gentle smile is meant, not open laughter. ↩
  46. The reading: vimarśa can mean 'deliberation', 'reflection' or 'doubt'; I chose 'deliberation' because the father then reflects (vimṛśya) and answers. The text is silent on the father's name here; it is supplied by the heading of the next verse, not by this verse. ↩
  47. The reading: tataḥ param can be read as "thereafter, in consequence" or "beyond that, further". I rendered it "a further loss beyond that", taking it with hāniḥ as a second loss that follows the loss of exertion. Verse 23.25 is also the end of a sentence begun in 23.24, where the nāga king speaks. The speaker line at 98.13 is a variant numbering in the e-text and is rendered as the opening of the speech. ↩
  48. manly effort: pauruṣa: a man's own exertion, his energy and initiative. The same word is used in the compound svapauruṣa, 'his own manly effort'. ↩
  49. fate: daiva: what is given by the gods, i.e. destiny or the results of past deeds, set against human effort (pauruṣa). ↩
  50. The reading: vyavasathitā is a likely misprint or irregular form for vyavasthitā ('rests, depends'); I translated it as vyavasthitā. mahāpayan is read as 'not letting go to waste', from the root hā in a causal sense (apahāpayan, 'letting be lost'), with the negative idea carried by the sense of the sentence. The text as printed is slightly uncertain. ↩
  51. my two dear sons: putrakau, vocative dual of putraka, the affectionate diminutive of putra ('son'). It is joined by sandhi to itaḥ ('from here, from now on') in the printed putrakāvitaḥ. The two youths addressed in the preceding verses are meant. ↩
  52. austerities: tapaścaryā, the practice of tapas (ascetic discipline, austerity), here undertaken to gain a particular result. ↩
  53. The reading: The printed putrakāvitaḥ is read as putrakau itaḥ: the vocative dual 'O dear sons' plus 'from here, from now on'. I chose this because only two sons are addressed, and the translation now says 'two' to show the dual. The reviewer is right that my earlier note named a vocative plural putrakāḥ, which did not fit the printed text or my own choice, and I have corrected it. The alternative putrakāḥ itaḥ (plural) would need the printed -āv- to be a misprint, so I set it aside. 'From now on' for itaḥ is somewhat uncertain; 'hence' or 'from here' are also possible. In yathaitat sādhyate the present indicative stands where a subjunctive or optative would be usual in a purpose clause, so I render it 'may be accomplished'. ↩
  54. Plakṣāvataraṇa: A sacred ford on the Himālaya, said to be the place where the river Sarasvatī descends; its name means 'the descent of the plakṣa (fig) tree'. ↩
  55. Himavat: The Himālaya, the mountain, here named in the genitive as the mountain that holds the tīrtha. ↩
  56. The reading: The Sanskrit has gireḥ ... himavataḥ, 'of the mountain, of Himavat', taken as apposition: the mountain Himavat. Plakṣāvataraṇa is taken as the name of the tīrtha (tīrtham in apposition), not as a separate place. The speaker sa nāgendraḥ is Aśvatara, who spoke in the preceding verses. tepe is taken as the perfect of tap, with tapas as its cognate object. ↩
  57. savanas: The three daily times of ritual bathing and worship: dawn, midday and evening. The compound triṣavaṇāplutaḥ means 'bathed at the three savanas'. ↩
  58. Sarasvatī: Goddess of speech and learning, here invoked through hymns; the verses that follow give Aśvatara's own praise of her. ↩
  59. The reading: gīrbhiḥ ('with words') is rendered 'with words of praise' to fit tuṣṭāva. The subject, the nāga king Aśvatara (from 23.28), is not named in this verse; 'he' stands for him. The verse begins with the main verb, but English places the participial phrases first. tatas and tatra are both rendered: 'Then, in that place' (the tīrtha of Himavat at Plakṣāvataraṇa). ↩
  60. whose source is Brahmā: Brahmayoni: a compound meaning 'having Brahmā as womb or source'. Sarasvatī is Brahmā's daughter or consort in the Purāṇas. It can also be read as 'having brahman (the Veda) as her womb', or as 'the source of brahman'. ↩
  61. The reading: brahmayoni can be a bahuvrīhi, 'whose womb/source is Brahmā' or 'whose womb is brahman (the Veda)', or a tatpuruṣa, 'source of brahman'. The draft's 'source of Brahmā' wrongly reversed the bahuvrīhi, and the bracketed 'or the Veda' mixed two analyses. I chose the bahuvrīhi with Brahmā, since Sarasvatī's descent from Brahmā is the common Purāṇic account. The Veda reading is given in the note rather than in the text. I also took Aśvatara as the speaker, although the stray label '98.20' in the context is misplaced. The verse continues his speech, so no speaker's line is added. Devī in the first half and Sarasvatī in the second are one goddess. The epithets 'auspicious' and 'sustainer of the world' are therefore attached to 'goddess', and 'Sarasvatī' is the object of 'shall praise'. ↩
  62. word: padam can mean 'word' or 'state, place'. Here it is read as 'word', in keeping with the praise of Sarasvatī as goddess of speech. ↩
  63. liberation: mokṣa: release from rebirth and bondage. Here mokṣavat means a word that carries or leads to liberation. ↩
  64. without conjunction, yet as though joined in yoga: asaṃyogaṃ and yogavat make a deliberate paradox. Everything rests in the goddess without being in contact with her, and yet it is as if united with her. ↩
  65. The reading: The printed 'say' is a misprint or corrupt reading. The sense and metre require 'yat' (kiñcit), so I read 'yat kiñcit', 'whatever'. 'sadasat' can mean 'being and non-being' or 'real and unreal'. 'padam' can mean 'word' or 'state'. I chose 'word', as explained in the note. ↩
  66. the imperishable: akṣara: the 'imperishable', also 'syllable'. Here the imperishable Brahman; the next verses link it with the syllable Om (oṅkārākṣara). ↩
  67. like an atom: paramāṇu: the smallest indivisible particle of matter; the following verse compares it with Brahman and the perishable world. ↩
  68. The reading: saṃsthitam has no stated locative; 'in you' is supplied from tvam and the context of 23.31 and 23.34 (tvayi sthitam). In pāda a, tvam akṣaram paraṃ could also be read as 'you are the supreme imperishable'; I take paraṃ as predicate with akṣaram. Pāda b is a relative clause, yatra sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitam, and I have rendered it with 'in whom' to match the feminine antecedent. The vocative devi is printed with a space and a mark (devi !), which I read as a plain vocative. ↩
  69. brahman: The absolute, the supreme reality. Here it is identified with the imperishable (akṣara), in contrast to the perishable universe. Aśvatara is addressing Sarasvatī. ↩
  70. Fire abides in wood, and the atoms are of the earth.: The verse is elliptical. These two images illustrate how the imperishable abides in the perishable world, as fire lies latent in wood and atoms in earthly things. The verse after it, 23.34, begins with 'tathā' ('so'), which completes the comparison. ↩
  71. The reading: The word 'bhaumāḥ' can mean 'earthly' or 'produced from or belonging to the earth'. I took it as 'of the earth', qualifying the atoms. The second half of the verse is elliptical, and I have kept it so. The 'viśvam' of the first half is the subject of the predicate 'kṣarātmakam'. Read this way, the verse sets the imperishable brahman against the perishable universe. An alternative would take 'akṣaram paramam brahma' as a vocative-like address, but the nominative is more natural. ↩
  72. brahman: The supreme, imperishable reality; here, as in the preceding verse, identified with the imperishable (akṣara) syllable, and so with the goddess Sarasvatī. ↩
  73. oṅkāra: The sacred syllable Oṃ. The word akṣara also means 'imperishable', so the verse plays on the syllable and the imperishable. ↩
  74. The reading: The last line is loosely constructed. 'yat tu ... sthirāsthiram' (what is steady and unsteady) could qualify 'jagat' or 'brahman'; 'oṅkārākṣarasaṃsthānam' is a neuter compound that could also be read as the object of the establishing. I took the whole line as describing the world, with the form (saṃsthāna) of the syllable oṅkāra. 'Akṣara' may also be taken as 'imperishable' rather than 'syllable'; I chose 'syllable' with a note. ↩
  75. There, in that syllable: tatra refers back to the syllable oṃ (oṅkārākṣara) of the preceding verse. ↩
  76. mātrā: The 'measure' or constituent element of the syllable oṃ, which is made up of three: a, u and m. The verses that follow list the triads that correspond to them. ↩
  77. the threefold knowledge: traividya is the knowledge contained in the three Vedas (Ṛg, Yajur and Sāma). ↩
  78. the three fires: The three sacrificial fires of the Vedic ritual: the gārhapatya, āhavanīya and dakṣiṇa fires. ↩
  79. The reading: Sanskrit 'yad devi nāsti ca' is read as 'what does not exist', with 'sarvam asti' as 'everything that exists'. The mention of three Vedas here is repeated in 23.36 (trayo vedāḥ) and may be a textual doubling. In the first line, the original has 'devi' (vocative), which I keep. The reading of 'tatra' as 'in that syllable' is an inference from the preceding verse. ↩
  80. varṇas: The social orders (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra). The verse does not state the number here, but in the series of triads it is taken as three, i.e. the three twice-born orders. ↩
  81. the three sources of dharma: dharmāgama: the authorities or sources through which dharma is known; the text does not name them. ↩
  82. guṇas: The three constituent qualities of nature: sattva, rajas and tamas. ↩
  83. the three Vedas: The verse repeats trayo vedāḥ from the previous verse; the word appears again here as in the Sanskrit. ↩
  84. āśramas: The stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer); here, in a series of triads, three are meant. ↩
  85. The reading: The verse gives 'trayaḥ/trayo' (three) syntactically to the whole list, so varṇāḥ and āśramāḥ are read as 'three' as well (the numeral governs the series); the Sanskrit states the number explicitly only for dharmāgamāḥ, guṇāḥ, śabdaḥ and vedāḥ. 'Śabdaḥ' is singular after 'trayaḥ' and is probably the three sounds (the three mātrās of Om) or three kinds of sound; I keep 'sounds'. Vedāḥ repeats the previous verse; no emendation is needed. I also render ca/tathā lightly with semicolons. ↩
  86. the ancestors: pitaraḥ is plural and means the ancestors or pitṛs. The reading is uncertain in this list of triads, which would call for a three-fold grouping of them. ↩
  87. mātrās: mātrā is the 'measure' or 'moment' of a syllable. Here it refers to the three elements (a, u, m) of the syllable oṃ, which the preceding verses make the pattern for every triad listed. ↩
  88. The reading: 'avasthāḥ' (states) is plural and has no number given. Since the list is of triads, I supplied 'three' in brackets. 'pitaro' is left as 'the ancestors', though it sits oddly among triads. 'aharniśādayaḥ' is read as 'day and night and the rest', meaning day, night and the other [divisions of time]. The line 99.9 printed among the following verses belongs to another chapter and is not part of this verse. ↩
  89. Brahman: brahman here is the neuter absolute, the supreme reality, and not the god Brahmā or a brahmin; the genitive brahmaṇaḥ is read as that of the neuter noun. ↩
  90. those who see things as distinct: vibhinnadarśin: those who perceive difference or plurality, as opposed to those who see the one reality. ↩
  91. The reading: The verse is a fragment with no stated subject; the neighbouring verses suggest the threefold mātrās or the sacrificial orders, but I have supplied only 'They are' and 'forms'. The grammar is also uneven: ādyā (feminine) beside sanātanāḥ (masculine plural) suggests a lost visarga or a corrupt text, and I read ādyā as ādyāḥ. Brahmaṇaḥ could also be read as 'of the brahmin' (brāhmaṇa) or as the god Brahmā; I chose neuter Brahman, which suits the context of the hymn. ↩
  92. modes: saṃsthā: an established form or type of rite. The soma rites, the oblation (havis) rites and the cooking (pāka) rites are traditionally counted as seven each. ↩
  93. brahmavādins: Expounders of the Veda or of brahman, those who speak of brahman; here, the Vedic ritualists. ↩
  94. half-mātrā: A mātrā is a prosodic 'measure' or mora. The three mātrās of Oṃ are a, u, m; the half-mātrā is the silent resonance after them, which stands for the supreme, unutterable aspect of the goddess. ↩
  95. The reading: Neuter anyad anirdeśyaṃ param ardhamātrānvitam has no noun. I take 'another' as a further form of the goddess, as 23.40 (tava etat paramaṃ rūpam) shows, and leave it without a bracketed noun. Taking it as a further 'measure' (mātrā) is also possible. ↩
  96. highest form of yours: This is the further form, joined with the half-measure (ardhamātrā) and beyond the three measures, which cannot be described (anirdeśya), as stated in verse 23.39. The address is to Sarasvatī, who is identified with the syllable Oṃ. ↩
  97. The reading: The compound avikāryakṣayam can be read as 'not subject to change and not subject to decay' (avikārya + akṣaya, two separate adjectives) or as 'without change or decay' taken together; I took it as two adjectives, 'unchangeable and imperishable'. The word yat is taken as relative to rūpam ('something that I am not able to express'). Because of the sandhi, yanna is read as yad na. ↩
  98. nor [by] its tongue: The transmitted text na cāsye na ca tajjihvā is probably corrupt. Asye is a locative, tajjihvā a nominative, and tāmroṣṭhādibhiḥ an instrumental, so the three members do not match. Possible repairs are nāsyaṃ na ca tajjihvā or na cāsyena na jihvayā. The sense is clear from 23.39–40: the supreme form cannot be uttered by the organs of speech. ↩
  99. the Vasus: A class of eight gods (Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, Prabhāsa) who personify natural phenomena such as earth, fire, wind, water and the sky. ↩
  100. The reading: (1) The first half is syntactically irregular. Asye is the locative of āsya ('mouth'), tajjihvā is a nominative feminine ('its tongue'), and tāmroṣṭhādibhiḥ is an instrumental, yet there is a single verb, ucyate. The reviewer is right that the draft should say plainly that the text is probably corrupt, and I now flag this in a textual note. I do not adopt the emendation nāsyaṃ or the 'mouth, tongue, lips' instrumental rendering in the text itself, because that would replace the transmitted cases with conjectured ones. My rendering keeps the three cases as they stand, supplies only 'by' in brackets for the nominative member, and carries over ucyate. The resulting sense is the same as the reviewer's: the supreme form is not expressed by mouth, tongue or lips. (2) The second half is a list of nominatives with no verb: Indra, the Vasus, Brahmā, the moon, the sun, and light. It may belong with the accusatives of 23.42 (viśvāvāsam etc.), but the connection is uncertain, so I supplied nothing ↩
  101. the doctrines of Sāṃkhya and Vedānta: Sāṃkhya and Vedānta are two schools of Indian philosophy; vāda means doctrine or school of argument. ↩
  102. made firm through many branches: bahuśākhā can mean many branches of the Vedic recensions or of learning; the sense is that the highest reality has been established by many traditions of teaching. ↩
  103. The reading: The verse has no finite verb and continues from the preceding verses, where the highest form (paraṃ rūpam) of the goddess is described; the accusative neuter forms agree with that 'form' (tava etat paramaṃ rūpam), so they are adjectives of it, not of a person. I supplied '[He is]' to make the English parse, but the grammatical subject may be 'that supreme form' (neuter). Also bahuśākhāsthirīkṛtam: 'made firm/established through many branches' (of the Vedas or schools), or 'made stable by many branches'; I took the first. ↩
  104. being and non-being: Translates sat and asat, 'what is' and 'what is not'. The verse says the supreme reality is not confined to either category; the Vedāntic and Sāṃkhya contrast is meant. ↩
  105. the divisions of existence: bhavabhedasamāśraitam: samāśraitam is metrically irregular for samāśritam. Bhava can mean 'existence' or 'worldly becoming'. ↩
  106. The reading: 1) sadasanna sadeva: I read sad-asat, then na sad eva, 'being and non-being, yet not being alone'. Another reading takes sadasat with na as 'neither being nor non-being', but the following eva then has no clear place. 2) samāśraitam is taken as a corrupt or metrical form of samāśritam, 'resting on, resorting to'. 3) The subject is not stated in the verse. Following 23.40, I supply 'It', meaning the supreme form of the Goddess, in brackets. ↩
  107. six guṇas: guṇa is a quality or strand. The six are probably the qualities of divine lordship (bhaga): sovereignty, dharma, glory, prosperity, knowledge and dispassion. Other sets of six are also known, such as the six expedients of policy. ↩
  108. groups: varga is a set or class. The text does not say which sets are meant. The commonest are the aims of life (dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa) and the classes of beings. ↩
  109. the three guṇas: The three strands of nature: sattva, rajas and tamas. ↩
  110. The reading: śakti: the glossary gives 'javelin', but here the word means 'power', the divine energy, and is rendered so. Śaktivaibhavika is a compound: 'belonging to the glory/splendour of power', or 'whose glory is power'. I chose 'whose glory is that of power'. The genitive plural nānāśaktimatām is read as partitive, 'among those endowed with manifold powers'. The six guṇas and the groups (varga) are not specified in the text, so the readings in the notes are tentative. The verse is a continuation of the accusative series of 23.42-43, describing the form (rūpa) of the Goddess, so the translation has no expressed subject. ↩
  111. Pleasure and non-pleasure: The compound sukhāsukham is read as 'pleasure and non-pleasure (pain)'; it could also mean 'pleasant and unpleasant'. It is a neuter singular that stands for the pair of opposites as one thing. Mahāsaukhyarūpam qualifies it, so the pair itself is said to have the form of great bliss. ↩
  112. The reading: The verse number 99.17 in the header does not match the chapter reference (23). The neighbouring verses are numbered 23.39–46, so the line probably belongs between 23.44 and 23.45, in the hymn addressed to the Goddess. I translated the line as given. Following the reviewer, I take mahāsaukhyarūpam as an adjective (a bahuvrīhi, 'having the form of great bliss') agreeing with sukhāsukham. There is no ca, and vibhāvyate is singular, so there is one subject and not two. Sukhāsukham is therefore a neuter nominative singular, the subject of the passive verb. Sukhāsukham itself can be read as 'pleasure and pain' or as 'pleasant and unpleasant'. I kept the literal 'pleasure and non-pleasure' and explained the reading in the note. ↩
  113. Devī: The Goddess, addressed here as the all-pervading supreme power; the hymn is addressed to her. ↩
  114. all that has parts and all that is without parts: sakala and niṣkala: the manifest, partite and the unmanifest, partless. ↩
  115. brahman: brahman: the supreme absolute reality; here it is said to abide both in non-duality (advaita) and in the dual world. ↩
  116. The reading: The verse has no finite verb. 'vyāptam' (pervaded) is neuter singular and agrees with 'sakalaṃ niṣkalaṃ ca yat', while 'brahma yac ca dvaite vyavasthitam' is a further object; I supplied 'is pervaded by you' for the second clause, in brackets, since the sentence otherwise does not parse. 'advaitāvasthitam' could also be read as 'established in non-duality'; I chose this reading as it matches the contrasting 'dvaite vyavasthitam'. ↩
  117. in the atmosphere: antarīkṣa: the middle realm between earth and heaven. ↩
  118. the apprehension: upalabdhi: perception, cognition or attainment of a thing. The goddess addressed is Sarasvatī, speech, through whom all objects are known and expressed. ↩
  119. The reading: The text reads 'yer'thā' for 'ye 'rthā' (ye arthāḥ), 'those things'. 'Anyato vā' is taken as 'elsewhere' (anyatas, in some other place). 'Upalabdhi' could be 'perception' or 'attainment'; I chose 'apprehension' because the context is the goddess of speech as the source of knowing. ↩
  120. formless: amūrta and mūrta are the unembodied or formless and the embodied or formed, a standard pair that together cover all existence. ↩
  121. through your vowels and consonants: svara and vyañjana are the two classes of Sanskrit sounds. The goddess is Sarasvatī as Speech, and the verse says that everything is connected with her through the letters of the alphabet. ↩
  122. The reading: yaddivyasti: read as yad divi asti, 'what is in heaven', with divi in the locative, which fits the series kṣmātale, khe, anyatas. The alternative, divya 'divine' with a stray -m, is less natural. bhūteṣv ekam ekaṃ ca kiñcit is compressed. I took it as 'whatever among beings is one, or any single thing', but 'whatever one thing, each one among beings' is also possible. ↩
  123. the tongue of Viṣṇu: Sarasvatī, goddess of speech, is called the tongue (jihvā) of Viṣṇu; here Viṣṇu is identified with Dattātreya, so she is his speech. ↩
  124. The reading: The Sanskrit has devī viṣṇorjihvā sarasvatī, which could be read as three separate items. I took viṣṇorjihvā as an appositive epithet of Sarasvatī ('the goddess Sarasvatī, the tongue of Viṣṇu'), since this is the usual identification. 'Tataḥ' is rendered 'then', alongside 'tadā', which is also 'then'; both are kept, so the sentence reads 'then ... [and] then' as one 'then' for the sake of English. ↩
  125. brother of Kambala: kambalabhrātaḥ is a vocative addressing Aśvatara as the brother of Kambala, the other nāga of this story. ↩
  126. lord of serpents: uragādhipa, a second vocative for Aśvatara, the king of the nāgas; uraga is a word for serpent. ↩
  127. The reading: The reference '100.3' is an e-text numbering irregularity; the line is only the speaker's formula, and I render it as such. In 'varaṃ te prayacchāmi' I take the present as an immediate, performative present ('I grant'). 'ucyatām' is an imperative passive, rendered 'let it be spoken', that is, 'say it'. I have changed the Kambala note as the reviewer asked, deleting the claim that the two are sons of a nāga king, which contradicts the glossary. ↩
  128. Kambala: Kambala is Aśvatara's brother. In 23.49 Sarasvatī addressed Aśvatara as kambalabhrātṛ, 'brother of Kambala'. ↩
  129. svaras: svara: the seven musical notes of the scale. The next verse lists them together with the grāmarāgas (modes), the kīrtanas and the mūrchanās. ↩
  130. The reading: 1) sahāyam is the object of dehi and me is the dative 'to me', as the reviewer says. I corrected the draft's possessive 'my' and the invented 'his'. 2) kambalam eva is taken as a second accusative with sahāyam: 'Kambala himself (alone) as a helper'. The alternative is 'give help first to Kambala alone', with Kambala as the recipient. I preferred the first because me is then the recipient and the verse parallels ubhayoḥ in the second half. The reading is not certain. 3) pūrvam could mean 'first' or 'as before' (Kambala having been his companion earlier). I kept 'first', which fits the sequence with ca in the second half. 4) ubhayoḥ is genitive dual, so I rendered 'the connection of both of us with all the svaras', not 'to both of us'. 'Both of us' means Aśvatara and Kambala; the Sanskrit says only ubhayoḥ, so this follows from context. 5) I removed 'brother' from the translation, since this verse does not say it; the relationship is given only in the note. ↩
  131. grāmarāgas: grāmarāga: a melodic mode in Indian musical theory, derived from a grāma (scale). The text gives only the number seven and does not name them. ↩
  132. kītakas: kītaka: an obscure technical term of the musical lore, possibly corrupt. The text gives only the number seven. ↩
  133. mūrcchanās: mūrcchanā: the ascending and descending arrangement of the seven notes within a scale; seven for each grāma. ↩
  134. tālas: tāla: musical time-measure or beat. The text gives the number forty-nine and does not list them. ↩
  135. grāmas: grāma: 'scale'. The three are traditionally the ṣaḍja, madhyama and gāndhāra scales. ↩
  136. layas: laya: tempo, of which three are counted: slow, medium and fast. ↩
  137. the triad of yati: The text reads 'yaditrayam'. I emend it to 'yatitrayam'. yati: a pattern of rhythmic arrangement within the tāla. ↩
  138. vowels and consonants: svara means 'note' in 23.51 but 'vowel' here, where it stands beside vyañjana 'consonant', as in 23.47 (svarair vyañjanaiś ca). The reference is to speech sounds. ↩
  139. The reading: 1. 'yaditrayam' (23.54): I keep my emendation to 'yatitrayam', the triad of yati, because the context is a list of musical terms and 'yadi' ('if') makes no sense here. It is flagged in a textual note, not by brackets in the translation, since square brackets are reserved for implied words. 2. 'svaravyañjanasaṃmitam' (23.55): I accept the reviewer's point. With vyañjana, svara means 'vowels', as in 23.47. 'Saṃmita' is taken as 'measured by' or 'comprised in'. 3. 'yat' (23.52, grāmatrayaṃ ca yat) is now rendered as 'that there are'. 4. 'caturvidhaṃ padaṃ tālam' (23.53): 'fourfold' may govern only pada, as I take it, or both pada and tāla. 'Triḥ prakāraṃ layatrayam' is taken as the three layas in three kinds. 5. 'Aparaṃ tathā' is read as 'and also the rest', introducing the list. 6. 'Kītakāni' is obscure and left transliterated. ↩
  140. O serpent: Singular vocative addressed to Aśvatara; the dual pannagau at the end of the verse includes Kambala. ↩
  141. the world of the gods: devaloka: the heavenly world, in the triple division here: nether worlds, heaven and earth. ↩
  142. The reading: The first line has no verb and no object. I supplied '[who has this]' from the preceding verses, which treat the gift of music; this is an inference. 'Anyasya' is genitive singular, so 'no one else' is a loose rendering of 'of no other'. Also, the speaker is Sarasvatī (from the speaker line at 100.7), but the vocative pannaga is singular and its referent is not explicit in the verse. I took it as the one being addressed, the elder serpent, which is a guess; the later dual pannagau covers both brothers. ↩
  143. who dwells on every tongue: Sarasvatī is the goddess of speech, and sarvajihvā ('of all tongues') marks her as present in the speech of all beings. ↩
  144. The reading: The Sanskrit says adarśanaṃ jagāma, 'went to non-sight', with nāgasya in the genitive. I render this as 'vanished from the sight of the nāga'. The nāga is Aśvatara, but the verse does not name him, so I keep the common noun. ↩
  145. pada, tāla and svara: Technical terms of music: pada is the word or verse of a song, tāla the beat or time-measure, svara the musical note. The compound ends in ādika ('beginning with'), so the list is open. ↩
  146. The reading: tadyathāvṛttam: I accept the reviewer's point that 'told' is not supported, since vṛtta means 'occurred, happened'. I now render 'as it had occurred', and make sarvam the subject of ajāyata, with vijñānam ubhayor agryam padatālasvarādikam in apposition, as the reviewer suggests. The phrase may be read as 'just as it had happened', or as 'just as it was (promised)', referring back to the goddess's gift in 23.52-56. I kept the plain sense and added no bracketed word. agryam is 'supreme', qualifying vijñānam, and ubhayoḥ is 'in both of them', taken with vijñānam. padatālasvarādikam is a neuter agreeing with vijñānam. ↩
  147. rhythm of the lute strings: tantrīlaya: tantrī is the string of a lute (vīṇā) and laya is musical time or tempo. The compound means accompanied by stringed instruments in proper time. ↩
  148. destroyer of the body of Anaṅga: Śiva burned Kāma (Anaṅga, the Bodiless One) to ashes with the fire of his eye when Kāma tried to disturb his meditation. The epithet anaṅgāṅgaharam refers to this. ↩
  149. Vṛṣadhvaja: 'He whose banner is the bull', an epithet of Śiva, whose emblem is the bull (vṛṣa). ↩
  150. The reading: (1) sptabhiḥ in 23.59 is a misprint for saptabhiḥ, 'with seven'; I read it so. (2) saṃhatavākkalau could be 'with voice and melody (kala, sweet sound) joined', which I chose, or 'with voice and the art of music united'. (3) ārirādhayiṣū is a desiderative dual ('wishing to propitiate'); I take 'the Lord on Kailāsa' (īśvaram) and 'the god Hara' as one person, the object of this wish. (4) prāheśo is prāha + īśaḥ: 'the Lord said'. ↩
  151. Śitikaṇṭha: 'Blue-throated', an epithet of Śiva, whose throat was darkened when he drank the poison produced at the churning of the ocean. ↩
  152. yoginī: A woman who practises yoga, a female adept. ↩
  153. a mother of yoga: yogamātā may mean a woman who is the source or teacher of yoga, or the mother of yogins. The literal 'mother of yoga' is kept. ↩
  154. The reading: The speaker uses the dual 'nau' ('us two', the two nāgas), but then 'me' and 'my house' in the singular. Aśvatara, the elder, evidently speaks the request for both, so the Sanskrit is kept as it stands. 'Yogamātā' can be read in more than one way (see note); the literal reading was chosen. ↩
  155. Mahādeva: 'The Great God', a name of Śiva. Here he answers the prayer of the two serpents, Aśvatara and Kambala. ↩
  156. best of serpents: Vocative of pannagaśreṣṭha, addressed to Aśvatara, who spoke for both in the prayer (23.62–65). ↩
  157. The reading: The verse reads 'sarvemetad' for sarvam etad (misprint or sandhi irregularity); I take it as 'sarvam etad', 'all this'. The vocative 'bhujaṅgama' is singular, so Śiva addresses Aśvatara alone, though both serpents asked for the boon. ↩
  158. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the deceased ancestors, in which rice-balls (piṇḍa) are presented to the forefathers. ↩
  159. best of serpents: phaṇiśreṣṭha: addressed to Aśvatara, the serpent who asked for the boon. The word phaṇin means 'hooded one', that is, a cobra. ↩
  160. rice-ball: piṇḍa: a ball of cooked rice offered to the ancestors in the śrāddha. The middle one is the one meant for the serpent to eat. ↩
  161. The reading: The particle tu is left untranslated as merely transitional. Ātmanā is rendered 'yourself', as an emphatic instrumental, rather than 'with your own [mind]'. The addressee is Aśvatara (the serpent of v. 62 and 66), not named in this verse. ↩
  162. middle hood: The nāga Aśvatara is addressed; the middle one of his hoods is to produce the reborn Madālasā once he eats the middle piṇḍa (rice-ball) offered at the śrāddha, as stated in the preceding verse. ↩
  163. auspicious woman: kalyāṇī, feminine, 'auspicious, fair one'; she is Madālasā, though the verse does not name her. ↩
  164. The reading: tathārūpā yathāmṛtā: 'of such a form as she was when dead' is taken to mean she will have the form she had at death, i.e. the same as Madālasā's former form. 'tasmin' is taken as referring to the piṇḍa of v. 67, which is understood though not stated in this verse. ↩
  165. libation to the ancestors: pitṛtarpaṇa: the tarpaṇa, a ritual offering of water to satisfy the departed forefathers, here part of the śrāddha rite. ↩
  166. the two: tau, dual: the nāga Aśvatara and his companion, his brother Kambala, who had come to Śiva together. ↩
  167. Maheśvara: 'Great Lord', a name of Śiva, the speaker in the preceding verses. ↩
  168. The reading: śvasataḥ is taken as the ablative singular of the participle śvasat, agreeing with phaṇāt ('from the breathing hood'). It could be read as a genitive qualifying an implied 'you' ('from the middle hood of you as you breathe'). The sense is almost the same; I chose the first because it agrees grammatically with phaṇāt. ↩
  169. Kambala's younger brother: Kambalānuja: the younger brother of the serpent Kambala. He is the serpent Aśvatara, who is addressed in this passage. ↩
  170. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the departed ancestors, centred on balls of rice (piṇḍa), which are mentioned in the preceding and following verses. ↩
  171. The reading: The verse does not name Kambala's younger brother. Identifying him as Aśvatara rests on the wider story (Kambala and Aśvatara are the two nāga brothers), not on this verse. ↩
  172. piṇḍa: The ball of cooked rice (with other food) offered to the departed ancestors in the śrāddha rite. Here the nāga eats the middle ball himself, as instructed in 23.67. ↩
  173. that slender-waisted woman: tanumadhyamā, 'slender in the middle', i.e. slim-waisted, refers to the woman who is to be born from the hood, the one described in 23.68–70. ↩
  174. did not tell anyone: kaṃsyacit is a misprint for kasyacit, 'to anyone'. ↩
  175. The reading: dhyāyaḥ in 23.72 is not a正 form; it is probably a corruption of dhyāyan ('meditating') or dhyātavān ('he meditated'). I render it as a finite 'meditated' joined by 'and' to the preceding clause, which has the same sense either way. kāma is taken as 'desire' (the wish to obtain the woman), as in kāmaṃ cemam of 23.69, and not as the god Kāma of the glossary. kaṃsyacit is read as kasyacit. ↩
  176. the lord of the nāgas: Nāgapati is Aśvatara, the nāga king and father of the two young nāgas, called Kambalānuja (younger brother of Kambala) in 23.71. ↩
  177. that prince: Here rājaputra is Ṛtadhvaja, the son of Śatrujit, the friend of the two nāga brothers. ↩
  178. The reading: nāgarājau (23.75) is dual and could qualify sutau, 'his two sons, the two nāga princes'. The singular nāgarājaḥ, 'the nāga king said to his two sons', may be the intended reading, since mudānvitaḥ and prāha are singular and the speaker is Aśvatara. I kept the transmitted dual and took the subject of prāha from 23.74. The sense is much the same either way. ↩
  179. the two: The dual tau and sakhyū refer to the two young nāga princes, sons of Aśvatara, who have gone to the city of Ṛtadhvaja at their father's urging. ↩
  180. The reading: kuvalayāśvaṃ tau kṛtvā kiñcitkathāntaram: the accusative Kuvalayāśvam is awkward with kṛtvā kathāntaram. I took it as 'having made some conversation with Kuvalayāśva', i.e. having talked a little with him. Other readings are possible, such as 'having turned Kuvalayāśva to some other topic'. praṇayopetam is taken adverbially, 'affectionately', rather than as an adjective of gamanam. tasya (his) is taken to be Ṛtadhvaja, since the princes visit his city. ↩
  181. O sons of a brahmin: Dvijasutau, dual vocative. Ṛtadhvaja addresses the two young nāgas as brahmin boys, which is how he knows them. ↩
  182. Fate: Daiva, the divine ordering of events, what is allotted to a person. The word is here a personified agent that cheats him. ↩
  183. The reading: 1. 'doyatām' in the e-text is a misprint for 'dīyatām' or 'deyatām'. I read it as 'let it be given', the third-person imperative passive of dā. 2. 'etāvatā' (instrumental of etāvat) can mean 'by this much', 'thus far' or 'in this respect'. Verse 82 shows what it refers to: the two do not treat his house as their own. I took it as 'In this much' and left the reference to the next verse. 3. 'Dvijasutau' is taken as 'sons of a brahmin', a vocative dual. The glossary's 'dvija = brahmins' fits this. ↩
  184. In that you two show no sense of ownership: The yad-clause gives the reason for the complaint at the end of 23.81 (etāvatā ... vañcito 'smi, 'by this much I am cheated'). ↩
  185. a sense of ownership: mamatva, literally 'my-ness': treating a thing as one's own. Ṛtadhvaja asks the two brahmin youths to treat his house and wealth as their own. In 23.80 he has already said that all his possessions are theirs. ↩
  186. The reading: 1) 'no' in 'mamatvaṃ no madīye' can be na (not) or naḥ (to us/by us, with visarga turned to o before m). I chose na, because the clause is the complaint begun in 23.81 and naḥ would add a pronoun nothing else in the sentence needs. 2) The reference '102.3' is evidently a faulty verse number in the GRETIL e-text. The half-verse 'taddhane mama gehe ca mamatvamanukalpyatām' follows 23.82 directly and completes its sentence, so I translate the two together. 3) 'taddhane' is read as tat + dhane. Tat is the 'then' that answers the two yadi clauses, and mama governs both 'wealth' and 'house' ('my wealth and my house'). I withdrew the earlier reading 'in that wealth', and the note built on it. ↩
  187. The reading: The line is loose and can be read in more than one way. (1) Reviewer's point on māmakam: accepted. Māmakam is the possessive of the first person ('my, mine'), not 'yours', so tan māmakam is 'that is mine'. The draft was wrong here. (2) Reviewer's point on yuvayoḥ: accepted. I take it as a genitive of possession, 'belonging to you two', in both places. The first is yuvayor yan madīyam, 'what of mine belongs to you two'. The second is yuvayoḥ svakam, '[it is] your own'. I did not use the reviewer's sample 'what is yours is your own', because it makes yuvayoḥ the subject of the first clause and so reads it inconsistently. (3) The draft's brackets '[and]' and '[your]' are removed. Only the copula in 'it is your own' is supplied, and it is not bracketed because English needs it. (4) Sense: the three members run as a series. What is mine and yours is mine and also your own, so ownership is shared, and this follows the plea of 23.82 for mamatva, a sense of ownership, in his house and wealth. ↩
  188. life-breaths moving outside [my body]: bahiścarāḥ prāṇāḥ: a common idiom for a dearest friend, who is felt to be one's own life itself, living outside the body. ↩
  189. O best of brahmins: dvijasattamau is a dual vocative, addressing both brothers, the two sons of the brahmin (dvijasutau, 23.81). English has no dual, so the sense is 'you two best of brahmins'. ↩
  190. The reading: vibhinnārtham ('with a different meaning') is taken as an adverbial accusative with vaktavyam: speaking as though 'mine' and 'yours' had separate meanings, i.e. as if their property and his were distinct. An alternative would be 'with a divided purpose', but the sense is much the same. The bracketed 'my body' is implied by bahiścarāḥ. The dual dvijasattamau is rendered 'O best of brahmins' for both brothers. ↩
  191. adjured: śāpitau: 'made to swear', 'bound by an oath'. Ṛtadhvaja binds the two youths by his own heart (hṛdayena me), a form of entreaty. ↩
  192. the king's son: nṛpateḥ putram: Ṛtadhvaja, son of King Śatrujit. He is the 'Ṛtadhvaja' addressed in the vocative and the 'Kuvalayāśva' of the next sentence. ↩
  193. as [he] said: yathāha: the subject of āha is not given. It may be the nāga father, whose wish was just quoted, or one of the youths. ↩
  194. The reading: (1) Finding on 23.85 accepted: matprasādaparau ... śāpitau ... me is Ṛtadhvaja's speech to the two youths, continuing 23.80–84, and the narration begins at tataḥ. The duals have no pronoun, so I supply '[You two,]'. The first-person words are no longer a shift of narrator, and the earlier pluperfect is dropped. (2) yathāha tāteti vadan: I now keep yathāha as a separate clause, 'as [he] said'. It is still uncertain who 'he' is. It could be the father who has said he wants to see Kuvalayāśva, or the youths, or Ṛtadhvaja's own earlier phrase. The bracketed '[he]' marks the guess. (3) svayam is rendered as an adverb, 'by our father himself', and proktam as a past tense, 'was said'. (4) kiñcit praṇayakopitau is rendered 'somewhat vexed out of fondness'. praṇaya can also mean 'request' or 'trust', but the context favours affectionate pique. ↩
  195. Father: Sanskrit tāta, an affectionate and respectful address for a father or an elder. Here it is Kuvalayāśva's address to the father of the two nāga youths, who in 23.87–88 is said to have expressed the wish to see him. It does not mean Kuvalayāśva's own father. In the wider narrative the nāgas' father is Aśvatara. ↩
  196. The reading: 1. The reference '102.10' is evidently a misprint in the e-text for the speaker's line belonging to 23.89. I treat it as the line introducing 23.89. 2. I accept the reviewer's correction on tāta. In 23.87 the youths speak of 'our father' (pitrā … mahātmanā), so the tāta of 23.89 is their father, not Kuvalayāśva's father Śatrujit. I have corrected the note and proposed no Śatrujit entry. 3. I read yat as causal or explanatory ('in that'), not as a result clause. I read pravaṇa as 'inclined', so manaḥ pravaṇaṃ karoti is 'makes his mind inclined'. The prefix abhi- in abhidraṣṭum is rendered by 'look upon'. ↩
  197. I swear by his two feet: Swearing by the feet of a revered elder, here the nāgas' father, is a binding form of oath. ↩
  198. [your] father's command: Sanskrit tāta, a respectful and affectionate word for 'father'. Kuvalayāśva uses it for the nāgas' father, Aśvatara, who wished to see him (23.88–89). It is not his own father Śatrujit. ↩
  199. The reading: (1) tātājñām: the draft took tāta as Ṛtadhvaja's own father. The reviewer is right. Tāta is the nāgas' father, who wished to see him (23.88–89), so I render '[your] father's command'. 'Your' is in brackets because the Sanskrit does not say it. (2) padebhyām: the form is irregular. The regular instrumental dual is padābhyām (from pāda) or padbhyām (from pad). padebhyām looks like a plural ending on pada, or a corruption of padābhyām. The sense 'by his feet' is clear. I follow the reviewer and keep the dual, 'two feet', reading it as the instrumental of the oath with śapāmi. (3) uttiṣṭhata is a plural imperative, but only the two nāga youths are addressed. A dual uttiṣṭhatam would be regular, so the plural is probably loose usage or metrical. I render 'rise, you two'. (4) iha is a light filler, 'here' or 'in this matter'. I keep 'here' literally. (5) There is no new speaker's line. The verse continues Kuvalayāśva's speech opened at 102.10. ↩
  200. Gomatī: A river, here the one beside which the city lies; it is the route by which the two young nāgas lead the prince down to Pātāla in the following verses. ↩
  201. The reading: The verse has prāptaśca ('and reached') with no expressed subject. I take the subject to be the prince (nṛpātmaja), who is also the subject of yayau. The note on Gomatī links forward to Pātāla, which appears only in the verses after (23.93) and is not in this verse. ↩
  202. the two sons of the lord of the nāgas and the king's son: The compound nāgendra-nṛpa-nandanāḥ is read as nāgendra-nandanau (the two sons of the nāga lord) together with nṛpa-nandana (the king's son), three persons in all. This accounts for the plural 'they'. The nāga lord is Aśvatara, father of the two nāga youths, and the king's son is Puṣkaramālin. ↩
  203. nāgas: nāga: serpent-beings who live in the underworld (Pātāla) and can take human form. ↩
  204. The reading: 1. Compound nāgendranṛpanandanāḥ: it could be one group, 'sons of the nāga lord who is a king', or a group of three, the two sons of the nāga lord plus the king's son. I chose the three-person reading because te ('they') must include the prince, who is already travelling with the two (23.91, saha tābhyām), and because rājaputra is then named separately in the second half. 2. ve is read as vai, an emphatic particle left untranslated. 3. tat and tasyāḥ: the antecedent is Gomatī (23.91), so 'it' is used without brackets; tasyāḥ is feminine and fits the river. I rendered pāre as 'on the other shore of it' and added asau as 'that prince'. ↩
  205. The reading: ākṛṣya is an absolutive, so its agent is the agent of the main verb. Since nīto is passive, that agent is tābhyām, the two serpent youths. The draft wrongly made the prince the one drawn, and I have corrected it. The object of ākṛṣya is not stated, so I supplied '[him]' in brackets, meaning the prince. I took pātālam as the goal of the drawing, which is the natural reading with ākṛṣya. The alternative, that they drew the nether world itself toward them, is unlikely. I accepted the reviewer's point on 'down': the Sanskrit has no word for it, so I removed it. I also made ca and ubhau explicit with 'and ... both'. I did not add 'the prince' as a separate subject for sa. 'He' already renders it, and nṛpātmajaḥ names the same man. I kept the glossary's 'son of a king' for nṛpātmaja. Here it is nominative, not the vocative the glossary entry mentions, but the person is the same. ↩
  206. svastika: An auspicious mark shaped like a cross with bent arms. Here it is a mark on the hoods of the two serpent youths. ↩
  207. best of the twice-born: The vocative dvijasattamau is addressed to the two serpent youths. Serpents are called dvija, 'twice-born', because they are born first as eggs and then hatch. The word also suggests the brahmins' status. ↩
  208. the lord of the serpents: pannageśvara. The next verse (23.96) names him as Aśvatara. ↩
  209. The reading: dvijasattamau: dvija could mean brahmins, or serpents as 'twice-born' through egg and hatching. The glossary takes dvija as brahmins, but here it is addressed to the two serpent youths, so I keep the literal 'twice-born' and explain it in a note. The object of kathayāmāsatuḥ is not stated in these verses. The father's description continues in 23.96, so I render only 'told their father, the lord of the serpents'. ↩
  210. the dwellers in heaven: divaukasām, literally 'those whose home is heaven', the gods. ↩
  211. The reading: 1) The text reads 'apasyat'; this is a misprint or an unsandhied spelling for 'apaśyat', and I translate it as 'saw'. 2) 'śāntam' and 'mānanīyam' could agree with either Aśvatara or pātāla. I take them with Aśvatara, the nāga king whom the prince now meets, and I take 'ramaṇīyam' with pātāla. The accusative endings alone do not settle this. 3) 'tataḥ' is read as 'then', not 'from there'. 4) 'Tranquil [king]' supplies 'king' from the earlier verses, where Aśvatara is called the lord of serpents (pannageśvara). ↩
  212. as the sky is adorned with stars: cārukuṇḍalahārābhiḥ agrees with nāgakanyābhiḥ. In the simile the maidens in their ornaments are the stars (tārābhiḥ) and the nether world is the sky (gaganam); upaśobhitam is understood from the first line. ↩
  213. lutes: vīṇā: a stringed instrument, a lute or similar; veṇu is a bamboo flute. ↩
  214. The reading: 1. kumāraiḥ taruṇaiḥ vṛddhair uragaiḥ: I took all three adjectives as qualifying uragaiḥ (serpents who were boys, young men and elders), not 'boys, young men and old serpents'. 2. anugaiḥ in vīṇāveṇusvanānugaiḥ may be 'following' or 'accompanying'. I took it as the songs accompanied by the sounds of lute and flute. 3. The reviewer asked for the verse-end marker ' //' to be removed. I kept it, because the series convention requires the passage to end with ' //'. 4. The reviewer's main point on the simile is accepted. The maidens are the stars and the nether world is the sky. ↩
  215. mṛdaṅga: A double-headed barrel drum, played with the hands. ↩
  216. paṇava: A small drum or tabor, often used with the mṛdaṅga. ↩
  217. the subduer of enemies: Translates arindama, here an epithet of the prince, Śatrujit's son. ↩
  218. The reading: ātodya (musical instrument) is taken as the predicate of pātāla: the nether world 'having mṛdaṅga and paṇava drums as its instruments'. The sense is that it resounds with them. The compound could also be read as 'with the music of mṛdaṅga and paṇava'. ↩
  219. The reading: sthitam can mean 'standing' or 'seated'. I chose 'seated' because 23.102 places him on a seat (āsane). In svacchamuktāphalalatāhārihāra, latā can mean 'creeper' or 'strand'. I took it as strands of pearls forming the necklaces. Taking hāri as 'charming' is also an assumption, since it could be read as 'captivating'. ↩
  220. cat's-eye: vaidūrya, a precious stone, usually identified as cat's-eye chrysoberyl, sometimes as beryl. ↩
  221. he was pointed out to him: sa is the nāga king, the subject of darśitaḥ. tasya is a genitive standing for a dative: the prince, to whom he is shown. ↩
  222. The reading: tasya: read as a genitive used for the dative, 'to him' (the prince), with darśitaḥ. The alternative, 'his father', does not fit asmākam ('our father'). rūpake: taken as 'form, appearance' of the seat in 23.102, with jālāntarita 'interspersed, set about with latticework'. The locative continues from āsane in the previous verse, so 'seated' is supplied in brackets. ↩
  223. Kuvalayāśva: 'He who has the horse Kuvalaya'; a name of Ṛtadhvaja, the prince, son of Śatrujit. ↩
  224. he was presented to their father: The verse continues the sentence of 23.103, where the two young nāgas point out their father to the prince. Here the two present the prince to their father; the agents, the two nāgas, are implied. The word asau is taken as 'he' (the prince), with ayam 'this' for the direct speech. ↩
  225. The reading: The word 'asau' (and ca) is read as 'and he [the prince]' joined with niveditaḥ, with 'ayam' in the quotation. Another reading would take 'asau' as referring to the father, 'and that one'. I chose the first because the sentence turns to the prince being introduced to the father. The speakers of the quotation are not named in the verse; they are the two nāgas of 23.103. ↩
  226. lord of the nāgas: nāgendra, 'chief of the nāgas', here Aśvatara, the father of the two young nāgas. ↩
  227. smelled his head: upāghrāya: smelling or kissing the crown of the head was a customary gesture of affection from an elder to a younger or inferior person. ↩
  228. The reading: The verse is a single sentence, so no segments are given. The adverbs balāt and gāḍham both qualify parīṣasvaje; I have rendered them as 'tightly and with force'. parīṣasvaje is a Vedic-style perfect of pari-√svañj, 'embraced'. ↩
  229. My child: vatsa, literally 'calf', is an affectionate address to a younger person. Here Aśvatara, the nāga king, speaks to Ṛtadhvaja. ↩
  230. The reading: nihatāmitravargaḥ is a bahuvrīhi in the nominative, 'you whose host of enemies has been slain'. It agrees with the unexpressed subject of kuru, the only finite verb, which is an imperative. I rendered it as an absolute phrase ('with the host of your enemies slain'), not as a wish, as the reviewer says. dhanyasya, parokṣasya and te are three genitives in agreement, 'of you, the fortunate one, who are unseen', so dhanya is not a separate predicate. The verse has no speaker line, because the speech continues from 23.105 with Aśvatara speaking, so none is added. parokṣa (literally 'beyond the eye') is rendered 'not present'. ↩
  231. The reading: The Sanskrit has no noun with asāmānyāḥ (feminine/neuter plural). I supply [qualities] from guṇāḥ in 23.106. Tvam eva anena can be read as 'you yourself, by this' (this conduct or these qualities) or 'you alone'. I chose 'you yourself ... by this', since eva stresses tvam and anena points to the reported qualities. ↩
  232. the great folk: mahājane, locative singular: the eminent, or people at large. The sense is the esteem and trust of society. ↩
  233. the ancestors: pitaraḥ: the pitṛ, the departed forefathers, who are honoured with offerings and depend on the good conduct of their descendants. ↩
  234. the afflicted: vikala: deficient, crippled or distressed. The compound mitrārthivikalādayaḥ is read as mitra, arthin, vikala and others. ↩
  235. The reading: mahājana can mean 'great people, eminent men' or 'the multitude'. I chose 'the great folk', which keeps the ambiguity. The finite verb for the final list (devatāḥ ... ādayaḥ) is icchanti in 23.110, so the passage is left grammatically open and the list is not translated as a clause. ↩
  236. likewise: Tathā links this verse to the previous one, where gods, ancestors, brahmins and others are also said to wish for the virtuous man's long life. ↩
  237. slander: Parivāda means slander, censure or speaking ill of others. It can also mean being blamed, so the phrase could instead mean 'free from blame'. ↩
  238. The reading: Parivādanivṛttānām: 'turned away from slander' (from parivāda = censure of others) or 'free from being blamed'. I chose the first because it fits the other qualities, compassion and giving refuge, which are things the virtuous do. Saṃśritānām vipadgataiḥ: I take the genitive as 'of those resorted to by those fallen into calamity', the instrumental being the agent of the passive participle. The verse as printed also has an irregular metrical form, which may reflect a textual disturbance. ↩
  239. Kuvalayāśva: The name of Ṛtadhvaja, 'he who has the horse Kuvalaya'. The serpent king Aśvatara is the speaker, and Kuvalayāśva is the hero he has just addressed. ↩
  240. The reading: The verse does not name the speaker. 'nāgendra' in 23.105 and 'bhujaṅgama' here refer to the same serpent king. 'putrau' is the dual, so two sons. 'Pūjā' is 'honour, worship', and I rendered it as 'honour' because it is directed at a guest. 'Vīra' qualifies the hero Kuvalayāśva, who is also the person addressed in 'taṃ', so it is one person. ↩
  241. Śatrujit's son: The prince Ṛtadhvaja, called Kuvalayāśva after his horse Kuvalaya. ↩
  242. approved that speech: The e-text reads anumena ca tanmauno, which does not parse and is probably corrupt. The rendering gives the sense the context requires (he approved the proposal just made) and is conjectural as to the exact original wording. ↩
  243. The reading: anumena ca tanmauno is a crux. Possible emendations are anumene ca tan mene, or anumene with tanmauno a corruption of some other word. I no longer read tanmaunaḥ as 'silent' (mauna), since that builds a meaning on a corrupt word and nothing in the context suggests silent assent. I render only the sense the context supports: the prince approved the speech (vacaḥ). A second doubt is whether nṛpatiḥ pannagānām is the same person as Śatrujitaḥ sutaḥ. I keep the serpent king as a separate subject of cakāra. Verse 23.111 has him making the proposal, and verse 23.115 has him joining his own sons and the king's son to feast, so a prince is not meant. I take tathā as 'so', meaning he acted in accordance with the proposal just made, and not 'as he had said'. ↩
  244. his own sons and the king's son: The compound ātmajabhūpanandanaiḥ is plural. It covers the serpent-lord's sons together with the prince Ṛtadhvaja (Kuvalayāśva), who is the king's son (bhūpanandana). ↩
  245. great serpents: mahoraga, 'great serpent', is a class of serpent-beings, here the nāgas of Pātāla. The lord meant is the serpent-king of the preceding verses. ↩
  246. The reading: (1) ātmajabhūpanandanaiḥ: I take it as two groups joined, the serpent's own sons (ātmaja) and the king's son (bhūpanandana), with the plural covering both. The alternative is a single compound qualifying tair, 'those sons, delighters of kings', which is less natural here. (2) bhogabhuk: it can mean 'enjoyer of pleasures', which I chose, or 'serpent', since bhoga also means a snake's coil. The sense 'serpent' would make the phrase an apposition for the lord of serpents. (3) The verses after (103.20, 104.1) are chapter colophon and numbering from the e-text and are not part of this verse. ↩
  247. Kuvalayāśva: 'He who has the horse Kuvalaya'; a name of Ṛtadhvaja, the prince, son of Śatrujit. ↩
  248. Pātāla: The nether worlds, the realm of the serpents (pannaga), where the prince goes in this chapter. ↩
  249. Madālasā episode: upākhyāna: a subsidiary tale told within the main narrative of a Purāṇa. The story of the maiden Madālasā, daughter of Viśvāvasu, is its subject. ↩
  250. The reading: The verse is a colophon, not a narrative verse. The compound kuvalayāśvapātālagamanam is taken as 'the going of Kuvalayāśva to Pātāla', with gamana as a verbal noun. The reading trayoviṃsa, given in the text as trayoviṃso, is taken as 'twenty-third'; the standard form is trayoviṃśa. ↩

Adhyāya 24

Sanskrit

चतुर्विशो ऽध्यायः

caturviśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Twenty-Four1

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

24.1

Sanskrit

कृताहारं महात्मनामधिपं पवनाशिनाम् । उपासाञ्चक्रिरे पुत्रौ भूपालतनयस्तथा ॥

kṛtāhāraṃ mahātmanāmadhipaṃ pavanāśinām | upāsāñcakrire putrau bhūpālatanayastathā ||

English

The two sons [of the serpent], and likewise the son of the king2, attended upon the lord of the great-souled wind-eaters3, who had finished his meal.4

24.2

Sanskrit

कथाभिरनुरूपाभिः स महात्मा भुजङ्गमः । प्रीतिं सञ्जनयामास पुत्रसख्युरुवाच च ॥

kathābhiranurūpābhiḥ sa mahātmā bhujaṅgamaḥ | prītiṃ sañjanayāmāsa putrasakhyuruvāca ca ||

English

With fitting conversations, that great-souled serpent produced pleasure in the friend of his sons, and spoke [to him].5

24.3

Sanskrit

तव भद्र ! सुखं ब्रूहि गेहमभ्यागतस्य यत् । कर्तव्यमुत्सृजाशङ्कां पितरीव सुतो मयि ॥

tava bhadra ! sukhaṃ brūhi gehamabhyāgatasya yat | kartavyamutsṛjāśaṅkāṃ pitarīva suto mayi ||

English

"Good youth6, you have come to my house. Tell me what is to be done for your comfort. Put aside your hesitation, as a son does with a father, [and speak] to me."7

24.4

Sanskrit

रजतं वा सुवर्णं वा वस्त्रं वाहनमासनम् । यद्वाभिमतमत्यर्थं दुर्लभं तद्वृणुष्व माम् ॥

rajataṃ vā suvarṇaṃ vā vastraṃ vāhanamāsanam | yadvābhimatamatyarthaṃ durlabhaṃ tadvṛṇuṣva mām ||

English

Silver or gold, clothing, a conveyance, a seat, or whatever else you greatly desire and find hard to obtain: ask me for it.8

Sanskrit

कुवलयाश्व उवाच

kuvalayāśva uvāca

English

Kuvalayāśva said:

24.5

Sanskrit

तव प्रसादाद्भगवन् ! सुवर्णादि गृहे मम । पितुरस्ति ममाद्यापिन किञ्चित् कार्यमीदृशम् ॥

tava prasādādbhagavan ! suvarṇādi gṛhe mama | piturasti mamādyāpina kiñcit kāryamīdṛśam ||

English

By your grace, venerable sir, there is gold and the like in my house; my father has [them]. Even now I have no need at all of anything of this kind.9

24.6

Sanskrit

ताते वर्षसहस्राणि शासतीमां वसुन्धराम् । तथैव त्वयि पातालं न मे याञ्चोन्मुकं मनः ॥

tāte varṣasahasrāṇi śāsatīmāṃ vasundharām | tathaiva tvayi pātālaṃ na me yāñconmukaṃ manaḥ ||

English

While my father10 has been ruling this earth for thousands of years, and likewise while you [rule]11 the pātāla realms, my mind is not eager to make a request.12

24.7

Sanskrit

ते स्वर्ग्याश्च सुपुण्याश्च येषां पितरि जीवति । तृणकोटिसमं वित्तं तारुण्याद्वित्तकोटिषु ॥

te svargyāśca supuṇyāśca yeṣāṃ pitari jīvati | tṛṇakoṭisamaṃ vittaṃ tāruṇyādvittakoṭiṣu ||

English

They are worthy of heaven and greatly meritorious, those whose father is alive, for whom, because of youth, wealth, even among crores of wealth, is equal to a crore13 of blades of grass.14†

24.8

Sanskrit

मित्राणि तुल्यशिष्टानि तद्वद्देहमनामयम् । जनिता ध्रियते वित्तं यौवनं किन्नु नास्ति मे ॥

mitrāṇi tulyaśiṣṭāni tadvaddehamanāmayam | janitā dhriyate vittaṃ yauvanaṃ kinnu nāsti me ||

English

Sanskrit

asatyarthe nṛṇāṃ yāñcāpravaṇaṃ jāyate manaḥ | satyaśeṣe kathaṃ yāñcāṃ mama jihvā kariṣyati ||

English

When there is no wealth, the minds of men become inclined to beg. When [everything] is present, with nothing lacking16, how will my tongue make a request?17

24.10

Sanskrit

English

24.11

Sanskrit

ye tu bālyāt prabhṛtyeva vinā pitrā kuṭumbinaḥ | te sukhāsvādavibhraṃśānmanye dhātraiva vañcitāḥ ||

English

24.12

Sanskrit

tadvayaṃ tvatprasādena dhanaratnādisañcayān | pitṛmuktān prayacchāmaḥ kāmato nityamarthinām ||

So, by your favour23, we give, according to their wish and always, to those who seek, the hoards of wealth, jewels and the like that our father has left us24.25†

Sanskrit

tat sarvamiha saṃprāptaṃ yadaṅghriyugalaṃ tava | maccūḍāmaṇinā spṛṣṭaṃ yaccāṅgasparśamāptavān ||

Sanskrit

jaḍa uvāca ityevaṃ prasṛtaṃ vākyamuktaḥ pannagasattamaḥ | prāha rājasutaṃ prītyā putrayorupakāriṇam ||

English

Jaḍa said: Addressed in these words, which had been spoken at such length, the best of the serpents28 spoke with affection to the king's son, the benefactor of his two sons29.30

nāga uvāca

24.15

yadi ratnasuvarṇādi matto 'vāptuṃ na te manaḥ | yadanyanmanasaḥ prītyai tadbrūhi tvaṃ dadāmyaham ||

bhagavaṃstvatprasādena prārthitasya gṛhe mama | sarvamasti viśeṣeṇa samprāptaṃ tava darśanāt ||

English

Its English is given with 24.16, above.

Sanskrit

Its English is given with 24.20–21, above.

Its English is given with 24.23, above.

tato 'sya patnī dayitā śrutvemaṃ vinipātitam | atyajaddayitān prāṇān vipralabdhā durātmanā ||

kenāpi kṛtavaireṇa dānavena kubuddhinā | gandharvarājasya sutā nāmnā khyātā madālasā ||

Sanskrit

अश्वतर उवाच

aśvatara uvāca

English

Aśvatara said:

Sanskrit

jaḍa uvāca

24.43

Sanskrit

ततः प्रहृष्टः प्रतिलभ्य कान्तां प्रणम्य नागं निजगाम सो ऽथ । सुशोभमानः स्वपुरं तमश्वम् आरुह्य संचिन्तितमभ्युपतेम् ॥

tataḥ prahṛṣṭaḥ pratilabhya kāntāṃ praṇamya nāgaṃ nijagāma so 'tha | suśobhamānaḥ svapuraṃ tamaśvam āruhya saṃcintitamabhyupatem ||

English

Then, greatly delighted at having regained his beloved, he bowed to the nāga and went to his own city, shining splendidly, having mounted that horse, which had come to him when he thought of it91.92

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे मदालसाप्राप्तिर्नाम चतुर्विशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe madālasāprāptirnāma caturviśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, named "The Regaining of Madālasā," in the venerable93 Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.94

  1. The reading: The line is a chapter heading, not a verse. The Sanskrit reads caturviśo 'dhyāyaḥ, 'the twenty-fourth chapter'. The reference [104.1] and the verse numbering of the e-text are irregular (the preceding colophon is numbered 103.20), but this does not affect the translation. ↩
  2. the son of the king: bhūpālatanaya refers to the prince Kuvalayāśva (Ṛtadhvaja), son of Śatrujit, who had been brought to Pātāla. ↩
  3. wind-eaters: pavanāśin, 'one who feeds on air', is a common name for serpents, who were believed to live on wind. Here it means the nāgas, and their lord is the serpent king of the preceding verses. ↩
  4. The reading: putrau (dual, 'two sons') is not said to be whose sons. I took it as the two sons of the serpent king, since 23.115 mentions his sons (ātmaja) together with the king's son. The verb upāsāñcakrire is plural because it has three subjects: the two sons and the prince. ↩
  5. The reading: putrasakhyuḥ is the genitive (or ablative) of putrasakhi, 'friend of his sons', i.e. Kuvalayāśva. The verse also contains the sandhi form uvāca ca. The genitive can be read two ways. (a) It can depend on prītim: 'produced pleasure in the friend of his sons'. (b) It can be objective: 'produced affection for the friend of his sons'. I chose (a), because the causative sañjanayāmāsa suggests that the guest was pleased by the talk. The unexpressed object of uvāca, 'to him', is supplied in brackets. ↩
  6. Good youth: Sanskrit bhadra, a vocative of address meaning 'good one' or 'auspicious one'. The serpent king addresses Kuvalayāśva, the prince who has come to his house. ↩
  7. The reading: The verse has no verb in the second half beyond utsṛja ('abandon'). 'Tell' (brūhi) governs 'what is to be done', and the phrase 'what is to be done for your comfort' renders tava sukhaṃ ... yat kartavyam. The words 'and speak' are supplied for the comparison 'as a son to a father'. Alternatively sukham could be read as an adverb, 'tell [me] at ease'. I took it as a noun, 'comfort', because it fits the host's offer in the next verse. ↩
  8. The reading: The word 'yadvā' (yad vā) is taken as 'or whatever', closing the list of things that may be asked for. 'Atyartham' is read adverbially with 'abhimatam', 'greatly desired'.
