The verse could also be read as 'whatever is desired and is exceedingly hard to obtain'. 'Vṛṇuṣva mām' is literally 'choose from me'; I render it 'ask me for it'. ↩
  9. The reading: (1) pitur asti: pituḥ is genitive, so I take it as possession ('my father has [them]'), not 'my father is alive'. I accept the reviewer's findings on the genitive, on deleting the bracketed 'is alive', and on adyāpi. The bracketed 'them' is needed to supply the object of asti, namely suvarṇādi. (2) Alternative reading: mama pituḥ, 'in my father's house', with gṛhe mama split off. The metrical break after gṛhe mama makes mama belong to the first line, so I keep 'in my house', as the reviewer also advises. (3) mamādyāpina is separated as mama adyāpi na. adyāpi ('even now') goes with the final clause, 'I have no need at all of anything of this kind' (na kiñcit kāryam īdṛśam). The father's being alive is not stated here; it only appears in 24.6. ↩
  10. my father: tāta here is Ṛtadhvaja's own father, King Śatrujit. The locative tāte with śāsatīm is a locative absolute. ↩
  11. while you [rule]: The verse has the locative absolute tvayi but no participle with it. The participle śāsati, 'ruling', is carried over from the first half, where pātālam is its object. ↩
  12. The reading: yāñconmukam is read as yāñcā + unmukam (unmukha, 'turned toward, eager for'), so 'eager to make a request'. The e-text's sandhi and the feminine participle śāsatīm (agreeing with vasundharām, not with tāte) look irregular. I take śāsatīm as a corrupt or loose form of the locative absolute tāte śāsati, 'while [my] father rules', and render it that way. ↩
  13. a crore: koṭi is ten million and is often used for any very large number. It occurs twice in the verse, once with wealth (vittakoṭiṣu) and once with blades of grass (tṛṇakoṭi). ↩
  14. The reading: 1. tāruṇyāt is an ablative, 'from youth' or 'because of youth'. A locative reading, 'in youth', is also possible. I follow the reviewer and choose 'because of youth': young men with a living father lack nothing and do not need to value wealth. Verse 8 ('wealth, youth, what do I lack?') names youth among the blessings and is compatible with either reading. 2. vittakoṭiṣu is a locative, 'among crores of wealth'. I render it concessively, 'even among crores of wealth', and use 'wealth' for both occurrences of vitta, as the reviewer asks. The sense is that wealth, even when it runs to crores, counts for no more than a crore of straws. 3. The relative yeṣām governs both the locative absolute pitari jīvati and the clause about wealth, so 'for whom' is carried into the second half without added words. The correlative te is kept as the main clause: 'They are worthy of heaven ... those whose father is alive'. 4. An alternative would be that youth outweighs crores of wealth. I did not choose it, ↩
  15. The reading: tulyaśiṣṭāni: the compound can be read as 'equal and well-bred/disciplined' (śiṣṭa in the sense of cultured), or as 'like the remainder', or 'equally taught'. I chose 'equals and well-bred' as the most natural sense in the context, which lists the advantages that a son whose father is alive enjoys. The sentence has no finite verb apart from dhriyate and nāsti, so the bracketed '[I have]' is implied from me. Also, dhriyate literally means 'is sustained, is held up', and I render it 'is alive'. ↩
  16. with nothing lacking: Read as sati aśeṣe, a locative absolute matching asati arthe in the first half. The sandhi satyaśeṣe hides the division. ↩
  17. The reading: asatyarthe is read as asati arthe, 'when wealth is not there'. satyaśeṣe is read as sati aśeṣe, 'when [wealth] is present without remainder', as the counterpart of asati arthe. A possible alternative is a compound satya-śeṣa, 'when the remainder is real'. That makes poor sense and breaks the parallel, so I rejected it. The bracketed 'everything' supplies the subject of sati. ↩
  18. the tree of their father's arm: A metaphor (pitṛbāhutaru): the father's arm is likened to a tree whose shade shelters the son, who therefore has no concern about wealth. ↩
  19. The reading: The text reads 'mama gehe' (in my house), while the plural relative 'yaiḥ' and 'te' refer to those sons who live under a father's protection. The first-person 'mama' is the speaker's own hypothetical thought ("in my house"), as in the quoted thought. I have kept it within the quotation. 'pitṛ' is rendered 'father' here, not 'ancestor' as in the glossary, because the context (24.7-24.9) concerns a living father. ↩
  20. heads of households: kuṭumbin, one who has a family (kuṭumba) to support; the glossary's 'servant or dependent' (bhṛtya) is not meant here. ↩
  21. Fate: dhātṛ, 'the Placer' or 'Ordainer', here the power that disposes human lots, and also a name of Brahmā. The word is understood here as Fate. ↩
  22. The reading: dhātrā may mean the creator Brahmā or Fate in general; I chose 'Fate' because the context concerns the lot of fatherless householders. sukhāsvādavibhraṃśāt is taken as an ablative of cause, 'through the loss of the taste of happiness'. Alternatively it could be read as 'because of falling away from', but the sense is much the same. ↩
  23. by your favour: prasāda: grace or favour; the speaker credits the prince's kindness for the freedom he now has to give. ↩
  24. that our father has left us: pitṛmuktān is read as 'left, released by the father' (pitṛ + mukta), qualifying sañcayān. The speaker, the young nāga, says that he and his brother give freely from what their father left. ↩
  25. The reading: pitṛmuktān: could mean 'left by the father' (my choice, fitting the preceding verses on paternal wealth) or 'freed from the ancestors/pitṛ'. The sense 'left by the father' is preferred. 'vayam' is plural, but the speaker is probably one of two brothers, so 'we' is retained. The pronoun 'tvat' refers to the prince, Puṣkaramālin. ↩
  26. crest-jewel: cūḍāmaṇi, the jewel worn on the top of the head. Touching the feet with it is a gesture of homage. ↩
  27. The reading: The verb āptavān is a masculine singular participle with no stated subject. I take the implied subject to be the speaker, 'I', in agreement with maccūḍāmaṇinā ('my crest-jewel'). An alternative would make the person addressed the one who gained the touch, but the context of thanks to the serpent and the first-person 'my' favour the speaker. ↩
  28. the best of the serpents: pannagasattama: the serpent king Aśvatara, who is addressing Puṣkaramālin; the verse itself does not name him. ↩
  29. his two sons: putrayoḥ is dual and in the genitive. It is taken with upakāriṇam, 'benefactor of the two sons', the serpent's own sons whom the prince had helped. ↩
  30. The reading: The verse does not name the serpent or the prince. I take pannagasattama as the serpent king (Aśvatara) and rājasuta as Puṣkaramālin, from context and the glossary. putrayoḥ upakāriṇam could also be read as 'who had done a service to the two sons' with the sons not necessarily the serpent's own. The serpent's own sons is the natural reading and is the one I chose. The phrase prasṛtaṃ vākyam, 'extended speech', is rendered 'spoken at such length', and the verb ukta is taken as passive, 'being addressed'. ↩
  31. The reading: The Sanskrit has no vocative in this verse; the speaker is the best of serpents (pannagasattama) of 24.14, speaking to the prince, so no name is added. 'ratnasuvarṇādi' is taken as 'jewels, gold and the like'. 'matto' is the ablative of 'mad', 'from me'. 'prītyai' is a dative of purpose, 'for the pleasure of the mind', rendered as 'would please your mind'. ↩
  32. Bhagavan: Vocative bhagavat, 'revered one', addressed here to the chief of the nāgas (pannagasattama, 24.14). ↩
  33. who have been asked [what I wish]: prārthitasya, genitive agreeing with mama: 'of me who am solicited', i.e. invited by the nāga to state a wish (24.15). Taken in this sense, not 'one who has made a request'. ↩
  34. The reading: prārthitasya may be passive ('of me who have been asked/solicited', answering the offer in 24.15) or, less naturally, 'of me who have desired/sought'. I chose the passive, since the nāga has just invited the prince to name a wish. 'viśeṣeṇa' could also qualify asti ('especially/particularly'); I took it with samprāptaṃ, 'above all obtained through the sight of you'. ↩
  35. a god: devasya: the speaker, Kuvalayāśva, addresses the chief of the serpents (pannaga) as a deva, a divine being. ↩
  36. The reading: The text reads 'yadaṅgasaṃśleṣam itas tava devasya'. 'itaḥ' is taken as 'from this [meeting]' / 'here', and the construction is read as 'I have obtained the embrace of your limbs'. The verb ('prāptaḥ' or similar) is not in the verse and is supplied in English as 'have come by'. 'Yat' is read as 'because'. The genitive 'tava devasya' is taken with 'aṅgasaṃśleṣam', 'the embrace of your limbs'. The word 'itaḥ' could also be read as 'hence, from now', but 'here' is the better sense. ↩
  37. lord of serpents: Vocative of pannageśvara, addressed to the Nāga king, who is the speaker of the preceding verses. ↩
  38. The reading: The sense of 'yad ... kṛtaṃ tenaiva' is taken as 'because a place has been made ... by that very thing'. The word 'iha' is taken as 'here', with 'āspadam'. The verse could also be read with 'yat' as relative, 'the place that was made ... by that very thing, what have I not obtained?'; the two readings give the same sense. The text reads 'yadihāspadam' (yad + iha + āspadam). ↩
  39. the impression of that meritorious act: saṃskāra here is the latent impression or memory a deed leaves in the mind. The "meritorious act" is probably his act of service to the nāga's sons, for which the nāga is rewarding him. ↩
  40. The reading: The compound tatpuṇyakarmasaṃskāraḥ can be read as 'the impression of that meritorious act' (tat modifying puṇyakarman, as chosen) or as 'the impression (saṃskāra) of that meritorious deed' with the sense of a disposition toward meritorious acts. I chose the first as simpler and fitting the context, where the previous verses speak of his service and the nāga's offer. The verse says only 'that', so the act itself is not named here. ↩
  41. unguents: The text reads anulepan, which is metrically and grammatically irregular. It is probably a misprint for anulepanam or anulepanāḥ, and the sense is the same. ↩
  42. the tree of merit: puṇya-vanaspati: puṇya is meritorious action, or the merit it yields. Vanaspati is a large forest tree, specifically one that bears fruit without visible flowers. The compound is read as a metaphor, with merit as the tree and these enjoyments as its fruit. ↩
  43. The reading: anulepan (24.20) is irregular; it is probably corrupt for anulepanam (or anulepanāni), and I translate 'unguents'. The compound cārumālyānulepan could also be taken as 'fair garlands and unguents' (two items) rather than as one phrase, and I have taken it as two items. The form mataṃ (24.21) is read as the participle 'held, considered' with mama as the agent ('by me, in my view'). ↩
  44. whose self is perfected: kṛtātman: one who has disciplined or perfected himself; it can also mean 'resolute'. ↩
  45. that [merit]: tanmūlaḥ, 'having that as its root', refers back to the tree of merit (puṇyavanaspati) of 24.21; the text prints 'tanmulaḥ' with a short u. ↩
  46. The reading: tanmulaḥ is read as tanmūlaḥ ('rooted in that'), the vowel being short in the e-text. kṛtātmanā: 'whose self is perfected' was chosen over 'resolute'. The verse has a metrical irregularity: kartavyaḥ seems to repeat kāryaḥ, so I have rendered it as an emphatic 'must be made'. ↩
  47. The reading: The reference '105.8' is evidently a misnumbering in the e-text; the line is the speaker's introduction to 24.23 (Aśvatara replying to the king's son). The vocative prājña is addressed to the king's son, who has just spoken at 24.17–22. In 24.23 'evaṃ bhaviṣyati' could also be read as 'it will be so [as you wish]' in reply to the request of 24.19 that the memory of meritorious deeds not leave his heart; I kept the plain rendering 'So it will be', which allows that reading. The phrase 'dharmāśritā matiḥ' is taken as 'mind resting on/grounded in dharma'. ↩
  48. The reading: The verse is spoken by Aśvatara (the speaker line 105.8 precedes 24.23). In 'yan mānuṣe loke duṣprāptaṃ bhavato matam', 'bhavato matam' is read as 'in your opinion / considered by you' (genitive of the agent with the participle matam), qualifying 'yat'. 'Madgeham āgatena tvayā' is an instrumental absolute-like construction ('by you who have come to my house'), rendered as a subordinate clause. ↩
  49. the prince: Nṛpanandana, 'delight of the king', means a king's son. The verse does not name him; he is the guest in Aśvatara's house. ↩
  50. looked at the faces: The text reads mukāvalokanam; mukha-avalokanam, 'looking at the faces', is meant. ↩
  51. the lord of serpents: Pannageśvara, 'lord of the pannagas', is Aśvatara, the nāga king who has just spoken; the two sons are the two youths of the glossary. ↩
  52. The reading: The text reads 'mukāvalokanam', which is not a word. I take it as a misprint for 'mukhāvalokanam' ('looking at the face'), which fits the sense: the prince glances at the two youths as if to consult them. Reading the compound as 'mūka-' ('dumb, silent') does not yield a sense that fits the grammar. ↩
  53. [their] father: pituḥ is a genitive. I take it as standing for the person addressed with kathayāmāsatuḥ ('told'), a loose use common in Purāṇic Sanskrit. It is not construed with praṇipatya. The father is Aśvatara. ↩
  54. The reading: 1) praṇipatya has no stated object. I now leave the bowing unspecified ('having bowed low') and no longer supply '[to the prince]'. The reviewer suggests 'bowed to their father', but that would mean construing the genitive pituḥ with praṇipatya, which normally takes an accusative or dative. I therefore keep pituḥ with kathayāmāsatuḥ, and the note says so. 2) pituḥ: the readings are (a) a genitive standing for the dative of the person addressed, with kath (chosen), or (b) a genitive with praṇipatya. 3) vīrau is now rendered 'the two brave ones', following the glossary, and 'sons' is removed from the wording. '[their]' is bracketed because the Sanskrit implies it without saying it. 4) matam is rendered 'intention', but 'wish' or 'opinion' are also possible. ↩
  55. his beloved wife: asya and imam in 24.27 both refer to the prince, the husband of Madālasā, whose story the two sons are telling their father. ↩
  56. deceived: The deception was a false report of her husband's death, told in an earlier episode of the Purāṇa; on hearing it she died. ↩
  57. The reading: 105.14 putrāpūcatuḥ: the sandhi is irregular. I read putrau ūcatuḥ, 'the two sons said', with the speakers being the two nāga youths addressing Aśvatara. In 24.27 asya and imam are both taken as the prince, the husband; the text does not name him in these verses. ↩
  58. The reading: The reading kutajño is probably a misprint for kṛtajño, "grateful", and I have translated it so. kutajña has no clear meaning here. The verse does not name the one who made the vow. The next verse (24.30) calls him Ṛtadhvaja, so "this one" is he. The glossary entry rājaputra, which gives "Puṣkaramālin", does not seem to fit here, and I have not used it. ↩
  59. hero: The vocative vīra is addressed to the father, not to Ṛtadhvaja, and is taken as a respectful address. The glossary's gloss of vīra as qualifying the husband does not fit the vocative here. ↩
  60. Father: tāta is the sons' address to their father, the nāga king Aśvatara. ↩
  61. The reading: The vocative vīra could address the father or qualify Ṛtadhvaja (vīra Ṛtadhvaja, 'the brave Ṛtadhvaja'). Since the vocative is marked in the text and tāta follows as a second vocative, I took vīra as addressed to the father. The reading of 'sarvāṅgī' as 'fair in all her limbs' follows cāru-sarva-aṅgī, a bahuvrīhi-derived feminine. Also, 'tat kṛtaṃ bhavet' is rendered 'it will have been accomplished', as an optative with a past participle, meaning the task would be done. ↩
  62. separated from beings: bhūtaiḥ here means living beings. One 'separated from beings' (viyogin) is a dead person, in this context Madālasā. The union spoken of is therefore one between the dead only. ↩
  63. Śambara: A dānava famed for his skill in illusion. His māyā is cited as the standard example of a deceptive appearance. ↩
  64. The reading: (1) bhūtair viyogino: bhūta can mean 'living beings' or 'the elements'. On either reading the viyogin is the dead. I kept 'beings' because it is the more natural complement of viyogin and gives the same sense. The draft's note hedged between the dead and the living; it now commits to the dead. (2) Reciprocity: I accepted the reviewer's point. tādṛśaiḥ ... tādṛśaḥ means that the union of such a one is of that kind only with those like him, so the translation now makes the correspondence explicit. (3) yogaḥ: here it means 'union', not the discipline, so it is rendered 'union' with no asterisks and no note, even though the glossary lists yoga as a technical term. (4) etat: I made 'this' explicit in the question. I kept 'except through' for vinā, since 'except' is a fair rendering of vinā with the accusative. (5) śambaroditām: rendered 'of which Śambara spoke', which does not imply that he uttered the illusion himself. The past participle may also be read as 'reported of Śamb ↩
  65. the son of Śatrujit: Ṛtadhvaja, the prince, named by his patronymic. ↩
  66. the lord of serpents: Bhujaṅgeśa, here Aśvatara, the nāga king, who has just spoken. ↩
  67. The reading: Mahātmānam is accusative and could in principle qualify bhujaṅgeśam or stand alone; I take it as in apposition to bhujaṅgeśam, the great-souled nāga king, who is the one addressed. ↩
  68. Father: tāta is a respectful address to an elder, here used by Ṛtadhvaja to the nāga king Aśvatara; it does not imply actual paternity. ↩
  69. made of illusion: māyāmayī, 'consisting of māyā': an illusory Madālasā, not the real woman. The possibility of an illusion or dream was raised in 24.31 (svapna, and the māyā of Śambara). ↩
  70. The reading: (1) api: I now take it with māyāmayīm ('even one made of illusion'), as the reviewer says, and not with the conditional clause. (2) darśayate: the subject is unstated. Because the vocative tāta addresses Aśvatara, I take 'you' as the subject and drop the earlier indefinite 'someone'. (3) mama can be read three ways: 'my Madālasā' (with madālasām), 'to me' with the causative darśayate (genitive in the sense of a dative), or 'a favour done to me' with kṛtam anugraham. I chose 'to me' with the showing, which also makes the favour his; the sense is the same either way. I rejected 'my Madālasā' because she is not yet his wife. (4) manye is rendered in the plain present, 'I consider'. The verse sits inside the speech that pratyuvāca opens in 24.32, so no speaker line is added. ↩
  71. my child: Vocative of vatsa, a form of address to a younger person; here Aśvatara speaks to Ṛtadhvaja. ↩
  72. guru: Here a person owed respect and honour, as a teacher or elder is; a guest, even a young one, is to be honoured in this way. The word is not the epithet Guru (Bṛhaspati). ↩
  73. The reading: The second line is elliptical. 'anugrāhyo bhavān' could be 'you are to be favoured' (as a guest), which I chose. 'gehaṃ' is accusative of goal with 'abhyāgataḥ' ('come to the house'). 'bālo 'pi ... guruḥ' is taken as a general maxim that even a young guest is a guru, not as a statement that Ṛtadhvaja is Aśvatara's guru. The text 'māyāñced' is read as māyāṃ ced. ↩
  74. The lord of the nāgas: Nāgendra, 'chief of the nāgas', is Aśvatara, who is speaking in the preceding verses. ↩
  75. in order to bewilder them: teṣām is not clearly resolved in this verse. It is taken as the people present, the intended objects of the bewilderment. ↩
  76. The reading: jjalpa is not a standard form. I take it as a misprint for jajalpa, the perfect of √jalp, 'he spoke', with nāgendraḥ as subject, and sphuṭam as 'plainly, clearly'. Another reading takes jalpa as a noun, 'talk', but then the clause lacks a verb. Also, teṣām has no clear antecedent in the verses given. ↩
  77. The reading: The verse has no speaker's verb. The words 'seyaṃ na veti te bhāryā rājaputra madālasā' are most naturally the nāga's speech, so I supplied 'saying' in brackets. The subject of darśayāmāsa is Aśvatara, the nāga lord of 24.35. 'Sā iyam' is read as 'this very one'. 'Na vā iti' is read as the alternative question 'or not', which is the usual force of 'na veti'. ↩
  78. the slender one: tanvī, here Madālasā as she appears to the prince; the figure shown is an illusion (see 24.33). ↩
  79. The reading: The verse is hypermetrical in the e-text. 'vācam udīrayan' is literally 'uttering the word'; I render it as 'calling out the word "Beloved!"'. 'Tatkṣaṇāt' is taken with 'vigatatrapaḥ' ('at that very moment'). The ablative 'tatkṣaṇāt' could also be read with 'yayau'; the sense is unchanged. ↩
  80. The reading: The reviewer is right that my earlier note was wrong. Nothing in the text supports a 'test of the prince'. Aśvatara presents Madālasā as a conjured semblance in order to bewilder the youths (v. 35, teṣāṃ saṃmohanārthāya). I have removed that note. māyā is already explained in the glossary, so I keep it in asterisks and give no new note. The verse has no speaker's line of its own. The speaker is Aśvatara, who is speaking in the preceding verse, so I add none. 'Mā sprākṣīḥ' is the aorist with mā, a prohibition ('do not touch'). 'Saṃsparśanādibhiḥ' is instrumental plural ('by touch and the like'). I now keep 'kathitaṃ tava' as a passive ('it was told to you'), as the Sanskrit has it, and not as 'I told you'. The word 'her' in brackets is implied by the verb. ↩
  81. the lady: bhāminī here is Madālasā, whom the prince has just seen; the glossary notes it as the woman of the city, but the context shows the one he mourns. ↩
  82. The reading: bhāminīm: the glossary glosses it as 'the woman of the city', but here the object of his thought is clearly Madālasā, the woman he has just seen and takes to be lost. cintayāmāsa could also be 'reflected on' or 'brooded over'; I chose 'thought of' as the plainest sense with the accusative. The subject changes in the second half: sa tu ... so 'tha both refer to the prince, so there is no change of agent. ↩
  83. this king: The speaker is not named in the verse. 'This king' is read as the prince, with the thought assigned to the lady of 24.39 (see doubts). ↩
  84. The reading: The speaker and the referent of asya nṛpateḥ are not certain. 24.39 has cintayāmāsa bhāminīm, 'he thought of the lady', and that accusative may be a corruption of bhāminī, 'the lady thought'. I follow the second reading: the lady thinks of the prince as 'this king' (mama upari = 'toward me'). Another reading takes the prince as the thinker and the nāga king as 'this king', but this fits mama upari and the felling by affection less well. I take pātano 'rīṇām as 'felling (i.e. destroying) enemies', an epithet of the prince. ↩
  85. through the working of wind, water, fire, earth and space: The instrumental ceṣṭayā governs the whole list of the five elements. The sense is probably that the elements acted as in a real body, so the appearance cannot be mere illusion. The line is compressed and open to other readings. ↩
  86. earth: The text reads bhumeḥ, a short-vowel form of bhūmeḥ, 'of the earth'. It is probably metrical or a misprint. ↩
  87. The reading: The verse is compressed. (1) mithyā may be an adverb with darśitā ('falsely shown as illusion') or a predicate of māyā ('that "it is illusion" is false'). I took the second, since mithyā māyeti sets the quoted word against the first māyeti. (2) The genitives vāyvambutejasāṃ bhumer ākāśasya are taken with ceṣṭayā, 'by the working of the five elements', although the logic is elliptical. (3) bhumeḥ is read as bhūmeḥ. ↩
  88. the serpent: bhujaṅgama, 'serpent', here stands for the nāga Aśvatara, who has been speaking in the preceding verses. ↩
  89. beginning with the restoring of the dead to life: mṛtasañjīvanādikam, 'having the restoring of the dead to life as its first item': the account began with this and went on to other matters, which the verse does not list. ↩
  90. The reading: The Sanskrit does not name Aśvatara in this verse; bhujaṅgamaḥ is taken as the nāga Aśvatara of 24.37, hence the bracketed name. 'Comforted' renders samāśvāsya, 'having consoled/revived', which suits Kuvalayāśva's fainting in 24.39. ↩
  91. which had come to him when he thought of it: The printed text reads abhyupatem, which is metrically and grammatically defective. It is emended here to abhyupetam, 'come, arrived', agreeing with aśvam and taken with saṃcintitam. ↩
  92. The reading: abhyupatem is a misprint or corruption. Reading abhyupetam, 'approached, arrived', agreeing with 'that horse', gives 'the horse that had come when thought of'. An alternative is to take saṃcintitam adverbially ('as he had intended') with a different ending, but the horse-summoning sense fits the story best. I chose the first reading. ↩
  93. venerable: śrī, an honorific prefixed to titles of works; here it qualifies the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa. ↩
  94. The reading: The verse is a colophon, not a verse of the text. In the GRETIL numbering it carries the stray reference 106.19. The e-text gives the chapter as 24, and the next heading reads 'twenty-fifth', which is consistent. The compound madālasāprāptiḥ literally means 'the obtaining (or attaining) of Madālasā'. I now render it 'Regaining', as the reviewer suggested, because in this chapter Ṛtadhvaja does not court her for the first time but gets her back after her apparent death; the preceding verse says he 'regained' (pratilabhya) his beloved. The Sanskrit has no prefix meaning 're-', so this is a contextual choice, and the literal sense is 'Obtaining'. I keep 'venerable' for śrī, as the reviewer accepts it. ↩

Adhyāya 25

Sanskrit

पञ्चविंशो ऽध्यायः

pañcaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Twenty-Five1

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

25.1

Sanskrit

आगम्य स्वपुरं सो ऽथ पित्रोः सर्वमशेषतः । कथयामास तन्वङ्गी यथा प्राप्ता पुनर्मृता ॥

āgamya svapuraṃ so 'tha pitroḥ sarvamaśeṣataḥ | kathayāmāsa tanvaṅgī yathā prāptā punarmṛtā ||

English

Having come to his own city, he then told his parents everything, without omission: how the slender-limbed woman, who had died2, was gained again.3†

25.2

Sanskrit

ननाम सा च चरणौ श्वश्रूश्वशुरयोः शुभा । स्वजनञ्च यथापूर्वं वन्दनाश्लेषणादिभिः ॥

nanāma sā ca caraṇau śvaśrūśvaśurayoḥ śubhā | svajanañca yathāpūrvaṃ vandanāśleṣaṇādibhiḥ ||

English

25.2–3And she, the auspicious one, bowed at the feet4 of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, and the slender-limbed woman honoured her own kin as before with salutations, embraces and the like, each according to what was proper and according to age. Then a great festival arose among the townspeople in that city.5

25.3

Sanskrit

पूजयामास तन्वङ्गी यथान्यायं यथावयः । ततो महोत्सवो जज्ञे पौराणां तत्र वै पुरे ॥

pūjayāmāsa tanvaṅgī yathānyāyaṃ yathāvayaḥ | tato mahotsavo jajñe paurāṇāṃ tatra vai pure ||

English

Its English is given with 25.2–3, above.

25.4

Sanskrit

ऋतध्वजश्च सुचिरं तया रेमे सुमध्यया । निर्झरेषु च शैलानां निम्नगापुलिनेषु च ॥

ṛtadhvajaśca suciraṃ tayā reme sumadhyayā | nirjhareṣu ca śailānāṃ nimnagāpulineṣu ca ||

English

25.4–6And Ṛtadhvaja delighted for a very long time with her, the slender-waisted one6, by the mountain streams and on the sandbanks of rivers, in lovely forests and likewise in groves. She too, wishing for the exhaustion of [her] merit7 through the enjoyment of desires, delighted with him, her exceedingly beloved one, in those lovely places. Then, after a long time, that Śatrujit, the lord of men,8

25.5

Sanskrit

काननेषु च रम्येषु तथैवोपवनेषु च । पुण्यक्षयं वाञ्छमाना सापि कामोपबोगतः ॥

kānaneṣu ca ramyeṣu tathaivopavaneṣu ca | puṇyakṣayaṃ vāñchamānā sāpi kāmopabogataḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 25.4–6, above.

25.6

Sanskrit

सह तेनातिकान्तेन रेमे रम्यासु भूमिषु । ततः कालेन महता शत्रुजित् स नराधिपः ॥

saha tenātikāntena reme ramyāsu bhūmiṣu | tataḥ kālena mahatā śatrujit sa narādhipaḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 25.4–6, above.

25.7

Sanskrit

सम्यक् प्रशास्य वसुधां कालधर्ममुपेयिवान् । ततः पौरा महात्मानं पुत्रं तस्य ऋतध्वजम् ॥

samyak praśāsya vasudhāṃ kāladharmamupeyivān | tataḥ paurā mahātmānaṃ putraṃ tasya ṛtadhvajam ||

English

25.7–8Having ruled the earth well, he [Śatrujit] met the law of time9. Then the citizens consecrated10 as king his son Ṛtadhvaja, the great-souled one, whose conduct and deeds were noble; and he protected his subjects well, as though they were his own sons born of his body.11

25.8

Sanskrit

अभ्यषिञ्चन्त राजानमुदाराचारचेष्टितम् । सम्यक् पालयतस्तस्य प्रजाः पुत्रानिवौरसान् ॥

abhyaṣiñcanta rājānamudārācāraceṣṭitam | samyak pālayatastasya prajāḥ putrānivaurasān ||

English

Its English is given with 25.7–8, above.

25.9

Sanskrit

मदालसायाः सञ्जज्ञे पुत्रः प्रथमजस्ततः । तस्य चक्रे पिता नाम विक्रान्त इति धीमतः ॥

madālasāyāḥ sañjajñe putraḥ prathamajastataḥ | tasya cakre pitā nāma vikrānta iti dhīmataḥ ||

English

Then a son, her first-born, was born to Madālasā. His father gave him, the wise child, the name "Vikrānta12."13

25.10

Sanskrit

तुतुषुस्तेन वै भृत्या जहास च मदालसा । सा वै मदालसा पुत्रं बालमुत्तानशायिनम् । उल्लापनच्छलेनाह रुदमानमविस्वरम् ॥

tutuṣustena vai bhṛtyā jahāsa ca madālasā | sā vai madālasā putraṃ bālamuttānaśāyinam | ullāpanacchalenāha rudamānamavisvaram ||

English

The servants were pleased with that [name]14, and Madālasā laughed. Then Madālasā said to her young son, who lay on his back weeping in a soft voice, under the pretext of coaxing him with a lullaby15:16

25.11

Sanskrit

शुद्धो ऽसि रे तात ! न ते ऽस्ति नाम कृतं हि ते कल्पनयाधुनैव । पञ्चात्मकं देहमिदं तवैतन् नैवास्य त्वं रोदिषि कस्य हेतोः ॥

śuddho 'si re tāta ! na te 'sti nāma kṛtaṃ hi te kalpanayādhunaiva | pañcātmakaṃ dehamidaṃ tavaitan naivāsya tvaṃ rodiṣi kasya hetoḥ ||

English

"You are pure17, O dear child18. You have no name, for it was made for you just now, by imagination. This body of five elements19 is yours, [but] you are not of it. For what reason do you weep?"20

25.12

Sanskrit

न वा भवान् रोदिति वै स्वजन्मा शब्दो ऽयमासाद्य महीशशूनुम् । विकल्प्यमाना विविधा गुणास्ते ऽगुणाश्च भौताः सकलेन्द्रियेषु ॥

na vā bhavān roditi vai svajanmā śabdo 'yamāsādya mahīśaśūnum | vikalpyamānā vividhā guṇāste 'guṇāśca bhautāḥ sakalendriyeṣu ||

English

Indeed you do not weep21. This sound, arisen of itself, has come upon the son of the lord of the earth22. Your various guṇas23 and non-guṇas, made of the elements, are being imagined in all the sense organs.24

25.13

Sanskrit

भूतानि भूतैः परिदुर्बलानि वृद्धिं समायान्ति यथेह पुंसः । अन्नाम्बुपानादिभिरेव कस्य न ते ऽस्ति वृद्धिर्न च ते ऽस्ति हानिः ॥

bhūtāni bhūtaiḥ paridurbalāni vṛddhiṃ samāyānti yatheha puṃsaḥ | annāmbupānādibhireva kasya na te 'sti vṛddhirna ca te 'sti hāniḥ ||

English

Here in the world, the very weak elements25 of a man come to growth through [other] elements, through food, drink of water and the like alone. Whose [growth] is it?26 For you there is no growth, and for you there is no decline.27†

25.14

Sanskrit

त्वं कञ्चुके शीर्यमाणे निजे ऽस्मिंस् तस्मिंश्च देहे मूढतां मा व्रजेथाः । शुभाशुभैः कर्मभिर्देहमेतन् मदादिमूढैः सञ्चुकस्ते ऽपिनद्धः ॥

tvaṃ kañcuke śīryamāṇe nije 'smiṃs tasmiṃśca dehe mūḍhatāṃ mā vrajethāḥ | śubhāśubhaiḥ karmabhirdehametan madādimūḍhaiḥ sañcukaste 'pinaddhaḥ ||

English

Do not fall into delusion about this tunic28 of yours that is wearing away, or about that body29. This body is a tunic tied on you by deeds, good and bad, [done by those] deluded by pride and the rest.30

25.15

Sanskrit

तातेति किञ्चित्तनयेति किञ्चिद् अम्बेति किञ्चिद्दयितेति किञ्चित् । ममेति किञ्चिन्न ममेति किञ्चित् त्वं भूतसङ्घं बहुमानयेथाः ॥

tāteti kiñcittanayeti kiñcid ambeti kiñciddayiteti kiñcit | mameti kiñcinna mameti kiñcit tvaṃ bhūtasaṅghaṃ bahumānayethāḥ ||

English

You would hold the host of beings31 in high regard, [calling] one "father," another "son," another "mother," another "beloved," one "mine," another "not mine."32

25.16

Sanskrit

दुः खानि दुः खोपगमाय भोगान् सुखाय जानाति विमूढचेताः । तान्येव दुः खानि पुनः सुखानि जानात्यविद्वान सुविमूढयेताः ॥

duḥ khāni duḥ khopagamāya bhogān sukhāya jānāti vimūḍhacetāḥ | tānyeva duḥ khāni punaḥ sukhāni jānātyavidvāna suvimūḍhayetāḥ ||

English

The man of deluded mind regards enjoyments, which are sufferings and lead to the attainment of suffering33, as [meant] for happiness. The ignorant man, utterly deluded in mind, regards those same sufferings again as pleasures.34

25.17

Sanskrit

हासो ऽस्थिसन्दर्शनमक्षियुग्मम् अत्युज्ज्वलं तर्जनमङ्गनायाः । कुचादिपीनं पिशितं घनं तत् स्थानं रतेः किं नरकं न योषित् ॥

hāso 'sthisandarśanamakṣiyugmam atyujjvalaṃ tarjanamaṅganāyāḥ | kucādipīnaṃ piśitaṃ ghanaṃ tat sthānaṃ rateḥ kiṃ narakaṃ na yoṣit ||

English

A woman's laughter is the display of bones35; her pair of eyes, very bright, is a menace36. That thick flesh, swollen at the breasts and elsewhere, is a place of sexual pleasure? Is a woman not a hell?37

25.18

Sanskrit

यानं क्षितौ यानगतञ्च देहं देहे ऽपि चान्यः पुरुषो निविष्टः । ममत्वबुद्धिर्न तथा यथा स्वे देहे ऽतिमात्रं बत मूढतैषा ॥

yānaṃ kṣitau yānagatañca dehaṃ dehe 'pi cānyaḥ puruṣo niviṣṭaḥ | mamatvabuddhirna tathā yathā sve dehe 'timātraṃ bata mūḍhataiṣā ||

English

A vehicle is on the earth, and the body is seated in the vehicle38; and in that body, too, another, the puruṣa39, is seated. The notion of "mine" is not felt toward them as it is toward one's own body. Alas, this is excessive delusion.40

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे मदालसोपाख्याने पञ्चविंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe madālasopākhyāne pañcaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, in the Madālasā episode41, in the venerable42 Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

  1. The reading: The line is only a chapter heading, 'pañcaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ' ('the twenty-fifth chapter'), with no verse content. The reference 107.1 is the e-text's running numbering; the chapter number 25 follows the Sanskrit. ↩
  2. who had died: punarmṛtā is sandhi for punar mṛtā. Here punar is taken with prāptā ('gained again'), and mṛtā ('dead') describes the woman. She died once, on the false report of Kuvalayāśva's death, and was restored. ↩
  3. The reading: punarmṛtā can be read in two ways: (a) punar with mṛtā, 'dead again'; (b) mṛtā alone as 'dead', with punar going with prāptā, 'regained'. I now take (b). The reviewer is right that she died only once, on the false news of his death, so 'dead again' has no basis in the story. The Sanskrit has one predicate, prāptā, so I add no second event. Since he had already won her once as a maiden, punar prāptā, 'gained again', fits. In the previous round I wrongly said that 'dead again' implied an earlier death, and I withdraw that claim. The subject of kathayāmāsa is so, Kuvalayāśva, as the context shows. 'Slender-limbed woman' is kept for tanvaṅgī, as in the glossary. ↩
  4. bowed at the feet: Touching or bowing at the feet (caraṇau) is the customary gesture of reverence to elders. ↩
  5. The reading: The sentence is built as a single clause whose verb is pūjayāmāsa in 25.3, while nanāma in 25.2 governs only the parents-in-law. Svajanam is the object of pūjayāmāsa, not of nanāma. I rendered it so: she bowed to her parents-in-law and honoured her own kin. The phrase 'bowed ... and her own kin' in the segment for 25.2 is only the fragment of this arrangement. Yathānyāyam is 'as was proper', and yathāvayaḥ is 'according to age'. I took the latter to qualify the whole honouring, i.e. each person by seniority. ↩
  6. slender-waisted one: Translates sumadhyā, 'fair-waisted', a common epithet of a beautiful woman. Here it refers to Madālasā. ↩
  7. exhaustion of [her] merit: puṇyakṣaya: puṇya is the store of merit from good deeds. Enjoyment of pleasures is taken to use up that store. ↩
  8. The reading: (1) atikāntena: I read ati-kānta, 'exceedingly beloved or handsome', as describing Ṛtadhvaja. The alternative is a corruption of atikrānta, 'passed, gone beyond', which gives poor sense here. (2) kāmopabogataḥ: 'upabogataḥ' looks like a misprint for upabhogataḥ, 'through enjoyment'. I translate it so. ↩
  9. met the law of time: kāladharma ('the law of time') is a common euphemism for death. ↩
  10. consecrated: abhiṣeka, the sprinkling of water that installs a king. ↩
  11. The reading: tasya in 25.8 (sampālayataḥ tasya) is a genitive absolute referring to Ṛtadhvaja, the new king, not Śatrujit. rājānam is the object of abhyaṣiñcanta, in apposition with putram Ṛtadhvajam. The adjective udārācāraceṣṭitam ('of noble conduct and deeds') qualifies rājānam. The word is neuter in form (ending -m) but agrees with the masculine accusative, as is normal for this compound. ↩
  12. Vikrānta: The name means 'valiant' or 'one who strides forth'. In the next two verses Madālasā laughs and, under the pretext of a lullaby (ullāpana), tells the crying child that he has no real name. ↩
  13. The reading: dhīmataḥ is a genitive in agreement with tasya, so 'wise' qualifies the child; the revised rendering 'him, the wise child' makes this explicit, as the reviewer asked. iti is the quotative, now shown by quotation marks around the name. sañjajñe is the perfect middle 'was born', and prathamajaḥ, 'first-born', agrees with putraḥ. The pitā is understood to be Ṛtadhvaja, the king of 25.7-8, though this verse does not name him. ↩
  14. that [name]: The name Vikrānta, which the father gave the child in the previous verse. ↩
  15. under the pretext of coaxing him with a lullaby: ullāpana is the soothing talk or song used to quiet a child. Madālasā uses it as a cover for teaching her son. Her words follow in the next verses. ↩
  16. The reading: avisvaram: read as 'not discordant', i.e. a soft or clear voice, and taken as an adverb with rudamānam. Another reading is 'without a loud cry' or 'faintly'. I chose 'in a soft voice' because it fits both senses. The sentence repeats sā vai madālasā; I rendered the repetition once and left out the emphatic vai. ↩
  17. pure: śuddha: free from the taint of name, body and their qualities. Madālasā's lullaby teaches the child that the self is distinct from both. ↩
  18. O dear child: re is a familiar particle of address; tāta is an affectionate vocative, here for a son. ↩
  19. five elements: pañcātmaka: composed of the five gross elements (earth, water, fire, air and ākāśa, 'space' or 'ether'). ↩
  20. The reading: (1) tavaitan naivāsya tvam: I now take 'tava etat' (this is yours) and 'na eva asya tvam' (you are not of it at all) as two separate clauses, as the reviewer asks. My earlier 'it is not yours' contradicted tava. Other recensions of this lullaby are often cited with 'na te 'sti' in place of 'tavaitan', which would read 'this body is not yours, nor are you its'. The GRETIL text reads tavaitan, so I translate that and do not call the verse corrupt. Asya (genitive) could also mean 'you are not its owner'. I keep the wider 'of it', meaning 'not belonging to it'. (2) kṛtaṃ hi te kalpanayā: kṛtam agrees with nāma. Hi is causal, so the clause now gives the reason for 'you have no name'. The agent is left unexpressed, as in the Sanskrit; the '[others]' I added before is removed. (3) Re tāta is now rendered 'O dear child', so that re is not lost. ↩
  21. you do not weep: bhavān, 'your honour', is the respectful form of address and takes a third-person verb (roditi). The subject is the child addressed. ↩
  22. son of the lord of the earth: The text reads mahīśaśūnum. This is probably a misprint for mahīśasūnum, 'son of the lord of the earth', and is translated so. The child is the son of King Ṛtadhvaja. ↩
  23. guṇas: guṇa: quality, here the good and bad qualities (virtues and faults, pleasant and painful states) that are wrongly ascribed to the self. aguṇa is its opposite. ↩
  24. The reading: svajanmā: it could agree with bhavān ('you, self-born') or with śabdaḥ. I now take it with śabdaḥ, 'this sound, arisen of itself', i.e. the word 'weeping' comes of its own accord and attaches to the child without any real cause in the self. The reviewer is right that the earlier reading was forced and that the teaching about the unproduced self was imported. na vā: I take it as a negation reinforced by vā ('not indeed', 'nor'), and vai as 'indeed', rendered once as 'Indeed' at the start. The sense of vā, 'or', is not clear in this context. śūnum: I take it as a misprint for sūnum, 'son', and say so in the note. The elliptical śabdo 'yam āsādya is rendered 'this sound has come upon', taking āsādya as 'having reached' in the sense of 'attaching to'. I have not added 'merely' or 'only', since the Sanskrit has no such word. ↩
  25. elements: bhūta: the gross elements (earth, water, fire, air, space) of which the body is made. The verse says that the body's elements are fed by the elements in food and drink. Verse 25.11 has already called the body 'made of five'. ↩
  26. Whose [growth] is it?: kasya is elliptical. It is read as a rhetorical genitive: the growth belongs to the body, not to the self addressed. ↩
  27. The reading: kasya is ambiguous. It could be 'whose?' (the growth is not yours) or 'for what reason?' (as in kasya hetoḥ in 25.11). I chose 'Whose [growth] is it?', supplying 'growth' and 'is it' in brackets. Another reading takes it as 'for whom is there no growth?', but that does not fit the sense of the following clause. ↩
  28. tunic: kañcuka (and sañcuka in the second half): a close-fitting garment or sheath. The body is likened to a garment that wears out and is put on the self by past action. ↩
  29. that body: tasmiṃś ca dehe: 'that' is read as the body itself, in parallel with the tunic-body of the first clause. The relation of the two is not made explicit. ↩
  30. The reading: madādimūḍhaiḥ (instrumental plural) has no clear noun. I take it as loosely qualifying karmabhiḥ, 'deeds [done by those] deluded by pride and the rest'. It could instead be read as an agent, 'by those deluded by pride etc.', or as 'by deeds born of delusion through pride etc.'. Also, deham etat with sañcukaḥ apinaddhaḥ is awkward; I read 'this body [is] a tunic tied on you'. The text may be slightly corrupt. ↩
  31. host of beings: bhūtasaṅgha can also mean 'aggregate of elements'. The preceding verses speak of the body as made of the five elements (bhūta), so both senses are present. ↩
  32. The reading: The verb bahumānayethāḥ is a causative optative middle, 2nd singular, 'you would/should esteem'. It could be read as a real injunction or as ironic. In the context of Madālasā's teaching, it describes the worldly habit of treating one aggregate of elements as 'father', 'son' and so on, so I took it as ironic and rendered it 'would'. The words tāta, tanaya, amba, dayita, mama and na mama are quoted terms, and the Sanskrit does not state 'calling'. I supplied it in brackets for the English to parse. ↩
  33. lead to the attainment of suffering: duḥkhopagamāya is a dative of purpose, 'for the attainment of suffering'. It is taken with bhogān, 'enjoyments', which are described as duḥkhāni, 'sufferings'. ↩
  34. The reading: The last word is printed suvimūḍhayetāḥ, which is evidently a misprint for suvimūḍhacetāḥ, 'utterly deluded in mind'; it echoes vimūḍhacetāḥ in the first half. I read it that way. The text also has the broken spellings duḥ khāni and duḥ khopagamāya, which I read as duḥkhāni and duḥkhopagamāya. The sense of duḥkhopagamāya is uncertain: I take it as 'for the attainment of suffering' (upagama = approach, attainment) rather than 'for relief of suffering'. The first half has no stated object for sukhāya, so I supply '[meant]' to make the English parse. ↩
  35. display of bones: Asthisandarśana: the bared teeth in laughter are treated as bones showing. The verse belongs to Madālasā's lullaby-teaching of detachment from the body. ↩
  36. a menace: Tarjana, 'threatening' or 'scolding', is predicated of the eyes: the bright glance is a threat. Another reading takes it as the woman's rebuke, separate from the eyes. ↩
  37. The reading: The syntax of 'akṣiyugmam atyujjvalaṃ tarjanam aṅganāyāḥ' is loose. I took akṣiyugmam as subject, atyujjvalam as its adjective, and tarjanam as predicate, with aṅganāyāḥ ('of the woman') governing all three. Alternatively atyujjvalam tarjanam could be read together, as 'very bright threatening'. In the last line, 'kiṃ ... na' is read as a rhetorical question, and 'sthānaṃ rateḥ' is taken as ironic ('a place of pleasure?'). ↩
  38. the body is seated in the vehicle: yānagatam dehaṃ is an accusative, but the sense is the body that has gone into or is seated in the vehicle. It is parallel to yānaṃ kṣitau, so the construction is elliptical, and it is read here as the verse's examples of things one treats as one's own. ↩
  39. puruṣa: The person or self dwelling in the body, distinct from the body; here the embodied self that is the true knower. ↩
  40. The reading: The syntax of the first half is elliptical: yānaṃ and dehaṃ are accusatives, while niviṣṭaḥ takes the puruṣa as subject. I read it as a series: a vehicle on the earth, the body in the vehicle, and the puruṣa in the body. The second half then says that the sense of "mine" is weaker for the first two than for one's own body. Also, 'na tathā yathā' is read as 'not so much as'; the verse is terse, and the comparison is implied rather than stated. ↩
  41. Madālasā episode: upākhyāna: a subsidiary narrative told within a larger work. The episode here concerns Madālasā, who teaches her sons detachment. ↩
  42. venerable: śrī in the colophon is an honorific prefix to the title, not part of the name. ↩

Adhyāya 26

Sanskrit

षड्विंशो ऽध्यायः

ṣaḍviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Twenty-Six

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

26.1

Sanskrit

वर्धमानं सुतं सा तु राजपत्नी दिने दिने । तमुल्लापादिना बोधमनयन्निर्ममात्मकम् ॥

vardhamānaṃ sutaṃ sā tu rājapatnī dine dine | tamullāpādinā bodhamanayannirmamātmakam ||

English

Day by day, that queen1 led her growing son, whose very nature was free of the sense of "mine"2, to awakening by lullabies3 and the like.4

26.2

Sanskrit

यथायथं बलं लेभे यथा लेभे मतिं पितुः । तथा तथात्मबोधञ्च सो ऽवापन्मातृभाषितैः ॥

yathāyathaṃ balaṃ lebhe yathā lebhe matiṃ pituḥ | tathā tathātmabodhañca so 'vāpanmātṛbhāṣitaiḥ ||

English

As he gained strength in due measure, and as he gained understanding from his father, so, step by step, he also attained knowledge of the Self5 through his mother's words.6

26.3

Sanskrit

इत्थं तया स तनयो जन्मप्रभृति बोधितः । चकार न मतिं प्राज्ञो गार्हस्थ्यं प्रति निर्ममः ॥

itthaṃ tayā sa tanayo janmaprabhṛti bodhitaḥ | cakāra na matiṃ prājño gārhasthyaṃ prati nirmamaḥ ||

English

Taught in this way by her from his birth onward, that son, who was wise and free of the sense of "mine," did not set his mind on the life of a householder7.8

26.4

Sanskrit

द्वितीयो ऽस्याः सुतो जज्ञे तस्य नामाकरोत्पिता । सुबाहुरयमित्युक्ते सा जाहस मदालसा ॥

dvitīyo 'syāḥ suto jajñe tasya nāmākarotpitā | subāhurayamityukte sā jāhasa madālasā ||

English

A second son was born to her, and his father gave him a name. When he said, "This one is Subāhu9," Madālasā laughed aloud.10

26.5

Sanskrit

तमप्येवं यथापूर्वं बालमुल्लापनादिना । प्राह बाल्यात् स च प्राप तथा बोधं माहमतिः ॥

tamapyevaṃ yathāpūrvaṃ bālamullāpanādinā | prāha bālyāt sa ca prāpa tathā bodhaṃ māhamatiḥ ||

English

In the same way as before, she addressed him too, the child, from his infancy, with lullabies11 and the like; and he, of great intellect, attained the same awakening12.13

26.6

Sanskrit

तृतीयं तनयं जातं स राजा शत्रुमर्दनम् । यदाह तेन सा सुभ्रुर्जहासातिचिरं पुनः ॥

tṛtīyaṃ tanayaṃ jātaṃ sa rājā śatrumardanam | yadāha tena sā subhrurjahāsāticiraṃ punaḥ ||

English

The king called his third son, who had been born, Śatrumardana14; at what he said, that fair-browed lady laughed again for a very long time.15

26.7

Sanskrit

तथैव सो ऽपि तन्वङ्ग्या बालत्वादवबोधितः । क्रियाश्चकार निष्कामो न किञ्चिदुपकारकम् ॥

tathaiva so 'pi tanvaṅgyā bālatvādavabodhitaḥ | kriyāścakāra niṣkāmo na kiñcidupakārakam ||

English

In the same way he too16, instructed from his infancy by the slender-limbed woman, free from desire, performed no act that was of any use17 [to worldly ends].18

26.8

Sanskrit

चतुर्थस्य सुतस्याथ चिकीर्षुर्नाम भूमिपः । ददर्श तां शुभाचारामीषद्धासां मदालसाम् । तामाह राजा हसतीं किञ्चित् कौतूहलान्वितः ॥

caturthasya sutasyātha cikīrṣurnāma bhūmipaḥ | dadarśa tāṃ śubhācārāmīṣaddhāsāṃ madālasām | tāmāha rājā hasatīṃ kiñcit kautūhalānvitaḥ ||

English

Then the king, wishing to give a name to his fourth son, looked at Madālasā, who was of auspicious conduct and wore a faint smile. Filled with curiosity, the king spoke to her as she smiled a little.19

Sanskrit

राजोवाच

rājovāca

26.9

Sanskrit

क्रियमाणे ऽसकृन्नाम्नि कथ्यतां हास्यकारणम् । विक्रान्तश्च सुबाहुश्च तथान्यः शत्रुमर्दनः ॥

kriyamāṇe 'sakṛnnāmni kathyatāṃ hāsyakāraṇam | vikrāntaśca subāhuśca tathānyaḥ śatrumardanaḥ ||

English

26.9–11When the naming was done again and again, let the reason for your laughter be told: Vikrānta20, and Subāhu, and the other, Śatrumardana. I think the names I gave are fine ones, suited to Kṣatriyas21 and full of the pomp of valour. But if these are not good, good lady, and if that is what you have in mind, then let a name be given to this fourth son of mine.22

26.10

Sanskrit

शोभनानीति नामानि मया मन्ये कृतानि वै । योग्यानि क्षत्रबन्धूनां शौर्याटोपयुतानि च ॥

śobhanānīti nāmāni mayā manye kṛtāni vai | yogyāni kṣatrabandhūnāṃ śauryāṭopayutāni ca ||

English

Its English is given with 26.9–11, above.

26.11

Sanskrit

असन्त्येतानि चेद्भद्रे ! यदि ते मनसि स्थितम् । तदस्य क्रियतां नाम चतुर्थस्य सुतस्य मे ॥

asantyetāni cedbhadre ! yadi te manasi sthitam | tadasya kriyatāṃ nāma caturthasya sutasya me ||

English

Its English is given with 26.9–11, above.

Sanskrit

मदालसौवाच

madālasauvāca

English

26.12Madālasā said: Your command must be carried out by me, Mahārāja. As you have spoken to me, so I shall make the name of your fourth son.23

26.12

Sanskrit

मयाज्ञा भवतः कार्या महाराज ! यथात्थ माम् । तथा नाम करिष्यामि चतुर्थस्य सुतस्य ते ॥

mayājñā bhavataḥ kāryā mahārāja ! yathāttha mām | tathā nāma kariṣyāmi caturthasya sutasya te ||

English

Its English is given with 26.12, above.

26.13

Sanskrit

अलर्क इति धर्मज्ञः ख्यातिं लोके प्रयास्यति । कनीयानेष ते पुत्रो मतिमांश्च भविष्यति ॥

alarka iti dharmajñaḥ khyātiṃ loke prayāsyati | kanīyāneṣa te putro matimāṃśca bhaviṣyati ||

English

Under the name Alarka, a knower of dharma24, he will attain fame in the world. This youngest son of yours will also be wise.25

26.14

Sanskrit

तच्छ्रुत्वा नाम पुत्रस्य कृतं मात्रा महीपतिः । अलर्क इत्यसम्बद्धं प्रहस्येदमथाब्रवीत् ॥

tacchrutvā nāma putrasya kṛtaṃ mātrā mahīpatiḥ | alarka ityasambaddhaṃ prahasyedamathābravīt ||

English

Having heard that name of his son, "Alarka26," which the mother had given, the king, finding it incoherent, laughed aloud and then said this:27

Sanskrit

राजोवाच

rājovāca

26.15

Sanskrit

भवत्या यदिदं नाम मत्पुत्रस्य कृतं शुभे । किमीदृशमसम्बद्धमर्थः को ऽस्य मदालसे ॥

bhavatyā yadidaṃ nāma matputrasya kṛtaṃ śubhe | kimīdṛśamasambaddhamarthaḥ ko 'sya madālase ||

English

"This name that you, auspicious lady, have given to my son: why is it so incoherent? What is the meaning of it, Madālasā28?"29

Sanskrit

मदालसोवाच

madālasovāca

English

Madālasā said:

26.16

Sanskrit

कल्पनेयं महाराज ! कृता सा व्यावहारिको । त्वत्कृतानां तथा नाम्नां शृणु भूप ! निरर्थताम् ॥

kalpaneyaṃ mahārāja ! kṛtā sā vyāvahāriko | tvatkṛtānāṃ tathā nāmnāṃ śṛṇu bhūpa ! nirarthatām ||

English

This designation30, great king, was made for practical use. Now hear, king, how meaningless the names given by you are.31

26.17

Sanskrit

वदन्ति पुरुषाः प्राज्ञा व्यापिनं पुरुषं यतः । क्रान्तिश्च गतिरुद्दिष्टा देशाद्देशान्तरन्तु या ॥

vadanti puruṣāḥ prājñā vyāpinaṃ puruṣaṃ yataḥ | krāntiśca gatiruddiṣṭā deśāddeśāntarantu yā ||

English

26.17–18Since wise men call the puruṣa32 pervasive, and krānti33 is declared to be motion, that which is from one place to another, and since the all-going one34 does not go forth, being the pervader, the lord of the body, therefore this name Vikrānta is held by me to be meaningless.35

26.18

Sanskrit

सर्वगो न प्रयातीति व्यापी देहेश्वरो यतः । ततो विक्रान्तसंज्ञेयं मता मम निरर्थिका ॥

sarvago na prayātīti vyāpī deheśvaro yataḥ | tato vikrāntasaṃjñeyaṃ matā mama nirarthikā ||

English

Its English is given with 26.17–18, above.

26.19

Sanskrit

सुबाहुरिति या संज्ञा कृतान्यस्य सुतस्य ते । निरर्था साप्यमूर्तत्वात् पुरुषस्य महीपते ॥

subāhuriti yā saṃjñā kṛtānyasya sutasya te | nirarthā sāpyamūrtatvāt puruṣasya mahīpate ||

English

The name Subāhu36 that was given to this other son of yours, that too is meaningless, O lord of the earth, because the puruṣa37 has no form.38

26.20

Sanskrit

पुत्रस्य यद् कृतं नाम तृतीयस्यारिमर्दनः । मन्ये तदप्यसम्बद्धं शृणु चाप्यत्र कारणम् ॥

putrasya yad kṛtaṃ nāma tṛtīyasyārimardanaḥ | manye tadapyasambaddhaṃ śṛṇu cāpyatra kāraṇam ||

English

As for the name Arimardana39 that was made for the third son, I consider that too unconnected; and listen to the reason for it here as well.40

26.21

Sanskrit

एक एव शरीरेषु सर्वेषु पुरुषो यदा । तदास्य राजन् ! क शत्रुः को वा मित्रमिहेष्यते ॥

eka eva śarīreṣu sarveṣu puruṣo yadā | tadāsya rājan ! ka śatruḥ ko vā mitramiheṣyate ||

English

When there is only one puruṣa41 in all bodies, then, O king, who is an enemy to him here, or who is thought to be a friend?42

26.22

Sanskrit

भूतैर्भूतानि मृद्यन्ते अमूर्तो मृद्यते कथम् । क्रोधादीनां पृथग्भावात् कल्पनेयं निरर्थिका ॥

bhūtairbhūtāni mṛdyante amūrto mṛdyate katham | krodhādīnāṃ pṛthagbhāvāt kalpaneyaṃ nirarthikā ||

English

Beings43 are crushed by beings; how can the formless one44 be crushed? Since anger and the rest exist as separate from him, this naming45 is without meaning.46

26.23

Sanskrit

यदि संव्यवहारार्थमसन्नाम प्रकल्प्यते । नाम्नि कस्मादलर्काख्ये नैरर्थ्यं भवतो मतम् ॥

yadi saṃvyavahārārthamasannāma prakalpyate | nāmni kasmādalarkākhye nairarthyaṃ bhavato matam ||

English

If an unreal name47 is devised for the sake of everyday dealings, why is meaninglessness held by you to lie in the name called Alarka?48

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

26.24

Sanskrit

एवमुक्तस्तया साधु महीष्या स महीपतिः । तथेत्याह महाबुद्धिर्दयितां तथ्यवादिनीम् ॥

evamuktastayā sādhu mahīṣyā sa mahīpatiḥ | tathetyāha mahābuddhirdayitāṃ tathyavādinīm ||

English

Addressed in this way by his queen, who had spoken well, that lord of the earth, of great intelligence, said "So be it" to his beloved, who spoke the truth.49

26.25

Sanskrit

तञ्चापि सा सुतं सुभ्रूर्यथा पूर्वसुतांस्तथा । प्रोवाच बोधजननं तामुवाच स पार्थिवः ॥

tañcāpi sā sutaṃ subhrūryathā pūrvasutāṃstathā | provāca bodhajananaṃ tāmuvāca sa pārthivaḥ ||

English

The fair-browed lady spoke to that son also, as she had to her earlier sons, [words] that produce awakening50; and that king said to her:51

26.26

Sanskrit

करोषि किमिदं मूढे ! ममाभावाय सन्ततेः । दुष्टावबोधदानेन यथापूर्वं सुतेषु मे ॥

karoṣi kimidaṃ mūḍhe ! mamābhāvāya santateḥ | duṣṭāvabodhadānena yathāpūrvaṃ suteṣu me ||

English

What is this that you are doing, foolish one? By giving harmful understanding52, as before in the case of my sons, you work for the non-existence of my line's continuity.53

26.27

Sanskrit

यदि ते मत्प्रियं कार्यं यदि ग्राह्यं वचो मम । तदेनं तनयं मार्गे प्रवृत्तेः सन्नियोजय ॥

yadi te matpriyaṃ kāryaṃ yadi grāhyaṃ vaco mama | tadenaṃ tanayaṃ mārge pravṛtteḥ sanniyojaya ||

English

If what pleases me is to be done by you, and if my word is to be accepted, then set this son on the path of activity54.55

26.28

Sanskrit

कर्ममार्गः समुच्छेदं नैवं देवि ! गमिष्यति । पितृपिण्डनिवृत्तिश्च नैवं साध्वि ! भविष्यति ॥

karmamārgaḥ samucchedaṃ naivaṃ devi ! gamiṣyati | pitṛpiṇḍanivṛttiśca naivaṃ sādhvi ! bhaviṣyati ||

English

The path of rites56 will not, in this way, come to destruction, O queen57; and the cessation of the offerings of rice-balls58 to the ancestors will not, in this way, come about, O faithful wife.59

26.29

Sanskrit

पितरो देवलोकस्थास्तथा तिर्यक्त्वमागताः । तद्वन्मनुष्यतां याता भूतवर्गे च संस्थिताः ॥

pitaro devalokasthāstathā tiryaktvamāgatāḥ | tadvanmanuṣyatāṃ yātā bhūtavarge ca saṃsthitāḥ ||

English

26.29–33A man who is established in ritual action, by giving rice-balls60 and water, always nourishes the ancestors who dwell in the world of the gods, those who have come to the state of animals, likewise those who have gone to the human state, and those who are established in the class of beings. He nourishes them whether they have merit or lack it, wasted by hunger and flooded by thirst. In the same way, fair-browed one, he nourishes the gods and guests as well. Man alone is lived upon by gods, men, ancestors, pretas61, and bhūtas together with guhyakas62, and by birds, worms and insects. Therefore, slender-limbed one, [you should] properly direct the son to that which is to be done by those born of the kṣatriya womb63, whose fruit belongs to this world and the next.64

26.30

Sanskrit

सपुण्यानसपुण्यांश्च क्षुत्क्षामान् तृट्परिप्लुतान् । पिण्डोदकप्रदानेन नरः कर्मण्यवस्थितः ॥

sapuṇyānasapuṇyāṃśca kṣutkṣāmān tṛṭpariplutān | piṇḍodakapradānena naraḥ karmaṇyavasthitaḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 26.29–33, above.

26.31

Sanskrit

सदाप्यायते सुभ्रु ! तद्वद्देवातिथोनपि । देवैर्मनुष्यैः पितृभिः प्रेतैर्भूतैः सगुह्यकैः ॥

sadāpyāyate subhru ! tadvaddevātithonapi | devairmanuṣyaiḥ pitṛbhiḥ pretairbhūtaiḥ saguhyakaiḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 26.29–33, above.

26.32

Sanskrit

वयोभिः कृमिकीटैश्च नर एवोपजीव्यते । तस्मात् तन्वड्गि ! पुत्रं यत्कार्यं क्षत्रयोनिभिः ॥

vayobhiḥ kṛmikīṭaiśca nara evopajīvyate | tasmāt tanvaḍgi ! putraṃ yatkāryaṃ kṣatrayonibhiḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 26.29–33, above.

26.33

Sanskrit

ऐहिकामुष्मिकफलं तत् सम्यक् प्रतिपादय ॥

aihikāmuṣmikaphalaṃ tat samyak pratipādaya ||

English

Its English is given with 26.29–33, above.

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

26.34

Sanskrit

तेनैवमुक्ता सा भर्त्रा वरनारी मदालसा । अलर्कं नाम तनयमुवाचोल्लापवादिनी ॥

tenaivamuktā sā bhartrā varanārī madālasā | alarkaṃ nāma tanayamuvācollāpavādinī ||

English

Thus addressed by her husband, the excellent woman Madālasā, speaking in a coaxing tone65, said to her son named Alarka:66

26.35

Sanskrit

पुत्र वर्धस्व मद्भर्तुर्मनो नन्दय कर्मभिः । मित्राणामुपकाराय दुर्हृदां नाशनाय च ॥

putra vardhasva madbharturmano nandaya karmabhiḥ | mitrāṇāmupakārāya durhṛdāṃ nāśanāya ca ||

English

"Grow, my son; gladden the mind of my husband with your deeds, for the benefit of your friends and for the destruction of evil-hearted foes."67

26.36

Sanskrit

धन्यो ऽसि रे यो वसुधामशत्रुर् एकश्चिरं पालयितासि पुत्र । तत्पालनादस्तु सुखोपभोगो धर्मात् फलं प्राप्स्यसि चामरत्वम् ॥

dhanyo 'si re yo vasudhāmaśatrur ekaściraṃ pālayitāsi putra | tatpālanādastu sukhopabhogo dharmāt phalaṃ prāpsyasi cāmaratvam ||

English

Ah68, you are fortunate, my son, you who, without an enemy, will alone protect the earth for a long time. From that protecting, let there be enjoyment of happiness; and from dharma you will obtain the fruit, and immortality69 as well.70

26.37

Sanskrit

धरामरान् पर्वसु तर्पयेथाः समीहितं बन्धुषु पूरयेथाः । हितं परस्मै हृदि चिन्तयेथाः मनः परस्त्रीषु निवर्तयेथाः ॥

dharāmarān parvasu tarpayethāḥ samīhitaṃ bandhuṣu pūrayethāḥ | hitaṃ parasmai hṛdi cintayethāḥ manaḥ parastrīṣu nivartayethāḥ ||

English

On the festival days71 you should gratify the gods of the earth72; you should fulfil what your kinsmen desire; in your heart you should contemplate what is good for another; and you should turn your mind away from the wives of others.73

26.38

Sanskrit

यज्ञौरनेकैर्विबुधानजस्त्रम् अर्थैर्द्विजान् प्रीणय संश्रितांश्च । स्त्रियश्च कामैरतुलैश्चिराय युद्धैश्चारींस्तोषयितासि वीर ॥

yajñauranekairvibudhānajastram arthairdvijān prīṇaya saṃśritāṃśca | striyaśca kāmairatulaiścirāya yuddhaiścārīṃstoṣayitāsi vīra ||

English

With many yajñas please the gods continually; with wealth please the brahmins and those who have taken refuge with you; and you shall satisfy women for a long time with incomparable pleasures, and your enemies with battles74, O brave one.75

26.39

Sanskrit

बालो मनो नन्दय बान्धवानां गुरोस्तथाज्ञानकरणैः कुमारः । स्त्रीणां युवा सत्कुलभूषणानां वृद्धो वने वत्स ! वनेचराणाम् ॥

bālo mano nandaya bāndhavānāṃ gurostathājñānakaraṇaiḥ kumāraḥ | strīṇāṃ yuvā satkulabhūṣaṇānāṃ vṛddho vane vatsa ! vanecarāṇām ||

English

As a child, gladden the minds of your kinsmen. Likewise, as a boy, [gladden the mind] of your teacher by carrying out his commands. As a youth, [gladden the minds] of women who are the ornaments of good families. And as an old man in the forest, my child, [gladden the minds] of the forest-dwellers76.77

26.40

Sanskrit

राज्यं कुर्वन् सुहृदो नन्दयेथाः साधून् रक्षंस्तात ! यज्ञैर्यजेथाः । दुष्टान्निघ्रन् वैरिणश्चाजिमध्ये गोविप्रार्थे वत्स ! मृत्युं व्रजेथाः ॥

rājyaṃ kurvan suhṛdo nandayethāḥ sādhūn rakṣaṃstāta ! yajñairyajethāḥ | duṣṭānnighran vairiṇaścājimadhye goviprārthe vatsa ! mṛtyuṃ vrajethāḥ ||

English

While ruling the kingdom, gladden your friends. Protecting the good, my son, worship with sacrifices78. Slaying the wicked and your enemies in the midst of battle, my child, may you meet death79 for the sake of cows and brahmins.

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे पुत्रानुशासनं नाम षड्विंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe putrānuśāsanaṃ nāma ṣaḍviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, named "The Instruction of the Son80," in the venerable Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

  1. that queen: Madālasā, wife of King Ṛtadhvaja, who is the mother of the child. The verse itself says only rājapatnī, "the king's wife". ↩
  2. free of the sense of "mine": nirmama: without mama, "mine", that is, without possessiveness or attachment. It echoes the mamatvabuddhi of 25.18. ↩
  3. lullabies: ullāpa is the soothing or coaxing speech with which a mother sings to a child. Here the lullabies carry the teaching of non-attachment, as in the preceding chapter. ↩
  4. The reading: nirmamātmakam: it can be read as a bahuvrīhi, "one whose self (ātman) is free of mamatā", or as "one of the nature of nirmama". I chose "whose very nature was free of the sense of 'mine'", which covers both. bodham anayat: bodha can mean "knowledge" or "awakening". I chose "awakening", in view of ātmabodha in 26.2. ↩
  5. knowledge of the Self: Translates ātmabodha, awareness of the Self (ātman) as distinct from body and possessions. This is the teaching Madālasā gives her son in the preceding verses. ↩
  6. The reading: Yathāyathaṃ is an unusual form; I read it as 'in due measure, as appropriate' (a variant of yathāyatham), qualifying balaṃ lebhe. The line yathā lebhe matiṃ pituḥ could also mean 'as he got intelligence from his father [by inheritance]', but 'gained understanding from his father' is the plainer reading. The sense of tathā tathā matches both clauses, 'in the same measure'. ↩
  7. the life of a householder: gārhasthya: the state of the householder (gṛhastha), the second of the four life-stages (āśrama). ↩
  8. free of the sense of "mine": nirmama: without mamatā, the sense of "mine," that is, of possession and attachment. It echoes the lullaby teaching of the preceding verses (26.1, nirmamātmakam). ↩
  9. Subāhu: The name means 'having fine arms'. Madālasā laughs, as she did at the naming of her first son, because the name attaches a bodily label to the self. ↩
  10. The reading: The verse does not say that this laugh is the same as at the first son's naming; the note's explanation is inferred from context and is not stated in the verse. The words 'ayam iti ukte' are a locative absolute: 'when [it] was said "This one [is Subāhu]"'. The speaker is understood to be the father, the subject of 'akarot', and I supply it in the translation as 'he said'. ↩
  11. lullabies: ullāpana: soothing or cajoling talk addressed to a small child. Here Madālasā uses it to teach the child while he is still an infant, as she did with her first son. ↩
  12. awakening: bodha: awakening, that is, knowledge of the Self and of the vanity of worldly attachment. It is the same bodha that her first son, Vikrānta, gained in verses 26.1–3. ↩
  13. The reading: The reading māhamatiḥ is not a regular Sanskrit word. I take it as a misprint or metrical lengthening for mahāmatiḥ, 'of great intellect', which fits the sense. Another possibility is māha-matiḥ, 'one whose mind is [Madālasā's]', but this is far less natural. The first son's teaching in 26.3 describes him as prājña, which supports 'great intellect'. ↩
  14. Śatrumardana: The name means 'crusher of enemies'. It is a warlike name, and this is why Madālasā laughs, as she did at Subāhu's name in the previous verse. ↩
  15. The reading: The words 'yad āha ... śatrumardanam' can be read as 'what he said, [namely] Śatrumardana', with the name as the object of 'āha' and 'tṛtīyaṃ tanayaṃ jātam' as the person named. I chose 'called the third son Śatrumardana', and took 'tena' as 'at that', the cause of her laughter. ↩
  16. he too: The third son, Śatrumardana, born in 26.6; like his two brothers he is taught by Madālasā from infancy. ↩
  17. no act that was of any use: Sanskrit upakārakam ("useful, beneficial") has no stated object; the sense is that he did nothing serving worldly or household ends, in keeping with the teaching of detachment given by his mother. ↩
  18. The reading: The verse has no stated antecedent for so 'pi: it is the third son, named Śatrumardana in 26.6. Upakārakam is neuter and may be read as the object of kriyāḥ ("no useful act") or adverbially; I take it as qualifying kriyāḥ. The words in square brackets are implied only, to make the English parse. The compound niṣkāmaḥ is rendered "free from desire". ↩
  19. The reading: The verse has three lines (a, b–c, d), so it is irregular as an anuṣṭubh. The sense is not affected. The reading hasatīṃ kiñcit, 'smiling a little', repeats īṣaddhāsām; I have kept both. In the second sentence 'tām āha' is taken with rājā, the king, as the subject. ↩
  20. Vikrānta: The name of the eldest son. His naming is not in the verses given here, but the king's list shows it. ↩
  21. Kṣatriyas: Sanskrit kṣatrabandhu, literally 'kinsman of the warrior class'. It is used here for members of the warrior class, the kṣatriyas. ↩
  22. The reading: asanti (26.11): read as the neuter plural of asat, 'not good, unsuitable', agreeing with etāni. The alternative, 'do not exist', gives a weaker sense. I chose 'not good' because the king is asking whether Madālasā laughed because she found the names unfit. ↩
  23. The reading: The reference "109.15" looks like a misnumbering in the e-text for the speaker's line (madālasauvāca) that opens the speech in chapter 26. I translated it as that line. The form āttha is from the perfect of √ah, "you have said", and is not from √as. The reading is clear. ↩
  24. dharma: Already explained in the glossary; no further note needed beyond its sense of right conduct. ↩
  25. The reading: kanīyān is a comparative ('younger', 'youngest'); here it refers to the fourth, youngest of the sons so far named, so I render 'youngest'. The construction 'alarka iti' is read as 'under the name Alarka', with dharmajñaḥ as the subject's qualifier. ↩
  26. Alarka: The name given by Madālasā to her fourth son. The king finds it odd and asks its meaning in the next verse. Elsewhere the word alarka means a mad dog (rabid), which may explain his reaction. ↩
  27. The reading: asambaddham: 'incoherent, unconnected, senseless'. It could qualify the name (nāma) as inapt, or Madālasā's act of naming; I take it as qualifying the name. Also, 'prahasya' (having laughed) is rendered 'laughed aloud'; the sense may be derisive or merely amused. ↩
  28. Madālasā: The king addresses his wife by name; she is the mother who named the fourth son Alarka, whose name he finds meaningless. ↩
  29. The reading: asambaddham ("incoherent", literally "unconnected") is taken as the king's complaint that the name has no connection with any sense or fitness. Other possible renderings are "inappropriate" or "senseless". The verse is the king's speech, but the Sanskrit gives no speaker's line before it; the previous verse (26.14) already introduces it with abravīt, so no speaker's line is added. ↩
  30. This designation: The text reads kalpanā kṛtā sā vyāvahārikī (feminine); the printed vyāvahāriko is a misprint. Madālasā means that the name Alarka was devised only as a convention for everyday dealings. ↩
  31. The reading: The printed vyāvahāriko is irregular. It should be the feminine vyāvahārikī, agreeing with kalpanā, and I translate it so. Also, kalpaneyaṃ is read as kalpanā + iyam, 'this designation'; sā is then a redundant repetition of the same subject and is not rendered separately. ↩
  32. puruṣa: Here the Self or spirit, said to pervade everything and to be the lord of the body, as distinct from the body itself. ↩
  33. krānti: 'Stepping, going', from the root kram. The first son's name Vikrānta (vi-krānta) comes from the same root. Madālasā argues that the name implies going or striding, which cannot be said of the all-pervading Self. ↩
  34. all-going one: sarvaga, 'going everywhere', hence 'present everywhere'. The argument rests on the pervader having no going: what is already everywhere has nowhere to go, so it does not go forth. ↩
  35. The reading: I accept the reviewer's point on yataḥ and now render the second clause as one ('since the all-going one does not go forth, being the pervader, the lord of the body'). The Sanskrit is compressed: yataḥ could also be taken with the whole of 26.17–18 as one reason ('because ...'). I keep it as two parallel 'since' clauses followed by 'therefore' (tataḥ). I keep 'wise men' for puruṣāḥ prājñāḥ. I render gati as 'motion' and do not carry it as a separate term. The note on 'all-going one' is relabelled 'term', as the reviewer asks, because it explains the word sarvaga rather than a grammatical point. 'Held by me' renders matā mama, and nirarthikā is 'meaningless'. I give no segment-by-segment reordering, since the verses stand in Sanskrit order. ↩
  36. Subāhu: 'Having fine arms'. Madālasā argues that a name praising the arms (bāhu) means nothing if the self has no body. ↩
  37. puruṣa: The person or spirit, the self within the body. The preceding verses use it for the all-pervading, bodiless self, in contrast to the embodied person. ↩
  38. The reading: The printed kṛtānyasya is read as kṛtā + anyasya, 'given to the other'. Here anyasya means 'other', that is, another son besides Vikrānta. ↩
  39. Arimardana: Literally 'crusher of enemies'; the name of the third son. ↩
  40. The reading: (1) 'yad kṛtaṃ': the reviewer is right that 'yad' before a voiceless k is a sandhi or print error. I read 'yat kṛtaṃ'. (2) 'ārimardanaḥ' is nominative masculine, standing in apposition to neuter 'nāma'; the name is quoted as a name. I take it as the name itself, 'Arimardana', and give it in the stem form. The sandhi 'tṛtīyasyārimardanaḥ' is resolved as 'tṛtīyasya' + 'arimardanaḥ'. (3) I dropped 'your' before 'third son'. The text says only 'putrasya … tṛtīyasya' (of the son, the third), and the identity of the one who gave the names is unclear. In 26.15 the king says 'bhavatyā … kṛtam' (made by you), which points to Madālasā. In 26.16 she says 'tvatkṛtānām … nāmnām' (of the names made by you), which points to the king. I have therefore removed the statement in the note that the king gave the name. (4) 'asambaddham' (unconnected, incoherent) is now rendered plainly as 'unconnected'. I removed the bracketed gloss 'with any reality', which was interpretive. ↩
  41. puruṣa: The spirit or self that pervades all bodies. Madālasā uses it to argue that names like "Arimardana" (crusher of enemies) have no real basis, since there is no second being to be an enemy. ↩
  42. The reading: puruṣa may mean 'man' or 'the spirit/self'. I chose the philosophical sense, since the verses before (26.17–19) speak of the all-pervading, formless puruṣa. 'asya' is read with 'śatruḥ' and 'mitram' as 'to him'. The genitive could also be read as 'of this [person]'. The 'iha' is taken as 'here', in this world or in this reckoning. ↩
  43. Beings: bhūta here means the embodied creatures, composed of the elements (bhūta); the word is used in both senses. ↩
  44. the formless one: amūrta: the puruṣa, the self, which has no body or form, and so cannot be struck or crushed by bodily beings. ↩
  45. this naming: kalpanā refers to the name Arimardana ('crusher of foes') given to the third son, discussed in the preceding verses. ↩
  46. The reading: krodhādīnām pṛthagbhāvāt is elliptical. I read it as 'because anger and the rest exist separately [from the self]', that is, they are not attributes of the puruṣa and so there is no enemy to be crushed. Another reading takes pṛthagbhāva as 'the diversity of anger and the like', but this fits the argument less well. Note also that the translation uses the term puruṣa only in notes; the verse itself does not contain it. ↩
  47. an unreal name: Sanskrit asannāma, 'a non-real name': a name that corresponds to no real entity. It could also be read as 'a name for what is not real'; the sense is much the same. ↩
  48. The reading: The compound asannāma may be read as 'a name that is unreal' or as 'a name for what is unreal'. I chose the first, taking it as a name with no true referent. I accept the reviewer's correction that Alarka is not the addressee: bhavataḥ is the king Ṛtadhvaja, and Alarka is his son, whose name is under discussion. The first draft's note and doubt wrongly identified the two, so I removed the name note. I dropped 'alone', which the Sanskrit does not have. I also restored the abstract nairarthya ('meaninglessness') and the passive matam ('is held'), with bhavataḥ as the agent ('by you'). The speaker is the queen Madālasā, as 26.24 shows. ↩
  49. The reading: The verse has no named speaker; the king (mahīpati) is presumably Ṛtadhvaja, but the verse does not say so. I kept the Sanskrit's 'lord of the earth' and did not supply a name. Sādhu may modify uktaḥ ('addressed well') or qualify the queen's speech; I took it as describing the manner of her speaking ('who had spoken well'). Alternatively it may be read adverbially with evamuktaḥ, 'rightly addressed'. ↩
  50. awakening: bodha: knowledge or awareness of the Self. Madālasā's teaching to her sons is that the Self is distinct from the body and from worldly pursuits. ↩
  51. The reading: bodhajananam is neuter accusative singular. It could qualify sutam ("the son, [one] who generates awakening"), but it more likely describes what she spoke, with vacas or something similar implied. I took it as the object of provāca and supplied "words" in brackets. The verse does not make clear which son tam sutam is: probably the third, Arimardana, of verse 20, but possibly the fourth. I kept "that son". ↩
  52. harmful understanding: duṣṭāvabodha: avabodha is awakening to knowledge. The king means the teaching of renunciation that Madālasā had given to the earlier sons, which he regards as harmful. ↩
  53. The reading: duṣṭāvabodhadānena: I read the compound as duṣṭa + avabodha + dāna, 'by the giving of faulty/harmful understanding'. The instrumental is kept ('by giving'). duṣṭa is the king's judgement on the teaching. It does not make the knowledge an active corrupter, so the draft's 'corrupting' is dropped, and so is the 'this' that the Sanskrit does not have. mamābhāvāya santateḥ: mama is taken with santateḥ ('my line's continuity'), and abhāvāya is the dative of purpose or result, 'for the non-existence of'. The reviewer's 'cutting off' is a paraphrase of abhāva, so I keep 'non-existence'. yathāpūrvaṃ suteṣu me: 'as before in the case of my sons', with suteṣu as a locative of reference. The comparison is with the teaching already given to the earlier sons, and the 'as' clause qualifies the giving of understanding. I have added no explanation of this in the sentence. mūḍhe: the vocative 'foolish one' (literally 'deluded one') is kept, and 'you' is added to the question as the finding asks. ↩
  54. the path of activity: pravṛtti, engagement in worldly action and ritual duty, as opposed to renunciation (nivṛtti). Madālasā had been urging her sons toward knowledge and withdrawal. ↩
  55. The reading: mārge pravṛtteḥ can be read as 'on the path of activity' (genitive of pravṛtti dependent on mārge) or 'to the path, from/for activity'. I took the first, which suits the context: the king wants the son turned to worldly duty and the continuity of offspring. ↩
  56. path of rites: karmamārga: the way of ritual and prescribed action, i.e. the householder's observances, as opposed to withdrawal from action. ↩
  57. O queen: devi, the vocative of address to Madālasā; the text of the verse marks it with a space before the exclamation mark. ↩
  58. rice-balls: piṇḍa: the balls of cooked rice offered to the departed forefathers in the śrāddha rite. ↩
  59. The reading: naivam: read as 'not in this way' (na evam), going with both clauses, meaning that the king's course of action, i.e. guiding the son to the active life, keeps the rites and offerings going. The speaker is the king and the person addressed is the queen Madālasā, inferred from context; the verse itself does not name her. ↩
  60. rice-balls: piṇḍa: balls of cooked rice offered to the ancestors in the śrāddha rites, together with water. ↩
  61. pretas: preta: a departed spirit, especially one not yet joined with the ancestors. ↩
  62. guhyakas: guhyaka: a class of semi-divine beings, attendants of Kubera. ↩
  63. kṣatriya womb: kṣatrayoni: those born in the warrior class; the verse sets out the duties proper to such a birth. ↩
  64. The reading: āpyāyate (26.31) is a middle form, passive or causative-middle. Since the ancestors in 26.30 are in the accusative, I take it as active in sense, with naraḥ as subject: 'he nourishes'. devātithonapi is read as devātithīn api, 'the gods and guests as well'. In 26.32–33 the syntax is loose (putraṃ yat kāryaṃ ... tat pratipādaya). I take tat as the object, 'direct the son to that', with yat kāryaṃ and aihikāmuṣmikaphalaṃ describing it. ↩
  65. speaking in a coaxing tone: ullāpavādinī: ullāpa can mean a tender, cooing address, a lullaby-like speech, or a call or taunt. Here it suits her soothing words to the child in the next verse. ↩
  66. The reading: ullāpavādinī: the readings are 'speaking in a coaxing, cooing way' and 'speaking in a taunting or calling way'. I chose the first because the next verse is an affectionate address to the child. ↩
  67. The reading: The verse is Madālasā's speech to her son Alarka, introduced by the previous verse (26.34, 'she addressed her son named Alarka'). Since that verse already introduces the speech, no speaker's line is added here. 'Mad-bhartuḥ' is 'of my husband', i.e. Ṛtadhvaja, Alarka's father; I kept the Sanskrit's literal 'my husband' because the speaker is Madālasā. ↩
  68. Ah: re is a familiar interjection of address, often abrupt when used to an inferior. Here a mother uses it affectionately to her son. It is not a vocative of putra. ↩
  69. immortality: amaratva: the state of the gods, here the heaven won by merit. The text does not say that it is final release. ↩
  70. The reading: (1) 're': the earlier draft left it out. I now render it as 'Ah' and explain it in a note. I do not take it as a vocative of 'putra'. (2) 'ekaḥ' is taken with 'pālayitāsi' ('will alone protect'), as the reviewer says, and 'aśatruḥ' stands apart as 'without an enemy'. (3) 'pālayitāsi' is a periphrastic future.
