'Pālana' is rendered 'protecting', consistently with 'pālayitāsi', and 'tat' refers back to the protecting of the earth (vasudhā). (4) The pronoun 'its' is removed, because the Sanskrit has only 'phalam', 'the fruit'. I do not accept the reviewer's reading of 'amaratvam' as being in apposition to 'phalam' ('the fruit, namely immortality'). The 'ca' in 'cāmaratvam' joins it to 'phalam' as a second item, and apposition would leave that particle unexplained. I therefore keep 'the fruit, and immortality as well'. Both readings give much the same sense. (5) 'astu' has no stated person to receive the enjoyment, so I left out the draft's added 'to you'. ↩
  71. festival days: parvan denotes the junctures of the lunar month (full moon, new moon and the like) and other festival occasions. ↩
  72. the gods of the earth: Dharāmara, literally 'immortals of the earth', is a common term for brāhmaṇas, who are gratified with gifts and food. ↩
  73. The reading: Optative second person singular (tarpayethāḥ, pūrayethāḥ, cintayethāḥ, nivartayethāḥ), rendered 'you should', the mother's counsel to Alarka. Following the reviewer, parasmai is now rendered as a singular dative, 'for another', and samīhitam as 'what ... desire', and parastrīṣu as the literal 'wives of others'. Bandhuṣu is a locative, taken as 'your kinsmen' with pūrayethāḥ. Dharāmarān could be read literally as 'immortals of the earth'; I take it as brāhmaṇas, since the following verse speaks of gratifying the twice-born. ↩
  74. your enemies with battles: A heroic idiom: to satisfy enemies with battles is to give them the fight they seek. ↩
  75. The reading: 1. striyaḥ: I now render 'women' (not 'wives'), as the reviewer asks, since the Sanskrit says only 'women'. 2. Which verb governs striyaḥ: the reviewer would have it as object of the imperative prīṇaya. I take it, with arīn, as object of toṣayitāsi, which closes the verse. The ca after striyaḥ and the ca in cārīn then join two objects of one verb, with kāmaiḥ and yuddhaiḥ as the matching instruments. Reading striyaḥ with prīṇaya is possible and would change only the English verb ('please' for 'satisfy'). 3. toṣayitāsi: I accept the point that the periphrastic future here is exhortatory, in keeping with the imperatives and optatives of the surrounding verses. I render 'you shall satisfy' and have dropped the note that treated the tense mixture as a problem. 4. I removed 'also' and joined the last clause with 'and'. 5. cirāya ('for a long time') is taken with the pleasures given to the women, as it stands beside them. ajasram is kept with the gods. ↩
  76. forest-dwellers: vanecarāṇām: literally 'those who move in the forest'. It can mean hermits and ascetics, or forest creatures generally. ↩
  77. The reading: (1) guru in 'gurostathā' can mean teacher or elder (including a father). I chose 'teacher' because it is the natural counterpart of kumāra, the boy's age of study. (2) vanecarāṇām may mean forest-dwelling ascetics or forest beings. I chose 'forest-dwellers', which leaves both readings open. (3) The verb nandaya and the object manaḥ stand only in the first quarter. I carry them over to the later clauses in square brackets. ↩
  78. worship with sacrifices: The verb yajethāḥ with the instrumental yajñaiḥ is a cognate construction, literally 'sacrifice with sacrifices'. The sense is 'worship the gods by performing sacrifices'. ↩
  79. may you meet death: The verbs nandayethāḥ, yajethāḥ and vrajethāḥ are optatives in the second person singular, used here as gentle injunctions and blessings. ↩
  80. The Instruction of the Son: Sanskrit putrānuśāsana: the counsel given by Madālasā to her son in the preceding verses of this chapter. ↩

Adhyāya 27

Sanskrit

सप्तविंशो ऽध्यायः

saptaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

The twenty-seventh chapter.

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

27.1

Sanskrit

एवमुल्लाप्यमानस्तु स तु मात्रा दिने दिने । ववृधे वयसा बालो बुद्ध्या चालर्कसंज्ञितः ॥

evamullāpyamānastu sa tu mātrā dine dine | vavṛdhe vayasā bālo buddhyā cālarkasaṃjñitaḥ ||

English

Being thus lulled and instructed1 by his mother day after day, that boy, who was named Alarka2, grew in age and in understanding.3

27.2

Sanskrit

स कौमारकमासाद्य ऋतध्वजसुतस्ततः । कृतोपनयनः प्राज्ञः प्रणिपत्याह मातरम् ॥

sa kaumārakamāsādya ṛtadhvajasutastataḥ | kṛtopanayanaḥ prājñaḥ praṇipatyāha mātaram ||

English

Then the son of Ṛtadhvaja4 reached boyhood. His sacred-thread initiation was performed5, and, being wise, he bowed down to his mother and spoke to her.

27.3

Sanskrit

मया यदत्र कर्तव्यमैहिकामुष्मिकाय वै । सुखाय वद तत् सर्वं प्रश्रयावनतस्य मे ॥

mayā yadatra kartavyamaihikāmuṣmikāya vai | sukhāya vada tat sarvaṃ praśrayāvanatasya me ||

English

Tell me all that I must do here, for happiness in this world and in the next6, for I stand bowed down in humility.7

Sanskrit

मदालसोवाच

madālasovāca

English

Madālasā said:

27.4

Sanskrit

वत्स ! राज्ये ऽभिषिक्तेन प्रजारञ्जनमादितः । कर्तव्यमविरोधेन स्वधर्मस्य महीभृता ॥

vatsa ! rājye 'bhiṣiktena prajārañjanamāditaḥ | kartavyamavirodhena svadharmasya mahībhṛtā ||

English

Madālasā said: My child, one who has been consecrated in the kingdom, a king, must first of all please the subjects, without conflict with his own dharma8.9†

27.5

Sanskrit

व्यसनानि परित्यज्य सप्त मूलहराणि वै । आत्मा रिपुभ्यः संरक्ष्यो बहिर्मन्त्रविनिर्गमात् ॥

vyasanāni parityajya sapta mūlaharāṇi vai | ātmā ripubhyaḥ saṃrakṣyo bahirmantravinirgamāt ||

English

Having given up the seven vices that take away the root10, one must protect oneself from enemies and from the going out of counsel11.12

27.6

Sanskrit

अष्टधा नाशमाप्नोति सुचक्रात् स्यन्दनाद्यथा । तथा राजाप्यसन्दिग्धं बहिर्मन्त्रविनिर्गमात् ॥

aṣṭadhā nāśamāpnoti sucakrāt syandanādyathā | tathā rājāpyasandigdhaṃ bahirmantravinirgamāt ||

English

27.6–7As [one] meets destruction eightfold13 from a chariot with good wheels, so too a king, without doubt, [meets destruction] from the going out of counsel14 to the outside. He should know the corrupt and the uncorrupt ministers through faults connected with the enemy15, and likewise the enemy's spies should be sought out with effort by spies.16†

27.7

Sanskrit

दुष्टादुष्टांश्च जानीयादमात्यानरिदोषतः । चरैश्चरास्तथा शत्रोरन्वेष्टव्याः प्रयत्नतः ॥

duṣṭāduṣṭāṃśca jānīyādamātyānaridoṣataḥ | caraiścarāstathā śatroranveṣṭavyāḥ prayatnataḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 27.6–7, above.

27.8

Sanskrit

विश्वासो न तु कर्तव्यो राज्ञा मित्राप्तबन्धुषु । कार्ययोगादमित्रे ऽपि विश्वसीत नराधिपः ॥

viśvāso na tu kartavyo rājñā mitrāptabandhuṣu | kāryayogādamitre 'pi viśvasīta narādhipaḥ ||

English

A king should not, however, place trust in friends, trusted kinsmen17 and relatives; yet, for the sake of an undertaking18, the ruler of men may trust even an enemy.19

27.9

Sanskrit

स्थानवृद्धिक्षयज्ञेन षाड्गुण्यगुणितात्माना । भवितव्यं नरेन्द्रेण न कामवशवर्तिना ॥

sthānavṛddhikṣayajñena ṣāḍguṇyaguṇitātmānā | bhavitavyaṃ narendreṇa na kāmavaśavartinā ||

English

A king should be one who knows the standing, the growth and the decline20 [of his realm], whose mind is trained in the sixfold policy21, and he should not be one who comes under the sway of desire22.23

27.10

Sanskrit

प्रागात्मा मन्त्रिणश्चैव ततो भृत्या महीभृता । जेयाश्चानन्तरं पौरा विरुध्येत ततो ऽरिभिः ॥

prāgātmā mantriṇaścaiva tato bhṛtyā mahībhṛtā | jeyāścānantaraṃ paurā virudhyeta tato 'ribhiḥ ||

English

First the king must conquer himself24, and his counsellors as well; then his servants; and after that the townspeople. Only then should he contend with his enemies.25

27.11

Sanskrit

यस्त्वेतानविजित्यैव वैरिणो विजिगीषते । सो ऽजितात्मा जितामात्यः शत्रुवर्गेण बाध्यते ॥

yastvetānavijityaiva vairiṇo vijigīṣate | so 'jitātmā jitāmātyaḥ śatruvargeṇa bādhyate ||

English

But the king who, without first conquering these26, wants to conquer his enemies, with his self unconquered and his ministers unconquered, is overwhelmed by the host of his enemies27.28†

27.12

Sanskrit

तस्मात् कामादयः पूर्वं जेयाः पुत्र ! महीभुजा । तज्जये हि जयो ऽवश्यं राजा नश्यति तैर्जितः ॥

tasmāt kāmādayaḥ pūrvaṃ jeyāḥ putra ! mahībhujā | tajjaye hi jayo 'vaśyaṃ rājā naśyati tairjitaḥ ||

English

Therefore, my son, a king must first conquer Kāma and the rest29. When they are conquered, victory is certain; but a king who is conquered by them is destroyed.30

27.13

Sanskrit

कामः क्रोधश्च लोभश्च मदो मानस्तथैव च । हर्षश्च शत्रवो ह्येते विनाशाय महीभृताम् ॥

kāmaḥ krodhaśca lobhaśca mado mānastathaiva ca | harṣaśca śatravo hyete vināśāya mahībhṛtām ||

English

Desire, anger, greed, pride31, arrogance32, and likewise elation: these are the enemies that bring about the destruction of kings.33

27.14

Sanskrit

कामप्रसक्तमात्मानं स्मृत्वा पाण्डुं निपातितम् । निवर्तयेत्तथा क्रोधादनुह्रादं हतात्मजम् ॥

kāmaprasaktamātmānaṃ smṛtvā pāṇḍuṃ nipātitam | nivartayettathā krodhādanuhrādaṃ hatātmajam ||

English

27.14–16The king, remembering Pāṇḍu34, who was struck down, should turn himself, attached to desire, back [from it]; and likewise from anger, [remembering] Anuhrāda35, whose son was slain; from greed, Aila36, who was slain; from arrogance, Vena37, slain by the brahmins; from pride, the son of Anāyuṣā38; from exultation, Bali and Purañjaya. By the great-souled Marutta39, when these were conquered, everything was conquered. Remembering [this], the king should shun these faults of his own.40

27.15

Sanskrit

हतमैलं तथा लोभान्मदाद्वेनं द्विजैर्हतम् । मानादनायुषापुत्रं बलिं हर्षात् पुरञ्जयम् ॥

hatamailaṃ tathā lobhānmadādvenaṃ dvijairhatam | mānādanāyuṣāputraṃ baliṃ harṣāt purañjayam ||

English

Its English is given with 27.14–16, above.

27.16

Sanskrit

एभिर्जितैर्जितं सर्वं मरुत्तेन महात्मना । स्मृत्वा विवर्जयेदेतान् दोषान् स्वीयान्महीपतिः ॥

ebhirjitairjitaṃ sarvaṃ maruttena mahātmanā | smṛtvā vivarjayedetān doṣān svīyānmahīpatiḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 27.14–16, above.

27.17

Sanskrit

काककोकिलभृङ्गाणां मृगव्यालशिखण्डिनाम् । हंसकुक्कुटलोहानां शिक्षेत चरित नृपः ॥

kākakokilabhṛṅgāṇāṃ mṛgavyālaśikhaṇḍinām | haṃsakukkuṭalohānāṃ śikṣeta carita nṛpaḥ ||

English

A king should learn the conduct of the crow, the cuckoo and the bee, of the deer, the snake41 and the peacock, and of the goose, the cock and the lohas42.43†

27.18

Sanskrit

कीटकस्य क्रियां कुर्यात् विपक्षे मनुजेश्वरः । चेष्टां पिपीलिकानाञ्च काले भूपः प्रदर्शयेत् ॥

kīṭakasya kriyāṃ kuryāt vipakṣe manujeśvaraḥ | ceṣṭāṃ pipīlikānāñca kāle bhūpaḥ pradarśayet ||

English

Against an enemy party, the lord of men should act as the worm does44; and at the proper time the king should display the conduct of ants.45

27.19

Sanskrit

ज्ञेयाग्निविस्फुलिङ्गानां बीजचेष्टा च शाल्मलेः । चन्द्रसूर्यस्वरूपेण नीत्यर्थे पृथिवीक्षिता ॥

jñeyāgnivisphuliṅgānāṃ bījaceṣṭā ca śālmaleḥ | candrasūryasvarūpeṇa nītyarthe pṛthivīkṣitā ||

English

For the purposes of nīti46, the king is to know the conduct of sparks of fire and the conduct of the seed of the śālmali47; [he is also to act] in the form of the moon and the sun48.49

27.20

Sanskrit

बन्धकीपद्मशरभशूलिकागुर्विणीस्तनात् । प्रज्ञा नृपेण चादेया तथा गोपालयोषितः ॥

bandhakīpadmaśarabhaśūlikāgurviṇīstanāt | prajñā nṛpeṇa cādeyā tathā gopālayoṣitaḥ ||

English

The king must take wisdom from the bandhakī50, the lotus, the śarabha51, the śūlikā52, and the breast of a pregnant woman, and likewise from the cowherd's woman.53

27.21

Sanskrit

शक्रार्कयमसोमानां तद्वद्वायोर्महीपतिः । रूपाणि पञ्च कुर्वोत महीपालनकर्मणि ॥

śakrārkayamasomānāṃ tadvadvāyormahīpatiḥ | rūpāṇi pañca kurvota mahīpālanakarmaṇi ||

English

In the work of protecting the earth, the king should take on five forms: those of Śakra, Arka54, Yama55 and Soma56, and likewise that of Vāyu57.58

27.22

Sanskrit

यथेन्द्रश्चतुरो मासान् तोयोत्सर्गेण भूगतम् । आप्याययेत्तथा लोकं परिहारैर्महीपतिः ॥

yathendraścaturo māsān toyotsargeṇa bhūgatam | āpyāyayettathā lokaṃ parihārairmahīpatiḥ ||

English

Just as Indra59, for four months, nourishes what is on the earth by releasing water, so should the king nourish the people by his remissions60.61

27.23

Sanskrit

मासानष्टौ यथा सूर्यस्तोयं हरति रश्मिभिः । सूक्ष्मेणैवाभ्युपायेन तथा शुल्कादिकं नृपः ॥

māsānaṣṭau yathā sūryastoyaṃ harati raśmibhiḥ | sūkṣmeṇaivābhyupāyena tathā śulkādikaṃ nṛpaḥ ||

English

Just as the sun takes water with its rays for eight months, and by a subtle means alone, so the king [should take] tolls and the like62.63

27.24

Sanskrit

यथा यमः प्रियद्वेष्ये प्राप्तकाले नियच्छति । तथा प्रियाप्रिये राजा दुष्टादुष्टे समो भवेत् ॥

yathā yamaḥ priyadveṣye prāptakāle niyacchati | tathā priyāpriye rājā duṣṭāduṣṭe samo bhavet ||

English

Just as Yama64 restrains both the one he loves and the one he hates when the time has come, so the king should be impartial toward the dear and the disliked65, the wicked and the not wicked.66

27.25

Sanskrit

पूर्णेन्दुमालोक्य यथा प्रीतिमान् जायते नरः । एवं यत्र प्रजाः सर्वा निर्वत्तास्तच्छशिव्रतम् ॥

pūrṇendumālokya yathā prītimān jāyate naraḥ | evaṃ yatra prajāḥ sarvā nirvattāstacchaśivratam ||

English

Just as a man becomes glad on seeing the full moon, so, wherever all the subjects are contented, that is the śaśivrata67.68

27.26

Sanskrit

मारुतः सर्वभूतेषु निगूढश्चरते यथा । एवं नृपश्चरेच्चारैः पौरामात्यादिबन्धुषु ॥

mārutaḥ sarvabhūteṣu nigūḍhaścarate yathā | evaṃ nṛpaścareccāraiḥ paurāmātyādibandhuṣu ||

English

As the wind moves hidden among all beings, so should a king move through spies69 among his townspeople, ministers and other kinsmen70.71

27.27

Sanskrit

न लोभाद्वा न कामाद्वा नार्थाद्वा यस्य मानसम् । यथान्यैः कृष्यते वत्स ! स राजा स्वर्गमृच्छति ॥

na lobhādvā na kāmādvā nārthādvā yasya mānasam | yathānyaiḥ kṛṣyate vatsa ! sa rājā svargamṛcchati ||

English

The king whose mind is not drawn away by greed, or by desire, or by wealth72, in the way that others draw it, my child, that king reaches heaven.73

27.28

Sanskrit

उत्पथग्राहिणो मूढान् स्वधर्माच्चलतो नरान् । यः करोति निजे धर्मे स राजा स्वर्गमृच्छति ॥

utpathagrāhiṇo mūḍhān svadharmāccalato narān | yaḥ karoti nije dharme sa rājā svargamṛcchati ||

English

The king who sets back in their own dharma74 those men who take the wrong road, who are deluded and are straying from their own dharma, goes to heaven.75†

27.29

Sanskrit

वर्णधर्मा न सीदन्ति यस्य राज्ये तथाश्रमाः । वत्स ! तस्य सुखं प्रेत्य परत्रेह च शाश्वतम् ॥

varṇadharmā na sīdanti yasya rājye tathāśramāḥ | vatsa ! tasya sukhaṃ pretya paratreha ca śāśvatam ||

English

In whose kingdom the duties of the varṇas76 and likewise of the āśramas77 do not decline, my child78, for him there is lasting happiness after death, in the next world and here as well.79

27.30

Sanskrit

एतद्राज्ञः परं कृत्यं तथैतत् सिद्धिकारकम् । स्वधर्मस्थापनं नृणां चाल्यन्ते ये कुबुद्धिभिः ॥

etadrājñaḥ paraṃ kṛtyaṃ tathaitat siddhikārakam | svadharmasthāpanaṃ nṛṇāṃ cālyante ye kubuddhibhiḥ ||

English

This is the highest duty of a king, and this is what brings success: the re-establishment in their own dharma of those men who are led astray80 by evil-minded people81.82

27.31

Sanskrit

पालनेनैव भूतानां कृतकृत्यो महीपतिः । सम्यक् पालयिता भागं धर्मस्याप्नोति यत्नतः ॥

pālanenaiva bhūtānāṃ kṛtakṛtyo mahīpatiḥ | samyak pālayitā bhāgaṃ dharmasyāpnoti yatnataḥ ||

English

By the protection of beings alone a king has done what was to be done83. One who protects them rightly obtains, through effort, a share of dharma84.85

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे पितापुत्रसंवादे आत्मविवेको नाम सप्तविंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe pitāputrasaṃvāde ātmaviveko nāma saptaviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, named "Ātmaviveka86" ("Discrimination of the Self"), in the dialogue between father and son87, in the revered Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.88

  1. lulled and instructed: ullāpyamāna is the passive participle of the causative of ud-√lap. It can mean 'being made to speak out', that is, addressed or sung to. Here it refers to the mother's lullaby-teachings in chapter 26. ↩
  2. Alarka: The son of Madālasā and Ṛtadhvaja, as verse 27.2 shows. His mother's counsel in chapter 26 was given in the form of lullabies. ↩
  3. The reading: ullāpyamāna: it can mean 'being lulled, sung to' or 'being addressed, taught'. I combined both senses because the context is the mother's lullaby-instructions. alarkasaṃjñitaḥ: 'named Alarka' is taken as the plain reading. ↩
  4. the son of Ṛtadhvaja: Alarka, named in the preceding verse (27.1), is the son of Ṛtadhvaja and Madālasā. The verse itself says only ṛtadhvajasuta. ↩
  5. His sacred-thread initiation was performed: upanayana, the rite of investiture with the sacred thread, which marks a boy's entry into Vedic study as a twice-born youth. ↩
  6. in this world and in the next: The compound aihikāmuṣmikāya is a single dative, 'for the happiness of this [world] and of the yonder [world]', qualifying sukhāya. ↩
  7. The reading: The speaker is Alarka, who is addressing his mother Madālasā (27.2). The verse has no speaker's line of its own; the verb 'said' (āha) is in 27.2. 'atra' may be read as 'here, in this life' or 'in this matter'; I chose 'here' as the simpler sense. Particle 'vai' is left untranslated as merely emphatic. ↩
  8. without conflict with his own dharma: svadharma: the duty proper to one's own station, here that of a king (kṣatriya). The sense is that pleasing the people must not contradict it. ↩
  9. The reading: The speaker's line [112.6] 'madālasovāca' stands before this verse and is translated here as its opening, since the speech begins in this verse. mahībhṛtā ('by the earth-supporter', i.e. a king) is in apposition to rājye 'bhiṣiktena; I render it 'a king' after the consecrated person. The instrumental agent construction (kartavyam ... mahībhṛtā) is rendered actively with 'must'. ↩
  10. the seven vices that take away the root: Vyasana means a fault or addiction that brings a king to ruin. The verse does not list the seven. The usual list, found in Manu (7.50–51) and Kāmandaka, is women, dice, hunting, drink, harsh speech, harsh punishment and waste of wealth. Mūla, 'root', is probably the basis of the king's power. ↩
  11. counsel: mantra here means secret counsel or state deliberation, not a sacred formula. The verse warns against the divulging of a king's plans. ↩
  12. The reading: 1. bahirmantravinirgamāt: I accept the reviewer's point. The ablative is read as separation, parallel to ripubhyaḥ, with saṃrakṣyaḥ governing both: 'from enemies and from the going out of counsel'. The bracketed 'preventing' is dropped, because it added a verbal idea the Sanskrit lacks. Verse 27.6 treats the leak as the cause of the king's ruin, which supports reading it as a danger. A causal reading is still possible grammatically. 2. bahiḥ is 'outside'. The English 'going out' already carries it, so I no longer add 'to the outside'. 3. ātmā is taken as the reflexive 'oneself', meaning the king, since Madālasā is instructing the anointed king. 4. mantra is rendered 'counsel' (not the glossary's ritual formula), as the context of state policy requires. 5. mūlaharāṇi is 'take away the root'. The gloss of mūla as kingdom and treasury was speculative and is now given only as the basis of the king's power. The note on Manu is corrected: his seven are the same. 6. vai is purely emphatic and ↩
  13. eightfold: aṣṭadhā. The text does not say what the eight kinds of destruction are, and the point of the chariot comparison is not explained. ↩
  14. counsel: mantra here means secret deliberation, the king's confidential plans, not a ritual formula. Its 'going out to the outside' (bahir vinirgama) is the leak against which 27.5 warns. ↩
  15. through faults connected with the enemy: aridoṣataḥ is ari, 'enemy', plus doṣa, 'fault', with the ablative suffix -taḥ. The text does not state how the two members relate. It may mean faults such as collusion with the enemy, or faults that the enemy can exploit. ↩
  16. The reading: (1) aṣṭadhā nāśam āpnoti sucakrāt syandanād yathā: The reviewer is right that sucakrāt syandanāt are ablatives and cannot be the subject of āpnoti. I have kept them as ablatives of source or cause, 'from a chariot with good wheels', with an indefinite subject '[one]'. My earlier note called the ablatives irregular and possibly corrupt, and I withdraw it. The real difficulty is that the verse has no stated subject and does not say how a chariot brings on an eightfold destruction. Taking syandana in the sense 'swift' or 'flowing' would not remove that difficulty. I have not tried to explain the simile within the translation. (2) aṣṭadhā: changed to 'eightfold', which keeps the adverb closer to the Sanskrit. (3) mantra: rendered 'counsel' rather than in the ritual sense of the glossary, because the context is secrecy and spies. (4) aridoṣataḥ: the reviewer accepted the sense. I changed the wording to 'through faults connected with the enemy' to avoid the ambiguous 'their'. The relation be ↩
  17. trusted kinsmen: Sanskrit āpta means a reliable or trusted person; it may also be read as 'close associates'. Here it is taken as a separate term between friends and relatives. ↩
  18. for the sake of an undertaking: kāryayogāt, literally 'by connection with a purpose'; that is, when the task in hand requires it. ↩
  19. The reading: mitrāptabandhuṣu: the compound can be read as three groups (friends, trusted persons, relatives) or as 'friends who are trusted relatives'. I chose three groups. The sense of 'tu' is contrastive and weak; I rendered it 'however'. The optative viśvasīta is rendered 'may trust', in contrast to the prohibition in the first half. ↩
  20. the standing, the growth and the decline: sthāna-vṛddhi-kṣaya: the three conditions of a state (stagnation, growth, decline), on which the choice among the six expedients depends. The compound can also be read as one: knowing the decline of growth of position; the threefold sense is preferred. ↩
  21. the sixfold policy: ṣāḍguṇya: the six expedients of royal policy: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking shelter, and dividing one's forces (or making peace with one and war with another). ↩
  22. desire: kāma here means desire or passion in general, and perhaps the vices born of it (hunting, dice, women, drink), not only the god Kāma. ↩
  23. The reading: sthānavṛddhikṣayajñena: could be 'knowing the standing, growth and decline' (three items; chosen, as in standard treatises) or 'knowing the decline of the growth of position'. guṇitātmānā: 'whose mind is trained/imbued' (chosen); a sense 'multiplied' is unlikely. ↩
  24. conquer himself: The text has prāgātmā, 'first the self'. The verb jeyāḥ, 'are to be conquered', is supplied from the second half of the verse and is understood with ātmā and mantriṇaḥ. The following verse (27.11) speaks of the ajitātmā, one who has not conquered himself. ↩
  25. The reading: mahībhṛtā is an instrumental agent ('by the king'), which I render as an active 'the king must'. virudhyeta is optative, 'should contend with', which I took as 'should fight or oppose'. The first pāda lacks an explicit verb, and I supplied jeyāḥ from pāda c. This is not marked in brackets, because the verb is plainly carried over: 'must conquer'. The word order has also been rearranged for English. ↩
  26. these: Refers back to the four named in 27.10: the king's own self, his ministers, his servants and the citizens, all of whom are to be mastered before the enemies. ↩
  27. the host of his enemies: śatruvarga: the group of enemies. The following verses (27.12–13) identify them with the inner foes, desire (kāma), anger, greed, pride and the rest. ↩
  28. The reading: The text reads jitāmātyaḥ, literally 'whose ministers are conquered'. That contradicts the sense of 27.10, where conquering the ministers is a duty, so I take it as ajitāmātyaḥ ('whose ministers are unconquered') with the avagraha lost after so 'jitātmā. A second possibility is 'conquered by his ministers', but I chose the emendation as the simpler one. ↩
  29. Kāma and the rest: kāmādayaḥ: 'Kāma and the others'. The verse that follows (27.13) lists them as desire, anger, greed, pride, conceit and elation, the six enemies of a king. ↩
  30. The reading: Kāma is taken as the name of the passion (desire), not strictly the deity Kāma. The glossary entry is for the god, but here the word means desire, the first of the group of enemies listed in 27.13. The translation keeps the IAST name 'Kāma' in line with the glossary, and the note explains the sense. Alternatively one could write 'desire and the rest'. ↩
  31. pride: mada is intoxicating pride, a self-satisfied conceit arising from birth, wealth, strength or learning. ↩
  32. arrogance: māna is self-esteem or haughtiness, an inflated sense of one's own standing. ↩
  33. The reading: kāma is rendered 'desire' (the lust of the sense-objects), not as the god Kāma of the glossary, since here it stands among the inner enemies. mada and māna are close in sense; I chose 'pride' for mada and 'arrogance' for māna to keep them distinct. harṣa is rendered 'elation' as an excess, not mere joy. ↩
  34. Pāṇḍu: The father of the Pāṇḍavas. He died when he embraced his wife Mādrī, despite a sage's curse that union would kill him. ↩
  35. Anuhrāda: A Dānava (Anuhlāda, in other spellings). The story of his anger and of his son's death is not told in this passage. ↩
  36. Aila: 'Son of Ilā', that is Purūravas. Tradition says he was killed by his own greed when he seized the wealth of brahmins. ↩
  37. Vena: A king whose arrogance led him to forbid sacrifice. The brahmins killed him with blades of kuśa grass consecrated by mantras. ↩
  38. the son of Anāyuṣā: The Sanskrit is anāyuṣāputra. Anāyuṣā is a wife of Kaśyapa, and the Dānava Vṛtra is sometimes counted among her sons, but the identification is uncertain. Nahuṣa is the other possibility. ↩
  39. Marutta: A famous king of the Solar line, known for his great sacrifice and his wealth. ↩
  40. The reading: (1) ātmānam in 27.14 is taken as the object of nivartayet ('turn himself back'), qualified by kāmaprasaktam. The ablative 'from desire' is not in the text and is supplied from the following krodhāt. Another reading takes ātmānam with smṛtvā, 'remembering himself attached to desire', but it would then have no function in the sentence. (2) The verb for the other items (lobhāt, madāt, mānāt, harṣāt) is understood from nivartayet and smṛtvā. (3) anāyuṣāputram is taken as 'the son of Anāyuṣā', and the person is uncertain: Vṛtra or Nahuṣa are both possible. (4) baliṃ harṣāt purañjayam is taken as two persons, Bali and Purañjaya, because the pattern is one example per vice. Purañjaya could instead be an epithet of Bali, 'conqueror of cities'. (5) hatātmajam is taken as a bahuvrīhi, 'whose son was slain', agreeing with Anuhrāda. The singular ātmaja could also stand for 'sons'. (6) In 27.16 ebhir jitaiḥ is taken as an instrumental absolute with maruttena as agent, 'by Marutta, these being conqu ↩
  41. snake: vyāla means a beast of prey or a snake. A snake is chosen here because the other words in the list are animals and birds. ↩
  42. lohas: The word lohānām is obscure. Possible readings are 'iron' (loha) or the name of a bird or animal, perhaps the red-feathered or red-eyed one. It stands in a list of creatures, so the translation keeps the Sanskrit word. ↩
  43. The reading: lohānām is uncertain. It may mean 'of iron' (as an instrument or metal), or be the name of a bird, or a corruption of another word. I keep it untranslated as loha. vyāla may mean 'beast of prey' or 'snake'; I chose 'snake' because mṛga is already 'deer' and the list is of creatures. The singular carita ('conduct') is taken as governing the whole genitive list, as carita for caritam (metrically and by the text's looseness), and the genitive depends on it. ↩
  44. act as the worm does: kīṭaka is a small worm or insect; the commentarial tradition is not given here, and the precise trait of the creature that the king is to imitate is not stated in the verse. ↩
  45. The reading: vipakṣe can mean 'against an enemy party' (locative of vipakṣa, opposition/adversary) or 'in the enemy's camp'. I chose 'against an enemy party', which fits both. kriyāṃ kuryāt is rendered 'act as ... does', literally 'perform the action of the worm'. Metrically, pipīlikānāñca is simply pipīlikānāṃ ca with the sandhi of the e-text. ↩
  46. nīti: Statecraft or political prudence: the conduct of government, including diplomacy and the use of force. ↩
  47. the seed of the śālmali: The śālmali is the silk-cotton tree. Its seeds travel on the wind in tufts of down, and sparks of fire likewise spread far from a small beginning. The verse seems to treat both as models of quiet, wide dispersal; it does not say so. ↩
  48. [he is also to act] in the form of the moon and the sun: The verse has no verb for this clause. 'Is to act' is supplied from the sense, and the king's acting like the moon and sun is understood from the parallel instructions in the following verses. The point of comparison is not stated. ↩
  49. The reading: The verse is elliptical and its text may be faulty. 'jñeyā' is feminine singular, so I take it as agreeing with an understood ceṣṭā ('conduct') from bījaceṣṭā, covering both agnivisphuliṅgānām and śālmaleḥ. 'pṛthivīkṣitā' is the instrumental of pṛthivīkṣit, 'king', the agent of 'is to be known'. The phrase 'candrasūryasvarūpeṇa' has no verb of its own, so I supplied 'he is also to act' in brackets. Other readings are possible: it may be read as 'by the king, who has the form of moon and sun', or with the moon and sun as the king's own nature. I chose the first reading because the following verses tell the king to take on the forms of several deities. ↩
  50. bandhakī: A term for an unchaste or wanton woman. It can also mean a woman who ties or binds. ↩
  51. śarabha: A fabulous eight-legged beast said to be stronger than the lion, or in some uses a kind of deer. ↩
  52. śūlikā: The word is unclear here. It may be a woman who roasts meat on a spit, a small spear, or a bird. It is left untranslated. ↩
  53. The reading: The long compound bandhakīpadmaśarabhaśūlikāgurviṇīstanāt ends in a single ablative, stanāt. Reading 1: a series of separate sources (bandhakī, padma, śarabha, śūlikā, gurviṇī, stana). Reading 2 (chosen): gurviṇīstana is one tatpuruṣa, 'breast of a pregnant woman', as the last item of the list. The sense of the lesson is not given in the verse. The word śūlikā is also uncertain (spit-roaster, spear or bird), and the text may be corrupt. ↩
  54. Arka: A name of the sun, Sūrya. ↩
  55. Yama: The god of death, who judges and restrains the wrongdoer. ↩
  56. Soma: The moon. ↩
  57. Vāyu: The wind. The verses that follow develop the comparisons with Indra and the sun; this verse only lists the five. ↩
  58. The reading: The verb kurvota is a Vedic-looking or irregular optative middle (for kurvīta); I take it as 'should take on, assume'. The text names only four deities with the genitive plural, which is then extended by tadvad vāyoḥ, making five forms in all. ↩
  59. Indra: Indra, here the god of rain, is the one of the five forms the king is to take (see 27.21, where he appears as Śakra). ↩
  60. remissions: parihāra means a waiver or exemption, such as remission of dues or taxes, or a grant of immunity. Another sense is 'protection' or 'avoidance'. Remission fits the parallel with the rain and with the taxes in 27.23. ↩
  61. The reading: parihāraiḥ can mean remissions or exemptions (of taxes and dues), or protection or avoidance. I chose 'remissions' because the verse compares it with Indra's releasing of rain, and the next verse deals with the sun's drawing of water as the king's taxation. 'bhūgatam' (what is on the earth, literally 'gone to the earth') is taken as a neuter object meaning what lives or grows on the earth, parallel to 'lokam' (the people). The words 'the people' for lokam is a choice; 'world' is also possible. ↩
  62. tolls and the like: śulkādikam: śulka is a toll, duty or tax on goods; ādika, "and the like", covers other levies. The king's gentle taxation is likened to the sun's unseen drawing of water, as the preceding verse likened his protection to Indra's rains. ↩
  63. The reading: The second half has no verb. I supply "should take" from harati in the first half. The Sanskrit could be read as a plain statement ("the king takes"), but the surrounding verses are precepts (śikṣeta, kuryāt, kurvīta), so I read it as a precept. I have rendered harati as "takes" in both halves so that the parallel stays exact. The reviewer named no specific fault, so the rest of the draft is unchanged. ↩
  64. Yama: Yama, god of death and judge of the dead, is the model of impartial restraint (niyamana) in the king's conduct; the verse is one of the five forms (rūpa) of the king listed in 27.21. ↩
  65. the dear and the disliked: The compound priyāpriye is a locative dvandva (priya + apriya), as is duṣṭāduṣṭe; the verse uses the locative of the object toward which impartiality is shown. ↩
  66. The reading: priyadveṣye can be read as a dvandva 'the dear and the hated' (taken here) or as 'the beloved who is hateful'. The dvandva fits the parallel with priyāpriye. Also, niyacchati has no stated object; 'restrains' is supplied from the sense of the verb and the object is the pair in priyadveṣye. ↩
  67. śaśivrata: Literally 'the moon-observance' or 'moon-vow'. It is the king's conduct modelled on the moon (Soma), the third of the five forms the king is to take on (27.21). Here it means a reign in which the subjects are pleased and at ease. ↩
  68. The reading: The e-text reads 'nirvattāḥ', which is not a regular form. I read it as 'nirvṛtāḥ' (or 'nirvṛttāḥ'), 'contented, at ease', which suits the comparison with the man made glad by the full moon. The text may be corrupt here. ↩
  69. spies: cāra: an agent who moves about unrecognized to gather information for the king. ↩
  70. townspeople, ministers and other kinsmen: The compound paurāmātyādibandhuṣu may be read as 'among townspeople, ministers and the like, and kinsmen', or with bandhu governing the whole series. Here 'ādi' is taken with the whole list, so that the kinsmen are the final item. ↩
  71. The reading: The compound paurāmātyādibandhuṣu can be divided in more than one way: 'townspeople, ministers, etc., and kinsmen', or 'townspeople, ministers and other kinsmen'. I chose the latter as the simplest reading, taking ādi with bandhu as 'and so on among the kinsmen'. ↩
  72. wealth: Artha: material interest, wealth, profit. It also means 'purpose'. Here it is the inducement or bribe by which others might sway the king. ↩
  73. The reading: yathānyaiḥ kṛṣyate: I accept the reviewer's main point. Anyaiḥ is an instrumental plural and the agent of the passive kṛṣyate, 'is drawn by others'. The draft's 'as in other men' turned it into a locative sense and invented a contrast with ordinary men, so I have withdrawn it. The sense is that the king's mind cannot be swayed by those around him, which fits the preceding verse on spies among citizens, ministers and kinsmen. The reviewer's point on yathā is partly right: it does not set up a comparison of the king with other men. I still translate it, as 'in the way that', so that no word is left out. The ablatives lobhāt, kāmāt and arthāt are ablatives of cause or means, and the Sanskrit does not say whose greed, desire or wealth is meant. They could be the king's own motives, which others exploit, or the inducements others offer. 'Greed, desire or wealth, in the way that others draw it' keeps both readings open. I accept the change of artha from 'gain' to 'wealth', since the context ↩
  74. their own dharma: svadharma, the duty proper to a man's own class (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama); nije dharme in the second half repeats the idea. ↩
  75. The reading: utpathagrāhiṇaḥ may mean 'taking the wrong road' (literally, grasping a path that is out of the way) or 'following wrong teachings'; I chose the literal sense, which suits the following 'straying from their own dharma'. ↩
  76. varṇas: The four social classes (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra), each with its own prescribed duties. ↩
  77. āśramas: The four stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant), each with its own prescribed duties. ↩
  78. my child: Vocative vatsa: the teacher addresses his pupil, as in the preceding verses. ↩
  79. The reading: pretya paratra iha ca: 'after death, in the next world and here' is taken as three adverbs describing where the happiness lasts. 'Pretya' may be read as 'having departed [this life]', which I render 'after death'. ↩
  80. led astray: Literally 'are made to move (away)'; the sense, as in 27.28, is of men who stray from their own dharma under bad influence. ↩
  81. evil-minded people: The plural instrumental kubuddhibhiḥ could also be read as 'by evil counsels'; the rendering takes it as persons. ↩
  82. The reading: kubuddhibhiḥ: 'by evil-minded persons' or 'by evil ideas/counsels'. I chose persons, since the agents who lead men astray are naturally people. Also, nṛṇām (genitive plural) is taken with svadharmasthāpanam ('re-establishment of men'), with ye as the relative clause describing those men; the relative ye and its antecedent nṛṇām are slightly irregular in construction. ↩
  83. has done what was to be done: Sanskrit kṛtakṛtya: one who has completed his duty, so that nothing further remains for him to accomplish. ↩
  84. a share of dharma: bhāgaṃ dharmasya: the genitive indicates the portion of merit (dharma) that arises from the protected subjects' righteous conduct; the king shares in it by protecting them. ↩
  85. The reading: The word 'yatnataḥ' (ablative of yatna) can attach to 'pālayitā' (one who protects with effort) or to 'āpnoti' (obtains through effort). I took it with 'āpnoti', as 'through effort', because 'samyak' already qualifies 'pālayitā'. 'Bhūtānām' is taken as 'of beings', meaning all the creatures or subjects a king protects. ↩
  86. Ātmaviveka: Literally 'discernment of the self': the distinction between the self (ātman) and what is not the self. This is the title the colophon gives to the chapter. ↩
  87. between father and son: The printed colophon reads pitāputrasaṃvāde, 'dialogue between father and son'. This does not fit the chapter, in which a mother instructs her son; the next chapter opens with Alarka hearing his mother's words (tanmātur vacanaṃ śrutvā so 'larko mātaram). The reading is probably a faulty or stock colophon, perhaps for mātāputrasaṃvāde. It is translated as printed. ↩
  88. The reading: 1. The Sanskrit has no verb. 'Thus ends' (iti ... adhyāyaḥ) is the usual colophon formula, and I supply it as English requires. 2. 'Śrī' is taken as an honorific of the Purāṇa's title, hence 'revered'. 3. The reviewer rightly noted that the speakers are mother and son, so my earlier note, which said that the address 'vatsa' fits 'father and son', was wrong. I have rewritten it. I still translate the printed pitāputra and flag the mismatch in the note, rather than emending to mātāputra. 4. I accept the grammatical correction: pitāputra is a dvandva (pitā ca putraś ca) forming the first member of the tatpuruṣa with saṃvāda, so 'between father and son' is the exact rendering. 5. The chapter title is kept in IAST with its meaning given in parentheses. ↩

Adhyāya 28

Sanskrit

अष्टाविंशो ऽध्यायः

aṣṭāviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Twenty-Eight1

Sanskrit

जड उवाच

jaḍa uvāca

28.1

Sanskrit

तन्मातुर्वचनं श्रुत्वा सो ऽलर्को मातरं पुनः । पप्रच्छ वर्णधर्मांश्च धर्मा ये चाश्रमेषु च ॥

tanmāturvacanaṃ śrutvā so 'larko mātaraṃ punaḥ | papraccha varṇadharmāṃśca dharmā ye cāśrameṣu ca ||

English

Having heard that speech of his mother, Alarka2 then asked his mother again about the duties of the social classes3, and about the duties that belong to the stages of life4.5

Sanskrit

अलर्क उवाच

alarka uvāca

English

28.2Alarka said: O greatly fortunate lady, you have told me this dharma that rests on the government of a kingdom6. I wish to hear that [dharma] which is based on the varṇas7 and the āśramas8.9

28.2

Sanskrit

कथितो ऽयं महाभागे ! राज्यतन्त्राश्रितस्त्वया । धर्मं तमहमिच्छामि श्रोतुं वर्णाश्रमात्मकम् ॥

kathito 'yaṃ mahābhāge ! rājyatantrāśritastvayā | dharmaṃ tamahamicchāmi śrotuṃ varṇāśramātmakam ||

English

Its English is given with 28.2, above.

Sanskrit

मदालसोवाच

madālasovāca

English

28.3Madālasā said: Generosity, study and yajña are held to be the threefold dharma of a brahmin. There is no other, fourth dharma; this is his dharma apart from [a time of] distress10.11

28.3

Sanskrit

दानमध्ययनं यज्ञो ब्राह्मणस्य त्रिधा मतः । नान्यश्चतुर्थो धर्मो ऽस्ति धर्मस्तस्यापदं विना ॥

dānamadhyayanaṃ yajño brāhmaṇasya tridhā mataḥ | nānyaścaturtho dharmo 'sti dharmastasyāpadaṃ vinā ||

English

Its English is given with 28.3, above.

28.4

Sanskrit

याजनाध्यापने शुद्धे तथा पूतप्रतिग्रहः । एषा सम्यक् समाख्यता त्रिविधा चास्य जीविका ॥

yājanādhyāpane śuddhe tathā pūtapratigrahaḥ | eṣā samyak samākhyatā trividhā cāsya jīvikā ||

English

Officiating at sacrifices12 and teaching are the two pure [means], and likewise the acceptance of pure gifts13. In this way the threefold livelihood of this [brahmin] has been rightly declared.14

28.5

Sanskrit

दानमध्ययनं यज्ञः क्षत्रियस्याप्ययं त्रिधा । धर्मः प्रोक्तः क्षिते रक्षा शस्त्राजीवञ्च जीविका ॥

dānamadhyayanaṃ yajñaḥ kṣatriyasyāpyayaṃ tridhā | dharmaḥ proktaḥ kṣite rakṣā śastrājīvañca jīvikā ||

English

For a kṣatriya15 too this dharma is declared to be threefold: generosity, study and yajña. His livelihood is the protection of the earth and living by weapons.16

28.6

Sanskrit

दानमध्ययनं यज्ञो वैश्यस्यापि त्रिधैव सः । वाणिज्यं पाशुपाल्यञ्च कृषिश्चैवास्य जीविका ॥

dānamadhyayanaṃ yajño vaiśyasyāpi tridhaiva saḥ | vāṇijyaṃ pāśupālyañca kṛṣiścaivāsya jīvikā ||

English

Giving, study and sacrifice: for the vaiśya17 too, that dharma is of these three kinds only. Trade, the tending of cattle and farming are his livelihood.18

28.7

Sanskrit

दानं यज्ञो ऽथ शुश्रूषा द्विजातीनां त्रिधा मया । व्याख्यातः शूद्रधर्मो ऽपि जीविका कारुकर्म च ॥

dānaṃ yajño 'tha śuśrūṣā dvijātīnāṃ tridhā mayā | vyākhyātaḥ śūdradharmo 'pi jīvikā kārukarma ca ||

English

28.7–8The dharma of the śūdra too has been explained by me as threefold: generosity, yajña, and service of the twice-born; and [his] livelihood is craftsman's work, and likewise service of the twice-born, maintenance19, and buying and selling. These dharmas of the varṇas20 have been declared; and let those based on the āśramas21 be heard.22

28.8

Sanskrit

तद्वद् द्विजातिशुश्रूषा पोषणं क्रयविक्रयौ । वर्णधर्मास्त्विमे प्रोक्ताः श्रूयन्तां चाश्रमाश्रयाः ॥

tadvad dvijātiśuśrūṣā poṣaṇaṃ krayavikrayau | varṇadharmāstvime proktāḥ śrūyantāṃ cāśramāśrayāḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 28.7–8, above.

28.9

Sanskrit

स्ववर्णधर्मात् संसिद्धिं नरः प्राप्नोति न च्युतः । प्रयाति नरकं प्रेत्य प्रतिषिद्धनिषेवणात् ॥

svavarṇadharmāt saṃsiddhiṃ naraḥ prāpnoti na cyutaḥ | prayāti narakaṃ pretya pratiṣiddhaniṣevaṇāt ||

English

A man who has not fallen away attains perfection23 from the dharma of his own order24; [a man] goes to hell after death through resorting to what is forbidden.25

28.10

Sanskrit

यावत्तु नोपनयनं क्रियते वै द्विजन्मनः । कामचेष्टोक्तिभक्ष्यश्च तावद् भवति पुत्रक ॥

yāvattu nopanayanaṃ kriyate vai dvijanmanaḥ | kāmaceṣṭoktibhakṣyaśca tāvad bhavati putraka ||

English

As long as the upanayana26 of a twice-born is not performed, so long, my son, he remains one whose actions, speech and eating are as he pleases27.

28.11

Sanskrit

कृतोपनयनः सम्यग् ब्रह्मचारी गुरुर्गृहे । वसेत्तत्र च धर्मो ऽस्य कथ्यते तं निबोध मे ॥

kṛtopanayanaḥ samyag brahmacārī gururgṛhe | vasettatra ca dharmo 'sya kathyate taṃ nibodha me ||

English

When the initiation28 has been properly performed, the brahmacārin29 should live in the house of his guru30. Here his dharma is being stated; listen to it from me.31

28.12

Sanskrit

स्वाध्यायो ऽथाग्रिशुश्रूषा स्नानं भिक्षाटनं तथा । गुरोर्निवेद्य तच्चान्नमनुज्ञातेन सर्वदा ॥

svādhyāyo 'thāgriśuśrūṣā snānaṃ bhikṣāṭanaṃ tathā | gurornivedya taccānnamanujñātena sarvadā ||

English

Recitation of the Veda by himself (svādhyāya32), attendance on the fire33, bathing, and likewise going about for alms; and that food, having been reported to the teacher, [is to be eaten] always by one who has been given permission.34

28.13

Sanskrit

गुरोः कर्मणि सोद्योगः सम्यक् प्रीत्युपपादनम् । तेनाहूतः पठेच्चैव तत्परो नान्यमानसः ॥

guroḥ karmaṇi sodyogaḥ samyak prītyupapādanam | tenāhūtaḥ paṭheccaiva tatparo nānyamānasaḥ ||

English

He is to be diligent in the service of the guru35, and he is to please him fully. When called by him, he is to study, intent on that and with his mind on nothing else.36

28.14

Sanskrit

एकं द्वौ सकलान् वापि वेदान् प्राप्य गुरोर्मुखात् । अनुज्ञातो ऽथ वन्दित्वा दक्षिणां गुरवे ततः ॥

ekaṃ dvau sakalān vāpi vedān prāpya gurormukhāt | anujñāto 'tha vanditvā dakṣiṇāṃ gurave tataḥ ||

English

28.14–15Having obtained one Veda, two, or even all the Vedas from the teacher's own mouth, having then been given leave, and having bowed and [given] the fee to the teacher, thereafter, if he desires the householder's stage of life, he should enter the householder āśrama37; or else he may enter the vānaprastha āśrama38, or the fourth39, as his own wish decides.40

28.15

Sanskrit

गार्हस्थ्याश्रमकामस्तु गृहस्थाश्रममावसेत् । वानप्रस्थाश्रमं वापि चतुर्थं चेच्छयात्मनः ॥

gārhasthyāśramakāmastu gṛhasthāśramamāvaset | vānaprasthāśramaṃ vāpi caturthaṃ cecchayātmanaḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 28.14–15, above.

28.16

Sanskrit

तत्रैव वा गुरोर्गेहे द्विजो निष्ठामवाप्नुयात् । गुरोरभावे तत्पुत्रे तच्छिष्ये तत्सुतं विना ॥

tatraiva vā gurorgehe dvijo niṣṭhāmavāpnuyāt | gurorabhāve tatputre tacchiṣye tatsutaṃ vinā ||

English

Or the brahmin may stay right there, in the teacher's house, until the end of his life41. In the absence of the teacher, [he may stay] in the house of the teacher's son, or in that of his pupil, failing the teacher's son.42

28.17

Sanskrit

शुश्रूषुर्निरभिमानो ब्रह्मचार्याश्रमं वसेत् । उपावृत्तस्ततस्तस्मात् गृहस्थाश्रमकाम्यया ॥

śuśrūṣurnirabhimāno brahmacāryāśramaṃ vaset | upāvṛttastatastasmāt gṛhasthāśramakāmyayā ||

English

Obedient and free of pride, he should live in the stage of the student [brahmacārin43]. Then, from that [stage], he should turn back44, with the desire for the householder's stage45.46

28.18

Sanskrit

ततो ऽसमानर्षिकुलां तुल्यां भार्यामरोगिणीम् । उद्वहेन्न्यायतो ऽव्यङ्गां गृहस्थाश्रमकारणात् ॥

tato 'samānarṣikulāṃ tulyāṃ bhāryāmarogiṇīm | udvahennyāyato 'vyaṅgāṃ gṛhasthāśramakāraṇāt ||

English

Then, for the sake of the householder's stage of life47, he should marry in accordance with the rule48 a wife who is not of the same sage-lineage as his own49, who is his equal, free from disease, and without any bodily defect.50

28.19

Sanskrit

स्वकर्मणा धनं लब्ध्वा पितृदेवातिथींस्तथा । सम्यक् सम्प्रीणयन् भक्त्या पोषयेच्चाश्रितांस्तथा ॥

svakarmaṇā dhanaṃ labdhvā pitṛdevātithīṃstathā | samyak samprīṇayan bhaktyā poṣayeccāśritāṃstathā ||

English

28.19–20Having obtained wealth by his own work, he should duly please the ancestors, the gods and likewise the guests with devotion, and likewise support those who depend on him: his servants, his children, his female relatives51, and also the wretched, the blind and the fallen52, giving food as far as his means allow, and [giving it] also to birds and animals53.54

28.20

Sanskrit

भृत्यात्मजान् जामयो ऽथ दीनान्धपतितानपि । यथाशक्त्यान्नदानेन वयांसि पशवस्तथा ॥

bhṛtyātmajān jāmayo 'tha dīnāndhapatitānapi | yathāśaktyānnadānena vayāṃsi paśavastathā ||

English

Its English is given with 28.19–20, above.

28.21

Sanskrit

एष धर्मो गृहस्थस्य ऋतावभिगमस्तथा । पञ्चयज्ञविधानन्तु यथाशक्त्या न हापयेत् ॥

eṣa dharmo gṛhasthasya ṛtāvabhigamastathā | pañcayajñavidhānantu yathāśaktyā na hāpayet ||

English

This is the dharma of the householder, and so is approaching [his wife] in her fertile season55. He should not neglect the ordinance of the five yajñas56, as far as his ability allows.57

28.22

Sanskrit

पितृदेवातिथिज्ञातिभुक्तशेषं स्वयं नरः । भुञ्जीत च समं भृत्यैर्यथाविभवमादृतः ॥

pitṛdevātithijñātibhuktaśeṣaṃ svayaṃ naraḥ | bhuñjīta ca samaṃ bhṛtyairyathāvibhavamādṛtaḥ ||

English

A man should himself eat, together with his servants and according to his means, the remainder of what has been eaten58 by the ancestors, the gods, guests and kinsmen, and he should do so with respect.59

28.23

Sanskrit

एष तूद्देशतः प्रोक्तो गृहस्थस्याश्रमो मया । वानप्रस्थस्य धर्मं ते कथयाम्यवधार्यताम् ॥

eṣa tūddeśataḥ prokto gṛhasthasyāśramo mayā | vānaprasthasya dharmaṃ te kathayāmyavadhāryatām ||

English

This is the stage of life60 of the householder, as I have described it to you in brief. Now I shall tell you the dharma of the forest-dweller61; let it be carefully grasped.62

28.24

Sanskrit

अपत्यसन्ततिं दृष्ट्वा प्राज्ञो चानतिम् । वानप्रस्थाश्रमं गच्छेदात्मनः शुद्धिकारणात् ॥

apatyasantatiṃ dṛṣṭvā prājño cānatim | vānaprasthāśramaṃ gacchedātmanaḥ śuddhikāraṇāt ||

English

Having seen the continuity of offspring and the bowing63, the wise man should go to the vānaprastha stage of life64, for the purification of himself.65

28.25

Sanskrit

तत्रारण्योपभोगश्च तपोभिश्चानुकर्षणम् । भूमौ शय्या ब्रह्मचर्यं पितृदेवातिथिक्रिया ॥

tatrāraṇyopabhogaśca tapobhiścānukarṣaṇam | bhūmau śayyā brahmacaryaṃ pitṛdevātithikriyā ||

English

28.25–26There, [in that stage,] one lives on the produce of the forest and wears down the body through austerities; one sleeps on the ground, practises brahmacarya66, and performs the rites for the ancestors, the gods and guests. One offers the homa67, bathes at the three pressings68, wears matted hair and bark garments, always devotes oneself to the practice of yoga69, and makes use of forest oils.70

28.26

Sanskrit

होमस्त्रिषवणस्त्रानं जटावल्कलधारणम् । योगाभ्यासः सदा चैव वन्यस्नेहनिषेवणम् ॥

homastriṣavaṇastrānaṃ jaṭāvalkaladhāraṇam | yogābhyāsaḥ sadā caiva vanyasnehaniṣevaṇam ||

English

Its English is given with 28.25–26, above.

28.27

Sanskrit

इत्येष पापशुद्ध्यर्थमात्मनश्चोपकारकः । वानप्रस्थाश्रमस्तस्माद् भिक्षोस्तु चरमो ऽपरः ॥

ityeṣa pāpaśuddhyarthamātmanaścopakārakaḥ | vānaprasthāśramastasmād bhikṣostu caramo 'paraḥ ||

English

Thus this vānaprastha71 āśrama72 exists for the purification of sin and is beneficial to oneself. After it73, the other and last is that of the mendicant.74

28.28

Sanskrit

चतुर्थस्य स्वरूपं तु श्रुयतामाश्रमस्य मे । यः स्वधर्मो ऽस्य धर्मज्ञैः प्रोक्तस्तात ! महात्मभिः ॥

caturthasya svarūpaṃ tu śruyatāmāśramasya me | yaḥ svadharmo 'sya dharmajñaiḥ proktastāta ! mahātmabhiḥ ||

English

Now hear from me the true nature of the fourth āśrama75, and the proper duty76 of this [order] that the great-souled knowers of dharma have declared, dear son.77

28.29

Sanskrit

सर्वसङ्गपरित्यागो ब्रह्मचर्यमकोपिता । यतेन्द्रियत्वमावासे नैकस्मिन् वसतिश्चिरम् ॥

sarvasaṅgaparityāgo brahmacaryamakopitā | yatendriyatvamāvāse naikasmin vasatiściram ||

English

28.29–30Renunciation of every attachment, celibacy (brahmacarya)78, freedom from anger, control of the senses, and not dwelling for long in any one dwelling; absence of undertakings79, and the taking of food that is received as alms, by means of one meal a day; the wish to know and understand the knowledge of the Self80, and likewise the contemplation of the Self.81

28.30

Sanskrit

अनारम्भस्तथाहारो भैक्षान्नेनैककालिना । आत्मज्ञानावबोधेच्छा तथा चात्मावलोकनम् ॥

anārambhastathāhāro bhaikṣānnenaikakālinā | ātmajñānāvabodhecchā tathā cātmāvalokanam ||

English

Its English is given with 28.29–30, above.

28.31

Sanskrit

चतुर्थे त्वाश्रमे धर्मो मयायं ते निवेदितः । सामान्यमन्यवर्णानामाश्रमाणाञ्च मे शृणु ॥

caturthe tvāśrame dharmo mayāyaṃ te niveditaḥ | sāmānyamanyavarṇānāmāśramāṇāñca me śṛṇu ||

English

This dharma of the fourth stage of life82 has been set out to you by me. Now hear from me what is common to the other classes83 and to the stages of life as well.84

28.32

Sanskrit

सत्यं शौचमहिंसा च अनसूया तथा क्षमा । आनृशंस्यमकार्पण्यं सन्तोषश्चाष्टमो गुणः ॥

satyaṃ śaucamahiṃsā ca anasūyā tathā kṣamā | ānṛśaṃsyamakārpaṇyaṃ santoṣaścāṣṭamo guṇaḥ ||

English

Truth, purity, non-violence, freedom from envy, forbearance, freedom from cruelty85, freedom from meanness86, and contentment as the eighth quality.

28.33

Sanskrit

एते संक्षेपतः प्रोक्ता धर्मा वर्णाश्रमेषु ते । एतेषु च स्वधर्मेषु स्वेषु तिष्ठेत् समन्ततः ॥

ete saṃkṣepataḥ proktā dharmā varṇāśrameṣu te | eteṣu ca svadharmeṣu sveṣu tiṣṭhet samantataḥ ||

English

These dharmas in the varṇas87 and āśramas88 have been told to you in brief. And one should stand firm in all respects in these, each in his own proper duties89.90

28.34

Sanskrit

यश्चोल्लङ्घ्य स्वकं धर्मं स्ववर्णाश्रमसंज्ञितम् । नरो ऽन्यथा प्रवर्तेत स दण्ड्यो भूभृतो भवेत् ॥

yaścollaṅghya svakaṃ dharmaṃ svavarṇāśramasaṃjñitam | naro 'nyathā pravarteta sa daṇḍyo bhūbhṛto bhavet ||

English

A man who transgresses his own dharma, which is designated by his own varṇa91 and āśrama92, and acts otherwise, is to be punished by the king93.94

28.35

Sanskrit

ये च स्वधर्मसन्त्यागात् पापं कुर्वन्ति मानवाः । उपेक्षतस्तान् नृपतेरिष्टापूर्तं प्रणश्यति ॥

ye ca svadharmasantyāgāt pāpaṃ kurvanti mānavāḥ | upekṣatastān nṛpateriṣṭāpūrtaṃ praṇaśyati ||

English

And as for those men who commit sin by abandoning their own dharma, the iṣṭāpūrta95 of the king who overlooks them is destroyed.96

28.36

Sanskrit

तस्माद्राज्ञा प्रयत्नेन सर्वे वर्णाः स्वधर्मतः । प्रवर्तन्तो ऽन्यथा दण्ड्याः स्थाप्याश्चैव स्वकर्मसु ॥

tasmādrājñā prayatnena sarve varṇāḥ svadharmataḥ | pravartanto 'nyathā daṇḍyāḥ sthāpyāścaiva svakarmasu ||

English

Therefore the king should take diligent care that all the varṇas97, if they act otherwise than according to their own dharma, are punished, and that they are established in their own duties.98

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे पुत्रानुशासने मदालसावाक्यं नामाष्टाविंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe putrānuśāsane madālasāvākyaṃ nāmāṣṭāviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, named "The Words of Madālasā," in the Instruction of the Son99, in the revered100 Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.101

  1. The reading: The 'verse' is only a chapter heading (aṣṭāviṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ, 'the twenty-eighth chapter'), not a verse of the text. It is rendered as a heading. The reference 114.1 belongs to the e-text's running numbering. ↩
  2. Alarka: A king of Kāśī, the son of Madālasā, who is instructed by his mother in this part of the Purāṇa. ↩
  3. duties of the social classes: varṇadharma: the duties of the four varṇas (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya and śūdra), the classes of Vedic society. ↩
  4. stages of life: āśrama: the four stages of life: student, householder, forest-dweller and renunciant. ↩
  5. The reading: The sentence is elliptical: 'dharmā ye cāśrameṣu ca' is rendered 'the duties that belong to the stages of life'. The verb 'papraccha' governs both accusatives, 'varṇadharmān' and the relative clause 'dharmā ye ... āśrameṣu'. Alarka's name is not spelled out in the verse apart from 'so 'larkaḥ', which I read as 'saḥ alarkaḥ'. ↩
  6. the government of a kingdom: Sanskrit rājyatantra: the machinery or administration of a kingdom. It refers to the royal duties Madālasā has just described. ↩
  7. varṇas: The four social classes: brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya and śūdra. ↩
  8. āśramas: The four stages of life: student (brahmacārin), householder, forest-dweller and renunciant. ↩
  9. The reading: The line has no word for 'which is' beside dharmam tam. I read varṇāśramātmakam as qualifying dharmam, 'having the varṇas and āśramas as its nature or basis', and supplied the second [dharma] to make the contrast with the royal dharma clear. The vocative mahābhāge is rendered 'O greatly fortunate lady' (glossary: mahābhāga). The e-text's 'rājyatantrāśritaḥ' is masculine nominative, agreeing with ayam (sc. dharmaḥ), but it is attached to dharmaṃ in sense; I took ayam as qualifying kathitaḥ in the Sanskrit's own construction. ↩
  10. distress: Sanskrit āpad: a time of calamity or necessity, when the normal rules of livelihood and conduct may be relaxed. The following verses go on to the brahmin's means of livelihood. ↩
  11. The reading: The second half (nānyaś caturtho dharmo 'sti; dharmas tasyāpadaṃ vinā) is terse. I take 'dharmas tasya' as 'this is his dharma', with 'apadaṃ vinā' meaning 'except in distress', and supply 'this' in brackets. It could also be read as 'there is no other, fourth dharma for him except in distress', with the exception attaching to the first clause. The sense is close in either reading. ↩
  12. Officiating at sacrifices: yājana is the performance of sacrifices for others as their priest. Together with teaching and the acceptance of gifts it makes up the brahmin's livelihood, as against the three duties of giving, study and sacrifice named in 28.3. ↩
  13. pure gifts: pūtapratigrahaḥ is a compound meaning acceptance of what is pure, that is, gifts received from a worthy giver and lawfully obtained. It could also be read as a pure act of accepting. ↩
  14. The reading: śuddhe is dual, agreeing with yājanādhyāpane. 'Pure' is not a separate item here; I take the two as the first and second means of livelihood. pūtapratigrahaḥ can mean 'acceptance of pure [gifts]' or 'pure acceptance'. I chose 'acceptance of pure gifts'. 'This [brahmin]' for asya is supplied from 28.3, where the brahmin is the subject. ↩
  15. kṣatriya: A member of the warrior and ruling class, the second of the four varṇas. ↩
  16. The reading: 1. dānam: I keep 'generosity', the glossary rendering, as the reviewer allows. 2. śastrājīvañca: I accept the reviewer's correction and read śastrājīvaṃ ca, 'and living by weapons' (the profession of arms), with ñ as a misprint or irregular spelling for the anusvāra. The compound is neuter, in apposition to rakṣā as a second item of the livelihood, and the translation is unchanged. 3. kṣite rakṣā: kṣite is an irregular form. I take it as the stem kṣiti, 'earth', shortened for the metre, so 'protection of the earth'. A possible alternative is 'protection of the injured' (kṣata), which echoes the traditional etymology of kṣatriya, but I prefer the first reading. ↩
  17. vaiśya: vaiśya: a member of the third of the four social classes (varṇa), traditionally merchants, herders and farmers. ↩
  18. The reading: saḥ ('that') refers back to the threefold dharma of the preceding verses; I rendered it as 'that dharma' to make the reference clear, supplying the noun from context. pāśupālya is literally 'herd-keeping, tending of animals'; I rendered it as 'tending of cattle', taking paśu in its common sense of livestock. ↩
  19. maintenance: poṣaṇa: maintaining or supporting others, such as dependents or livestock. The exact sense is not fixed here. ↩
  20. varṇas: The four social orders (brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra). Dharma tied to one's varṇa is the subject of 28.3–8. ↩
  21. āśramas: The stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant). The next section of the discourse treats the duties attached to them. ↩
  22. The reading: 1. The reviewer would take dvijātīnām tridhā mayā vyākhyātaḥ as 'the threefold dharma of the twice-born, as explained by me'. I keep my reading. The threefold set here is dāna, yajña and śuśrūṣā. The twice-born's own three duties were already given in 28.3, 5 and 6 as dāna, adhyayana and yajña, and śuśrūṣā is not among them. Also, vyākhyātaḥ is singular and agrees with śūdradharmaḥ, so tridhā belongs with the śūdra's dharma. Hence dvijātīnām goes with śuśrūṣā ('service of the twice-born'), and 28.8 (dvijātiśuśrūṣā) confirms that service is owed to the twice-born. 2. I have accepted the other findings: the threefold list now follows 'threefold' with a colon, 'now' is removed, 'craftsman's work' and 'likewise' are repositioned, and 'based on the āśramas' now matches the note. 3. poṣaṇa could mean maintaining dependents or rearing animals; I chose the general 'maintenance'. 4. 'his' is bracketed because jīvikā has no stated possessor but clearly belongs to the śūdra. ↩
  23. perfection: saṃsiddhi: complete accomplishment, perfection, success. ↩
  24. order: varṇa: one of the four orders of society (brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra), each with its own prescribed duties, as set out in the preceding verses. ↩
  25. The reading: 'na cyutaḥ' is taken as the nominative qualifier of naraḥ, 'one who has not fallen away [from it]', with na negating the participle and not prāpnoti. My earlier reading ('one who has fallen away does not attain') was wrong, since it would need na to stand before the verb. In the second half naraḥ is the implied subject of prayāti, so I supply '[a man]'. The text does not name the fallen man, and I do not add him. 'Saṃsiddhi' could also be 'success' or 'final accomplishment'; I chose 'perfection'. 'Pratiṣiddhaniṣevaṇāt' is an ablative of cause: 'through resorting to what is forbidden'. ↩
  26. upanayana: The rite of initiation, in which a boy of the upper three classes is invested with the sacred thread and taken to a teacher. It makes him 'twice-born' and begins his period of studentship. ↩
  27. whose actions, speech and eating are as he pleases: Rendering the compound kāmaceṣṭoktibhakṣya, with kāma ('as one wishes, at will') governing ceṣṭā (conduct), ukti (speech) and bhakṣya (food). Here kāma is the common word 'desire', not the god Kāma. ↩
  28. initiation: upanayana, the rite of investiture with the sacred thread, by which a boy of the three upper orders is made a student and a "twice-born". ↩
  29. brahmacārin: A student in the first stage of life (āśrama), living with his teacher in chastity and study; the stages of life are the subject of the verses that follow. ↩
  30. guru: The teacher who has performed the initiation and instructs the student in the Veda. This is the common noun, not the epithet Guru (Bṛhaspati). ↩
  31. The reading: The verse is addressed to Putraka (vocative in 28.10), but the vocative is not repeated here. In kathyate the verb is passive: "is being stated", with the speaker implied by me. The compound gurur gṛhe is read as guror gṛhe ("in the guru's house"), with the nominative gurur understood as a sandhi or printing variant of the genitive guroḥ, since a nominative cannot parse with gṛhe. A reading with the guru as the subject does not fit the syntax. ↩
  32. svādhyāya: The student's own daily recitation and study of the Veda, learned from the teacher and repeated by heart. ↩
  33. attendance on the fire: agniśuśrūṣā: the student's daily care of the sacred fire, tending it and feeding it with fuel morning and evening. ↩
  34. The reading: The verse has no finite verb. The list of duties continues the 'dharma' of the student announced in 28.11, and 'anujñātena' (instrumental, 'by one who has been permitted') has no stated verb. I supplied '[is to be eaten]' in brackets, which fits 'annam' and 'nivedya'. Here 'guru' is the common noun 'teacher', not the glossary's Guru (Bṛhaspati). ↩
  35. guru: Here the teacher in whose house the student lives (see 28.11), not Bṛhaspati, the divine Guru of the glossary. ↩
  36. The reading: The verse has no finite verb in its first half: sodyogaḥ and prītyupapādanam are nominal, and the subject is the brahmacārin of 28.11. I supplied 'is to be' and 'is to please' as the sense of an injunction. 'Guru' here is the human teacher, not the glossary's Guru (Bṛhaspati), so I use lower-case guru. tenāhūtaḥ: 'called by him' refers to the guru. ↩
  37. āśrama: One of the four stages of life: student (brahmacārin), householder (gṛhastha), forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and renunciant. ↩
  38. vānaprastha āśrama: The stage of the forest-dweller, in which a man withdraws to the forest after householder life. ↩
  39. the fourth: The text does not name it here; it is the stage of the renunciant (saṃnyāsa). ↩
  40. The reading: The Sanskrit has no verb for dakṣiṇāṃ; 'given' is supplied in brackets (vanditvā governs gurave, dakṣiṇām implies 'having offered'). In 28.15 'caturthaṃ ca icchayā ātmanaḥ' I read 'by his own wish' as governing all three choices, not only the fourth. ↩
  41. until the end of his life: Sanskrit niṣṭhā, literally 'attainment of the end'. Here it means the lifelong stay as a student, the naiṣṭhika life of the brahmacārin. It is not a fourth stage of life. ↩
  42. The reading: 1. Reading of 'tatsutaṃ vinā': I take 'tat' throughout as the teacher (guru). The sequence is: teacher; in his absence, his son (tatputre); his pupil (tacchiṣye), if there is no son of his (tatsutaṃ vinā). The reviewer's alternative, 'excluding the son's own son', has no basis, since 'tatsuta' simply repeats 'tatputra'. I therefore keep the three-step sequence, but I have dropped the draft's redundant doublet and render 'vinā' as 'failing'. 2. 'niṣṭhām avāpnuyāt': I accept the reviewer's point that 'final stage' could be mistaken for a fourth āśrama. I now render 'stay ... until the end of his life' and explain it in a note. 3. 'gurorabhāve': I accept the point and now use 'in the absence of the teacher', not 'no longer living'. 4. Locatives: I accept the point and render 'in the house of' the son and the pupil. The bracketed words are limited to what is needed for the English to parse. ↩
  43. brahmacārin: The celibate student who lives in the teacher's house studying the Veda. The verse names the stage as brahmacāryāśrama, the student's stage of life. ↩
  44. he should turn back: upāvṛttaḥ is a past participle, literally 'having turned back, returned'. It refers to the same student, who returns from the teacher's house. The translation renders it with a finite verb in English. ↩
  45. householder's stage: Gṛhastha-āśrama, the second of the four stages of life (āśrama): the life of the married man with a household. ↩
  46. The reading: The reading upāvṛttas tatas tasmāt (ablative 'from that') is unmetrical in places, but it is taken as 'from that stage'. Brahmacāryāśramam is accusative with vaset ('live in'), and I take it as a compound of brahmacārin and āśrama, 'the student's stage'. The verb 'turn back' is supplied from the participle upāvṛtta, treated as the main verb with an implied 'he should be'. I rendered it as a modal to parallel vaset. ↩
  47. householder's stage of life: gṛhastha-āśrama, the second of the four life-stages (āśrama): student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant. ↩
  48. in accordance with the rule: nyāyataḥ, 'according to rule or propriety', i.e. by one of the approved forms of marriage. ↩
  49. not of the same sage-lineage as his own: Sanskrit asamānarṣikulā: a wife whose family does not descend from the same ṛṣi (gotra/pravara) as the husband's. The rule forbids marriage within the same lineage. ↩
  50. The reading: tulyām ('equal') is left unspecified in the Sanskrit; it probably means equal in birth and class (varṇa) and in qualities. I kept the plain 'equal'. The ablative gṛhasthāśramakāraṇāt is rendered 'for the sake of', as a purpose clause. ↩
  51. his female relatives: jāmayaḥ: from jāmi, 'kinswoman', which can mean sisters, daughters-in-law or women of the family in general. The form is nominative plural, but the sense requires the accusative. ↩
  52. the fallen: patita: one who has fallen from caste or status through grave offence, an outcast. ↩
  53. birds and animals: vayāṃsi paśavaḥ stand in the nominative, but are to be taken as objects of the giving of food, like the earlier accusatives. This is the usual Purāṇic looseness. ↩
  54. The reading: jāmayaḥ and paśavaḥ are nominative forms where the syntax needs accusatives (jāmīḥ, paśūn). I took them as accusatives, as objects of poṣayet and of the giving of food, and treated the irregularity as metrical or Purāṇic usage. jāmayaḥ could in principle be a nominative, but no verb supports that. vayāṃsi is taken as 'birds' rather than 'ages'; the pairing with paśavaḥ makes this clear. svakarmaṇā could mean 'by his own work' or 'by the work proper to his own class'; I kept the plainer sense. ↩
  55. approaching [his wife] in her fertile season: ṛtau abhigama: marital intercourse restricted to the wife's fertile period after menstruation, a duty of the householder. ↩
  56. five yajñas: The pañcayajña, the five daily sacrifices of the householder: to the brahman (study of the Veda), to the ancestors, to the gods, to beings, and to guests (men). The Sanskrit does not list them here. ↩
  57. The reading: The Sanskrit has 'ṛtau abhigamaḥ' without naming the wife; 'his wife' is supplied in brackets from the context of 28.18. 'Tu' in 'vidhānantu' is merely emphatic and is left untranslated. ↩
  58. the remainder of what has been eaten: The compound bhuktaśeṣa, 'remainder of what has been eaten', governs the four groups named before it. The sense is that the householder eats only after these have been served. ↩
  59. The reading: bhuktaśeṣam is read as the object of bhuñjīta, 'let him eat the remainder'. The ancestors, gods, guests and kinsmen are taken as those for whom food is first set aside or served. Strictly the gods and ancestors receive offerings and do not eat, so bhukta is read loosely as 'what has been enjoyed or offered'. The adverbial phrase yathāvibhavam, 'according to his means', is taken with the whole act of eating. ↩
  60. stage of life: āśrama: one of the four stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer). The householder's stage (gṛhasthāśrama) has just been described. ↩
  61. forest-dweller: vānaprastha: one who has left household life to live in the forest, the third stage of life. ↩
  62. The reading: The verse is a closing and a transition. The imperative avadhāryatām is passive ("let it be grasped"), and I kept the passive form. The addressee is te, "to you", the same person as in the preceding verses. ↩
  63. the bowing: The pāda 'prājño cānatim' is metrically short and probably corrupt. Ānati means bowing, salutation or submission, and its sense and agent here are uncertain. See the doubts. ↩
  64. vānaprastha stage of life: The third of the four āśramas (stages of life): the forest-dweller, who leaves household life for a life of austerity in the forest. The verses that follow describe its observances. ↩
  65. The reading: The reviewer agrees that the crux is real and that the literal rendering should stand, so I keep the reading and make no change of substance. I have only removed the bracketed 'his' before 'offspring' in this version, since the Sanskrit does not require it. The pāda 'prājño cānatim' has five syllables where eight are expected, so a word may have dropped out. 'Prājño' before ca would normally be 'prājñaś'. I take it as prājñaḥ, nominative singular, 'the wise man'. For 'cānatim' I read ca + ānatim, 'and the bowing', which is the literal sense. Ānati means bowing or submission, and it is not attested for the bent posture of old age. The bowing may be the obeisance of the offspring, or the word may be corrupt. Manu 6.2 lists wrinkles and grey hair (valīpalita) along with the sight of one's children's children as the signs for entering the forest life. That suggests that a word for old age was lost or altered here. I do not emend on that model, because the printed text does not support it. ↩
  66. brahmacarya: Celibacy and continence; here the forest-dweller's chastity, not the student stage. ↩
  67. homa: Oblation poured into the consecrated fire. ↩
  68. the three pressings: triṣavaṇa: the three daily soma-pressing times (dawn, noon, evening), used for the three daily ablutions. ↩
  69. yoga: Discipline of body and mind aimed at concentration and liberation. ↩
  70. The reading: triṣavaṇasnānam is printed 'triṣavaṇastrānaṃ' (a misprint for snānam); I read 'bathing at the three pressings'. 'anukarṣaṇa' (drawing along, wasting) is taken as wearing down the body by austerities. 'vanyasnehaniṣevaṇam' read as use of forest oils (snehā), the other possible sense being affection for forest things; oils chosen as the usual ascetic practice of anointing. ↩
  71. vānaprastha: The forest-dweller, who withdraws to the forest after seeing the continuity of his line assured. The preceding verses describe his duties. ↩
  72. āśrama: A stage of life. The four are the student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the renouncer (bhikṣu, yati). ↩
  73. After it: tasmāt is ablative and can mean 'therefore' or 'after that'. Here it is read as 'after that', since the verse introduces the fourth and last stage, which the following verses describe. ↩
  74. The reading: tasmāt: 'therefore' or 'after that'. I chose 'after it' because the verse leads into the fourth stage. ātmanaḥ: taken with upakārakaḥ ('beneficial to oneself'), not with pāpa. ↩
  75. āśrama: One of the four orders or stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant). The fourth is that of the mendicant renunciant (bhikṣu, yati), mentioned in the previous verse. ↩
  76. proper duty: svadharma: the duty or conduct proper to this particular order. ↩
  77. The reading: The text of 28.28 has tāta with a stray space and exclamation mark; I read it as a vocative. The 'this' in 'this [order]' (asya) could refer to the fourth āśrama or to its follower, the renunciant; I took the order, which is the natural referent given caturthasyāśramasya. ↩
  78. celibacy (brahmacarya): brahmacarya: chastity, continence; also the name of the first life-stage, the student's. Here it is a discipline of the ascetic, the fourth stage described in 28.28. ↩
  79. absence of undertakings: anārambha: not beginning or undertaking enterprises, whether ritual or worldly, that bind a person to action and its fruits. ↩
  80. the Self: ātman: the Self, the inner real being, as distinct from body and mind. ↩
  81. The reading: In 28.29 'vasatiś ciram' could be read as 'he dwells long', with the negative 'na' going with 'ekasmin' (not long in one place). I took 'na ... ciram' together: he does not dwell for long in any one dwelling. Also 'akopitā' (here 'freedom from anger') is a noun in -tā from akopa; the form is slightly irregular but the sense is clear. 'Ekakālinā' I took as 'having one time [of eating] a day', i.e. one meal daily. ↩
  82. fourth stage of life: The āśrama is a stage of life. The fourth is that of the renunciant (bhikṣu, yati), which follows the student, householder and forest-dweller (vānaprastha). ↩
  83. other classes: anyavarṇānām may also be read as 'of the other classes' (i.e. all classes besides the one under discussion) or as 'of all the classes'. The sense here is the duties common to every class. ↩
  84. The reading: anyavarṇānām: 'of the other classes' or 'of all classes'; I chose 'other classes', following the literal sense of anya, and the sense of the passage is the same either way. The e-text reads sāmānyam as one word with anyavarṇānām; I take it as 'what is common' to the classes and stages, with ca linking āśramāṇām. ↩
  85. freedom from cruelty: Translates ānṛśaṃsya, literally the quality of not being cruel or harsh; also understood as kindness or compassion toward others. ↩
  86. freedom from meanness: Translates akārpaṇya, absence of miserliness or wretched pettiness, including not behaving abjectly. ↩
  87. varṇas: The four social classes: brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya and śūdra. ↩
  88. āśramas: The four stages of life: student (brahmacarya), householder, forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and renouncer (bhikṣu). ↩
  89. each in his own proper duties: svadharmeṣu sveṣu: the duties proper to one's own class and stage; the plural, with the locative eteṣu, distributes them to each person. ↩
  90. The reading: samantataḥ ('from all sides, in every way') is rendered 'in all respects'. The speaker's address to a single listener (te) is rendered 'to you'. tiṣṭhet is an optative with an indefinite subject, so 'one should stand'. ↩
  91. varṇa: One of the four social classes (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra). ↩
  92. āśrama: A stage of life: student (brahmacārin), householder, forest-dweller, renunciant. ↩
  93. is to be punished by the king: Literally 'he would be one to be punished by the earth-supporter (bhūbhṛt)'; bhūbhṛt is an epithet of the king, 'sustainer of the earth'. The verse is followed by the statement that the king must keep all classes to their duties. ↩
  94. The reading: svavarṇāśramasaṃjñitam could be taken as qualifying dharma ('called by the name of his own varṇa and āśrama', i.e. the duty defined by them), which I follow; the sense 'known as the dharma of his varṇa and āśrama' is the same. Reading anyathā pravarteta as 'acts otherwise [than his dharma]'. ↩
  95. iṣṭāpūrta: The merit of iṣṭa, Vedic sacrifice and offerings, together with pūrta, works of public piety such as digging wells and tanks, building temples and planting groves. ↩
  96. The reading: upekṣataḥ is a genitive singular present participle agreeing with nṛpateḥ ('of the king who overlooks'). tān is its object, referring to the men who abandon their own dharma. The verse has no adharma in the text, so the glossary entry for it is not used. The word 'sin' renders pāpa. ↩
  97. varṇas: The four social classes (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra), each with its own prescribed duties. ↩
  98. The reading: Syntax: 'pravartanto 'nyathā' (nominative plural participle) agrees with 'sarve varṇāḥ'; 'svadharmataḥ' is read as 'according to their own dharma' with 'anyathā' ('otherwise'), i.e. departing from it. 'svakarmasu' ('in their own duties') is taken with 'sthāpyāḥ'. The first 'daṇḍyāḥ' is conditional on the participle 'pravartantaḥ'. ↩
  99. Instruction of the Son: Putrānuśāsana, the section in which Madālasā instructs her son; here Alarka, as the next chapter's opening speaker suggests. ↩
  100. revered: Śrī is an honorific prefixed to the title of the work in the colophon. ↩
  101. The reading: The colophon does not name the son. Alarka is inferred from the next verse, 117.2, where he is the speaker, and is used only in the note. Śrī is rendered 'revered' as an honorific for the Purāṇa. ↩

Adhyāya 29

Sanskrit

ऊनत्रिंशो ऽध्यायः

ūnatriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Twenty-Nine1

Sanskrit

अलर्क उवाच

alarka uvāca

English

Alarka said:

29.1

Sanskrit

यत् कार्यं पुरुषाणाञ्च गार्हस्थ्यमनुवर्तताम् । बन्धश्च स्यादकरणे क्रियाया यस्य चोच्छ्रितिः ॥

yat kāryaṃ puruṣāṇāñca gārhasthyamanuvartatām | bandhaśca syādakaraṇe kriyāyā yasya cocchritiḥ ||

English

29.1–2Tell me, who am asking, exactly what is to be done by men who follow the householder's life2, what would be a bond if it were not done, and the action whose result is exaltation; what is for the benefit of men, what is to be avoided at home by a good man, and how that is done.3

29.2

Sanskrit

उपकाराय यन्नृणां यच्च वर्ज्यं गृहे सता । यथा च क्रियते तन्मे यथावत् पृच्छतो वद ॥

upakārāya yannṛṇāṃ yacca varjyaṃ gṛhe satā | yathā ca kriyate tanme yathāvat pṛcchato vada ||

English

Its English is given with 29.1–2, above.

Sanskrit

मदालसोवाच

madālasovāca

English

Madālasā said:

29.3

Sanskrit

वत्स ! गार्हस्थ्यमादाय नरः सर्वमिदं जगत् । पुष्णाति तेन लोकांश्च स जयत्यभिवाञ्छितान् ॥

vatsa ! gārhasthyamādāya naraḥ sarvamidaṃ jagat | puṣṇāti tena lokāṃśca sa jayatyabhivāñchitān ||

English

Madālasā said: "My child4, a man who has taken up the householder's life5 sustains this whole world by it, and he wins the worlds he desires."6

29.4

Sanskrit

पितरो मुनयो देवा भूतानि मनुजास्तथा । कृमिकीटपतङ्गाश्च वयांसि पशवो ऽसुराः ॥

pitaro munayo devā bhūtāni manujāstathā | kṛmikīṭapataṅgāśca vayāṃsi paśavo 'surāḥ ||

English

29.4–5The ancestors (pitṛs7), sages, gods, beings, and likewise human beings, worms, insects and moths, birds, animals, and asuras8 all live in dependence on the householder. From him they attain satisfaction. And they look to his face, [thinking]: "Will he not give something to us?9"10†

29.5

Sanskrit
