गृहस्थमुपजीवन्ति ततस्तृप्तिं प्रयान्ति च । मुखं चास्य निरीक्षन्ते अपि नो दास्यतीति वै ॥

gṛhasthamupajīvanti tatastṛptiṃ prayānti ca | mukhaṃ cāsya nirīkṣante api no dāsyatīti vai ||

English

Its English is given with 29.4–5, above.

29.6

Sanskrit

सर्वस्याधारभूतेयं वत्स ! धेनुस्त्रयीमयी । यस्यां प्रतिष्ठितं विश्वं विश्वहेतुश्च या मता ॥

sarvasyādhārabhūteyaṃ vatsa ! dhenustrayīmayī | yasyāṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ viśvaṃ viśvahetuśca yā matā ||

English

29.6–8This cow, my son, made of the three Vedas11, is the support of all; the universe is established in her, and she is held to be the cause of the universe. She has the Ṛc verses as her back, the Yajus formulas as her middle, and the Sāman chants as her mouth and neck; the iṣṭa and the pūrta12 are her horns, and the good hymns are the hair of her body. Śānti and puṣṭi13 are her dung and urine, and she stands established on the varṇas14 as her feet. Though the worlds live on her, she is imperishable and does not diminish.15†

ṛkpṛṣṭhāsau yajurmadhyā sāmavaktraśirodharā | iṣṭāpūrtaviṣāṇā ca sādhusūktatanūruhā ||

Its English is given with 29.6–8, above.

In this way, child, this cow made of the three Vedas26 nourishes [all].27

Sanskrit

Sanskrit

Sanskrit

29.34

Sanskrit

Having the ancestors in view89, he should feed brahmins, or even a single brahmin. Having taken out the first portion of the food90, he should present it to a brahmin.91

Sanskrit

Sanskrit

29.38–40One should feed the disabled, children and the aged, and likewise the sick; and [one should give] whatever food another destitute man, his self afflicted by hunger, desires. And in the evening, too, the rite103 must be performed, and there the guest brought by the sun104 [one should honour]105

English

Its English is given with 29.38–40, above.

29.44

Sanskrit

ता शृणुष्व महाभाग ! गृहस्थाश्रमसंस्थिताः । देवान् पितॄंश्चातिथींश्च तद्वत् सम्पूज्य बान्धवान् ॥

tā śṛṇuṣva mahābhāga ! gṛhasthāśramasaṃsthitāḥ | devān pitṝṃścātithīṃśca tadvat sampūjya bāndhavān ||

English

29.44–45Listen to those [verses], greatly fortunate one, about those established in the householder's stage of life110. Having duly worshipped the gods, the ancestors, the guests, and likewise the kinsmen, the women of the family111 and the preceptor, a householder, when he has means, should scatter [food] on the ground for dogs, for dog-cookers112 and for birds.113

29.45

Sanskrit

जामयश्च गुरुञ्चैव गृहस्थो विभवे सति । श्वभ्यश्च श्वपचेभ्यश्च वयोभ्यश्चावपेद् भुवि ॥

jāmayaśca guruñcaiva gṛhastho vibhave sati | śvabhyaśca śvapacebhyaśca vayobhyaścāvaped bhuvi ||

English

Its English is given with 29.44–45, above.

29.46

Sanskrit

वैश्वदेवं हि नामैतत् कुर्यात् सायं तथा दिने । मांसमन्नं तथा शाकं गृहे यच्चोपसाधितम् । न च तत् स्वयमश्नीयाद्विधिवद्यन्न निर्वपेत् ॥

vaiśvadevaṃ hi nāmaitat kuryāt sāyaṃ tathā dine | māṃsamannaṃ tathā śākaṃ gṛhe yaccopasādhitam | na ca tat svayamaśnīyādvidhivadyanna nirvapet ||

English

This indeed is called the vaiśvadeva114; one should perform it in the evening and likewise by day. Whatever is prepared in the house, whether meat115, cooked grain or vegetables, one should not eat that oneself if one has not offered it according to rule.116

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे मदालसोपदेशो नामोनत्रिंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe madālasopadeśo nāmonatriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter117, named "The Instruction of Madālasā," in the venerable118 Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.119

  1. The reading: The line is a chapter heading, not a verse: 'ūnatriṃśaḥ' is the ordinal 'twenty-ninth', and 'adhyāya' means 'chapter'. The sandhi form 'ūnatriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ' reads 'the twenty-ninth chapter'. The Sanskrit ūnatriṃśa (literally 'less by one than thirty') is rendered simply as 'twenty-ninth'. The number 117.1 is a GRETIL running count and does not match the chapter numbering (29). ↩
  2. householder's life: gārhasthya: the second stage of life (āśrama), the life of the married man who keeps a household and maintains the rites and duties tied to it. ↩
  3. The reading: bandha ("bond") in 'bandhaś ca syād akaraṇe' could mean bondage in the sense of sin or obligation incurred by omission. I kept the literal 'bond'. 'kriyāyā yasya ca ucchritiḥ' is literally 'and of which action there is elevation'. I took ucchriti as the exaltation (prosperity, merit) that results from the action, not as the elevation of the action itself. ↩
  4. My child: vatsa, literally 'calf', is an affectionate address to a son. Madālasā is answering Alarka's questions in 29.1–2. ↩
  5. householder's life: gārhasthya: the state of the householder (gṛhastha), the second of the four life-stages (āśrama), in which a man keeps a household, marries, and supports others. ↩
  6. The reading: The speaker's line 'madālasovāca' stands in the verse numbered 117.5 just before this verse, so it is placed here at the opening. The verse has two clauses (tena puṣṇāti, sa jayati); the second is a separate main clause. 'tena' is taken as 'by it', that is, by the householder's life. 'lokān' is taken as the object of jayati, qualified by abhivāñchitān ('desired'), though puṣṇāti could also take it: 'sustains the worlds, and he wins [what he desires]'. I chose the first reading, because abhivāñchitān agrees with lokān in the same clause as jayati, and the world (jagat) is already the object of puṣṇāti. ↩
  7. pitṛs: The deceased forefathers, who are nourished by offerings of water and rice-balls made by their descendants. ↩
  8. asuras: A class of powerful beings, often rivals of the gods (devas). ↩
  9. Will he not give something to us?: The Sanskrit is 'api no dāsyati iti': 'api' introduces a hopeful question, and 'iti' closes the thought. 'Vai' is only emphatic. ↩
  10. The reading: bhūtāni in 29.4 can mean 'beings' in general or 'spirits' (ghosts and the like). Since the list already names humans, worms and animals separately, 'spirits' may be meant, but I kept the wider 'beings'. vayāṃsi is 'birds'. ↩
  11. made of the three Vedas: Trayī, the triple Veda (Ṛg, Yajur and Sāma), here the substance of which the cow of the householder's duties is made. The cow stands for the whole system of Vedic rites that sustains the world. ↩
  12. iṣṭa and the pūrta: Iṣṭa is the Vedic sacrifice and its rites; pūrta is meritorious public work, such as digging wells and tanks, building temples and giving charity. Together they make up the householder's religious merit. ↩
  13. Śānti and puṣṭi: Śānti is the rite or act that brings peace and averts evil; puṣṭi is the rite or act that brings prosperity and growth. ↩
  14. varṇas: The four social orders (brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra), taken as the four feet of the cow. ↩
  15. The reading: sādhusūktatanūruhā: sādhusūkta can be read as "good (well-spoken) hymns" or as "hymns of the good (sādhu)". I took it as "good hymns". The compound ends in tanūruhā, "body hair". In 29.8 sākṣayā is sa + akṣayā, "imperishable", not a separate word sākṣa. The genitive jagatām with ājīvyamānā is read as the agent, "by the worlds". ↩
  16. svāhākāra: The utterance of svāhā, the exclamation with which an oblation is offered into the fire to the gods. ↩
  17. svadhākāra: The utterance of svadhā, the exclamation accompanying offerings to the ancestors (pitṛ). ↩
  18. vaṣaṭkāra: The utterance of vaṣaṭ, the call made by the hotṛ priest at the moment of offering in Vedic sacrifice. ↩
  19. hantakāra: The utterance of hanta, the word used when offering a gift or food to human beings. ↩
  20. her four udders: The cow is the threefold Veda (trayīmayī) of verse 29.6; the next verse assigns each udder to its drinkers: gods, ancestors, sages, and men. ↩
  21. The reading: The text prints tasyāḥstanacatuṣṭayam with a misplaced visarga-sandhi; I read tasyāḥ stanacatuṣṭayam, 'her group of four udders'. Putraka is a affectionate vocative ('my son'), rendered so. ↩
  22. svāhākāra: The exclamation svāhā, uttered when an oblation is poured into the fire for the gods. Here it is the first of the four teats of the cow of the sacrifice (see 29.9). ↩
  23. svadhā: The exclamation (svadhā) with which offerings are made to the ancestors (pitṛ). Here it is the second teat. ↩
  24. vaṣaṭkāra: The ritual cry vaṣaṭ, uttered at the moment of offering in Vedic sacrifice. Here it is the third teat. ↩
  25. hantakāra: The cry hanta, an expression of giving or offering. Here it is the fourth teat, associated with the gift of food to humans. ↩
  26. made of the three Vedas: trayīmayī: made of the trayī, the threefold Veda (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma), as set out in 29.7. ↩
  27. The reading: The compound devabhūtasuretarāḥ is ambiguous. It could mean (a) 'gods, beings, and those other than the gods'; (b) 'the divine beings and those other than the gods (asuras)', with sura repeating deva; or (c) 'the beings of the gods and of the non-gods'. I chose (b): the divine beings and the non-gods, who drink the vaṣaṭkāra teat with the sages. Devas have already been given the svāhākāra teat, so I do not take 'gods' as a separate member of the list. The compound has no case ending of its own, and I read it as the subject of the same verb 'drink' as the sages. ↩
  28. them: teṣām refers back to those who drink at the four teats of the cow in 29.9–11: the gods, the pitṛs, the sages and the other beings, and men. ↩
  29. Andhatāmisra: Andhatāmisra ("blind darkness") and Tāmisra ("darkness") are names of hells in the Purāṇic lists of narakas. ↩
  30. The reading: tamasi may be the locative of the common noun tamas, 'in darkness', serving as a general term. I read it as a third hell named Tamas, parallel to the two names that follow, since all three are in the locative with ca. Both readings give the same sense of a descent into darkness. ↩
  31. this cow: The cow is the Vedic triad (trayī) of the preceding verses, with her four udders: the offering-cries svāhā, svadhā, vaṣaṭ and hanta. To make her drink is to nourish the gods, ancestors, sages and others with these offerings. ↩
  32. the immortals and the others: amarādibhiḥ: the calves are the gods (the immortals) and the other classes of beings named in verses 29.10-11, namely the ancestors, the sages and human beings. ↩
  33. The reading: upapadyate with the dative svargāya is read as 'is reborn for heaven', that is, becomes fit for or attains heaven. Another reading is 'is fitted for heaven'. Svairvatsaiḥ is taken as the instrument, 'through her own calves', in apposition with amarādibhiḥ. ↩
  34. the gods, the sages, the ancestors, human beings: The compound devarṣipitṛmānavāḥ can be read as 'gods, sages, ancestors and men', as here, or 'divine sages, ancestors and men'. The following verse (29.15) lists devas, ṛṣis and pitṛs separately, which supports the first reading. ↩
  35. The reading: devarṣi- may be a single word, 'divine sage' (like Nārada), or two words, 'gods and sages'. I chose the second, because verse 29.15 speaks of offerings to gods, sages and ancestors (devarṣipitṛtarpaṇa). The bracketed 'other' is implied by the contrast of bhūtāni with the preceding groups. ↩
  36. tarpaṇa: The rite of satisfying divine beings and the dead with offerings of water (with sesame for the ancestors). ↩
  37. Prajāpati: 'Lord of creatures', the creator deity. He is a single further recipient of the rite. ↩
  38. with water: The text reads ādibhaḥ, which I emend to adbhiḥ, the instrumental plural of ap, 'water'. The metre and the sense of tarpaṇa both support the emendation. ↩
  39. The reading: (1) 'strātaḥ' is a misprint for 'snātaḥ' ('bathed'), and I have translated it so. (2) 'ādibhaḥ' is corrupt: the form is not a correct instrumental, and the pāda has nine syllables where eight are required. I accept the reading 'prajāpates tathaivādbhiḥ', which restores the metre and the meaning. This replaces my earlier conjecture 'and the others', which had no support. Prajāpati therefore stands alone as the further recipient, and 'with water' is the means of the rite. (3) 'prajāpateḥ' is read as a genitive dependent on 'tarpaṇam', parallel to the compound 'devarṣipitṛ-'. (4) 'devarṣi-' is taken as 'gods and sages' in a dvandva, since the preceding verse lists the gods, sages and ancestors separately. 'Divine sages' is possible but less likely. ↩
  40. flowers, perfumes and blossoms: The compound sumanogandhapuṣpaiḥ is read as a list of three: sumanas 'flowers' (also 'jasmine'), gandha 'perfumes', puṣpa 'blossoms'. ↩
  41. tarpaṇa: tarpaṇa is an offering meant to satisfy or gratify a deity or ancestor, here with an oblation to Agni. The same word is used for the offerings to gods, sages and ancestors in 29.15. ↩
  42. bali: bali is a food offering set out for deities, spirits and beings, distinct from the oblation poured into the fire. The next verses name the recipients and the quarters. ↩
  43. The reading: sumanogandhapuṣpaiḥ: (a) a three-member list, 'flowers, perfumes, blossoms'; (b) a single phrase, 'with fragrant jasmine and other flowers', or 'fragrant flowers'. I chose (a). The reviewer is right that the draft was incoherent in treating gandha as an adjective and making sumanas 'jasmine' while also splitting the compound in three. The revision takes sumanas in its usual sense 'flowers' (jasmine is secondary) and gandha as a noun, 'perfumes'. The overlap between sumanas and puṣpa is not unusual in such lists. Reading (b) remains possible. The reviewer's point about 'likewise' for tathā is accepted. I kept 'are to be given' for the gerundive deyāḥ. ↩
  44. bali: An offering of food (usually cooked rice) set out or thrown down for gods, spirits and creatures, part of the daily household rites. ↩
  45. Viśvedevas: A group of deities, 'All-gods', regularly given a share in domestic offerings and in the offerings to the ancestors. ↩
  46. Dhanvantari: The physician of the gods, who rose from the churning of the ocean. ↩
  47. in the north-east: prāgudīcyām, a compound of east and north, is the intermediate quarter between them, the north-east (aiśānī). ↩
  48. The reading: The Sanskrit has no explicit verb for the first two datives; kṣipet governs the whole verse and baliṃ is shared. 'Brahmaṇe' is taken as dative of Brahmā (the creator). The particle 'tu' is left untranslated. 'Samuddiśya' is rendered 'dedicating it to', governing Dhanvantari. ↩
  49. bali: A food offering set out for gods, spirits and beings, not poured into a fire; one of the daily household offerings. ↩
  50. Yama: God of the dead, lord of the southern quarter. ↩
  51. Soma: The moon-god, here guardian of the north. ↩
  52. The reading: yāmyāyām (south, 'the quarter of Yama') is taken as the direction, with prācyām, pratīcyām and uttarataḥ as the other directions. The verb āharet is used with the first bali and is understood for the later ones; 'should offer' is supplied in each clause. Śakra is given in the dative, 'to Śakra'. No reading is in doubt. ↩
  53. offering: bali: the food-offering set out for gods, spirits and beings, part of the daily household rites. ↩
  54. Dhātṛ: Dhātṛ, 'the Establisher', is a divine figure often named with Vidhātṛ; here both receive the bali at the door. ↩
  55. Aryaman: Aryaman is one of the Ādityas, a god associated with hospitality and ancestors; here he receives the offering outside the house. ↩
  56. The reading: gṛhebhyaḥ (dative plural, 'to the houses') is odd as a recipient. It may mean the deities of the houses, or the offering is meant for the dwellings. I kept the literal reading. The text may be corrupt. ↩
  57. from the sky: Sanskrit ākāśataḥ: the offering is cast up into the open air, not placed on the ground. ↩
  58. set out: Sanskrit nirvapet is the verb used for ritual offerings to the ancestors, here understood as an offering of food, as in the śrāddha context. The object is not stated in the verse. ↩
  59. The reading: Object of nirvapet is not stated; I supply "[an offering]" from balim in the first half. Nirvapet could also be read as 'should pour out', which is a possible alternative for the libation. Pitṝṇām is read as a dative-sense genitive ('for the ancestors'). ↩
  60. rinsing of the mouth: ācamana: the ritual sipping or rinsing with water, done for purification. Here the water is poured out at the places of the offerings for the deities' ācamana. ↩
  61. bali: An offering of food or grain set out for deities, spirits and beings as part of the daily household rites. The preceding verses name the recipients and the directions. ↩
  62. the master of the house: The text reads hṛhapatiḥ, an evident misprint for gṛhapatiḥ. The word is a second designation of the same person as the householder (gṛhastha) of 29.21. ↩
  63. The reading: hṛhapatiḥ in 29.22 is read as gṛhapatiḥ, a misprint of the e-text. tatparaḥ could mean 'intent on that' (the rite) or 'devoted to them' (the deities); I took the rite. The Sanskrit does not say whose rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) is meant; it is presumably that of the deities, but I left it unstated. ↩
  64. release [of food]: utsarga: a giving up or letting go; here the setting aside of food for beings, after the bali offerings, without a named recipient. ↩
  65. dog-cookers: śvapaca: literally 'dog-cooker', a member of a very low, outcaste group; here the householder's offering reaches even those excluded from ordinary society. ↩
  66. The reading: utsarga: 'release', 'gift' or 'discharge'; I take it as the setting aside of food for beings, with the object 'food' implied from the context and the following avāpet. kuryāt and avapet are both optative, 'should'; the subject, the householder (gṛhapati) of the preceding verse, is carried on. ↩
  67. vaiśvadeva: The daily householder's offering of food to the Viśvedevas, the "All-gods". Here it is taken to be the offerings described in the preceding verses. ↩
  68. The reading: (1) The reference 118.7 does not fit chapter 29, and the line is not among 29.18–25. It may be a numbering artifact of the e-text, or the line may belong to another passage; I translated it as given. (2) I accept the reviewer's points on the participle. udāhṛtam is now a single sense, "declared", and it is no longer split into "called" and "prescribed". "Prescribed" is removed because the Sanskrit does not say it. (3) nāma is kept as the word for the name, "named", and hi as "indeed". The phrase vaiśvadevaṃ nāma etat can also be read idiomatically as "this is what is called vaiśvadeva", with nāma as a particle meaning "by name"; the two readings give the same sense, and I chose the one closer to the words. (4) The earlier bracketed "rite" is dropped, since etat is neuter and agrees with vaiśvadevam, so no supplied word is needed. (5) I accepted the correction on the note and removed "household fire", which the context does not support. I kept the gloss "Viśvedevas" because it explains ↩
  69. sipped water: ācamana, the ritual sipping of water for purification, done before and after rites and meals. ↩
  70. look out toward the door: dvārāvalokana: the look toward the door is made to see whether a guest is arriving; the next verse says he should wait for an eighth part of a muhūrta. ↩
  71. The reading: The subject of kuryāt is not named; 'prājñaḥ' (the wise man) is the householder (gṛhastha) of the preceding verses, so 'householder' is supplied in brackets. 'ca' is rendered with 'And'. ↩
  72. muhūrta: A division of time, one thirtieth of a day, about forty-eight minutes. An eighth part of it is about six minutes. ↩
  73. The reading: udīkṣyo 'pi atithir bhavet: udīkṣyaḥ is a gerundive ("to be looked for, waited for"), so I took atithiḥ as its subject, with bhavet as "may become" and api as "even". The alternative is that the householder, as an unexpressed subject, should look out for a guest for an eighth of a muhūrta; the sense is much the same. The accusative muhūrtasyāṣṭamaṃ bhāgam is read as expressing duration. ↩
  74. guest: atithi, a guest. The following verse (29.29) gives the traditional etymology: one who stays for no fixed time. ↩
  75. gotra: gotra: the patrilineal clan or lineage, traced to a Vedic seer, which fixes a brahmin's ancestry. ↩
  76. caraṇa: caraṇa: the Vedic school or branch to which a brahmin belongs through the recension of the Veda he learns. ↩
  77. The reading: tatkālasamupasthitam: 'arrived at that very time' (the time of the meal, or the time the offerings were just made) is the literal sense. I kept it as stated, without adding 'mealtime', since the Sanskrit does not say so. āgatam after bubhukṣum is a separate word, 'come', and is not redundant if it means 'come from elsewhere'. I rendered it 'come from afar', which slightly extends the Sanskrit. ↩
  78. Prajāpati: 'Lord of creatures', the creator god. The guest is to be honoured as the creator himself, whatever his looks. ↩
  79. atithi: 'Guest'. The verse explains the word by a popular etymology: a-tithi, one whose stay is not governed by a fixed lunar day (tithi), or who stays for an uncertain time (anityam). ↩
  80. The reading: anityam sthitaḥ: taken as 'staying for an uncertain or no fixed time', the etymological explanation of atithi (a-tithi). Alternative: 'being impermanent'. I chose the former because it suits the etymology. The subject 'he' is the brahmin guest of the preceding verse, supplied from taṃ. ↩
  81. the householder: gṛhāśramin, one who is in the householder's stage of life (āśrama), the second of the four stages. ↩
  82. the sacrifice to men: nṛyajña, the sacrifice to men, is the duty of hospitality to guests, one of the five daily great sacrifices of the householder. Failure to perform it leaves a debt (ṛṇa). ↩
  83. The reading: The word 'adattvā' has no stated object; I supply 'to the guest' in brackets from the context of the preceding verses. 'Kilviṣabhuk' is taken as 'eater of sin', a compound of kilviṣa and bhuj. Verse 31 confirms this reading with 'pāpaṃ kevalaṃ bhuṅkte'. ↩
  84. he eats filth: The man who eats without giving to the guest is said to be reborn eating excrement (purīṣa); the verse continues the preceding statement about one who eats without giving (29.30). ↩
  85. The reading: The verse is a single sentence whose relative clause (atithir yasya ... pratinivartate) is placed after the main clause. I put 'sa' as 'he' and the relative as 'the man from whose house', with the subject being the same householder. 'Kevalam' is taken as 'only' qualifying pāpam (sin and nothing else), not as an adverb of bhuṅkte. ↩
  86. his own evil deed: duṣkṛta means a bad deed and the guilt arising from it. The guest, turned away, passes his guilt to the host and takes the host's merit in exchange. ↩
  87. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the deceased ancestors (pitṛ). Here it is enjoined as a daily observance. ↩
  88. The reading: In 29.32a 'sa' could refer to the host of 29.31 or to the guest (atithi). I took it as the guest, because 'tasmai' (to him) then refers to the host, and 'gacchati' (departs) suits a guest who leaves. In 29.32cd the second 'sa' (svayam) is the householder. 'Yad vā' is read as 'or with whatever'. 'Annādya' is taken simply as 'food'. ↩
  89. Having the ancestors in view: The absolutive uddiśya means 'designating' or 'intending'; the feeding is done for the ancestors (the pitṛ), as in a śrāddha. ↩
  90. the first portion of the food: agra: the first portion set aside from the cooked food before the meal; verse 29.35 defines it as four mouthfuls. ↩
  91. The reading: Verse 29.34 has viprāṃśca ... viprameva vā: 'brahmins, or even a single brahmin'. The verse says nothing about the number of brahmins in the first alternative; I take it as plural, with vā offering the smaller option. The word tat in taduddhṛtya is taken as 'that [food]' and left untranslated, since annasya already gives the object. Both brāhmaṇa and vipra are rendered 'brahmin', following the glossary. ↩
  92. wandering ascetics: Sanskrit parivrāj, a renunciant who has left home and wanders; the fourth stage of life. ↩
  93. brahmacārins: Students of the Veda who live in celibate discipline, here as mendicants. ↩
  94. agra: The 'first portion' of food set aside and offered to a brahmin, as in the preceding verse; it is defined here as four mouthfuls (grāsa). The following verse gives it a fourfold measure again. ↩
  95. The reading: The verb dadyāt is singular, with the subject carried over from the previous verses (the householder). In the verse, 'agraṃ grāsacatuṣṭayam' is read as 'an agra should be a set of four mouthfuls'; the verse supplies 'syāt' only once, and I have repeated it for the second clause. 'Parivrāḍbrahmacāriṇām' is taken as a dvandva compound, 'of wandering ascetics and brahmacārins', in the genitive plural agreeing with yācatām. ↩
  96. hantakāra: A portion of food offered to a brahmin with the invitation hanta, 'here, take this'. By the measure given here it is four times the agra, hence sixteen mouthfuls. ↩
  97. agra: The 'first portion' of food, set aside for a guest or brahmin. According to the preceding verse it equals four mouthfuls. ↩
  98. bhikṣā: Alms; according to verse 29.35, a single mouthful (grāsa). ↩
  99. The reading: The syntax of the first half is compact: agraṃ caturguṇam ... hantakāram. I take hantakāra as the predicate ('they call the agra fourfold hantakāra'), which gives hantakāra = 4 × agra. In the second half, bhojanaṃ hantakāraṃ vā ... agraṃ bhikṣām athāpi vā is elliptical, with no verb. I supply '[One may give]' and read the three as alternative forms of giving. Another reading takes bhojanaṃ as a full meal equal to the hantakāra. ↩
  100. the dear ones: iṣṭān is taken as a separate class, 'those held dear'. It could also qualify the guests ('welcome guests'), but the series of accusatives favours a separate class. ↩
  101. kinsmen, relatives: jñāti denotes kin of the same family or lineage, bandhu more broadly relatives by blood or marriage. ↩
  102. The reading: iṣṭān: 'dear ones' as a separate class (chosen), or an adjective of atithīn ('welcome guests'). Since jñātīn, bandhūn and arthinaḥ are listed separately, a separate class seems more natural. 'Giving' (adattvā) has no stated object; it is understood from the preceding verses (food to guests, ascetics and others), and I have left it without one. ↩
  103. the rite: vidhi here is the prescribed procedure, the evening hospitality, and not 'destiny' as elsewhere. ↩
  104. the guest brought by the sun: sūryoḍha, literally 'carried by the sun': a guest who arrives at sunset, when he can find no other lodging. The verb governing him, 'should honour', is in 29.41. ↩
  105. The reading: (1) 'sīdatā yad kṛtaṃ tena': 'yad' before 'kṛtam' is a hiatus or misprint for 'yat'. I did not take 'tena' as 'on that account', as the reviewer suggests. It agrees with 'sīdatā': 'by him, being in distress'. The sin is what the distressed relative did in his need, and 'sa' is the householder who did not feed him and so incurs it. 'Tena' is therefore rendered once, as 'by him'. (2) In 29.38 I took 'yat' with 'annam' as the object of 'vāñchate' ('desires'), as the reviewer says. The bracketed '[one should give]' is needed because the Sanskrit does not give a verb for this object. 'Bhojayet' could also govern it ('feed with whatever food ...'), which would give a similar sense. (3) In 29.39 'yaḥ' is a plain relative whose antecedent is the implied subject of 'bhojanīyaḥ', 'the relative'. Both 'jñāti' are translated 'relative'. (4) 'Vidhi' is glossed 'destiny', but here it means a prescribed rite, so I render it 'the rite'. (5) 'Sāyaṃ caiva': 'eva' is rendered as 'too', since 'ca eva' her ↩
  106. the Creator: Vidhātā, 'the Ordainer, Disposer', is a name of Brahmā, the creator god. It is related to vidhi, 'destiny'. ↩
  107. Atri: Atri is one of the ancient seers, a mind-born son of Brahmā and a speaker of Vedic hymns. ↩
  108. verses: Gāthā: a stanza or verse, here one sung by a sage, which the next verses give. ↩
  109. The reading: (1) pūjayīta has no object in the verse. I take it as the guest (atithi) of 29.40, who arrives at sunset, and mark him in brackets. (2) 'uddavahataḥ' looks like a misprint or a metrical doubling of 'udvahataḥ', the genitive of the participle 'carrying'. I translated it as that. (3) Verse 42 has no finite verb. I took 'śreyo 'bhivarṣiṇaḥ' ('showering down good') as the predicate of the gods, ancestors and the rest, and 'tṛptāḥ' in 29.43 as the predicate for the animals and insects, supplying 'are'. ↩
  110. the householder's stage of life: gṛhasthāśrama: the second of the four stages of life (āśrama), in which a man marries, keeps a household and supports others. ↩
  111. the women of the family: jāmayaḥ: plural of jāmi, women of one's own family, such as sisters and daughters-in-law. The sense is not exact. ↩
  112. dog-cookers: śvapaca: 'dog-cooker', a name for people outside the caste order who were held to be lowly. ↩
  113. The reading: 1) tā: read as tāḥ with the visarga lost, i.e. feminine plural 'those [gāthās]', the verses of 29.43. gṛhasthāśramasaṃsthitāḥ is feminine plural and I take it to qualify those verses (verses about those in the householder's stage). It could instead be a masculine plural meaning 'householders established in the stage', agreeing with the subject of sampūjya, but the singular gṛhasthaḥ in 29.45 makes that less likely. 2) guruṃ: 'preceptor' or 'elder'. I chose 'preceptor'. 3) jāmayaḥ: taken as accusative plural, a further object of sampūjya. 4) avaped has no stated object; '[food]' is supplied, as 29.46 confirms. ↩
  114. vaiśvadeva: The daily household offering made to the Viśvedevas, the "All-gods", from the food prepared for the meal, before the householder eats. The text here defines it by the offering of food to beings, as in the preceding verse. ↩
  115. meat: māṃsa, "meat", is read as it stands in the e-text. Some readers take it as a general term for edible flesh or pulp, but no variant is given here. ↩
  116. The reading: nirvapet: "offer, distribute". The verb is used for offering to gods, ancestors and beings, and I take it so. The verse's first half is also loosely connected to the preceding one; I take "this" (etat) as pointing back to the offerings described in 29.45. The e-text's reading hi nāmaitat is kept. ↩
  117. twenty-ninth chapter: The compound is read as ekonatriṃśa, 'twenty-ninth' (literally 'one less than thirty'); the text has onatriṃśa, which is a variant of ekonatriṃśa. ↩
  118. venerable: śrī- is an honorific prefix in the colophon, attached to the title of the work. ↩
  119. The reading: The colophon reads onatriṃśa for the usual ekonatriṃśa. I take it as 'twenty-ninth' (one less than thirty), which also suits the next chapter, called triṃśa, 'thirtieth'. The verse number 119.11 is a GRETIL running count, and the colophon is not a verse proper. ↩

Adhyāya 30

Sanskrit

त्रिंशो ऽध्यायः

triṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Thirty1.

Sanskrit

मदालसोवाच

madālasovāca

English

30.1Madālasā said: "Listen, my son, to the duty of a householder: the regular2 [duty], the occasional3, and likewise the regular-occasional4."

30.1

Sanskrit

नित्यं नैमित्तकञ्चैव नित्यनैमित्तिकं तथा । गृहस्थस्य तु यत् कर्म तन्निशामय पुत्रक ! ॥

nityaṃ naimittakañcaiva nityanaimittikaṃ tathā | gṛhasthasya tu yat karma tanniśāmaya putraka ! ||

English

Its English is given with 30.1, above.

30.2

Sanskrit

पञ्चयज्ञाश्रितं नित्यं यदेतत् कथितं तव । नैमित्तिकं तथैवान्यत् पुत्रजन्मक्रियादिकम् ॥

pañcayajñāśritaṃ nityaṃ yadetat kathitaṃ tava | naimittikaṃ tathaivānyat putrajanmakriyādikam ||

English

The regular rite5 that has been described to you rests on the five yajñas6. The occasional rite7 is another kind, beginning with the rites at the birth of a son.8

30.3

Sanskrit

नित्यनैमित्तिकं ज्ञेयं पर्वश्राद्धादि पण्डितैः । तत्र नैमित्तिकं वक्ष्ये श्राद्धमभ्युदयं तव ॥

nityanaimittikaṃ jñeyaṃ parvaśrāddhādi paṇḍitaiḥ | tatra naimittikaṃ vakṣye śrāddhamabhyudayaṃ tava ||

English

The learned should know that the nityanaimittika9 rite is that which begins with the śrāddha10 of the parvan days11. Of these, I shall now tell you of the occasional rite, the śrāddha for prosperity (abhyudaya12).13†

30.4

Sanskrit

पुत्रजन्मनि यत्कार्यं जातकर्मसमं नरैः । विवाहादौ च कर्तव्यं सर्वं सम्यक् क्रिमोदितम् ॥

putrajanmani yatkāryaṃ jātakarmasamaṃ naraiḥ | vivāhādau ca kartavyaṃ sarvaṃ samyak krimoditam ||

English

What men must do on the birth of a son, which is the same as the jātakarma14, and what must be done at a wedding and the other [occasions] that follow it: all of this has been properly stated in due order15.16

30.5

Sanskrit

पितरश्चात्र सम्पूज्याः ख्याता नान्दीमुखास्तु ये । पिण्डांश्च दधिसंमिश्रान् दद्याद् यवसमन्वितान् ॥

pitaraścātra sampūjyāḥ khyātā nāndīmukhāstu ye | piṇḍāṃśca dadhisaṃmiśrān dadyād yavasamanvitān ||

English

And here17 the ancestors who are renowned as Nāndīmukhas18 are to be duly honoured; and one should offer piṇḍas19 mixed with curds and accompanied by barley.20

30.6

Sanskrit

उदङ्मुखः प्राङ्मुखो वा यजमानः समाहितः । वैश्वदेवविहीनं तत् केचिदिच्छन्ति मानवाः ॥

udaṅmukhaḥ prāṅmukho vā yajamānaḥ samāhitaḥ | vaiśvadevavihīnaṃ tat kecidicchanti mānavāḥ ||

English

30.6The sacrificer, attentive, [is to be] facing north or facing east; some men want that [rite]21 to be without the Vaiśvadeva22; and here the brahmins are to be engaged in even numbers, and they are to be honoured keeping them to the right23.24

Sanskrit

युग्माश्चात्र द्विजाः कार्यास्ते च पूज्याः प्रदक्षिणम् ।

yugmāścātra dvijāḥ kāryāste ca pūjyāḥ pradakṣiṇam |

English

Its English is given with 30.6, above.

30.7

Sanskrit

एतन्नैमित्तिकं वृद्धौ तथान्यच्चौर्ध्वदेहिकम् ॥

etannaimittikaṃ vṛddhau tathānyaccaurdhvadehikam ||

English

This is the occasional rite (naimittika)25 at a time of increase26; and there is another, the one belonging to the funeral rites for the departed27.28

30.8

Sanskrit

मृताहनि च कर्तव्यमेकोद्दिष्टं शृणुष्व तत् । दैवहीनं तथा कार्यं तथैवैकपवित्रकम् ॥

mṛtāhani ca kartavyamekoddiṣṭaṃ śṛṇuṣva tat | daivahīnaṃ tathā kāryaṃ tathaivaikapavitrakam ||

English

And on the day of a death the ekoddiṣṭa29 is to be performed; listen to that. It is to be done without the gods30, and likewise with a single pavitra31.32

30.9

Sanskrit

आवाहनं न कर्तव्यमग्नौकरणवर्जितम् । प्रेतस्य पिण्डमेकञ्च दद्यादुच्छिष्टसन्निधौ ॥

āvāhanaṃ na kartavyamagnaukaraṇavarjitam | pretasya piṇḍamekañca dadyāducchiṣṭasannidhau ||

English

No invocation is to be made, [the rite being] devoid of the agnaukaraṇa33. One should give a single rice-ball34 for the dead man, near the leavings of the meal35.36

30.10

Sanskrit

तिलोदकं चापसव्यं तन्नामस्मरणान्वितम् । अक्षय्यममुकस्येति स्थाने विप्रविसर्जने ॥

tilodakaṃ cāpasavyaṃ tannāmasmaraṇānvitam | akṣayyamamukasyeti sthāne vipravisarjane ||

English

30.10–11Sesame-water [should be offered] in the apasavya37 manner, accompanied by recollection of his name; and "[May this be] inexhaustible for so-and-so"38 [should be said] in place of [the usual formula] at the dismissal of the brahmins. One should say, "Rest content,"39 and they should answer, "We are indeed content." This should be done by men every month, up to the year.40

30.11

Sanskrit

अभिरण्यतामिति ब्रूयाद् ब्रूयुस्ते ऽभिरताः स्म ह । प्रतिमासं भवेदेतत् कार्यमा वत्सरं नरैः ॥

abhiraṇyatāmiti brūyād brūyuste 'bhiratāḥ sma ha | pratimāsaṃ bhavedetat kāryamā vatsaraṃ naraiḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 30.10–11, above.

30.12

Sanskrit

अथ संवत्सरे पूर्णे यदा वा क्रियते नरैः । सपिण्डीकरणं कार्यं तस्यापि विधिरुच्यते ॥

atha saṃvatsare pūrṇe yadā vā kriyate naraiḥ | sapiṇḍīkaraṇaṃ kāryaṃ tasyāpi vidhirucyate ||

English

Then, when the year is complete, or whenever it is performed by men, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa41 is to be done; the rule for that too is now stated.42

30.13

Sanskrit

तच्चापि दैवरहितमेकार्घ्यैकपवित्रकम् । नैवाग्नौकरणं तत्र तच्चावाहनवर्जितम् ॥

taccāpi daivarahitamekārghyaikapavitrakam | naivāgnaukaraṇaṃ tatra taccāvāhanavarjitam ||

English

That [rite] too is to be done without the deva offerings43, with a single arghya44 water-vessel and a single pavitraka45. In it there is no agnaukaraṇa46 at all, and it too is without the invocation.47

30.14

Sanskrit

अपसव्यञ्च तत्रापि भोजयेदयुजो द्विजान् । विशेषस्तत्र चान्यो ऽस्ति प्रतिमासं क्रियाधिकः ॥

apasavyañca tatrāpi bhojayedayujo dvijān | viśeṣastatra cānyo 'sti pratimāsaṃ kriyādhikaḥ ||

English

In that rite too he should perform the offering with the sacred thread over the right shoulder48, and he should feed brahmins of uneven number49. There is, moreover, another special rule there, which exceeds the monthly rite in its procedure50.51

30.15

Sanskrit

तं कथ्यमानमेकाग्रो वदन्त्या मे निशामय । तिलगन्धोदकैर्युक्तं तत्र पात्रचतुष्टयम् ॥

taṃ kathyamānamekāgro vadantyā me niśāmaya | tilagandhodakairyuktaṃ tatra pātracatuṣṭayam ||

English

Listen with one-pointed attention to that52, as it is being told by me while I speak: there, a set of four vessels53 furnished with sesame, perfume and water54

30.16

Sanskrit

कुर्यात् पितॄणां त्रितयमेकं प्रेतस्य पुत्रक । पात्रत्रये प्रेतपात्रमर्घ्यञ्चैव प्रसेचयेत् ॥

kuryāt pitṝṇāṃ tritayamekaṃ pretasya putraka | pātratraye pretapātramarghyañcaiva prasecayet ||

English

One should make a set of three [vessels] for the fathers and one for the dead man55, my son56. Into the three [fathers'] vessels one should pour [the contents of] the dead man's vessel and also the arghya57.58

30.17

Sanskrit

ये समाना इति जपन् पूर्ववच्छेषमाचरेत् । स्त्रीणामप्येवमेवैतदेकीद्दिष्टमुदाहृतम् ॥

ye samānā iti japan pūrvavaccheṣamācaret | strīṇāmapyevamevaitadekīddiṣṭamudāhṛtam ||

English

Muttering "ye samānāḥ59," he should perform the rest as before. This same ekoddiṣṭa60 rite is declared for women also in just this way.61

30.18

Sanskrit

सपिण्डीकरणं तासां पुत्राभावे न विद्यते । प्रतिसंवत्सरं कार्यमेकोद्दिष्टं नरैः स्त्रियाः ॥

sapiṇḍīkaraṇaṃ tāsāṃ putrābhāve na vidyate | pratisaṃvatsaraṃ kāryamekoddiṣṭaṃ naraiḥ striyāḥ ||

English

For those women, when there is no son, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa62 does not exist. The ekoddiṣṭa63 for a woman is to be performed by men every year.

30.19

Sanskrit

मृताहनि यथान्यायं नृणां यद्वदिहोदितम् । पुत्राभावे सपिण्डास्तु तदभावे सहोदकाः ॥

mṛtāhani yathānyāyaṃ nṛṇāṃ yadvadihoditam | putrābhāve sapiṇḍāstu tadabhāve sahodakāḥ ||

English

30.19–20On the day of death, according to rule, as has been stated here for men: in the absence of a son, the sapiṇḍas64; in their absence, the sahodakas65; and those who are the mother's sapiṇḍas, and those who are the mother's sahodakas, and the daughter's son of a sonless man, should perform this rite66 properly.67

30.20

Sanskrit

मातुः सपिण्डा ये च स्युर्ये च मातुः सहोदकाः । कुर्युरेनं विधिं सम्यगपुत्रस्य सुतासुतः ॥

mātuḥ sapiṇḍā ye ca syurye ca mātuḥ sahodakāḥ | kuryurenaṃ vidhiṃ samyagaputrasya sutāsutaḥ ||

English

Its English is given with 30.19–20, above.

30.21

Sanskrit

कुर्युर्मातामहायैवं पुत्रिकास्तनयास्तथा । द्व्यामुष्यायणसंज्ञास्तु मातामहपितामहान् ॥

kuryurmātāmahāyaivaṃ putrikāstanayāstathā | dvyāmuṣyāyaṇasaṃjñāstu mātāmahapitāmahān ||

English

30.21–22Thus the appointed daughters, and likewise the sons, should perform [the rites] for the maternal grandfather. Those called dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa68 should honour the maternal and paternal grandfathers according to rule, with śrāddhas69, even the occasional70 ones. When there is none of all these, women should perform [the rite] for their own husbands, without mantras.71

30.22

Sanskrit

पूजयेयुर्यथान्यायं श्राद्धैर्नैमित्तिकैरपि । सर्वाभावे स्त्रियः कुर्युः स्वभर्तॄणाममन्त्रकम् ॥

pūjayeyuryathānyāyaṃ śrāddhairnaimittikairapi | sarvābhāve striyaḥ kuryuḥ svabhartṝṇāmamantrakam ||

English

Its English is given with 30.21–22, above.

30.23

Sanskrit

तदभावे च नृपतिः कारयेत् स्वकुटुम्बिना । तज्जातीयैर्नरैः सम्याग् दाहाद्याः सकलाः क्रियाः ॥

tadabhāve ca nṛpatiḥ kārayet svakuṭumbinā | tajjātīyairnaraiḥ samyāg dāhādyāḥ sakalāḥ kriyāḥ ||

English

30.23–24In their absence, the king should have all the rites, beginning with the cremation, properly performed by a member of his own household72 and by men of the same community as the deceased, since the king is the kinsman of all the varṇas73. These rites, both the obligatory and the occasional74, have been told to you, child.75

30.24

Sanskrit

सर्वेषामेव वर्णानां बान्धवो नृपतिर्यतः । एतास्ते कथिता वत्स ! नित्यनैमित्तकास्तथा ॥

sarveṣāmeva varṇānāṃ bāndhavo nṛpatiryataḥ | etāste kathitā vatsa ! nityanaimittakāstathā ||

English

Its English is given with 30.23–24, above.

30.25

Sanskrit

क्रियां श्राद्धाश्रयामन्यां नित्यनैमित्तिकीं शृणु । दर्शस्तत्र निमित्तं वै कालश्चन्द्रक्षयात्मकः । नित्यातां नियतः कालस्तस्याः संसूचयत्यथ ॥

kriyāṃ śrāddhāśrayāmanyāṃ nityanaimittikīṃ śṛṇu | darśastatra nimittaṃ vai kālaścandrakṣayātmakaḥ | nityātāṃ niyataḥ kālastasyāḥ saṃsūcayatyatha ||

English

Now hear of another rite, which rests on the śrāddha76 and is both regular and occasional77. The new moon78 is its occasion, a time marked by the waning of the moon. The fixed time of that rite then points to its regular character.79

Sanskrit

इति श्रीमार्कण्डेयपुराणे अलर्कानुशासने नैमित्तिकादिश्राद्धकल्पो नाम त्रिंशो ऽध्यायः

iti śrīmārkaṇḍeyapurāṇe alarkānuśāsane naimittikādiśrāddhakalpo nāma triṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, named "The Procedure for the Occasional and Other Śrāddhas80," in the Instruction of Alarka81, in the revered Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.82

  1. Chapter Thirty: This is the chapter heading (triṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ, 'the thirtieth chapter'). The e-text's verse numbering at this point is irregular: the reference 120.1 stands for chapter 30, verse 0. ↩
  2. regular: nitya: a duty performed daily or at fixed times, without any special occasion, such as the five daily sacrifices mentioned in the next verse. ↩
  3. occasional: naimittika: a duty performed only on a particular occasion, such as the birth of a son (see 30.2). ↩
  4. regular-occasional: nityanaimittika: a duty that is regular but falls on a particular occasion, such as the rites at the lunar junctures (see 30.3). ↩
  5. regular rite: nitya: a rite performed every day or at fixed times, as opposed to the naimittika, performed only on a particular occasion. ↩
  6. five yajñas: The five daily great sacrifices of the householder, described in the preceding chapter: to the gods, the ancestors, living beings, humans and the Veda or brahman. ↩
  7. occasional rite: naimittika: a rite required by a particular occasion, such as a birth. ↩
  8. The reading: The verse has no verb in the second half; 'is another kind' is supplied from the construction, as 'asti' is implied. 'putrajanmakriyādikam' is taken as a bahuvrīhi qualifying naimittikam ('having the rites at the birth of a son as its first'). ↩
  9. nityanaimittika: A rite both regular and occasional: obligatory, yet performed on a particular occasion, such as the parvan days (new moon and full moon). ↩
  10. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the ancestors (pitṛ). ↩
  11. parvan days: The junctures of the lunar month: the new-moon and full-moon days, and the like. ↩
  12. abhyudaya: A śrāddha performed at occasions of good fortune, such as the birth of a son or a marriage. It is also called nāndīmukha, as verse 30.5 says. ↩
  13. The reading: The verse has no speaker's line; Madālasā continues from 30.1. 'Tava' (to/for you) is taken with 'vakṣye' (I shall tell you). 'Paṇḍitaiḥ' with 'jñeyam' is an agent in the instrumental: 'should be known by the learned.' 'Parvaśrāddhādi' is read as 'having the parvan-śrāddha as its beginning', that is, the class headed by it; 'nityanaimittikaṃ' is in apposition to it. The translation states this in the active voice, which keeps the sense. ↩
  14. jātakarma: The birth rite performed for a newborn child, before the cutting of the umbilical cord. The verse says that the rites at a son's birth follow the same procedure. ↩
  15. in due order: The text reads krimoditam, which gives no sense. It is probably a corruption of kramoditam, 'stated in sequence'. ↩
  16. The reading: krimoditam is not a Sanskrit word as it stands. Possible readings: kramoditam 'stated in order' (chosen, the simplest emendation), or kriyoditam 'stated as rites'. Both give much the same sense. Also, vivāhādau 'at marriage and the like' needs a supplied noun in English, so I added [occasions] in brackets. ↩
  17. here: atra refers to the śrāddha for prosperity (abhyudaya) announced in 30.3. ↩
  18. Nāndīmukhas: Nāndīmukha is the name of the ancestors honoured in the śrāddha (rite for the ancestors) performed on auspicious occasions such as a birth or a marriage, called the ābhyudayika or vṛddhi śrāddha. The name is a technical one, and it is the context that makes the occasion clear. ↩
  19. piṇḍas: piṇḍa: a ball of food offered to the ancestors in a śrāddha. The verse does not say what the food is, apart from the curds and barley. ↩
  20. The reading: I accept the reviewer's point about 'balls of rice': the text names no grain, and barley is mentioned separately, so I now write 'piṇḍas' with a note. I now render the relative 'ye' ('who are renowned as') and the connecting 'ca' ('And ... and'). I leave 'tu' untranslated: it is a mild, contrastive particle here, and it adds no meaning that English needs. 'Dadyāt' has no stated subject; I take it as the general optative 'one should offer', which would be the householder or sacrificer of the next verse. 'Atra' is 'here', meaning in this rite. ↩
  21. that [rite]: tat refers to the Nāndīmukha rite of 30.5, with its offering of rice-balls to the Nāndīmukha ancestors. ↩
  22. the Vaiśvadeva: The offering to the Viśvedevas, a group of gods who are normally given a place and an oblation in a śrāddha. Some authorities omit it in the ābhyudayika (Nāndīmukha) rite. ↩
  23. keeping them to the right: pradakṣiṇam means moving with the right side towards the person honoured, that is, a clockwise circuit. It is the auspicious direction of ritual, in contrast to the prasavya order of funeral rites. ↩
  24. The reading: 1) The verse number 120.9 is evidently a misnumbering in the e-text, since the verse belongs to chapter 30 and continues the instruction of 30.6. I translated it as given, as the continuation of the same passage. 2) 30.6 has no finite verb for the sacrificer clause; I supplied '[is to be]' in brackets. 3) vaiśvadevavihīnam is taken as 'without the Vaiśvadeva', qualifying tat (the rite). 4) yugmāḥ is taken as 'even in number' (2, 4 and so on), against 'in pairs'; kāryāḥ is rendered 'are to be engaged'. The sense is the same either way. 5) mānavāḥ is taken simply as 'men'. ↩
  25. occasional rite (naimittika): A naimittika rite is one performed on a particular occasion, here the śrāddha for a son's birth or a marriage, in contrast to the nitya, the regular daily rite. ↩
  26. time of increase: vṛddhi is the occasion of increase or prosperity (birth of a son, marriage). The rite is the vṛddhi or ābhyudayika śrāddha announced in 30.3. ↩
  27. funeral rites for the departed: aurdhvadehika means 'belonging to the departed one's after-body'. It denotes the rites after death. The next verses go on to the ekoddiṣṭa rite. ↩
  28. The reading: The verse has no verb. I supply 'is' and 'there is'. The Sanskrit says only 'another', so 'rite' is understood from naimittikam. I read 'vṛddhau' as 'at a time of increase' (locative) and 'aurdhvadehikam' as qualifying the other rite. ↩
  29. ekoddiṣṭa: The śrāddha offered for one single deceased person on the day of death, as distinct from the pārvaṇa rite for the three ancestors together. ↩
  30. without the gods: daivahīna: without the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadeva), the gods who otherwise take part in a śrāddha; compare the Sanskrit of verse 30.6, where the rite is described as vaiśvadevavihīna. ↩
  31. pavitra: A ring or strand of kuśa grass, used for purification; ekapavitraka means that only one is used, not the usual two. ↩
  32. The reading: ekapavitraka (neuter, 'with a single pavitra') is taken as a predicate of kāryam, parallel to daivahīnam. Some may take pavitra as the kuśa blades held in the hand; the sense is the same. The Sanskrit tat ('that') refers to the ekoddiṣṭa rite which follows in the next verses. ↩
  33. agnaukaraṇa: The offering made into the fire, with the brahmins' leave, before they are fed; it is a regular step of the ordinary śrāddha. The verse itself says it is omitted here, in the rite of the single ancestor (ekoddiṣṭa, 30.8). ↩
  34. rice-ball: piṇḍa: the ball of cooked food offered to the dead in a śrāddha. ↩
  35. the leavings of the meal: ucchiṣṭa: food left over after the meal. The commentarial tradition takes this to be what is left on the brahmins' leaves or plates; the verse itself says only that the rice-ball is given near it. ↩
  36. The reading: 1. agnaukaraṇavarjitam is neuter singular and could agree with āvāhanam, but the sense is that the whole rite lacks the agnaukaraṇa. I now give it literally, as 'devoid of the agnaukaraṇa', and bracket the supplied words '[the rite being]'. The earlier wording 'the rite is to be done' is dropped. 2. The reviewer would have āvāhana specified as 'of the deities/ancestors'. The verse does not say whom the invocation addresses, and the commentators differ, so I keep the bare 'invocation' rather than add an object that is not in the Sanskrit. 3. In ucchiṣṭasannidhau, sannidhi means nearness or proximity, so I write 'near'. That the leavings are the brahmins' is now marked in the note as the commentarial view. 4. dadyāt is optative, with the subject left unexpressed, hence 'one should give'. ↩
  37. apasavya: The reverse of the ordinary (savya) direction: the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder and the action turns to the south. It is the manner used in rites for the dead. ↩
  38. "[May this be] inexhaustible for so-and-so": The formula akṣayyam amukasya: the officiant says the deceased's name in place of amuka ("so-and-so"). It belongs to the rite for a single deceased person, in which it stands in place of a formula of the general śrāddha. ↩
  39. "Rest content,": The text reads abhiraṇyatām, taken as a form of abhiramyatām, the imperative "may you take pleasure, rest content". The brahmins' reply abhiratāḥ sma means "we are content". ↩
  40. The reading: 1) sthāne in 30.10 can mean "in place of" (the usual formula of the general śrāddha) or "in the proper place". I now follow the first reading, as the reviewer proposed, because it construes better with the locative vipravisarjane. The text does not say which formula is replaced, so I supply only "[the usual formula]". The alternative remains possible. 2) abhiraṇyatām, with ṇ, looks like an altered or misprinted abhiramyatām. I translated it as that, and the note and the translation now use the same rendering ("Rest content"). 3) The reviewer asked for ha to be rendered. I give it as "indeed" in "We are indeed content", though it may be only a filler particle. 4) I kept the structure with the formula as a separate element of the rite, with the verbs supplied in brackets. ↩
  41. sapiṇḍīkaraṇa: The rite of 'making sapiṇḍa', in which the deceased's single piṇḍa is joined with those of the father, grandfather and great-grandfather, admitting him among the ancestors (pitṛ). ↩
  42. The reading: The Sanskrit's 'yadā vā kriyate naraiḥ' is elliptical; I take it as 'or whenever it is performed by men', i.e. the rite may be done at another time than the completed year. 'Tasya api' is rendered 'for that too', taking tasya as referring to the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa. ↩
  43. deva offerings: daivarahita: without the daiva portion, i.e. without the brahmins who represent the Viśvedevas (the gods) at the śrāddha; only the pitṛ side is served. ↩
  44. arghya: The water of respectful offering, with sesame, perfumes and the like, placed in a vessel; in the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa the single vessel of the dead man is later mixed with those of the ancestors (see the verses that follow). ↩
  45. pavitraka: A ring or strainer of kuśa grass worn or used in rites for purification. ↩
  46. agnaukaraṇa: The rite of offering into the fire, the formal oblation made before the piṇḍas in an ordinary śrāddha. ↩
  47. The reading: taccāpi: 'that too' refers to the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite announced in 30.12. 'Deva offerings' is a rendering of daiva, which more precisely means the portion for the Viśvedevas, hence the note. The verse is a single sentence with a repeated 'tat'; the second tat (tacca) I take as the rite again, 'it too'. ↩
  48. with the sacred thread over the right shoulder: apasavya: the ritual posture used in rites for the dead, with the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder, in contrast to the usual savya posture of rites for the gods. ↩
  49. of uneven number: ayujaḥ: an odd number of brahmins (1, 3, 5, etc.), as is prescribed for rites for the dead. ↩
  50. which exceeds the monthly rite in its procedure: pratimāsaṃ kriyādhikaḥ is literally 'greater in action than the monthly [rite]'. It may mean that the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa involves more procedure than the monthly rite, and the next verses give the added detail (the four vessels). The sense is taken from them. ↩
  51. The reading: The last phrase pratimāsaṃ kriyādhikaḥ can be read as 'exceeding the monthly [śrāddha] in rite' (chosen, as the following verses add a fourth vessel and the like) or as 'a further rite to be done every month'. The first fits the context better. Also, 'apasavyaṃ' could be an adverb ('in the apasavya manner') or the object of an implied verb; I take it as the manner of performing the rite. ↩
  52. that: taṃ refers back to the additional feature of the monthly rite mentioned in 30.14 (viśeṣa ... kriyādhikaḥ). ↩
  53. a set of four vessels: pātra: the ritual vessels of the rite, which 30.16 divides into three for the ancestors and one for the dead man. ↩
  54. The reading: 1. 'taṃ kathyamānam' is the object of 'niśāmaya' ("listen to that, as it is being told"). The reviewer is right, and my earlier 'listen to me' was a misreading. 'me vadantyā' is the agent: 'by me, as I speak' (instrumental 'me', with the feminine participle agreeing). It does not take 'niśāmaya' as its object. I now render the two as a single clause. 2. 'taṃ' is taken to refer to the extra feature of the monthly rite in 30.14. This is an inference from context, since the verse does not name it. 3. The sentence runs on into 30.16, where the verb 'kuryāt' appears. I no longer supply 'prepare' from there; the passage opens the sentence with 'there, a set of four vessels furnished with ...'. 4. 'tilagandhodakaiḥ' is a plural dvandva, 'sesame, perfume (fragrant substance) and water'. I keep 'perfume' for 'gandha', since the compound lists three separate items, and not 'perfumed water'. 5. My earlier remark that the speaker is a bird-mother was wrong. The speaker is a mother instructing her ↩
  55. the dead man: preta: the deceased who, until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, has not yet been joined with the ancestors. ↩
  56. my son: putraka: an affectionate diminutive vocative. The speaker is Madālasā, instructing her son Alarka. ↩
  57. arghya: The honorific offering of water, here the water prepared in the vessels for the ancestors. ↩
  58. The reading: 1) The Sanskrit gives no noun with tritayam and ekam. I supply 'vessels' in brackets from pātratraye and the 'four vessels' of 30.15. 2) Pātratraye is read as the three vessels of the fathers, in contrast with the single vessel of the preta. 'Fathers'' is bracketed because it is implied by the context and not stated. 3) Pretapātram is the object of prasecayet, 'one should pour/sprinkle'. What is poured is the contents of the vessel, which I supply in brackets, as I do with 'vessels'. 4) The reviewer's point about 'Then' is accepted: the Sanskrit has only ca eva, so I now write 'and also'. 5) The reviewer's point about the vocative is accepted: the speaker is Madālasā addressing her son Alarka, and 'Madālasā-like' and the bird were my error. The vocative putraka is rendered 'my son', since the diminutive here is affectionate and the addressee is her son. ↩
  59. ye samānāḥ: The opening words of the Yajurvedic mantra 'ye samānāḥ samanasaḥ pitaro yamarājye' (cf. Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 19.45 and its parallels), used in the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite that joins the deceased with the ancestors. ↩
  60. ekoddiṣṭa: The rite offered for a single deceased person, without the ancestors being included. The text reads ekīddiṣṭa, an irregular form of ekoddiṣṭa; 30.18 has ekoddiṣṭa. ↩
  61. The reading: The reading ekīddiṣṭam is a misprint or irregular form for ekoddiṣṭam (30.18 has ekoddiṣṭam); I translated it as ekoddiṣṭa. 'ye samānāḥ' is cited as the opening of a mantra, with iti marking the quotation; the Sanskrit gives no subject, so 'he' is implied. Strīṇām apy evam evaitat could be taken as 'for women too, just so', which I followed. I accepted the reviewer's correction on the mantra's source: I removed the Ṛgveda 10.57.3 reference and cite the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 19.45 with 'cf.', since I cannot verify every parallel. ↩
  62. sapiṇḍīkaraṇa: The rite, performed after the first year, that joins the deceased to the three ancestors who receive the piṇḍa offerings and so makes him or her a sapiṇḍa; it is described in the preceding verses. ↩
  63. ekoddiṣṭa: The śrāddha offered to one single deceased person, without the ancestors who are joined in the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa. ↩
  64. sapiṇḍas: Kinsmen related through the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to common ancestors. By the usual reckoning they are the relatives within seven generations. ↩
  65. sahodakas: Kinsmen who share the water-offering (udaka): more distant relatives, beyond the sapiṇḍa degrees. ↩
  66. this rite: The ekoddiṣṭa rite, the single-person śrāddha described in the preceding verses. ↩
  67. The reading: sutāsutaḥ is singular, and the verb kuryuḥ is plural. I take it as sutāyāḥ sutaḥ, 'daughter's son', one more of the persons who perform the rite. The text does not say whether aputrasya means a sonless man or a sonless woman. I took it as 'sonless man' because verse 19 speaks of men (nṛṇām), and ekoddiṣṭa for women has just been dealt with. enaṃ vidhim is taken as the ekoddiṣṭa rite. ↩
  68. dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa: Literally 'descendant of two fathers': a son who belongs to both his natural father and the man who adopted him or begot him on his behalf. He owes rites to both lines. ↩
  69. śrāddhas: Rites of food-offering to the deceased forefathers (pitṛ), with piṇḍa and water. ↩
  70. occasional: naimittika: performed on a particular occasion or cause, as opposed to the regular (nitya) rites. The chapter ends by summarising both kinds (30.24). ↩
  71. The reading: putrikāstanayāstathā: the visarga-sandhi shows two separate words, putrikāḥ and tanayāḥ ('appointed daughters' and 'sons'), not a compound putrikā-tanayāḥ ('sons of an appointed daughter'). The compound would be the more natural sense for rites to the maternal grandfather, and some readers may prefer it. I followed the sandhi as it stands. mātāmahapitāmahān is read as a dvandva, 'maternal and paternal grandfathers'. The other possible sense, 'the maternal grandfather's father', is less likely. amantrakam is taken as the object of kuryuḥ: 'the rite without mantras'. ↩
  72. a member of his own household: svakuṭumbinā is a singular instrumental. 'His own' is taken to refer to the king, so a man of the king's household; see doubts. ↩
  73. varṇas: The four social classes (brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra). Here the king, as protector of all of them, acts as kinsman of anyone who has no relatives left. ↩
  74. the obligatory and the occasional: Sanskrit nitya (rites performed regularly, as a standing duty) and naimittika (rites performed on a particular occasion or cause). The next verse begins the treatment of the nitya-naimittika śrāddha. ↩
  75. The reading: svakuṭumbinā: 'his own' could refer to the king (a man of the king's household) or to the deceased (a member of the dead person's own family). Since the family has just been exhausted (tadabhāve), I chose the king's household. The singular svakuṭumbinā and the plural tajjātīyair naraiḥ are taken as two agents joined by implied 'and'; they could also be read as alternatives ('or'). ↩
  76. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the dead ancestors. ↩
  77. both regular and occasional: nityanaimittika: a rite that is nitya (obligatory, performed at fixed times) and also naimittika (performed on a particular occasion). Here the occasion is the new moon, and the fixed recurrence makes it regular. ↩
  78. The new moon: darśa: the day of the new moon, when the moon is not seen (or is just seen). ↩
  79. The reading: The verse is metrically irregular and the compound 'nityātām' is awkward. I take 'nityātām' as an abstract noun, 'regularity', governed by 'saṃsūcayati'. 'Atha' is rendered 'then'. 'Vai' is left out as emphatic. ↩
  80. Śrāddhas: Śrāddha: rite of offerings to the deceased ancestors. Naimittika means occasional, performed on a particular occasion, as opposed to nitya, regular. ↩
  81. Instruction of Alarka: Alarkānuśāsana: the section of the Purāṇa in which Alarka is instructed by his mother Madālasā; the chapter belongs to it. ↩
  82. The reading: The colophon is a title, not a verse. 'Naimittikādiśrāddhakalpa' is rendered 'The Procedure for the Occasional and Other Śrāddhas' (kalpa as ritual procedure); 'ādi' might also be read as 'beginning with the occasional', which is the same sense. The text's 'alarkānuśāsane' is taken as a locative: in the Instruction of Alarka (a subsection of the Purāṇa). I did not mark śrāddha with asterisks in the translation, treating it as an English-used word, and the note explains it. ↩

Adhyāya 31

Sanskrit

एकत्रिंशो ऽध्यायः

ekatriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ

English

Chapter Thirty-One1.

Sanskrit

मदालसोवाच

madālasovāca

English

Madālasā said:

31.1

Sanskrit

सपिण्डीकरणादूर्ध्वं पितुर्यः प्रपितामहः । स तु लेपभुजो याति प्रलुप्तः पितृपिण्डतः ॥

sapiṇḍīkaraṇādūrdhvaṃ pituryaḥ prapitāmahaḥ | sa tu lepabhujo yāti praluptaḥ pitṛpiṇḍataḥ ||

English

After the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa2, the father's great-grandfather, cut off from the piṇḍa3 of the ancestors, goes to the eaters of the wipings4.5

31.2

Sanskrit

तेषामन्यश्चतुर्थो यः पुत्रलेपभुजान्नभुक् । सो ऽपि सम्बन्धतो हीनमुपभोगं प्रपद्यते ॥

teṣāmanyaścaturtho yaḥ putralepabhujānnabhuk | so 'pi sambandhato hīnamupabhogaṃ prapadyate ||

English

Among them, the other one, the fourth6, who eats the food of the son's lepa7-eaters, he too obtains, by reason of the relationship, a diminished share of enjoyment.8

31.3

Sanskrit

पिता पितामहश्चैव तथैव प्रपितामहः । पिण्डसम्बन्धिनो ह्येते विज्ञेयाः पुरुषास्त्रयः ॥

pitā pitāmahaścaiva tathaiva prapitāmahaḥ | piṇḍasambandhino hyete vijñeyāḥ puruṣāstrayaḥ ||

English

The father, the grandfather and likewise the great-grandfather: for these three men are to be known as connected with the piṇḍa9.10

31.4

Sanskrit

तेपसम्बन्धिनश्चान्ये पितामहपितामहात् । प्रभृत्युक्तास्त्रयस्तेषां यजमानश्च सप्तमः ॥

tepasambandhinaścānye pitāmahapitāmahāt | prabhṛtyuktāstrayasteṣāṃ yajamānaśca saptamaḥ ||

English

And the other three, who are connected through the lepa11, are said to begin from the grandfather's grandfather12; and among them the sacrificer13 is the seventh.14

31.5

Sanskrit

इत्येष मु नभिः प्रोक्तः सम्बन्धः साप्तपौरुषः । यजमानात् प्रभृत्यूर्ध्वमनुलेपभुजस्तथा ॥

ityeṣa mu nabhiḥ proktaḥ sambandhaḥ sāptapauruṣaḥ | yajamānāt prabhṛtyūrdhvamanulepabhujastathā ||

English

Thus this relationship of seven generations has been declared by the sages15, reckoned upward from the sacrificer16, and likewise [that of] the successive sharers in the wipings17.18

31.6

Sanskrit

ततो ऽन्ये पूर्वजाः सर्वे ये चान्ये नरकौकसः । ये च तिर्यक्त्वमापन्ना ये च भूतादिसंस्थिताः ॥

tato 'nye pūrvajāḥ sarve ye cānye narakaukasaḥ | ye ca tiryaktvamāpannā ye ca bhūtādisaṃsthitāḥ ||

English

31.6–7Then all the other forefathers, and those others who dwell in hell, and those who have fallen into the state of animals, and those who remain in the condition of spirits and the like19: the sacrificer20, performing the śrāddha21 according to rule, fully satisfies all of them. Listen, child, to that—by what means, by each of which he does so.22

31.7

Sanskrit

तान् सर्वान् यजमानो वै श्राद्धं कुर्वन् यथाविधि । समाप्याययते वत्स ! येन येन शृणुष्व तत् ॥

tān sarvān yajamāno vai śrāddhaṃ kurvan yathāvidhi | samāpyāyayate vatsa ! yena yena śṛṇuṣva tat ||

English

Its English is given with 31.6–7, above.

31.8

Sanskrit

अन्नप्रकिरणं यत् तु मनुष्यैः क्रियते भुवि । तेन तृत्पिमुपायान्ति ये पिशाचत्वमागताः ॥

annaprakiraṇaṃ yat tu manuṣyaiḥ kriyate bhuvi | tena tṛtpimupāyānti ye piśācatvamāgatāḥ ||

English

Those who have attained the state of piśācas23 find satisfaction through the scattering of food that human beings perform on the earth.24

31.9

Sanskrit

यदम्बु स्त्रानवस्त्रोत्थं भूमौ पतति पुत्रक ! । तेन ये तरुतां प्राप्तास्तेषां तृप्तिः प्रजायते ॥

yadambu strānavastrotthaṃ bhūmau patati putraka ! | tena ye tarutāṃ prāptāsteṣāṃ tṛptiḥ prajāyate ||

English

The water that comes from the bathing-cloth25 and falls on the ground, my child, satisfies those in the family who have attained the state of trees; by it their contentment is produced.26†

31.10

Sanskrit

यास्तु गात्राम्बुकणिकाः पतन्ति धरणीतले । ताभिराप्यायनं तेषां ये देवत्वं कुले गताः ॥

yāstu gātrāmbukaṇikāḥ patanti dharaṇītale | tābhirāpyāyanaṃ teṣāṃ ye devatvaṃ kule gatāḥ ||

English

And the drops of water from the body that fall on the surface of the ground: by these there is nourishment for those in the family who have attained the state of gods27.28†

31.11

Sanskrit

उद्धृतेष्वथ पिण्डेषु याश्चान्नकणिका भुवि । ताभिराप्यायनं प्राप्ता ये तिर्यकत्वं कुले गताः ॥

uddhṛteṣvatha piṇḍeṣu yāścānnakaṇikā bhuvi | tābhirāpyāyanaṃ prāptā ye tiryakatvaṃ kule gatāḥ ||

English

31.26–29The one who has broken his vow of celibacy72, the sick man, the one deficient in a limb and likewise the one with an extra limb, the son of a remarried woman, the one-eyed man, the kuṇḍa73 and the gola74, my son; the betrayer of a friend, the one with deformed nails, the impotent man, the one with dark teeth, the one of defective form, the one denounced by his father, the slanderer, the seller of soma; the defiler of a maiden, the physician, the one who has abandoned his teacher and his father, the one who teaches for hire, the enemy, the husband of a woman previously married to another; the one who has abandoned the Veda, the one who has given up the sacred fires, the one defiled by a husband of a vṛṣalī75, and others who follow forbidden occupations: these brahmins are to be excluded from the rites for the ancestors.76

31.31–33They, and he who79 will perform the śrāddha80, must be self-controlled. He who, having given the śrāddha, resorts to sexual intercourse, and he who, having eaten, [resorts to it]: the ancestors of those two, however81, lie for a month in that semen. And he who, having gone to a woman, eats at the śrāddha, and he who goes [to her]: for that month the ancestors of those two have food made of semen and urine. Therefore the invitation should be made first by a wise man.82

31.34–39Men addicted to women are to be avoided; and [they are to be avoided] even if [other brahmins] are not found on that day. Or, at the proper time, he should feed self-controlled ascetics who have come for alms, having won them over with prostrations and the like, with a disciplined mind. Just as the dark fortnight is dearer to the ancestors than the bright, so the afternoon surpasses the forenoon for the ancestors. Having honoured with a welcome these brahmins who have come to his house, he should seat them on seats, after they have sipped water83, with the purifier in his hand84: for the ancestors an uneven number, as he wishes; for the gods an even number of the best of brahmins. Or [he may seat] one each for the ancestors and for the gods, according to his means, and likewise for the maternal grandfathers; or the Vaiśvadevika85 may be the same [for both]. Some other men wish it to be separate for those two. He should make those designated for the gods face east, and those of the ancestors face north.86
