Sanskrit

सोमाय वै पितृमते स्वाहेत्यन्या तथा भवेत् । यमाय प्रेतपतये स्वाहेति त्रितयाहुतिः ॥

somāya vai pitṛmate svāhetyanyā tathā bhavet | yamāya pretapataye svāheti tritayāhutiḥ ||

English

"To Soma, who is accompanied by the ancestors103, svāhā104": so the second offering shall be. "To Yama, lord of the departed105, svāhā": this is the third offering.

31.48

Sanskrit

हुतावशिष्टं दद्याच्च भाजनेषु द्विजन्मनाम् । भाजनालम्भनं कृत्वा दद्याच्चान्नं यथाविधि ॥

hutāvaśiṣṭaṃ dadyācca bhājaneṣu dvijanmanām | bhājanālambhanaṃ kṛtvā dadyāccānnaṃ yathāvidhi ||

English

He should give what remains of the oblation into the vessels of the twice-born; and, having made the touching of the vessels106, he should give the food according to the rule.107

31.49

Sanskrit

यथा सुखं जुषध्वं भो इति वाच्यमनिष्ठुरम् । भुञ्जीरंश्च ततस्ते ऽपि तच्चित्ता मौनिनः सुखम् ॥

yathā sukhaṃ juṣadhvaṃ bho iti vācyamaniṣṭhuram | bhuñjīraṃśca tataste 'pi taccittā mauninaḥ sukham ||

English

"Eat at your ease, sirs, as it pleases you": this should be said, gently and without harshness. And then they too, with their minds fixed on it108 and keeping silent, should eat at ease.109

31.50

Sanskrit

यद्यदिष्टचतमं तेषां तत्तदन्नमसत्वरम् । अक्रुध्यंश्च नरो दद्यात् सम्भवेन प्रलोभयन् ॥

yadyadiṣṭacatamaṃ teṣāṃ tattadannamasatvaram | akrudhyaṃśca naro dadyāt sambhavena pralobhayan ||

English

Whatever food is most desired by them, he should give them each such food, without haste and without anger. The man should give it, tempting them according to what is available110.111

31.51

Sanskrit

रक्षोघ्रांश्च जपेन्मन्त्रांस्तिलैश्च विकिरेन्महीम् । सिद्धार्थकैश्च रक्षार्थं श्राद्धं हि प्रचुरच्छलम् ॥

rakṣoghrāṃśca japenmantrāṃstilaiśca vikirenmahīm | siddhārthakaiśca rakṣārthaṃ śrāddhaṃ hi pracuracchalam ||

English

He should recite the mantras that destroy the rakṣas112, and scatter sesame seeds over the ground, and also white mustard seeds, for protection; for the śrāddha113 is open to much trickery114.115

31.52

Sanskrit

पृष्टैस्तृप्तैश्च तृप्ताः स्थ तृप्ताः स्म इति वादिभिः । अनुज्ञातो नरस्त्वन्नं प्रकिरेत् भुवि सर्वतः ॥

pṛṣṭaistṛptaiśca tṛptāḥ stha tṛptāḥ sma iti vādibhiḥ | anujñāto narastvannaṃ prakiret bhuvi sarvataḥ ||

English

When the guests have been asked, "Are you satisfied?" and those who are satisfied have answered, "We are satisfied," the man, having received their leave, should scatter the food on the ground116 on every side.117

31.53

Sanskrit

तद्वदाचमनार्थाय दद्यादापः सकृत् सकृत् । अनुज्ञाञ्च ततः प्राप्य यतवाक्कायमानसः ॥

tadvadācamanārthāya dadyādāpaḥ sakṛt sakṛt | anujñāñca tataḥ prāpya yatavākkāyamānasaḥ ||

English

31.53–54In the same way, he should give water, once to each, for the rinsing of the mouth118. Then, having received permission, with speech, body and mind restrained, he should offer the piṇḍas119 with food mixed with sesame, with the left [hand], my son, on darbha grass120 near the leavings121, in the name of the ancestors.122

31.54

Sanskrit

सतिलेन ततो ऽन्नेन पिण्डान् सव्येन पुत्रक ! । पितनुद्दिश्य दर्भेषु दद्यादुच्छिष्टसन्निधौ ॥

satilena tato 'nnena piṇḍān savyena putraka ! | pitanuddiśya darbheṣu dadyāducchiṣṭasannidhau ||

English

Its English is given with 31.53–54, above.

31.55

Sanskrit

पितृतीर्थेन तोयञ्च दद्यात्तेभ्यः समाहितः । पितॄनिद्दिश्य यद्भक्त्या यजमानो नृपात्मज ॥

pitṛtīrthena toyañca dadyāttebhyaḥ samāhitaḥ | pitṝniddiśya yadbhaktyā yajamāno nṛpātmaja ||

English

And the sacrificer123, [himself] composed, should give water to them by the pitṛtīrtha124, having dedicated it to the ancestors with devotion, O prince.125

31.56

Sanskrit

तद्वन्मातामहानाञ्च दत्त्वा पिण्डान् यथाविधि । गन्धमाल्यादिसंयुक्तं दद्यादाचमनं ततः ॥

tadvanmātāmahānāñca dattvā piṇḍān yathāvidhi | gandhamālyādisaṃyuktaṃ dadyādācamanaṃ tataḥ ||

English

In the same way, having given the rice-balls (piṇḍa)126 in due order to the maternal grandfathers127 as well, he should then give water for rinsing the mouth128, accompanied by perfumes, garlands and the like.

31.57

Sanskrit

दत्त्वा च तक्षिणां शक्त्या सुस्वधास्त्विति तान् वदेत् । तैश्च तुष्टैस्तथेत्युक्त्वा वाचयेद्वैश्वदेविकान् ॥

dattvā ca takṣiṇāṃ śaktyā susvadhāstviti tān vadet | taiśca tuṣṭaistathetyuktvā vācayedvaiśvadevikān ||

English

Having given the fee (dakṣiṇā)129 according to his means, he should say to them, "May the svadhā130 be well [given]." When they, being satisfied, have said, "So be it," he should have the Vaiśvadevika [brahmins]131 recite.132

31.58

Sanskrit

प्रीयन्तामिति भद्रं वो विश्वेदेवा इतीरयेन् । तथेति चोक्ते तैर्विप्रैः प्रार्थनीयास्तदाशिषः ॥

prīyantāmiti bhadraṃ vo viśvedevā itīrayen | tatheti cokte tairvipraiḥ prārthanīyāstadāśiṣaḥ ||

  1. Chapter Thirty-One: The e-text gives this chapter heading as verse 122.1; the preceding colophon (121.9) names the thirtieth chapter, and the next verse (31.1) is numbered within chapter 31. The heading is not a verse of the Sanskrit text proper. ↩
  2. sapiṇḍīkaraṇa: The rite performed after the first year of mourning, in which the deceased is joined to the ancestors who share the piṇḍa (rice-ball) offering; the piṇḍa of the deceased is merged with those of his father, grandfather and great-grandfather. ↩
  3. piṇḍa: The ball of cooked rice offered to the ancestors in śrāddha. ↩
  4. eaters of the wipings: lepabhuj: those who consume the lepa, the traces of food wiped from the hands onto the sacred grass after the piṇḍa offering. They are the three ancestors beyond the three who receive the piṇḍa; the verse says the father's great-grandfather joins them, being dropped from the piṇḍa line. ↩
  5. The reading: The speaker's line (Madālasā uvāca) belongs to the preceding verse. The singular 'lepabhujo' is taken as accusative plural (lepabhujaḥ), 'goes to [the class of] the eaters of the wipings', with yāti governing an accusative; the text as printed has the genitive/ablative-looking form lepabhujo, probably a sandhi form of lepabhujaḥ before 'yāti' (-aḥ + y → -o y?). I read it as the plural accusative or as a nominative-type class-name. 'sa tu' is an emphatic/contrastive pair and is rendered by the topic of the sentence. ↩
  6. the fourth: The fourth ancestor in the ascending line, counting from the father. Verse 31.1 has just described the father's great-grandfather being removed from the piṇḍa and passing to the lepa-eaters. ↩
  7. lepa: The remnant of rice smeared on the kuśa grass when the balls of rice (piṇḍa) are offered. It is the portion given to the three ancestors beyond the great-grandfather, the 'eaters of the smear' (lepabhuj). ↩
  8. The reading: The compound putralepabhujānnabhuk is obscure. It can be taken as 'eater of the food of the son's lepa-eaters' (putra-lepabhuj-anna-bhuj), which I chose as the most literal. Another reading takes putra as the offerer and the fourth ancestor as a food-eater next after the lepa-eaters. Teṣām ('among them') most likely refers to the lepa-eating ancestors of 31.1. ↩
  9. piṇḍa: The ball of cooked rice offered to the departed ancestors in the śrāddha rite. ↩
  10. The reading: I accepted the finding on hi and now render it as "for", since it gives the reason for the preceding list. On the second finding I did not reword the note on the grandfather but removed it. The glossary already explains pitāmaha, and the rules say not to explain a listed term again. The word is singular here, so the plural sense of the paternal line does not apply. I use the glossary's "grandfather" in place of my earlier "paternal grandfather". ↩
  11. lepa: The 'smear', meaning the traces of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) offering wiped off onto the sacred grass. The three remote ancestors beyond the piṇḍa-sharers receive these. The text reads tepa-, which is probably a misprint for lepa-; see the doubts. ↩
  12. the grandfather's grandfather: pitāmahapitāmaha: the paternal grandfather of the grandfather, that is, the fourth ancestor in the ascending line. The three lepa-sharers are counted from him upward. ↩
  13. the sacrificer: yajamāna: the one who performs the rite, here the performer of the śrāddha. Counting him with the six ancestors gives the seven generations of the sāptapauruṣa relationship. ↩
  14. The reading: The text reads tepasambandhinaḥ. Since 31.1, 31.2 and 31.5 speak of lepabhuj and anulepabhuj, and the verse contrasts these with the piṇḍa-sharers of 31.3, I take tepa- as a misprint for lepa- and translate 'connected through the lepa'. Also, 'begin from the grandfather's grandfather' renders pitāmahapitāmahāt prabhṛti; uktāḥ is taken as 'are said [to begin]'. ↩
  15. has been declared by the sages: The e-text reads mu nabhiḥ, which is a misprint for munibhiḥ. ↩
  16. the sacrificer: yajamāna: the person who performs the rite, here the one offering the śrāddha. He is the seventh in the line, counting the three piṇḍa-sharers and the three wiping-sharers above him. ↩
  17. the successive sharers in the wipings: anulepabhuj: those who share in the lepa, the remnants wiped from the hands onto the grass after the piṇḍas are offered. This is the group named in verses 31.2 and 31.4. The compound is elliptical, and the prefix anu is taken as 'successive'. ↩
  18. The reading: The e-text reads 'mu nabhiḥ'; I emend to munibhiḥ, 'by the sages'. The second half is elliptical: anulepabhujaḥ is nominative plural with no verb. I take it as parallel to sambandhaḥ ('and likewise [the relationship of] the anulepabhuj'). The verses that follow (31.6) pick up with 'then all the other forefathers', which fits this reading. anu- is read as 'successive'; 'those who share afterwards' is another possible sense. ↩
  19. spirits and the like: bhūtādi: beings such as bhūta (ghosts, spirits); the following verses go through these classes, including piśāca, and the means that satisfies each. ↩
  20. the sacrificer: yajamāna, the person on whose behalf the rite is performed; here the descendant who offers the śrāddha, counted as the seventh in the line in 31.4. ↩
  21. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the departed forefathers, with the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), performed by a descendant. ↩
  22. The reading: tato 'nye pūrvajāḥ: 'tataḥ' could be 'then/thereafter' or 'beyond them' (further up the line, after the seven generations). I took it as 'then', marking the continuation from the seven-generation line in 31.5. Also, 'yena yena' is left in the same relative construction ('by what means, by each of which'), as its correlative continues in 31.8 onward. Madālasā is the presumed speaker of the discourse (see 122.2) and is not named in these verses. ↩
  23. piśācas: A class of flesh-eating demons or ghosts. Here they are among the departed kinsmen who have fallen into such a state, and who are nourished by the food strewn on the ground in the śrāddha. ↩
  24. The reading: The printed text has tṛtpim (for tṛptim); I read it as tṛptim, 'satisfaction'. The verse does not say when the food is scattered. The context, a śrāddha (verse 31.7), implies it, but I have added nothing to the translation. The word śrāddha is not used in this verse, so the note is brief. Its standard explanation may belong with verse 31.7. ↩
  25. bathing-cloth: The text reads strāna-vastra; strāna is evidently a misprint for snāna, 'bath', so the compound means the cloth worn or wrung out after bathing. ↩
  26. The reading: strānavastrotthaṃ: the e-text's strāna is not a standard word; I take it as a misprint for snāna ('bath'), giving 'arisen from the bathing-cloth'. Putraka is a diminutive vocative, 'dear son', here addressed to the listener; I render it 'my child'. ↩
  27. the state of gods: Devatva: the condition of a deva. The verse lists the several conditions into which departed members of the family may have passed, each fed by a different residue of the śrāddha. ↩
  28. The reading: gātrāmbukaṇikāḥ is a compound, 'drops of water from the body' (gātra + ambu + kaṇikā). It is taken to refer to water dripping from the body of the sacrificer after bathing, as the preceding verse mentions water from bathing clothes. The text does not state this, so the translation keeps 'from the body' only. kule gatāḥ is taken with 'in the family' as locative, 'who have gone, in the family, to godhood'; the alternative 'gone into the family' is not natural here. ↩
  29. rice-balls: piṇḍa: the ball of cooked rice (with other food) offered to the ancestors in the śrāddha. The verse speaks of the crumbs left after the balls are lifted from the ground. ↩
  30. The reading: uddhṛteṣu piṇḍeṣu is a locative absolute: 'when the piṇḍas have been lifted up'. 'Rice-balls' is chosen for piṇḍa to fit the context, since the sense is of balls of cooked food. The verb for the crumbs is implied (bhuvi 'on the ground'), so 'fall' is bracketed. tiryakatvam is read as 'the state of animals' (the animal birth, tiryagyoni). The reading tiryakatvam for metrical tiryaktvam is as printed. ↩
  31. fit for the rites: kriyāyogyāḥ: old enough for the funeral and post-funeral rites (kriyā) to be performed for them. ↩
  32. without the sacraments: asaṃskṛtāḥ: not having received the saṃskāras, the purificatory rites of childhood, such as tonsure and initiation. ↩
  33. the water of the sweeping: saṃmārjanajala: the water used in cleansing the ground after the rite. The compound can also be divided otherwise; see the doubts. ↩
  34. The reading: (1) The reviewer would read 'adagdhāḥ' and 'bālāḥ' as two separate classes ('uncremated, or children'). I keep 'vā' as 'or', now rendered as such at the head of the verse, linking this class to those in the preceding verses. The text has no second 'ye' or 'vā' between 'adagdhāḥ' and 'bālāḥ', and 'kriyāyogyā hy asaṃskṛtāḥ' describes children. So I take 'bālāḥ' as in apposition to 'adagdhāḥ': uncremated children. The comma-separated English can be read either way. (2) 'hi' is folded into 'yet', marking the contrast between fitness for the rites and absence of the sacraments. (3) 'Annavikirasaṃmārjanajalāśinaḥ' is read as 'eaters of scattered food and of the water of the sweeping', with 'saṃmārjana-jala' as one unit. The alternative is 'eaters of scattered food, of sweepings, and of water'. I chose the first because the preceding verses name the waters that fall on the ground. (4) 'Vipannāḥ' is rendered 'have perished' once only. The draft's 'died without having been cremated' is replaced ↩
  35. And others: anye ("others") takes up the departed kinsmen of the preceding verses, who are in various states of existence; the verb "attain" is carried by prayānti. ↩
  36. The reading: The verse is syntactically compressed: bhuktvā cācāmatām is a genitive plural absolute-type phrase, 'of those who, having eaten, rinse their mouths' (ācamatām agreeing with brāhmaṇānām). Taken so, 'the water of the brahmins after they have eaten and rinsed' is what is meant. tathaiva anye could alternatively mean 'in the same way, others [i.e. other beings]'; I take 'others' as the subject of prayānti. 'Attain' is supplied from prayānti. ↩
  37. the sacrificer: yajamāna: the person for whom a rite is performed and who bears its cost. Here he is the householder who offers the śrāddha. ↩
  38. mere leavings: ucchiṣṭa: food or water left over or touched after eating. The verse says that even this, scattered on the ground, nourishes the relatives. ↩
  39. śrāddha: śrāddha: the rite of offering food and water to the departed ancestors, usually with rice balls (piṇḍa) and the feeding of brahmins. ↩
  40. The reading: The genitive plural śrāddhakriyāvatām ("of those who have the śrāddha rite") could qualify tatkule (the family) or stand loosely with the sentence. I took it as describing the family of those who perform the rite, which is the sense of the surrounding verses. Samyak could also go with prayānti ("attain fully"). I took it with śrāddhakriyāvatām, as the rite performed properly. ↩
  41. cāṇḍāla: A member of one of the lowest, excluded classes. The tradition says such people are born of unions against the order of the classes. Here the word names a birth into which an ancestor may have been reborn. ↩
  42. pukkasa: Another despised, excluded class, often named together with the cāṇḍāla. ↩
  43. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the dead ancestors, with the feeding of brahmins. ↩
  44. The reading: The subject of tṛpyante is not expressed. I supply "[ancestors]" from verses 31.10–15, which speak of the dead who have gone into other births. The compound cāṇḍālapukkasādyāsu qualifies yoniṣu, so it means "in births beginning with cāṇḍāla and pukkasa", not "in the wombs of cāṇḍālas". Yoni can mean "womb" or "birth". I chose "birth" because the verse is about the condition into which the dead have been reborn. The relative–correlative pair yat śrāddham ... tena is turned into a main clause with a relative clause, as English requires. For arthaiḥ I keep artha, following the glossary. The plural is rendered as a collective. I take anyāyopārjita to mean "acquired unjustly". ↩
  45. nourishment: āpyāyana: literally 'swelling, filling up', that is, the sustaining and satisfaction of the departed in their various states of existence. ↩
  46. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the deceased ancestors, performed with faith (śraddhā) and with rice-balls (piṇḍa). ↩
  47. The reading: The printed 'kurvadibhaḥ' (kurvadibhar) is a misprint; I read kurvadbhiḥ, the instrumental plural of the present participle of kṛ, agreeing with bāndhavaiḥ ('relatives who perform'). 'bahūnām' has no noun; I supply 'beings' in brackets to mean the many departed and those in other births, as verses 31.11–16 show. 'annāmbubindu-' is taken as 'drops of food and water' (anna + ambu + bindu), though 'grains of food and drops of water' is also possible. ↩
  48. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the dead ancestors, performed with faith (śraddhā). ↩
  49. even if only with vegetables: śākaiḥ api: 'even with vegetables' means that even the humblest offering suffices when made with devotion. ↩
  50. The reading: kurvota is an irregular optative (ātmanepada) of kṛ, 'should perform'. sīdati, 'sinks', is rendered 'comes to grief', meaning falls into distress or ruin. ↩
  51. its times: tasya refers to the śrāddha, the ancestral rite spoken of in the preceding verses. ↩
  52. regular and the occasional kind: nitya rites are those prescribed as obligatory at fixed times, such as the monthly new-moon śrāddha; naimittika rites are performed on a particular occasion, such as an eclipse. The compound nityanaimittikātmakān qualifies kālān 'times'. ↩
  53. The reading: Verse 31.19 carries no speaker's line, so none is given. tasya ("its") is taken to refer to the śrāddha of 31.18. nibodha me is rendered "learn from me"; me could also be read as "to me", but it goes with the imperative as the ablative-type sense of hearing from the speaker. ↩
  54. Śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the deceased ancestors (pitṛs), usually with the feeding of brahmins. ↩
  55. new-moon day: Amāvāsyā, the day of the new moon, the principal monthly occasion for the śrāddha. ↩
  56. Aṣṭakās: The eighth days of the dark fortnights of certain months (traditionally the winter and cold-season months), on which ancestral rites are prescribed. ↩
  57. The reading: udupakṣaye (literally 'in the waning of the star-lord, i.e. the moon') could mean the dark fortnight in general or the new-moon day itself. I took it as 'at the waning of the moon', in apposition to amāvāsyā and māsi māsi, without narrowing it. icchākālam is a compound ('time of one's own wish', optional occasions); I rendered it as 'the occasions that are optional', which fits verses 31.21–22 that follow. ↩
  58. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the deceased ancestors, performed with brahmins as invited guests. ↩
  59. at the sun's passage into a new sign: saṃkrānti, the sun's entry into a new zodiacal sign. ↩
  60. vyatipāta: An astrological conjunction, regarded as inauspicious, when the sun and moon are at a certain relation to each other; it is held to be a time especially suited to śrāddha. ↩
  61. my child: putraka, a form of address to the pupil by the speaker, here the instructing teacher. ↩
  62. The reading: janmarkṣagrahapīḍāsu: could mean 'afflictions by planets to the birth star' (chosen) or 'afflictions of the birth star and of the planets'. Since the compound is a single tatpuruṣa, I took the planets as causing the affliction to the birth star. Also, the manuscripts have cecchayā, read ca icchayā 'and at will'; I have rendered icchayā 'at will' and let the 'and' stand in the list. ↩
  63. śrotriya: A brahmin learned in the Veda who has studied his own recension of it, and is therefore well qualified to be invited to a rite. ↩
  64. jyeṣṭhasāmaga: A singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, a particular Sāmaveda chant. The term is traditionally explained as a brahmin who knows that chant. ↩
  65. triṇāciketa: One who has studied the three sections of the Nāciketa, a Vedic text (Yajurveda), and kept the Nāciketa fire three times. Some explain it as one who knows the Nāciketa portion in three ways. ↩
  66. trimadhu: A brahmin who knows three Vedic hymn-groups whose verses begin with 'madhu' (the three 'honey' passages, e.g. madhu vātā ṛtāyate). Explained in commentaries as a Ṛgvedic or Yajurvedic study. ↩
  67. trisuparṇa: One who knows the three Suparṇa hymns of the Veda (the Suparṇa verses, used in the Yajurveda). In the śrāddha texts it designates a brahmin of high merit. ↩
  68. the five fires: The pañcāgni: either the five ritual fires (the three sacrificial fires with the sabhya and āvasathya fires) or the 'five-fire' meditation. The text's meaning is a brahmin who keeps these rites. ↩
  69. tapas: Austerity or ascetic discipline. ↩
  70. śrāddha: The rite in which food and water are offered to the departed ancestors, with brahmins fed on their behalf. ↩
  71. The reading: viśiṣṭaḥ may be an adjective ('eminent') qualifying the whole list or the first item of it. I took it as the first item of the list, as the singular and the list's asyndeton suggest. ketanakṣamāḥ: ketana is 'invitation, summons' (also 'house, sign'). I chose 'fit to be invited' because the context is the choice of brahmins for the śrāddha. The wording of 31.24 (jāmātṛ, svasrīya, śvaśura, mātula) is clear, but it presumes the brahmin is a relative. The 'six limbs' (ṣaḍaṅga) are the six Vedāṅgas, supplied in brackets for clarity. ↩
  72. broken his vow of celibacy: avakīrṇin: a student (brahmacārin) who has lost his chastity and so broken the vow of celibacy. ↩
  73. kuṇḍa: In the law books, a son born of adultery while the mother's husband is alive. ↩
  74. gola: In the law books, a son born of adultery after the mother's husband has died (also golaka). ↩
  75. vṛṣalī: A woman of low birth, here a śūdra woman. The compound vṛṣalīpatidūṣita is ambiguous; see doubts. ↩
  76. The reading: (1) avakīrṇo in 31.26 is a sandhi form for avakīrṇī (nominative of avakīrṇin); I took it as avakīrṇī. (2) nirākṛtiḥ can mean 'shapeless, of defective form' or 'one who has been repudiated' (from nirākṛ); I chose 'of defective form' because it fits the list of bodily defects. (3) abiśastaḥ is for abhiśasta, 'denounced, accused of a grave sin' (or 'cursed'). tu tātena makes 'by his father' the agent. I chose 'denounced'. (4) vṛṣalīpatidūṣitaḥ could be read as one defiled by (association with) a vṛṣalī's husband, or as two items, 'husband of a vṛṣalī' and 'defiled one'. I kept it as one compound with the instrumental sense. (5) gurupitroḥ is a dual, 'of teacher and father', and I took it so rather than as 'of his two parents'. ↩
  77. the assignment to the divine [rite] and to the ancestral [rite]: niyoga means appointment or assignment. Here it is the assigning of the invited brahmins to the śrāddha rite's two parts, the one for the gods (daiva) and the one for the ancestors (pitrya). ↩
  78. The reading: niyoge with daive ... pitrye ca: (a) daive and pitrye are two adjectives both qualifying niyoge, 'in the divine and the ancestral assignment'; (b) niyoge is a locative of occasion meaning 'in the rite', with daive and pitrye as two separate rites. I now take (a), as the reviewer asks. It gives niyoga its ordinary sense of 'appointment', and it fits upakalpayet, which is then the act of appointing. The noun 'rite' after daive and pitrye is supplied in brackets, as Sanskrit leaves it implied. I kept 'appoint' for upakalpayet rather than adding 'to their places', since the Sanskrit does not say that. The reviewer's tathaiva point needed no change: 'likewise' already renders it. For dvijasattamān I now use 'most excellent brahmins', to match dvijottamāḥ in 31.25. ↩
  79. They, and he who: 'They' (taiḥ) are the brahmins invited in the preceding verses. The instrumental with the gerundive bhāvyam means 'must be'. ↩
  80. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the departed ancestors, at which brahmins are invited and fed on their behalf. ↩
  81. those two, however: Here tayoḥ means the giver of the śrāddha and the eater at it, each of whom has resorted to intercourse (31.31cd). The tayoḥ of 31.33b is a different pair: the man who eats at the śrāddha after going to a woman, and the man who goes to her (31.32cd). ↩
  82. The reading: (1) saṃyatibhiḥ is taken as the instrumental plural of saṃyatin, 'self-controlled', a variant of saṃyata or saṃyamin (compare saṃyamino in 31.34). (2) The reviewer's finding is accepted: tayoḥ in 31.32b needs two antecedents in the English. The singular yaḥ with the two absolutives dattvā and bhuktvā is read distributively, as the giver (cf. yaś ca śrāddhaṃ kariṣyati) and the eater. I make the two men explicit and supply '[resorts to it]' for the second, in brackets, since the verb anugacchati is stated once. The alternative, that one man both gives and eats, does not fit the dual tayoḥ. The two occurrences of tayoḥ refer to different pairs: 31.32b to the giver and the eater of 31.31cd, and 31.33b to the two men of 31.32cd. (3) yaś ca gacchati in 31.32d has no stated object, and '[to her]' is supplied from yoṣitam. (4) tu in 31.32b is rendered 'however' because it contrasts the ancestors' fate with the offender's act. The tu in tasmāt tu (31.33c) is only transitional and is left out. ( ↩
  83. after they have sipped water: ācamana: the ritual sipping of water for purification, here done by the guests before they are seated. ↩
  84. with the purifier in his hand: pavitra: a ring or small bundle of kuśa grass worn on the hand to make the performer ritually pure. ↩
  85. the Vaiśvadevika: vaiśvadevika: the rite or offering addressed to the Viśvedevas, the 'gods' of the śrāddha, whose place is taken by the brahmins seated for the gods. ↩
  86. The reading: aprāptau taddine cāpi: 'if [others] are not obtained on that day' is my reading, with the object (suitable brahmins) implied. It could also mean 'if [the invited] do not arrive on that day'; the sense is nearly the same. atirityate is read as atiricyate, 'is superior, exceeds', a Purāṇic form. tayoḥ in 31.39 is taken to mean the ancestors and the maternal grandfathers, so Vaiśvadevika may be shared or separate for the two lines. ↩
  87. kuśa: A sacred grass (Poa cynosuroides), used in rituals for seats, purification and offerings. ↩
  88. arghya: The respectful offering of water, usually with other items, made to a guest or to a deity. ↩
  89. pavitraka: A ring or small twist of kuśa grass worn or given for ritual purity. ↩
  90. The reading: tebhyaḥ ('to them') is read as the invited brahmins who sit for the gods and for the maternal grandfathers. The verses give no separate noun for it. Budhaḥ (31.40) and prājñaḥ ... dvijaḥ (31.41) are taken as one person, the performer of the rite. The verses leave 'them' as the object of pūjya unexpressed, so I supply it in brackets. ↩
  91. arghya: The water, with other materials such as barley, offered in homage to a god or an honoured guest. ↩
  92. Viśvedevas: A class of gods who receive a share in the śrāddha; vaiśvadevikam means 'belonging to the Viśvedevas'. ↩
  93. apasavya: The reverse of the usual order: the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder and acts are done with the right side turned toward the object, as is proper in rites for the dead. ↩
  94. The reading: vaiśvadevikam: taken as an adjective of arghyam ('the arghya for the Viśvedevas'); it could also be read as a neuter noun, 'the Vaiśvadeva rite'. dviguṇān: 'double measure' is chosen over 'doubled over, folded in two'; both fit. 'tebhyaḥ' refers to the brahmins invited, as in 31.41. The text gives sadipakam, with a short i, for sadīpakam, which is metrical. ↩
  95. apasavya: Performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder and the right side turned toward the offering, the manner used in rites for the dead, the reverse of the savya manner used for the gods. ↩
  96. arghya: The water of respectful welcome offered to a guest or to a god or ancestor, here prepared with sesame in place of barley. ↩
  97. O greatly fortunate one: Vocative mahābhāga, addressed to the listener; the Sanskrit does not name him in these verses. ↩
  98. The reading: The sentence is elliptical. 'Niṣpādayet' governs āvāhana, arghya and the sesame preparation, and 'kāryam' in 31.45 has no clear finite verb, so I supplied 'he should then perform the rite in the fire' (kuryāt understood from 31.44). The reading 'pitṝṇām' (printed pitṝṇaṃ) is taken as a genitive plural. 'Yavārthaṃ ... tilaiḥ' is read as 'sesame in place of barley'; an alternative is 'for the purpose of barley, with sesame'. ↩
  99. according to the rule: Yathāvidhi, 'in accordance with the prescribed procedure'. It is a different word from the glossary's vidhi as destiny. ↩
  100. the bearer of the offerings to the ancestors: Kavyavāha, 'carrier of kavya'. Kavya is the oblation meant for the ancestors, as distinct from havya, which is meant for the gods. ↩
  101. svāhā: The exclamation that ends a formula of offering into the fire. ↩
  102. The reading: The text reads 'svaheti', with a short a. I have emended it to svāhā iti, as the parallel verses 31.47 and 31.48 require. The compound vyañjanakṣāravarjyam could also be read as 'free of condiments and alkali'. I chose 'seasonings and salt' because kṣāra commonly means salt in ritual food rules. ↩
  103. who is accompanied by the ancestors: Translates pitṛmat, 'possessing, or accompanied by, the pitṛs'; an epithet of Soma in the offerings to the ancestors. ↩
  104. svāhā: The exclamation that ends an oblation offered into the fire to the gods; the offerings of the ancestors in this passage are likewise made with it. ↩
  105. lord of the departed: Translates pretapati; Yama, ruler of the dead, is addressed by this title. ↩
  106. the touching of the vessels: bhājanālambhana: the rite in which the host touches the vessels (or the brahmins' dishes) as he serves the food. The exact manner is not stated here. ↩
  107. The reading: bhājanālambhanam: 'touching of the vessels' is the literal sense; the compound could also be read as 'taking hold of the vessels'. I chose the former, the usual sense of ālambhana as touching. 'dvijanmanām' is taken as the brahmins invited to the rite, in the genitive depending on 'bhājaneṣu'. ↩
  108. with their minds fixed on it: taccittāḥ: 'with their minds on that', that is, on the meal and the rite. The brahmins eat attentively and without talking. ↩
  109. The reading: The verse does not name who says the words or who eats. Context (31.48) shows the host speaks and the brahmin guests eat, and so I read 'te' as the brahmins; I added nothing in brackets. 'Sukham' is taken adverbially with bhuñjīran, 'at ease'. 'Tataḥ' is read as 'then', after the host has spoken. ↩
  110. according to what is available: sambhavena is instrumental. It can mean 'according to one's means, as far as is possible', which is the sense taken here. A reading 'with affection' is less likely. ↩
  111. The reading: The text reads iṣṭacatamam, which is not a word. It is probably a misprint for iṣṭatamam, 'most desired', and I translated it so. Also, sambhavena may mean 'according to what is available' (chosen, as the usual sense in rules for the śrāddha meal) or 'with affection/respect'. pralobhayan, 'tempting', I read as inviting the guests to eat more, though the object is not stated. ↩
  112. rakṣas: Malevolent beings, demons, who are believed to disturb and defile rites; the mantras recited here are those that drive them away. ↩
  113. śrāddha: The rite of offering food and water to the departed ancestors (pitṛ), the subject of this passage. ↩
  114. much trickery: The text reads pracuracchalam, 'having much deceit or opportunity for mischief'; the sense is that malign beings may find occasion to intrude upon the rite. ↩
  115. The reading: The subject of the verbs is not stated; it is the same man (nara) as in the previous verses, so 'He' is used. 'pracuracchalam' is read as a bahuvrīhi, 'having much trickery', agreeing with śrāddham; 'open to' renders the sense of the compound. ↩
  116. scatter the food on the ground: The text has the verb prakiret, 'should strew'. This is the scattering of food for the departed, done after the guests have eaten; the next verses go on to the rites of water-rinsing and the offering of the piṇḍas. ↩
  117. The reading: Syntax: pṛṣṭaiḥ tṛptaiś ca ... vādibhiḥ is an instrumental construction (those who were asked, and who are satisfied, saying). The text reads 'tṛptāḥ stha' as the question ('are you satisfied?') and 'tṛptāḥ smaḥ' as the reply. I took the instrumentals as qualifying the guests, who are the implied agents of the answer, and supplied 'the guests' in the English. The form 'prakiret' (for prakiret / prakireta) is irregular but the sense is clear. The text of 'narastvannaṃ' is read as naraḥ tu annaṃ, with tu left untranslated as merely emphatic. ↩
  118. rinsing of the mouth: ācamana: the ritual sipping or rinsing of water, taken at the end of a meal or rite for purification. ↩
  119. piṇḍas: piṇḍa: a ball of cooked rice or other food, offered to the ancestors in the śrāddha. ↩
  120. darbha grass: darbha: a sacred grass, used as a seat and spread for offerings in ritual. ↩
  121. the leavings: ucchiṣṭa: the remains of the food left by the brahmins who have eaten; the piṇḍas are set near the place where it lies. ↩
  122. The reading: savyena (31.54) has no noun: it may mean 'with the left hand' or 'in the savya manner' (the sacred thread on the left shoulder). I chose 'with the left [hand]', the usual reading with the verb dadyāt. The text reads pitanuddiśya, an evident misprint for pitṝn uddiśya, 'in the name of the ancestors'; I have translated the latter. ↩
  123. sacrificer: yajamāna, the person for whom the rite is performed and who bears its cost, here the performer of the śrāddha. ↩
  124. pitṛtīrtha: The part of the hand sacred to the ancestors, the base of the thumb and forefinger edge, by which water is poured in offerings to the departed. ↩
  125. The reading: The relative 'yad' in the second half has no clear correlative; it is taken as a loose connective (or a corruption for 'yat'), and left untranslated. 'Nṛpātmaja' is the glossary's vocative for Puṣkaramālin, rendered 'O prince'. Note too that 'samāhitaḥ' is taken as qualifying the sacrificer (composed, attentive). ↩
  126. rice-balls (piṇḍa): piṇḍa: the balls of cooked rice, mixed here with sesame, offered to the departed in the śrāddha rite. ↩
  127. maternal grandfathers: mātāmaha: the mother's father and, in the rite, his father and grandfather, who receive their own offerings after the paternal line. ↩
  128. water for rinsing the mouth: ācamana: the sipping or rinsing of water for purification, offered to the guests at the end of the meal. ↩
  129. fee (dakṣiṇā): The text reads takṣiṇām, evidently a misprint for dakṣiṇām, the priestly fee or gift. ↩
  130. svadhā: The ritual exclamation and offering made to the departed ancestors (pitṛ); the wish is that it be well offered. ↩
  131. Vaiśvadevika [brahmins]: The brahmins who represent the Viśvedevas, the class of gods honoured in the Vaiśvadeva part of the śrāddha; the next verse gives the words they are to be made to recite. ↩
  132. The reading: takṣiṇām is read as a misprint for dakṣiṇām, 'fee', which the sense requires. susvadhāḥ (nominative plural feminine in the text; the verse has susvadhāstviti) is taken as su-svadhā, 'may the svadhā be good', with 'given' supplied in brackets. Vaiśvadevikān is taken as the brahmins who stand for the Viśvedevas, not the gods themselves, since they are made to recite (vācayet). ↩
